...is therefore concluded: But whatever exists is, in a certain way, being and good; therefore, it is not "not good." Furthermore, you deny that it is true what Aristotle says in the *Categories* <note>original: *prædicamentis*; Aristotle's work on the classification of things</note>—namely, that good and evil are the *genera* <note>The primary classes or categories</note> of contraries. Yet neither Boethius <note>A 6th-century philosopher who bridged the gap between Classical and Medieval thought</note> nor the Latin commentators dare to deny this. <margin>You indeed: Are you, who are accustomed to be a follower of Boethius and a ridiculer of "barbarians" <note>A term humanists used for the "uncultured" medieval scholastic writers</note>, now so cold that you follow the Greek interpreters while setting aside the Latins? But even your Thomas [Aquinas] is not only a Latin, but the foremost among the Latins; he not only relates Simplicius's explanation but also proves it. You, however, not only disagree with Simplicius or Thomas, but you even claim the Latin commentators do not dare to deny it. You are a strange man.</margin> You, however, having set aside the Latin interpreters, take refuge in Simplicius <note>A 6th-century Greek Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle</note> alone, who says that for this reason good and evil are the genera of contraries: because of two contraries, one is always good—that is, it is better—and the other is evil—that is, it is worse. This is something that Blessed Thomas [Aquinas] also relates from Simplicius. But if one may oppose Simplicius: it is to the contrary that Aristotle says in the same place that not only is good the contrary of evil, but sometimes even an evil is contrary to an evil. If Aristotle calls that which is "better" the "good," and that which is "worse" the "evil," then the good will always be the contrary to the evil. Furthermore, if the good and the evil which Aristotle says are the genera of contraries are simply "the better" and "the worse," they would be placed in the category of *relatives* <note>Things that exist only in relation to something else, like "bigger" or "smaller"</note>, among which are the better and the worse, which are relative terms. Yet Aristotle truly says that good and evil are not *in* a genus, but are themselves *genera*. <margin>You wonder: Who would not wonder? I wondered then, when I had not yet perceived your sharp wit; now I do not wonder at many similar things.</margin> Finally, you wonder that good and evil are affirmed by me as contraries, even according to the opinion of Thomas; and what is more, you say I wander from the truth: you say I falsely allege Simplicius, and that I also falsely say Blessed Thomas proves by his testimony that evil and good are mutually contrary. But take care that you do not err, you who have weighed my small mind or my words; for the words written to you in the second letter read in this sequence: I say therefore again, and I approve, that good and evil are mutually contrary. This is not in the same way as white and black, or hot and cold, which are all truly qualities; <margin>I might allege falsely: And you admit below that you have alleged falsely, but you say this is of no consequence; how then does your mind escape me? I confess that it escaped me that it was of no consequence to ascribe to Simplicius things he does not say. For I believed that he who said "Simplicius says this" was in error if Simplicius never said it.</margin> but rather in the way that the healthy and the sick, the strong and the weak, the rare and the dense, the beautiful and the ugly, and many similar things are. Nor does Blessed Thomas deny this; rather, that most eminent man, in the first question *On Evil* <note>Aquinas's *De Malo*</note> regarding the solution to the second argument, shows how good and evil—even if they oppose each other as a privation and a habit <note>Privation is the absence of a quality that should be there (like blindness), while habit/possession is the presence of the quality (like sight)</note>—are nevertheless accustomed to be counted among contraries; and he confirms this by the authority of Simplicius. # **GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...that health and sickness are numbered by him among contraries: by this reasoning, therefore, by which Aristotle separates <term>contraries</term><note>In Aristotelian logic, "contraries" are opposites that belong to the same category (like black and white), whereas "privations" are the simple absence of a quality (like blindness being the absence of sight).</note> from the remaining kinds of opposition. I have affirmed that good and evil are contraries; and I confess it once more. And this is also what the <term>Divine Thomas</term><note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher whose "Summa Theologica" and "De Malo" (On Evil) are referenced here.</note> said in the first question *On Evil*: Good and evil are contraries, just like health and sickness, but not like sight and blindness.

But you say: "I will show you how evil is entirely ignorant of the property of a contrary." For although a certain evil can seem contrary to a certain good—as sickness to health—because it leaves something of the good behind, I will nevertheless offer a certain evil that can in no way be opposed to good by this reasoning: namely, death and blindness. 

But indeed, I do not know if you are pretending. For if you have read Thomas’s words more accurately, it can be plainly understood how neither blindness nor death, nor any other evil, can take away the good entirely. Blindness indeed takes away sight, and entirely so; but not life nor the body. Death indeed takes away life completely, but neither the body nor <term>prime matter</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "prime matter" is the most basic substance of the universe that lacks any form or qualities of its own but has the potential to become anything.</note>. # ON BEING AND THE ONE

<margin>Or if true, why then do you not frankly admit that you have erred? For it is no wonder; you are human.</margin>

<margin>Whether a chimera: In that chimera <note>The "chimera" was a standard example in medieval logic for an impossible or non-existent thing.</note> of yours, you imagine many chimeras.</margin>

<margin>To be created: If a chimera can be created by God, this power is not in the chimera, but in God.</margin>

<margin>Furthermore, the Chimera: The notion I form of a chimera—insofar as it is something—is good; but the chimera itself—insofar as it is nothing—is likewise not good.</margin>

<margin>Aristotle, Book 4 of the *Metaphysics*. Good and evil, according to you, are contraries, and each of the contraries is something positive; therefore, what is good is something positive and what is evil is something positive. And according to you, non-being is good; therefore, according to you, non-being is something positive. And "something" and "being" are interchangeable; therefore, according to you, non-being is positive being. See where your chimera has led us!</margin>

<margin>Furthermore, evil is: But according to you, it is a contrary, not a privation <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that ought to be present, like blindness in an eye, whereas a "contrary" is a positive opposing force.</note>.</margin>

<margin>Augustine says: He did not say evil is good, but [exists] in good <note>original: "in bono"</note>.</margin>

<margin>Furthermore, if evil is: It is a privation insofar as privation is formally a negation.</margin>

<margin>Show it: Reread your earlier letters, and you will see this was shown to you in them, perhaps even more than you might wish.</margin>

...therefore Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, who says that Simplicimus <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> calls those things properly **contraries** of which each is something else—since he explains the reason why "healthy" and "sick" are numbered among contraries—it is necessary to conclude from Simplicius that he does not include "blind" and "seeing." He interprets Aristotle on this point; whether that is true or false is a matter of little importance that needs no wandering.

But since, in your last letters, you seem to call "evil" that which is a negation of "good"—meaning an evil that is entirely evil—and in the same way you ask about "falsehood" as divided from the one "truth," I want to ask you: Do you think a **chimera** is entirely a non-being? If you deny it, you must contradict yourself, for you said before that a chimera is entirely non-being and false. But if you grant that it is entirely non-being, I shall proceed in this way: non-being and "entirely evil" are equal; but a chimera is entirely non-being, therefore it is also entirely evil. But this cannot be. For a chimera does not include a logical contradiction; therefore, it can be created by God. That which can exist, its existence is good; therefore, that which can be created can be good. But the **potential** for good is itself good; therefore, a chimera is not entirely evil.

Furthermore, a chimera can be understood both by God and by us; it can therefore exist in our mind and soul. Therefore, it can exist in some way, and that which can exist in some way participates in some way in goodness; therefore, a chimera is not entirely evil. Furthermore, nothing can be evil unless it is to be avoided; but nothing can be avoided or shunned unless it is known, either by the one who flees or by God, who implanted the natural instinct for flight. It is necessary, therefore, that every evil can be known in some way; but knowledge is a certain kind of good, and therefore to be able to be known is also a good. For the potential for a good is itself a certain good.

Furthermore, Aristotle in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* says that negations and privations are "in a way" beings; indeed, he even says that non-being itself is in a way a being, the sign of which, he says, is that we say "non-being *is* non-being." But what is in any way a being is in some way good; therefore the chimera, to which the name of non-being is truly applied, is in some way a being and good.

Furthermore, evil is the <term>privation</term> <note>original: "privatio"; the lack of a required good.</note> of good; but every privation is the negation of a form in a subject suited by nature to have that form and habit. Therefore, nothing can be evil that is not capable and suited for good; but capacity and aptitude for good are themselves good. Therefore, evil cannot be entirely evil; whence Augustine says that evil is always in a good [subject].

Furthermore, if evil is a privation of good as you say, how can it be a "negation" of good? For the opposition of **privation** and **habit** is one thing; the opposition of **affirmation** and **negation** is quite another.

Furthermore, it is your task to show that the argument you made earlier was valid—the one by which you tried to prove from Aristotle and Thomas that God is not "being" <note>original: "ens"</note>. For I have weakened both of your points, and it is not enough to say: "I know that sometimes God is called 'being' by the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>, but I also know that among them God is sometimes not included in the naming of 'being'." Show me, I ask, in what place either Aristotle or the Aristotelians do not consider God under the name of "being"?

Otherwise, if you have time, explain how you defend that God is and is One, yet God is not God. For if the word is understood, it is necessary that some description be formed by the mind; which, once given, it follows immediately that God is God...

-># 10. MIRANDOLA<-

Simonides the poet, when asked by a tyrant <note>This refers to the story of Simonides of Ceos and Hiero of Syracuse; when asked "What is God?", Simonides continually doubled the time needed to answer, concluding that the more he meditated, the more obscure the subject became.</note> what God is, requested time to respond so that he might first grasp the interpretation of the name and a concept in his mind. For in every question, the first thing to establish is the meaning of the word. Furthermore, if God is "one," then God is something other than "The One" itself; yet nothing can be "one" unless it is God. Likewise, if God exists and yet is not God, He would be something other than God—it would therefore be necessary for Him to be something other than Himself. Furthermore, if the reason God is not "God" is because the name of God is a "concrete" term <note>In scholastic logic, a "concrete" term (like 'human') refers to a subject possessing a quality, whereas an "abstract" term (like 'humanity') refers to the quality itself.</note> signifying something else, then it must be conceded that God is nothing. For there is nothing in the nature of things that is "God" by merely participating in divinity. Finally, you will demonstrate how you either prove or defend against the contradiction of "God not being" and "gold being." Such a dispute would be pleasing to me, and it should not be troublesome to you; for a dispute is the **sieve of truth**, the sweetest food of the soul, containing nothing unpleasant. Farewell.

<margin>A: Fourth Objections.</margin>
It was not said that God is "not being" <note>original: "deuʒ ens non esse"</note> because "being" in God is through His essence; rather, it is because His "being" is not different from His "essence," which is quite another matter. Otherwise, the very "being" of a stone—which is its essence—would neither be "being" nor "good." For the being of a stone is not its essence in the same way, but is its own being and its own essence. If we cannot ask "what they are" regarding negations and privations—and since knowing that a thing exists is not enough to form the question "what is it?"—one must know both that it *is* and *what* it is. Therefore, it is ridiculous and irrational to answer "being" or "something," whether "being" is taken in the first or second sense. If one asks what "sin" is, the question concerns the word rather than the thing. If something is "being," then according to your position, it is "being" because its being is a different thing from its essence. You say humanity is one thing, a man is another; whiteness is one thing, a white object is another. Therefore, if an "Idea" <note>Referring to the Platonic theory of Forms or Ideas.</note> is "being," it is "being" because the being of the Idea is different from the Idea itself. But the Idea is God; therefore the being of the Idea is different from God. This would mean there is a real composition in God, not just a conceptual one. According to the definition of derivative terms <note>original: "denominatiuorum"</note>, "one" is derived from "unity." Yet according to your position, God is called "one" by a likeness to unity. Therefore, the predication does not belong to the substance of God, as the Platonists say "God is one." Furthermore, when we say "God is one," you think it signifies not *what* He is, but *how* He is. But "how" (manner) belongs to the category of "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a quality that does not belong to the essence of a thing (like being tall), whereas "substance" is what the thing is.</note>; therefore the word "one" in God is not substantive, nor does it pertain to His reality. I do not say this because I have not studied the Platonic sect or am ignorant of the Greek language, for that is not enough to defend the discipline of the Academics <note>The "Academics" refers to the school of skeptics in the Platonic tradition.</note>. If God did not exist and gold did exist, you say that gold would both be gold and not be gold; therefore it would be gold. If, then, the definition of truth stands, it will be a truth that corresponds to no "Idea." If Socrates sits, it is neither true nor false because it is not necessary; indeed, I will defend that not every affirmation or negation is true, for in some cases, neither one nor the other holds a necessary truth. If "good" and "evil" are in things, but "true" and "false" are in the soul, where is your opposition of affirmation and negation? For a negation posits nothing. How then is a "Chimera" <note>A mythological beast used in logic to represent a "non-being" or something that cannot exist.</note> in both things and the soul if it is entirely a non-being and false, since you think non-being and evil are interchangeable? If it is true that "blindness is blindness," who does not see that blindness is a truth? For they are the same thing. By the very fact that blindness is posited, "blindness is blindness" is posited; and if it is removed, the statement is removed. By the same reasoning, Socrates and "Socrates being Socrates" are the same, and both are generated by the same generation. So too, God and "God being God" are the same; for both are eternal and the **First Truth**.

But pay attention: I will soon explain that when you conceive of "God" through this word, you are only grasping what is signified by the name. This word does not function as a **predicate** but as a **subject**. For the subject is that about which one asks what can or should be stated, not that which is stated about something else. Therefore, this was not unknown to Simonides nor to the tyrant who consulted him. Likewise, when you ask whether God—if He cannot be called "God"—is something other than God, I ask you: what do you conceive by this word "God" which you state about God? If you conceive nothing, you do not err, because you say nothing. If you conceive something, I say that God is something other than what you conceive and explain through this word "God," since He is **above everything** that can be conceived by us.

**On God not being:** Let us come then to your "gold," which you do not wish to lose even if God were lost. It is impossible for anything to exist if "Being" itself does not exist. Therefore, it is impossible for gold to exist if God does not exist. Furthermore, if God does not exist, then He is the infinite. If He is the infinite, He is nothing. For if He is infinite, He is not finite; but if He is infinite, He is not infinite, because the infinite destroys itself—just like other things that contain a contradiction. If "nothing" exists, then gold does not exist. I believe this is enough for you, a man who is as ingenious as you wish to be. Farewell.

# **ON BEING AND THE ONE**

If every falsehood is simply divided <note>In scholastic logic, "divided" often refers to the separation of concepts in a proposition.</note>, as you do not deny has been proven, it ought not to be said that something is false only under this condition—that is, only as long as it is false. For if every man is simply and absolutely capable of laughter, it is not necessary to add a condition to restrict it, saying: "Every man is capable of laughter as long as he is a man." Nor should that restriction be added because not all false things are equally divided; for even though not all beings are equally good, nonetheless all things are absolutely good. How it is concluded that good and evil are contraries will be easily established if you follow the argument: if "pursuing" and "fleeing" are contraries, and if the rationale of contrary motions <note>The author is using the physics of motion to explain moral or metaphysical categories.</note> has been sufficiently understood by you. Why are you surprised if I say that the Latin thinkers do not deny Aristotle—whom Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 AD), a Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle.</note> denies, but Boethius does not? Am I not, for that reason, either imitating Boethius or exalting the barbarians? <note>original: "barbaros". In the Renaissance, humanists often called the medieval Scholastic philosophers "barbarians" due to their unpolished Latin style. The author is likely defending his use of Scholastic logic.</note> Do you call me a man of wonders? Indeed, I should call you wonderful: for while I imitate Boethius, having set aside Simplicius for a time, you think I despise Boethius and follow the barbarians. If good and evil are contraries, you wish to prove that the chimera <note>A mythological beast used in philosophy to represent an "impossible object" or something that cannot exist in reality.</note> is something that exists in the nature of things. But if it were understood by what rationale I called good and evil contraries—which you either do not yet wish to or cannot understand—you would have proven nothing from the chimera. <margin>Pri-</margin> <gloss>Privations</gloss> You wonder greatly that certain <term>privations</term> <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present in a subject, like blindness in an eye.</note> are called "half-full" by me, and you prove they are nothing in this way: "Evil is nothing; therefore, it is not a half-full privation." I, however, following your argument, shall say this: sickness is evil; therefore it is nothing? Therefore it is not a half-full privation? But sickness is a certain privation. Therefore, it is not a half-full privation of either health or some good, but rather a full and perfect one? That cannot be. Therefore, privations are imperfectly "half-full," such as sickness, rarity, ugliness, or blindness—which are perfect in respect to the evil, but imperfect in respect to the good. For it does not take away the whole good which is in the one who sees.

If it is true, as you write, that every evil leaves something of the good, then the chimera—which is entirely a non-being—would also retain something of the good. If indeed it preserves something of the good, it is not entirely evil, nor entirely non-being. Even if the potential by which it can be created and exist is in God, and the notion by which it can be understood is in the mind, it does not stop the chimera from being "good" and "being" in potential. For the potential of God and the potential of the chimera are one and another thing by different rationales. Nor do we deny that the Antichrist is good in potential, whose power by which he can exist is partly in matter and partly in the heavens and in man.

Furthermore, how is the Chimera? If, for a moment, all thought and the power of God were excluded, it is entirely non-being and evil. For if it is non-being, it certainly cannot be evil. For evil is a privation which exists in a subject, and that subject must necessarily participate in goodness. Otherwise, it could not be a subject. For that which does not exist at all cannot be a subject.

You have not yet disproven what was said by me, even though you confirm it with the authority of Simplicius, except for what you say Simplicius does not say. But there was no need to boast of that; for I did not say Aristotle felt that every being whatsoever exists either <term>per se</term> <note>By itself; essentially.</note> or <term>per accidens</term> <note>By accident; non-essential attributes.</note>, nor did I falsely ascribe anything to Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> on that account.

Although every privation is a certain negation, it is not yet established that there is no other opposition between affirmation and negation, and another between privation and <term>habitus</term> <note>The presence or "possession" of a quality, the opposite of privation.</note>. Therefore, if evil is the privation of good, it is not necessary that "evil" and "not-good" are interchangeable terms.

Your defense, by which you wish to protect the idea that "God is not God," I neither [yield] to truth nor to the Blessed... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence.</note>

<meta>This page concludes a technical philosophical debate regarding the nature of God and begins a new letter from Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola to Antonio Faventino regarding the legacy and manuscripts of his late uncle, the famous Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</meta>

->**OF PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**<-

I think these things are consistent with Dionysius <note>Refers to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century whose works were central to medieval mysticism.</note>, nor did the blessed Dionysius ever deny that God is God. But as Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> interprets it, no name can fully explain the nature of God; nor for any other reason does he think that affirmations about the gods are "incompact" <term>incompactas: a technical term in logic referring to fragmented or non-composite propositions</term>. But you say that the name of God, if it has a description, has the quality of a subject and not also of a predicate. But even if this is granted, the argument stands: for let *a* be the definition of the name, and let it be said in this way: "God is *a*." For the definition of anything is predicated of that which it defines. Therefore, by a simple conversion, "*a* is God." Therefore, "God is God." 

Likewise, you say when it is asked whether God is something other than God or not, one must know what is conceived by the name of God. Whatever else is given, you say, I will call God. For He is above everything that can be conceived. But does not a solution of this kind conflict with itself? For if you admit a proposition of this sort—which is "God is above that which can be conceived"—do you not openly affirm something about God? Let it be done, then, and let the definition of the name be that speech which is "above that which can be conceived," and the argument will still hold. Furthermore, it follows that "God is above everything that can be conceived"; therefore, God cannot be conceived, otherwise He would be above Himself. Therefore, He cannot be loved or worshipped. 

Finally, you might think the power of gold <note>original: "auri potentia." Pico is likely mocking a specific logical sophistry or "word game" his opponent used involving the existence of gold to prove the existence of God.</note> is so great that, whether we wish it or not, it necessarily drags God along with it in this way: "Gold is. Therefore, Being itself is. Therefore, God is." Likewise: "God is. Therefore, the infinite is. The infinite is. Therefore, nothing is." If an infinite being is, you say, then the finite is not—as if you were arguing "the finite is not, therefore nothing is." Then you say: "The infinite is, therefore the infinite is not," for you say the infinite destroys itself. Indeed, I think if anyone had written arguments of this kind to Nicoletto <note>Nicoletto Vernia (c. 1420–1499), a famous professor of philosophy at Padua known for his strict Aristotelianism.</note>, he would have answered nothing. Nor will I oppose anything against them, lest where the matter seems clearer to me than light, I might seem to doubt anything. But if you prove your "refining" <note>original: "politionem." Likely a pun on refining gold and refining an argument.</note> with these same arguments, I truly fear you are wasting your gold.

If you wish, respond something to these objections, best of friends, so that we may now bring an end to the dispute; for we have played enough. Furthermore, I would not want you to think I have turned to these things out of hatred or ill-will. I know you remember that before I wrote anything to you, I asked if you were willing. Indeed, I call God to witness that I love and venerate my Mirandolan companion <note>Referring to his uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note>. If you ever care to put me to the test, you will find I have told no lie.

**GIOVANNI FRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO THE DISTINGUISHED PHILOSOPHER ANTONIO FAVENTINO, GREETINGS.**

**A**lthough by the death of my uncle Giovanni Pico, all the eagerness and hope of my studies—which had been almost entirely placed in him—has withered; for while he was living, I hoped that the study of philosophy might be recalled to its pristine purity, but enriched with great resources, and that the Christian faith, having eliminated all errors and driven out heresies, might be fortified with the strongest towers against its enemies. Yet I was not so devastated in spirit that I did not labor with all my strength to ensure that all the vigils and the begun works of scholarship, which had flowed from that man who was admired everywhere in literature, did not utterly perish. 

Wherefore, lookng out for myself and our people, I hurried to Florence by the greatest journeys possible. I took care, by whatever means I could, that whatever had been noted down by him, even if unpolished and unexamined, should be permitted into our power. Our efforts were not entirely in vain; for even if the accounts were not yet opened, nor a known heir appointed, the chests were nevertheless such that we could inspect and turn over all the commentaries. We saw in those scattered paper volumes the incredible zeal of the man: a reading of every kind, and concepts admirable beyond the grasp of the human mind. Truly, however, in the organizing of his writings, there was a lack of care that is not to be praised; everything was thrown about and scattered here and there. But concerning these things, another time. While these things [were being done] diligently...

<meta>This page serves as an introduction to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s treatise *De Ente et Uno* (On Being and the One), likely written by his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico. # ON BEING AND THE ONE

While we were carefully reviewing his short work **On Being and the One** <note>original: "de uno & ente"</note>, which was published nearly four years before his death, a certain collection fell into my hands. This included three letters you wrote regarding the work, along with the replies to them. Because the matter was so new to me, I did not merely read them; I "drank them in"—or rather, as the saying goes, I devoured them. (I had heard rumors that this exchange existed, but I had not yet fully explored how significant its impact was.) 

I began to reflect and debate with myself whether I should hand this work over to the printers to be published publicly alongside the other writings I have collected and edited, without making any mention of your objections. Or, would it be wiser if the book went out into the public sphere "fortified"—challenged by criticisms on one side and defended by counter-arguments <note>The author uses architectural metaphors here: "offensaculis" (little obstacles/attacks) and "propugnaculis" (bulwarks/defenses).</note> on the other? 

After a long consideration of the matter, a final decision at last took hold in my mind. Indeed, to the eyes of learned men, the work might seem to carry a stain of disgrace if it appeared to fear its accusers—or if, through a lack of inner confidence, it did not dare to summon those critics to judgment. Therefore, it seemed appropriate for the work to be accompanied by these responses, serving as witnesses to defend the cause of its innocence.

...declared that they can be called created things and beings. Therefore, by his followers—most notably **Capreolus** <note>Jean Capreolus (c. 1370–1444), a major Dominican theologian known as the "Prince of Thomists."</note>—when the question of the distinction between being and essence is raised, the very "act of being" of created things is ruled to be included neither in the number of true beings nor in the number of creatures. For if it does not receive the name of "being," then it undoubtedly does not receive the name of "good," since "being" and "good" follow one another and are reciprocal in their scope.

<margin>Solution to the second objection</margin>
In the second place, you argue in this manner: if, in the case of negations and privations <term>privation: the absence of a quality or good that should naturally be present, like blindness being the privation of sight</term>, one cannot ask "what they are"; and since they nonetheless "are," then it is not enough to form the question "What is it?" simply to know that the thing being asked about exists. Rather, the person asking "What is it?" must further know both that it "is" and that it is "something." Therefore, it is a ridiculous and irrational response to say it is "a being" or "something," whether one takes "being" in the first sense or the second. <note>In Scholastic philosophy, the "first mode" of being refers to the essence or substance of a thing; the "second mode" refers to the truth of a proposition (stating that something exists, even if it has no physical essence).</note> And if it is asked "What is sin?", the question concerns the word rather than the reality. To this objection, we respond that he never said one could not ask what they were in the case of privations and negations.

<margin>Thomas, Giles</margin>
But rather, he said that it cannot be answered "what" they are. This he brought forward for the sake of **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, whom he cited when you were doubting this very point in previous letters—specifically, whether it was true or false—using these words: "You must admit it is true unless you abandon your own Thomas." We have found this same point asserted by **Giles of Rome** <note>Egidius Romanus (c. 1243–1316), a prominent philosopher and student of Aquinas.</note> in the second book of his commentaries on the *Sentences* <note>The "Sentences" of Peter Lombard was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note>. For it is sufficient to form the question "What is it?" to know that the thing being inquired about exists. Nor is it necessary for the person who is about to investigate what a thing is to know that the thing exists or is "something" in the first sense; it is enough that it exists in the second sense—that is, that it has existence in thought or logic. However, if you were to contend that you understood this question as one that can only be formed when it can be answered affirmatively and correctly: first, if you think that question cannot be correctly formed unless the thing being asked about is such that a response can be given through it, I do not agree with you.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
For it is the opinion of **Aristotle** that one can ask whether a centaur exists or not; yet a centaur is not the kind of thing that can provide an answer to the question "Does it exist?", since it is a mere fable, a pure figment of the imagination <note>original: "mera ſit fabella merū figmentū"</note>. Likewise, I am opposed if you believe that the seeker must already know this same thing; for (as we have shown) the person who correctly asks "What is a thing?" does not need to know more than that it exists. Therefore, for someone who knows a thing exists, it is not a ridiculous answer to tell someone who does not know and is asking about it that it is "something." Indeed, it happens that we are not accustomed to teaching those who ask "What is a thing?" that it is "a being" or "something" in an absolute sense; for having already discovered that it is something, they would still be searching for what kind of being it might be. We satisfy, therefore, not only their express request but also their desire for investigation when we dissolve their questions—both those conceived in the mind and those not yet spoken—by anticipating them with our responses. However, those words—"if it is asked what sin is, the question is of the word rather than the thing"—which were used in that objection against you, seem to carry little weight. For when you previously argued from the opinion of Thomas: namely, that "being" is called that which answers the question "What is it?", and that to one asking what it is that preserves and moves the world, "God" is reasonably answered. From this, you concluded that God is "being" and "something" in the first sense. He replied: see how much you are deceived; "evil," according to Thomas, is not the kind of thing that allows us to answer "something" or "being" to one asking what it is. And yet, to someone asking "What is sin?", we can answer that it is "evil." Therefore, your response does not help you—namely, that if "What is sin?" is asked, it is a question of the name rather than the thing. For the question "What is it that governs the world?" is no more a question of a name (though the reasoning differs here and there) than "What is sin?", since He who governs the world—namely God—does not have a "quiddity" <term>quiddity: the 'what-ness' or essential nature of a thing</term> as the more recent thinkers speak. This is confirmed most clearly by everyone except those who would place Him in a "category" <note>In Aristotelian logic, "categories" are the classifications of finite things (like substance, quality, quantity). Many theologians argued God is "beyond category."</note>.

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
And as the most holy **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential 5th-6th century Christian mystic and philosopher.</note> says—our prince of theology after the apostles—He has neither a name nor a definition. Furthermore, even in those things you said before, your...

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's defense of his philosophical positions, likely from his work "On Being and the One" (De Ente et Uno). He is responding to a series of scholastic objections regarding the nature of God, specifically how God can be called "Being" or "the One" without implying that God is composed of different parts.</meta>

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

This response is consistent when you have previously said that evil itself is not "nothing" but something positive; but now you admit that the question is formed only regarding the name itself.

<margin>Objection</margin> You object thirdly with these words: "If something is a being <term>ens; a thing that exists</term>, then according to your position it is a being because its 'to be' <term>esse; the act of existing</term> is, <margin>Third [objection].</margin> in reality, something other than its essence." You ask whether humanity is one thing and "man" another, or whether "whiteness" is one thing and a "white thing" another. Therefore, if the Idea <note>In this context, "Idea" refers to the divine archetype or God himself as the pattern for creation.</note> is a being, it will be a being because the "to be" of the Idea is different from the Idea itself. But the Idea is God; therefore, the "to be" of the Idea is something other than God. Thus, there is a "real composition" <note>A "real composition" in scholastic philosophy means a thing is made of distinct parts or principles, which would contradict the belief that God is absolutely simple and undivided.</note> in God, not just a "conceptual" one.

To these things, we say the answer has already been given. <margin>Solution</margin> For when you argued with almost the same means you are now using in your third letter, he responded that the composition of "being" and "essence" in divine things is conceptual <note>original: "secundum rationem"; meaning it exists in our way of thinking about God, rather than in God's actual nature.</note>, not real. Regarding this hypothetical syllogism you bring forward, we deny that the first proposition is true. For even if in created things "essence" differs from "to be" in reality, it does not necessarily follow from this that whatever can be called a "being" in any way must be composed of essence and "to be" (or existence) as if from parts. Therefore, essence and existence do not meet as distinct things in the "Idea," which is the model for created things. 

But this composition is made by us when we consider the Idea as the exemplary cause of "essence" and "being" (or "to be" and "existence") which are found in created things. We apply this composition and distinction equally even to the simplest things, and we call it "conceptual" when our intellect has fashioned it. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> use this very frequently as a common saying, which, as he says, was repeated by <margin>Antipater</margin> Antipater, <margin>Peripatetics</margin> mentioned by Posidonius, and recorded in the letters of Seneca. For that reason, we can say in this manner that the Idea is composed of essence and existence "conceptually," and we can call it a "being"—specifically, as we consider it the model for creatures <margin>Antipater</margin> composed of "to be" and "essence" which differ in reality. We do not place this composition in God when we contemplate Him not as the model of others, but as enjoying Himself in the innermost <margin>Posidonius</margin> sanctuary of His own divinity. <margin>Seneca</margin>

<margin>Fourth objection</margin> Fourthly, you say that according to the definition of "denominative" terms <note>A denominative term is a name derived from a quality, like "strong" from "strength."</note>, "one" is a denominative from "unity." Or, according to your position, God is called "one" from a likeness to unity. Therefore, the preaching by which the Platonists say "God is one" does not regard the substance of God. Furthermore, when we <margin>Solution to the fourth objection</margin> say "God is one," you think it signifies not *what* He is, but *how* He is. But "mode" or "how" belongs to the category of accidents; therefore, the word "one" in God is not substantive. You say this as if I have either not learned the Platonic sect or am ignorant of the Greek language; for that is not enough to defend the discipline of the Academics. 

But the response is easy: since it has been said by the Platonists that the "One" which is predicated of God is substantive and not merely denominative, it has been correctly asserted. And again, since it has been maintained that He is called "One" because He is like unity, this is not incongruous. It cannot be said to be non-substantive for that reason. For even if a name is adapted to something because of a property or likeness to another thing, it does not necessarily follow that the name is not substantive when it is accepted as a substantive name—that is, one which signifies not by way of an attachment <note>original: "per modum adiacentis"; an adjective or accidental quality.</note> but as standing by itself. It is clear that the "One" which is predicated of God is understood not as something inherent but as something standing by itself in God, so that it needs no proof. 

Thus, you have the property from which the name is taken, which does not take away the fact that it is substantive for the thing it is applied to. For your Thomas <margin>Thomas</margin>—or rather, *our* Thomas <note>Refers to St. Thomas Aquinas. Pico is signaling his respect for the Dominican tradition despite his Platonic leanings.</note>—both in other places and in the *First Part* [of the Summa], reports that the thing a name is imposed to signify differs from the property by which the name is imposed. For example, he explains that this name "stone" <note>original: "lapis"</note> is imposed to signify that substance which is so named, but it is called so from a property related to it: namely, that it "hurts the foot" <note>A common medieval folk-etymology: *lapis* as *laedens pedem* (hurting the foot).</note>. Hence, in another place, he teaches that it is used by grammarians to write that a name denotes "substance with quality," which John Scotus <margin>John Scotus</margin> also affirms in the first book of his commentaries on the *Sentences*.

<summary>Pico defends the simplicity of God against the charge that calling God "Being" or "the One" introduces complexity or accidents into the divine nature. He argues that distinctions between essence and existence in God are conceptual tools used by the human mind, and that "the One" refers to God's very substance rather than a mere quality.</summary>

**APOLOGIA**
<note>original: "Apologia" — This title translates to "A Defense" or "Justification." In this context, it is likely a formal intellectual defense of a specific philosophical or theological position.</note>

Therefore, my dear Antonio, when we declare that God is "one," we speak truly and use the word as a substantive noun <note>original: "substantiuū nomē" — In grammar, a substantive refers to a word that functions as a noun, indicating that "One" is not just a quality God has, but expresses his very essence.</note>. We declare this because we both conceive and speak of Him in the manner of something that "stands" or exists in its own right. Furthermore, when we say that "truth" is assigned to Him by analogy to the properties of unity, we come as close as is divinely permitted. This is because we use a fitting term to indicate that deity which is far beyond all created things; for just as the "unit" <note>original: "unitas" — In medieval mathematics, the number one was often called the 'unit' or 'monad,' the source of all other numbers.</note> is the beginning of all numbers, so too is He the beginning of all things that exist. From these words, you will also gather the solution to your other argument concerning "mode," where you claim that it can only belong to the category of accidents. <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "mode" usually describes *how* something is (an accident), rather than *what* it is (a substance).</note> In this declaration—"God is one"—one can signify *how* God is one, while the word "one" nevertheless remains a substantive term for God. If you consider from what source the name is derived and what it is attributed to denote, you can also recognize a very brief solution to your doubt from the words of my uncle. 

<margin>A brief solution from the words of the uncle.</margin>

When he says, "How can you say I follow the reasoning of the Platonists or rather of Dionysius <note>Referencing Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian mystic and philosopher who blended Christian thought with Neoplatonism.</note>, when you have never even read Dionysius or the Platonists, though you boast of it so loudly?" Yet you should know that among the Platonists, "Unity" is the archetype of God, and according to Dionysius, God is "all things uniquely." No one could rightly ask for a more direct solution; for when it is said that Unity is the archetype of God, it refers to His likeness and manner of being. But when it is said that God is "all things uniquely," it must be referred to His substance—yet these two are asserted to be entirely the same thing. Furthermore, in the Greek language (which he knew well), the same word can sometimes signify both the abstract and the concrete.

<margin>Solution to the fifth objection.</margin>

To provide the solution to your fifth doubt, there is no need for many words. He says: "If God did not exist and gold did exist, gold would be gold and gold would not be gold." <note>This is a classic "impossible" thought experiment used in medieval logic to test the relationship between the existence of a Creator and the essence of created things.</note> You add these words: "Therefore gold would be gold." If the definition of truth holds, this would be a truth corresponding to no "Idea." <note>term: Idea — In the Platonic sense, a divine blueprint or eternal form.</note> Please add also these few words which he said followed from his own remarks, and you will recognize how it would be a truth corresponding to no Idea. What is impossible, I say, gives birth to the impossible. Therefore, it is no wonder if you make whatever you wish follow from your impossible proposition. For if God did not exist and gold did exist, it will be a truth corresponding to no Idea, since the impossible is born from the impossible; not only logicians but also theologians agree with this. 

<margin>John of Baconthorp.</margin>

For if you were to ask John of Baconthorp <note>A 14th-century English Carmelite monk known as the "Prince of Averroists."</note>, the Carmelite, whether it could happen that gold exists and God does not exist, he would answer you in the first book of his *Sentences* that no thing at all, whatever it may be, can be understood unless God is understood first. Since God is involved in the understanding of all things, you can gather whether it can be pronounced—without any controversy, even among novice logicians—that it is impossible for gold to be and God not to be. But we shall speak of this again at the end of the work, if you later consult the Cardinal of Cambrai. <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a famous philosopher, theologian, and cardinal.</note> You will hear that man, who was well-practiced in all philosophy, saying in his first commentary on the *Sentences* that a contradiction follows from any impossible premise.

<margin>Solution to the sixth objection.</margin>

In the sixth place, you said that if it were neither true nor false that "Socrates is sitting" (which he had asserted on the grounds that it was not a necessary event), you could defend the idea that a negation or affirmation is not true in every case, since in some cases neither one nor the other has a necessary truth. Solving this objection, we reply that this statement—namely, "Socrates is sitting"—does not necessarily determine its own truth or falsehood by itself. It does not follow from this that an affirmation or negation is not true for every case. Nevertheless, if you understand it in the way he teaches, you will even be able to deny that an affirmation or negation is true in every case in such a way that one side is *necessarily* true. For he says: "That I am sitting is always either true or false, because I am always either sitting or not sitting." And when it is said that "my sitting" is neither true nor false, this means that this proposition does not, out of itself, possess truth or...

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's defense of certain philosophical theses, specifically addressing objections regarding the nature of truth, falsehood, good, and evil. It transitions from a discussion on indeterminate propositions to a specific debate about whether truth resides in the mind or in things.</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...determined by falsehood; this is what necessary propositions do. But since it can be true when, for example, I sit, and false when I do not sit, the proposition is in itself indeterminate toward either possibility.

Furthermore, you pressed against several of his words concerning good and evil, truth and falsehood, which he had proposed regarding things <margin>Seventh objection</margin> and the soul, in this manner: "If good and evil are in things, and truth and falsehood <margin>and solution</margin> are in the soul, where is your opposition of affirmation and negation? For negation posits nothing, just as a chimera is in things and in the soul. If it is entirely non-being, then you must think that falsehood, non-being, and evil are interchangeable." 

But I pray you, pay attention and notice that evil and good are pronounced to be "in things" because they are considered in relation to the things themselves, whereas truth and falsehood are not so in the soul. For truth and falsehood are not in things—as Aristotle writes in the sixth book of *First Philosophy* <note>original: "sexto priæ phiæ [primæ philosophiæ] libro"; this refers to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>—but in the mind. Nor does it necessarily follow from this that a thing which is entirely evil is therefore a "true thing." Indeed, that "truth" and "falsehood" of which Aristotle makes mention in that place are complex <term>complexa (propositions or sentences made of multiple parts, rather than single words)</term>. 

Neither does it follow <margin>Aristotle</margin> that if good and evil are in things, they cannot therefore be opposed contradictorily. For the evil that is pronounced to be in things is not said to be in them in the sense that it is understood to be some "thing" or substance. Rather, it is because it is observed and considered in relation to the things themselves—that is, insofar as a thing is deprived of its perfections <margin>il [referring to the argument]</margin> and is rendered "not good." 

A chimera <note>A mythological monster; in philosophy, a standard example of an impossible object that exists only in the imagination.</note> is not itself in reality, because it is entirely non-being and entirely evil; yet, if it were possible for nature to produce it as a thing, it would be both a thing and good. It is "false" only insofar as it exists as nothing at all and fits no Idea <note>A reference to the Platonic Ideas or divine archetypes.</note>. Nor do we affirm that the chimera itself is in the soul, but rather the *notion* of the chimera. That notion, as a certain thing in itself, is both good and true; but it is "false" only in the sense that it represents a chimera, since the chimera itself is both nothing and evil.

After this, you believed you could prove that "blindness" is true—something he had denied. <margin>Eighth objection</margin> Even if he had not denied nor conceded that "blindness is blindness" is true, he would have said these two statements are very different. <margin>with solution</margin> You argued in this way: "If 'blindness is blindness' is true, who can fail to see that blindness is true? For they are the same thing. If blindness alone is posited, then 'blindness is blindness' is posited; if it is taken away, the other is taken away. By the same reasoning, Socrates and 'Socrates is Socrates' are the same thing. Both are produced by the same act of generation. Similarly, God and 'God is God' are the same, for both are eternal and the First Truth."

But I, my dear Antony, contend the opposite. I deny that these things you claim are the same are indeed the same. For when one of those you bring forward is posited, the other is not necessarily posited. If blindness alone were posited, and no intellect were considering it, blindness would indeed exist, yet this proposition—"blindness is blindness"—would not exist. 

For this reason, the argument concerning God and the generation of Socrates is also resolved. For Socrates is generated in himself, but the proposition "Socrates is Socrates" is not generated, since complex propositions <term>complexa (logical statements)</term> are not "generated" like physical things. Even if I were to grant you that they are the same, we say it still does not follow what you were concluding, because of the different way of signifying "complexly" and "incomplexly." Such an argument would be of no value: "Blindness and 'blindness is blindness' are the same; but this proposition is true; therefore blindness is true." By that same logic, it would follow: "This is a complex proposition; therefore blindness is a complex proposition," which is absurd, since "blindness" is a simple name, not a complex statement or an enunciation. 

Therefore, it is one thing for "blindness to be true" and another for "blindness is blindness" to be true. Although these points should suffice for the defense of my uncle, nonetheless, do not believe that ways of defending and fighting for him are lacking. So that a more complete response may come to you, I would have you know <margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin> that I could have spoken according to the opinion of Gregory of Rimini: even if "blindness is blindness" were posited whenever blindness is posited, it does not necessarily follow that they are the same thing. For he denies this consequence—and many others of this kind—where, setting aside everything else other than God, "God is" therefore "God is that God is." <margin>Cardinal of Cambrai</margin> The Cardinal of Cambrai also denies all <margin>of Cambrai</margin> statements in which something is enunciated about an infinitive phrase used significatively...

<summary>Pico distinguishes between metaphysical reality (good/evil) and logical truth (true/false), arguing that truth exists in the mind rather than in objects themselves. He further refutes the idea that a thing (like blindness) is identical to a logical proposition about that thing.</summary>

APOLOGIA

<margin>
The ninth objection and the solution to the objection.
</margin>

...and he asserts them to be both false and incongruous, as can be seen in his first book of the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* by Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook in medieval and Renaissance universities.</note>. Then you complain that the "false" ought not to have been pronounced "divided" <note>In medieval logic, "divided" often refers to the separation of terms in a proposition.</note> with this condition—that is, "so long as it is false." You explain this in these words: "If everything false is simply divided, which you do not deny has been proven, it should not have been said that a certain falsehood is divided only with this condition—namely, so long as it is false." For if every man is simply and absolutely capable of laughter <note>original: *risibilis*; a technical term in logic for a "proprium," a characteristic that belongs to all humans and only humans (the capacity for humor), even if they aren't laughing at that moment.</note>, it is not necessary to add a condition by which you restrict it, saying "every man is capable of laughter as long as he is a man." Nor should a restriction have been added because not all false things are equally divided or false. For not all beings are equally good, yet all are absolutely good. 

But weigh his words carefully, through which you can cast away all scruple and doubt. He says: every false thing is divided, yet not every false thing is equally false, because they are not equally divided when they are not necessarily and always false—and those things which are always and necessarily false. Therefore, Antonius <note>Likely referring to the author or a contemporary scholar involved in the debate.</note>, that phrase "as long as" was rightly added for those things that are not always and necessarily false; things which, even if false, can become true and united either by nature or by the work of a craftsman—as you also said in the second objections. Nevertheless, as long as they are divided, they are false; but those things that can never return to friendship <note>A metaphorical way of describing the union of terms or concepts.</note> are always false, as is seen abundantly in the response to the second objection. Nor does the comparison regarding beings and the capacity for laughter support you much. For beings are always and absolutely good. Although they are not equally good and some participate more in the nature of "the good" than others, they are nevertheless always and necessarily good; for insofar as they are beings, they are good, and they cannot become non-beings and non-good unless they are reduced to nothing. But what consists in a "false and divided" complex <note>Likely referring to a logical proposition or a complex of ideas.</note> can conveniently become "undivided and true." The comparison, therefore, does not fit. For although not all false things are equally divided, they are nevertheless false insofar as they are not united and not true. Add to this that this objection ought to trouble us little. For who would doubt that it can be pronounced that a man (who is absolutely and always capable of laughter) will be capable of laughter with the condition "so long as he is a man"? Or will this way of speaking be disapproved of by learned men: "a man is capable of laughter so long as he is a man"?

<margin>
Solution to the tenth objection.
</margin>

The tenth head of your objections brings nothing else against him except that what you said could have been easily established if the logic of contrary motions had been sufficiently understood by him. But he, unless he has forgotten, complained that you did not prove what you so often said would follow: namely, that from the contrariety of pursuing and fleeing, the contrariety of good and evil is inferred. For he asks: by what reasoning is "good" to be sought and "evil" to be fled? And since fleeing and seeking are contraries, how do you prove from this that good and evil are contraries? This is what you must prove; yet you have never said a word to prove it, nor do you do so now. This he denies—namely, the form of your argument—perhaps for this reason: that seeking and fleeing are not properly contrary motions from which it can be gathered that the terms are contraries. 

<margin>
Aristotle.
</margin>

And also by Aristotle himself, some contrariety of changes is assigned in the sixth book of the *Physics* <note>original: *Physicae Auscultationis*; the standard title for Aristotle's *Physics*.</note> where the terms are not contraries but contradictories: namely, "being" and "non-being," when generation proceeds from non-being to being, and corruption falls from being into non-being. But you have treated this contrariety of good and evil again and brought no other proof. Furthermore, do not doubt that he has diligently looked into the reasoning of contrary motions since his "fingernails" <note>original: *ab ipsis unguiculis*; a Latin idiom meaning "from early childhood" or "from the very beginning."</note>. On the contrary, he has quite often not only repelled your arguments against him regarding this contrariety, but he also acted against you when, in the second letter, he deduced that your proof implies not only that evil and good are contraries, but that contradictories are contraries. Second, when he turned your own weapons back against you...

<meta>This page continues a philosophical defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s positions, likely written by his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico. It focuses on the metaphysical status of "evil" as a privation of being rather than a positive substance, citing a lineage of authorities from Simplicius to Thomas Aquinas.</meta>

-># OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...it follows in this manner: good and evil are opposites in themselves; and each of these opposites is something positive; and non-being in itself is [not] good; therefore, non-being in itself is something positive. Since "being" and "something" are interchangeable <note>A fundamental rule in Scholastic philosophy: whatever exists (being) is also a "thing" (something).</note>, it follows that non-being in itself is something positive.

When you stated in your third letter that he <note>Referring to the author's uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> retreated to Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia, a 6th-century Greek commentator on Aristotle.</note>, leaving behind the Latin commentators <margin>Eleventh</margin> regarding the opposition of good and evil, he replied as if in wonder: <margin>of the objection</margin> why should you, who used to be a follower of Boethius <margin>solution.</margin> and a mocker of "barbarians," <note>Humanists often called medieval Scholastics "barbarians" for their rough Latin style.</note> now mock those who followed the Greek commentators instead of the Latins? You would find it most inconvenient to feel that Greek philosophers should not be held in high esteem, given that Boethius—whom you hold in such great value and highest honor—always held them in the highest regard. <margin>Boethius</margin> He used them as both teachers and guides. You reply that this is nothing to wonder at, for you would say the Latins do not deny Aristotle, whom Simplicius also does not deny, and so on.

But it does not seem to me that Simplicius denies Aristotle, as he interprets him correctly; nor does it appear that the Latin commentators vary from Simplicius's view, for they embrace and follow it with their whole minds in their works. If he was amazed by your claim that the Latin expositors do not follow Simplicius, he would perhaps have fallen into an even greater stupor if he had understood you to mean that the Latins do not deny Aristotle, while Simplicius does. 

Furthermore, Simplicius and those who followed him clearly illuminate Aristotle’s mind when he said that good and evil are opposites; for one of the opposites always holds the character of evil and deficiency. For this reason, in the first book of the *Physics*, he taught that opposites are always compared to one another according to the ratio of the "better" and the "worse." In this, he imitated the Pythagoreans, <margin>Pythagoras</margin> who established two orders of things: one contained under the good, the other under the evil. He frequently used external examples for this exposition in his logical books. As your own Thomas <margin>Thomas</margin> <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> says—who is not only Latin, but the chief among the Latins—he not only reports this but proves it. To him, we also add Giles <margin>Giles</margin> <note>Aegidius Romanus, or Giles of Rome.</note> in his second book on the *Sentences*, and many others including Walter Burley <margin>Burley</margin> and Esculanus <margin>Esculanus</margin> <note>Likely the astronomer and poet Cecco d'Ascoli.</note> who hold the same view. 

Even John Duns Scotus, <margin>John Duns Scotus</margin> explaining Aristotle’s *Categories*, agrees with our view, saying that if "good" is taken as being interchangeable with "being," then "evil" is nothing, and thus it is not an opposite to the good. For since it is beyond controversy that each of two opposites must be something positive, it is necessary that something which is "nothing" in the nature of things—which is what evil is—cannot be declared an opposite. 

And although you denied that evil is "nothing," appealing to Thomas Aquinas, he himself not only fails to support your opinion but abundantly refutes it. My uncle <note>original: "patruus"; Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> showed this sufficiently in the margin of his third letter. However, we do not think it out of place to touch upon even a few points in passing for my uncle's opinion, showing that not only was Thomas of the opinion that evil is "nothing," but that crowds of many other illustrious philosophers and theologians have descended into this same view "with hands and feet" <note>An idiom meaning "totally" or "with full agreement."</note>. 

We find that Augustine, <margin>Augustine</margin> discussing the *Morals of the Manichaeans*, said that no nature is evil. A little later, lest there be any ambiguity about what he understood by "nature," he added: "nature itself is nothing other than that which is understood to be something in its own kind." We have seen that Giles of Rome, <margin>Giles</margin> in his first book of commentaries on the *Sentences* of the Fathers, left it written that evil, insofar as it is evil, is a pure <term>privation</term> <gloss>the absence of a quality that should be present</gloss> and not a "something." It can only be called "something" in the same way that "nothing" itself can be called something—when both can be designated by a name. In the second book of those same commentaries, he affirms that evil does not have (to use his words) <term>quiddity</term> <gloss>essence or "what-ness"</gloss>, and for that reason, one cannot answer the question "What is it?" He states that evil is nothing other than a name and words. He likewise interprets Aristotle’s views on the opposition of good and evil according to my uncle’s mind, and he agrees with the dogma of Simplicius <margin>Simplicius</margin> and other upright interpreters of Aristotle, pronouncing that they are not distinct <term>genera</term> <gloss>categories or classes</gloss> but belong to other opposites...

The author cites a wide array of authorities, including Simplicius, Augustine, and Thomas Aquinas, to show that this view is consistent with both Greek and Latin traditions.</summary>

**THE DEFENSE**

[Main Text]

<margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin> ...that these ought to be called types <note>of opposites</note>, since one has the character of a positive while the other does not, and that no contrary is, in itself, "non-being," but rather possesses some nature and existence. Gregory of Rimini <note>A 14th-century theologian known for his rigorous reading of St. Augustine.</note> testifies to this very thing in his commentaries on the second book of the *Sentences* <note>original: "sententiarum" — The *Sentences* of Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</note>: namely, that evil itself is not "any entity"—to use his own word—but pure privation <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that should normally be present, like blindness being the privation of sight.</note>. Robert Holkot, a man of the most piercing intellect, felt the same way in the first question of his own commentaries on the second book of the theological *Sentences*. Many others have judged likewise, but to bring them all forward now would perhaps cause weariness for me in writing and for you in reading later. It will be enough for the present business to have enumerated these few, especially since it will be necessary to speak of this again when we resolve other objections in those places where mention of evil occurs.

But to return to the point from which we digressed: of all the Latin authors, you seem to summon only Boethius <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose works bridged the gap between Classical Antiquity and the Middle Ages.</note> to testify against the "Simple Ones" and the other illustrious interpreters. If you deign to count him among the Latins, he will be the only Latin expositor—not "the Latin expositors" plural—who seems to support your opinion. Add to this that even he, if his mind is properly examined, does not protest our view, since he neither weighs this question exactly nor searches it out with a final judgment. Rather, he only declares what Aristotle’s words, when grasped strictly and narrowly, demand. This was his most familiar habit in his first editions: to leave the various opinions of the Greek interpreters to be examined scrupulously and anxiously in a second edition.

<margin>Solution to the twelfth objection.</margin> Furthermore, I believe he not only proved but demonstrated that whenever it is granted that "good" and "evil" are contraries, it can be announced without any controversy that a "Chimera" <note>Here used to mean a logical absurdity or a thing that cannot exist in reality.</note> is something in the nature of things. To his arguments, you respond only that it was "not perceived"—that is, he did not understand by what reasoning you called good and evil contraries. You offer nothing else for yourself, and for that reason, I will do nothing against you except to point out that he both saw and perceived everything you had written, and when he pleased, he reviewed the many things you had said about contraries. Indeed, my plan in this business is to dissolve your final objections against my uncle, but to pass over in silence those to which he had already responded in some way. Nevertheless, if anything seems to you not fully clarified by him which you wish and demand to be opened by me, we will attempt to satisfy your desire. Through these things, we will move through your arguments by both dissolving and responding to them as best we can; for he did not judge it unsuitable for even every tiny detail of your words to receive a response. He confesses in his first letters that certain things were omitted to which no response was given, lest he waste words on trivial matters; some things were treated lightly, as he is a man who thought philosophical matters should be indicated rather than explained. I would like those words to be interpreted by you in this way: that some points of controversy are well known even to common philosophers, and it was not worth the effort for you, a noble philosopher, to bring them against a man most celebrated in both learning and fame who was conducting a discourse on the highest matters—a man who would descend to discuss these lowest things not without a loss to his meditations on the most difficult subjects. However, regarding this "contrariety" of yours, we shall say something in the following response when we speak of "incomplete privations."

<margin>Solution to the thirteenth objection.</margin> You wonder, moreover, why he marveled at your "incomplete privations" <note>original: "semiplenas priuationes" — literally "half-full privations." These are states where a good is partially but not entirely absent.</note>. I believe he turned to wonder at this not so much at that time, but after you proved you were attempting it again (if indeed your final objections were seen by him). He had said against you: "Evil is nothing; therefore, it is not an incomplete privation." You, however, pursue his argument in this way: "Sickness is evil, therefore it is nothing. Therefore, it is not an incomplete privation. But sickness is a certain privation; therefore, it is not an incomplete privation of either health or some good, but rather a full and perfect one." Since that cannot be, you argue that "imperfect privations are incomplete, such as sickness, rarity, ugliness, or blindness..." <note>The text cuts off here as it transitions to the next point.</note>

<meta>This page continues a philosophical debate, likely addressed to Antonio Pizzamano, regarding the nature of evil and privation. It picks up mid-sentence from the previous page's discussion of "the word."</meta>

# **GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...word. But I, my dear Antonio, would say freely that these words of yours either do nothing against him, or to see it more clearly, I will review them point by point. You say first, from his own words, that evil is nothing; therefore, it is not a partial privation <note>original: *semiplena priuatio*; a state where some of the intended "good" or "form" remains.</note>. You proceed correctly; again, sickness is evil, therefore it is nothing: therefore it is not a partial privation. Up to here you also progress well, because sickness, insofar as it is evil, is to that extent "nothing." Again you say: but a certain sickness is a privation, therefore not health, etc., all the way to the end; in which words, by your leave, I believe a falsehood is being constructed, which we shall endeavor to show.

For blindness is not only a perfect privation of sight, as you say, but it can also be called a perfect privation of "good," because it takes away all of that good which it is naturally meant to take away—namely, sight. Ophthalmia <note>An inflammation of the eye.</note> does not do this, even though it also destroys the good it is naturally meant to take away; however, it cannot be called a privation of that which it is not suited to destroy, whether you call it partial or full.

<margin>Privation is to be considered in two ways.</margin> For privation is considered either absolutely—that is, as it regards "habit" <note>original: *habitum*; in scholastic philosophy, a "habit" is a stable quality or disposition that a subject possesses, such as health or sight.</note> in general—or as it is restricted to a certain and limited kind of being, such as the health of the whole body, or the eye, or beauty, and other things of that sort. 

<margin>Dionysius</margin> Taken in the first way, it does not deprive a person of any particular habit, because an all-encompassing privation, as Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian whose "On the Divine Names" argued that evil has no independent existence but is a deficiency of good.</note> says in his book *On the Divine Names*, fails entirely in its powers. Taken in the second way, which is called "singular" by Dionysius (distinguishing it against the "universal"), it deprives that specific habit which it regards. In this way, this kind of habit—which the privation is naturally meant to oppose—is a full privation and not otherwise; for the thing itself, it is partial. For who would dare to say that blindness is a partial privation of a human being, or of any other good that might be in a human? Therefore, absolute privation regards habit absolutely, while a proper and particular privation regards a proper and particular habit, and does not exceed its limits.

For this reason, sickness is a full privation, not a partial one, whether you ascribe it to the whole body or to a particular limb. For a fever is the perfect privation of that temperature <note>The "balance of humors" or qualities required for health.</note> which it is naturally meant to corrupt. Ophthalmia, too, even if it does not take away the "total good" that is in the eye, is nevertheless a perfect and proper privation of *some* good: because it destroys all of that good which it is naturally meant to destroy, even when it does not take away the sight, but only the perfect health of the eye. 

Deformity also is a perfect privation, because it takes away all that good which it can take away—namely, the perfect composition of parts which is called beauty; and consider it likewise in other things. We might also say this in abundance: blindness, insofar as it is blindness, is an evil; insofar as it is an evil, it is nothing; insofar as it is nothing, it is not a partial privation, because if it were partial, it would leave something positive behind, which evil does not do. 

Furthermore, no privation in itself actually deprives *all* good; therefore, all privations would be "partial" privations, which goes against you, because you contend that some are full and some are partial. This is an excellent and necessary connection, and we prove what we have assumed with this argument: since no good would ever be found if a total and universal privation were discovered in the nature of things (as we hinted a little earlier from the words of Dionysius). For evil deprives a particular good, since evil exists within a "good" [subject], and a universal evil would destroy universal good—if indeed it could be found, which is impossible. And thus, conclude that privations of their own proper habits are always found to be full, not partial.

<margin>Solution to the fourteenth objection.</margin> To the fourteenth objection, which contains several questions, I respond point by point. First, that not every evil leaves something of good behind, unless you understand that "subject" in which the evil itself does not reside, or you take that subject whose habit is destroyed by the evil itself... <note>The text cuts off as Pico begins to cite a previous response from a second letter.</note>

<summary>Pico argues against the concept of "partial privation," asserting that while an evil (like blindness) doesn't destroy all good in a person, it is a "full" privation of the specific quality (sight) it opposes. Following Dionysius the Areopagite, he maintains that evil is a lack of a specific intended good rather than a positive substance.</summary>
