<meta>This page continues a philosophical defense (Apologia), likely within a Scholastic context, regarding the metaphysical nature of evil and the distinction between "being" and "non-being." It responds to an opponent's arguments concerning whether impossible or non-existent things (like a Chimera) can be considered "good" because of God's power to create.</meta>

->**DEFENSE**<-

...moved concerning this matter, writing in this manner: you surely ought to have considered that what is conceded regarding certain imperfect evils—on account of the mixture of goodness they still retain—must not be transferred to the unmixed and absolute nature of evil itself. 
<margin>Evil is understood in two ways.</margin> 
And so that you may perceive the truth more clearly, I will not be loath to explain the force of the distinction: evil can be considered in two ways. First, absolutely and under the proper definition of evil, which is insofar as it is nothing. Second, insofar as it is a <term>privation</term><note>In medieval philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a good that should normally be present, like blindness is the privation of sight. It is not a "thing" in itself, but a lack in something else.</note> of some good; this is a particular evil, and evil understood in this way leaves at least some "subject" (an existing thing) as its base. The other kind of evil does not do this, for it is entirely <term>non-being</term><note>Something that has no existence at all.</note> and nothing, just as we call the <term>Chimera</term><note>original: "chymera." A mythological beast used by philosophers as a standard example of an impossible object that can be thought of but cannot exist in reality.</note> a "nothing" since it does not refer to any actual subject or state of being. And for this reason, he calls "absolute evil" that which is the unmixed nature of evil. 
<margin>Dionysius</margin> 
He says this evil is—to use the words of <term>Dionysius</term><note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential 5th-century Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> in his book *On the Divine Names*—that which "in no way, nowhere, is a non-existent nothing" because it lacks any subject to exist in. The Chimera, even if it could be called "good" in <term>potential</term><note>The capacity to become something or be created, as opposed to "actuality," which is being real right now.</note> because of the power to produce it which exists in God, nevertheless can be named neither a "being" nor "good." For if this connection—namely, "something is potentially good, therefore it is good"—were valid, it would be a strong weapon that could be turned back against its author. It would force him to admit that all things which ought to be created by God, but are not (by some force of nature), and even things that have been destroyed, would simultaneously "be something" and "not be something." For if, according to him, they were both "beings" and "good" because of the creator's power, then they would necessarily "be something"; after all, "being something" and "being good" are interchangeable and cover the same ground. 

I shall argue as follows that such a thing cannot "be something": nothing can be made out of nothing before it is created; according to you, a Chimera cannot exist unless it is created; therefore, it is created out of nothing; therefore, before it was created out of nothing, it was not "something." Therefore, on account of the power of goodness which is in the Creator, a thing cannot be named "absolutely good"; otherwise—to use the language of our <term>dialecticians</term><note>The "dialecticians" were the Scholastic logicians of the university system.</note>—it would be a <term>fallacy of the qualified to the absolute</term><note>original: "fallatia secundum quid ad simpliciter." A logical error where one assumes that because something is true in a specific, limited case (it is "good" as a thought in God's mind), it must be true in an absolute, general sense (it is an "actual good").</note>. 

I deliberately pass over those arguments brought against that opinion regarding "eternal essences" (so to speak) and "objective potentiality," even if your opinion could perhaps be weakened by those very same reasons. For it is enough for our purpose if I have proved that a Chimera cannot be called "good." 
<margin>Averroes</margin> 
Add that we can also follow <term>Averroes</term><note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher Ibn Rushd, famous for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> on this point and say that "being in potential" is not "being," since in his commentaries on the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*, in the fifteenth section, he said that "that which is not in act is not being." 

Regarding what you add—namely, that a Chimera is a "being" because, although the power to produce the Chimera is in God, the power of God and the power of the Chimera exist by different definitions—I reply first that I can deny that God's power and the power of producing a Chimera are different in their definitions. Secondly, even if I were to grant you freely that those powers are different, your reasoning still proves nothing: for a Chimera can in no way be called a "being" on account of a "power to produce itself" that exists in God. Since that power is absent [from the Chimera itself], neither the Chimera nor anything intrinsic to it can be spoken of; indeed, they are infinitely distant. 

Furthermore, you add that if we exclude God's power and our own thought, a Chimera is not "evil," since evil is a privation that exists in a subject participating in goodness. To this I would reply with the same distinction as before: while a Chimera does not refer to any subject but is absolutely "bad" (non-existent), we can still say that the *notion* of the Chimera which we hold in our minds is "something" and therefore "good," even while we pronounce that the Chimera itself is neither "anything" nor "good."

<margin>Solution to the fifteenth objection</margin> 
Furthermore, you seem to take pleasure in the idea that what you brought forward was not disproved, and that the only response was that "simple people do not say that." Likewise, you say you did not claim that Aristotle felt that every being whatsoever exists either through itself or by accident, and that you did not ascribe anything false to Thomas [Aquinas] because of it. Truly, even if so many things have been said on this matter by that man whom we are defending that it does not seem necessary for me to speak further...

<summary>The author argues that absolute evil and non-existent concepts like the "Chimera" possess no "being" or "goodness" in themselves, refuting the idea that potential existence in God's mind constitutes actual reality. He utilizes the logic of Aristotle, Averroes, and Pseudo-Dionysius to distinguish between something that is "nothing" and something that is merely a "lack of good."</summary>

<keywords>Metaphysics, Nature of Evil, Non-being, Chimera, Privation, Potentiality vs Actuality, Pseudo-Dionysius, Averroes, Scholastic Logic, Thomas Aquinas</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of the author's uncle, likely Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, against a scholarly opponent. The text focuses on the metaphysical definition of "Being" and the nature of "Evil" as a privation of Good.</meta>

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

And since I have proposed once and for all not to retract things already discussed by him in whatever way, I might nonetheless say these things as an extra measure on behalf of my uncle regarding Simplicius <note>original: "Simpliciū." A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and one of the most important commentators on Aristotle.</note>. For he, whom you have so often cited as a witness in your judgment against us, has more often born witness against you, as my uncle frequently points out in his responses. Again, I would like to know whether you have undertaken to defend the idea that not every "being" <term>being: the Latin "ens," referring to anything that exists</term> is either "by accident" or "in itself" <term>original: "per accidens aut per se." A fundamental Aristotelian distinction between things that exist by their own nature and things that happen by chance or external circumstances.</term> according to the mind of Aristotle. For he, in the fifth book of his *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics* was traditionally called "First Philosophy."</note>, divides "being" into "being in itself" and "being by accident," and finally they divide these into substance and accidents. Since these were contained in the first member of the partition—as that "being in itself" is divided into ten categories, one of which is substance and the others are accidents—I would now most gladly be taught by you: what sort of "being" would it be that is neither "in itself" nor "by accident"? 

For if perhaps you were to say that this division into "being in itself" and "being by accident" is an assignment of a "complex being" <term>complex being: an "ens complexum," or a proposition/statement, rather than a single simple thing like "a tree."</term>, as you put forward in your first objections, I would not hesitate to respond that you truly cannot show this. You cannot support your opinion either by any sentiment of Aristotle or by suitable reason, since in that passage Aristotle divides "being in itself" into ten categories, of which one is substance and nine are accidents, which no one believes to be "complex beings," especially when they are distinguished against "complex" things. In that same place, Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher Ibn Rushd, famous for his extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note> says that "being in itself" is divided through terms signifying the categories of the predicaments; but a single term is not a "complex being." In the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, this same Averroes says that the first division of "being" is into "in itself" and "by accident"; but it could not be the "first" if a division of "complex being" preceded it. Nor is it found in the works of Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian.</note>, in his commentary on the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*, that "complex being" is divided in the way you asserted. 

Indeed, it cannot be believed—when "being" is first partitioned into "being in itself" and "being by accident," and that "in itself" is sub-divided into ten categories which we have shown to be "incomplex" <note>Simple or non-propositional.</note>—that a division of "complex being" is assigned in that place, since it is necessary that the thing which is divided be predicated of the members that divide it. These things have been said because, even if they pertain little to the business at hand, your dogma seems to me at first glance to be consistent neither with the views of the Aristotelian interpreters nor with reason. But if by chance you prove the contrary, it will be most pleasing to have learned something from a philosopher as serious as I truly consider you to be.

Furthermore, he [the uncle] said that evil is a privation <term>privation: the lack or absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness is the privation of sight.</term> insofar as privation was formally a negation. To this you object <margin>Solution to the tenth and sixth objections.</margin>, saying it is not established that there is no other opposition of affirmation and negation than that of privation and habit <note>original: "habitus." The state of possessing a quality.</note>. Nor, for that reason, if evil were a privation of good, would it be necessary for "evil" and "not-good" to be interchangeable. To these things I would like to respond that there is one opposition for privation and another for negation, and he did not claim they were the same opposite; but for this reason it still follows that if evil is opposed to good in a privative way, "evil" and "not-good" must be interchangeable. For privation, as Albert the Great <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century Dominican friar and teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note> <margin>Albert the Great</margin> says in the first book of *Natural Philosophy* <note>original: "physicæ auscultationis," referring to Aristotle's *Physics*.</note>, insofar as it is a privation, is not something from itself or by itself, because from itself it has "non-being." Moreover, it is even asserted by Aristotle in his *First Philosophy* that privations belong to the category of "non-beings," since privation by its nature becomes the other extreme of a contradiction. And therefore, since evil is a privation of good and consequently a "non-being," insofar as evil is evil, "evil" and "not-good" are interchangeable. For "evil" and "nothing," as has been proven, are the same; "nothing" and "non-being" are the same; likewise, "non-being" and "not-good" are the same because "being" and "good" are the same <note>A core medieval concept: existence and goodness are fundamentally the same thing viewed from different angles.</note>. Wherefore my uncle most rightly said that negation is a privation insofar as privation would formally be negation. For although they differ in this—that one of them, namely contradiction, has no middle ground <note>The Law of the Excluded Middle: something is either A or not-A.</note>, as the Philosopher [Aristotle] says in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*, while the other might have one in a certain way since it occurs together with its opposite regarding the same subject—nonetheless, as far as the present proposal is concerned, they would be the same since privation by its nature is a negation and...

The arguments of my uncle are these, which I will soon explain: it is impossible for anything to be if it is not "Being itself"; <note>original: "ipsum esse" — a technical term in medieval philosophy meaning the pure act of existence, which theologians identified with God.</note> but God is Being itself. Since it has been proved that there is some one thing from which all receive their being and their finite nature, if that is removed, nothing exists and nothing is finite. For if it is infinite, this means it is not terminated or made finite by that First Principle by whose help all things are both made to be and are finished and bounded. It follows that the infinite is not. Therefore, the infinite destroys itself. Since there is nothing else to be said of the "infinite" in the way it is taken here, it follows that it is nothing. For if it is neither finite nor God, it is beyond controversy that it is absolutely nothing.

These are the things, Anthony, which I have brought forward for the sake of grasping my uncle's opinion, which perhaps contains other doctrines as well; for it is not within everyone's reach to attain what he had conceived. And let us hold to what we have written while performing the duty of an interpreter, which, since they are satisfactory, will also conclude my response, after first bringing forward certain points that both strengthen my uncle's opinion and equally confirm and elucidate my own interpretation of his words that I offered before.

But if true things tend toward nothingness, beings likewise are not saved from destruction, since they move within an equal boundary. Likewise, if that which communicates both being and life to things is removed, who would not see those same things as mere paintings <note>Likely meaning "shadows" or "unreal images" rather than actual physical objects.</note> [rather than reality]?

->ORATION<-
->ORATION OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA.<-

[Decorated initial L with floral motifs] I have read, Most Honorable Fathers, in the records of the Arabs, that when Abdallah <margin>Abdallah</margin> the <term>Saracen</term> <margin>the Saracen</margin> <note>original: "Abdalam sarracenum"; "Saracen" was a common medieval term for Muslims.</note> was asked what he found most worthy of wonder on this stage of the world, as it were, he replied that nothing is more wonderful to behold than man. This quote comes from the Hermetic corpus, a collection of mystical and philosophical texts.</note> When I pondered the reason for these sayings, I was not satisfied by the many arguments offered by many others concerning the excellence of human nature: <margin>The dignity of man</margin> that man is the intermediary between creatures, the intimate of the higher beings, the king of the lower ones, perceptive through the sharpness of his senses, curious through the investigation of his reason, and the interpreter of nature through the light of his intellect. He is the interval between stable eternity and flowing time; and (as the <margin>The Persians</margin> say) the bond, or rather the <term>hymenaeus</term> <note>A Greek term for a wedding song or union; here, man is the "marriage bond" of the universe.</note> of the world, and according to the testimony of <margin>David</margin> David, "a little lower than the angels." <note>A reference to Psalm 8:5.</note> These things are certainly great, but they are not the principal reasons—that is, those which may rightfully claim the privilege of the highest admiration. For why should we not admire the angels themselves and the most blessed choirs of heaven even more? At last, I seemed to understand why man is the most fortunate of animals and consequently worthy of all admiration, and what precisely is that condition which he has been allotted in the sequence of the universe—a condition to be envied not only by the brutes but by the stars and the minds beyond this world. It is a thing beyond belief and wonderful. And why not? For it is for this reason that man is rightly called and considered a great miracle and a truly wonderful animal. But hear, Fathers, what this condition is, and grant me your attention with favorable ears, according to your kindness.

Already the Supreme Father, God the Architect, had fashioned this worldly house we see—this most august temple of divinity—according to the laws of secret wisdom. He had adorned the region above the heavens with minds; He had animated the celestial spheres with eternal souls; He had filled the excremental and dreg-filled parts of the lower world with a crowd of animals of every kind. But, when the work was finished, the Craftsman desired that there be someone to weigh the reason of such a great work, to love its beauty, and to admire its vastness. Therefore, when all things were finished (as <margin>Moses</margin> Moses and <margin>Timaeus</margin> Timaeus <note>Pico is synthesizing the biblical account in Genesis with Plato's "Timaeus," a Greek dialogue about the creation of the universe.</note> bear witness), He finally thought of creating man. But there was no pattern left among the archetypes from which He might fashion a new offspring, nor was there anything in His treasures which He might grant to His new son as an inheritance, nor was there a seat in the whole world where this contemplator of the universe might sit. All places were already full; all things had been distributed among the highest, the middle, and the lowest orders. But it was not in the nature of the Father's power to fail, as if exhausted, in His final creation; it was not in the nature of His wisdom to waver in a necessary matter through lack of a plan; it was not in the nature of His beneficent love that he who was to praise the divine liberality in others should be forced to condemn it in himself. At last, the Best of Craftsmen decreed that he to whom nothing could be given as his own property should share in whatever had been particular to each individual. Therefore, He took man as a creature of indeterminate image and, placing him in the middle of the world, addressed him thus: "We have given you, O Adam, no fixed seat <margin>Free will in man.</margin> nor a form of your own, nor any gift peculiar to you alone, so that whatever seat, whatever form, and whatever gifts you yourself shall desire, these you may have and possess according to your own wish and decision. The nature of all other beings is limited and constrained within the laws prescribed by us. You, constrained by no limits, shall define your nature for yourself according to your own free will, in whose hand I have placed you. I have set you in the center of the world so that from there you might more easily look around at whatever is in the world. We have made you neither heavenly nor earthly, neither mortal nor immortal, so that, like a free and sovereign artificer and molder of yourself, you may fashion yourself into whatever form you prefer. You will have the power to degenerate into the lower forms, which are the brutes; you will have the power to be reborn into the higher forms, which are divine, according to the judgment of your own mind." O the supreme liberality of God the Father! O the supreme and wonderful happiness of man! To him it is granted to have whatever he chooses, to be whatever he...

->ORATION<-

<margin>Lucilius</margin>
Brute beasts, as soon as they are born, bring with them from their mother's womb (as Lucilius says) all that they will ever possess. The highest spirits <note>referring to angels</note> were, either from the beginning or shortly thereafter, that which they are destined to be for all eternity. But to man, at his birth, the Father instilled seeds of every kind and germs of every form of life. Whatever seeds each person cultivates, those will grow and bear their fruit within him. If they are vegetative, he will become a plant. If they are sensual, he will grow brutish. If they are rational, he will turn into a heavenly creature. If they are intellectual, he will be an angel and a son of God. And if, happy with the lot of no created thing, he withdraws into the center of his own unity, he becomes one spirit with God, in the solitary darkness of the Father <note>A mystical reference to the "Divine Darkness" beyond human understanding</note> who is set above all things, and he shall surpass them all. 

<margin>Note:</margin>
Who would not admire this **chameleon** <term>chameleon|A metaphor for man's ability to change his nature and assume any form through his will</term> of ours? Or who could altogether admire anything else more? 
<margin>Asclepius of Athens.</margin>
It was not without reason that Asclepius of Athens said that man was symbolized in the mysteries by Proteus <note>A Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will</note>, on account of his changing and self-transforming nature. 
<margin>Hebrews. Pythagoreans.</margin>
Hence those famous "metamorphoses" celebrated among the Hebrews and the Pythagoreans. For the more secret theology of the Hebrews at one moment transforms the holy Enoch into an angel of the divinity (whom they call [blank space] <note>The original manuscript likely intended to name Metatron here</note>) and at other moments transforms others into different divine beings. 
<margin>Empedocles.</margin>
The Pythagoreans transform wicked men into brute animals and, if we believe Empedocles, even into plants. 
<margin>Muhammad.</margin>
Imitating them, Muhammad often had this saying on his lips: that he who turns away from the divine law becomes a brute; and rightly so. 
<margin>Note</margin>
For it is not the bark that makes the plant, but its dull and senseless nature; nor is it the hide that makes the beast of burden, but its brutal and sensual soul; nor is it the spherical body that makes the heavens, but its right reason; nor is it the separation from the body that makes the angel, but his spiritual intelligence. 

If you see someone crawling on his belly, devoted to his appetite, it is a shrub you see, not a man. If you see someone blinded by the vain illusions of fantasy, as if by Calypso <note>The nymph in Homer's Odyssey who enchanted Odysseus</note>, and lulled by seductive allurements, enslaved to his senses, it is a brute you see, not a man. If you see a philosopher discerning all things by right reason, revere him; he is a heavenly, not an earthly, being. If you see a pure contemplator, oblivious to the body and withdrawn into the inner sanctuary of the mind, this is neither an earthly nor a heavenly creature; he is a more august divinity clothed in human flesh.

<margin>The Mosaic and Christian writings.</margin>
Who then would not admire man? He who is not undeservedly designated in the sacred Mosaic and Christian writings sometimes by the name of "all flesh" and sometimes by that of "every creature," since he fashions, shapes, and transforms himself into the appearance of all flesh and into the character of every creature. 
<margin>Euantes the Persian. The Chaldeans.</margin>
Therefore, Euantes the Persian <note>Likely a reference to a source on Zoroastrian or Persian lore</note> writes, where he explains Chaldean theology, that man has no single native image of his own, but many that are foreign and external; hence that saying of the Chaldeans:
[blank space] 
that is, "man is a creature of a varied, multiform, and fickle nature." 

<margin>Note.</margin>
But to what end is all this? So that we may understand that, since we are born with the condition that we may be whatever we wish to be, we should take the greatest care of this: that it never be said of us that, while we were in a position of honor, we did not realize we had become like the beasts and senseless cattle. 
<margin>Asaph the prophet.</margin>
But rather let us remember the saying of Asaph the prophet: "You are all gods and sons of the Most High," lest by abusing the most indulgent generosity of the Father—that free choice He gave us—we make for ourselves a harmful choice instead of a saving one. 

Let a certain sacred ambition invade our souls, so that, not content with the mediocre, we may pant after the highest things and strive with all our might to attain them (since we can, if we will). Let us disdain earthly things, despise the celestial, and finally, leaving behind everything that is of this world, let us fly to the court beyond the world, nearest to the most eminent Divinity. 
<margin>Seraphim. Cherubim. Thrones.</margin>
There, as the sacred mysteries hand down to us, the **Seraphim**, **Cherubim**, and **Thrones** occupy the first places; let us, incapable of yielding to them and impatient of second place, emulate their dignity and glory. When we wish it, we shall be in no way inferior to them. 

<margin>Seraph. Cherub. Throne.</margin>
But in what way, or by doing what? Let us see what they do, what life they live. If we also live that life (for we can), we shall then have equaled their lot. The Seraph burns with the fire of charity; the Cherub shines with the splendor of intelligence; the Throne stands firm in the steadfastness of judgment. Therefore, if we, dedicated to an active life, undertake the care of lower things with a right examination...

<summary>Pico explains that unlike animals, humans have no fixed nature and can ascend to divinity or descend to brutality based on their free will. He calls on humanity to pursue the highest spiritual heights, emulating the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones through love, intelligence, and justice.</summary>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...we shall be established in the steady stability of the <term>Thrones<note>original: "thronorum". In the traditional celestial hierarchy, the Thrones represent divine justice and the steadfastness of God's throne.</note></term>. If, resting from outward actions and meditating on the <term>Maker<note>original: "opificem". Pico uses this term to describe God as a supreme craftsman or architect of the universe.</note></term> within His work, and the work within the Maker, we occupy ourselves in the leisure of contemplation, we shall flash on every side with <margin>Throne</margin> **Cherubic** light. If we burn with love for the Maker alone, we shall suddenly be set ablaze into a **Seraphic** likeness by His fire, which consumes all. Upon the Throne—that is, the just judge—God sits as the judge of the ages. Above the **Cherub**—that is, the contemplator—He flies, and fosters him as if by hovering over him. For the Spirit of the Lord moves over the waters—those waters, I say, which are above the heavens, and which in the Book of <margin>Job</margin> <note>Job 38:7</note> praise the Lord with hymns before the dawn. He who is a **Seraph**—that is, a lover—is in God, and God is in him; indeed, God and he are one. Great is the power of the **Thrones**, which we attain by the act of judging; highest is the sublimity of the **Seraphim**, which we attain by the act of loving.

<summary>Pico explains how humans can transcend their earthly nature by imitating the virtues of the three highest angelic orders: the stability of the Thrones, the wisdom of the Cherubim, and the burning love of the Seraphim. This process of imitation allows the human soul to achieve intellectual light and mystical union with the Creator.</summary>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...of His saints <margin>saints</margin>—or rather, that death, if it should even be called death, which is the fullness of life, the meditation upon which the wise have said is the study of philosophy. Let us also cite Moses <margin>Moses</margin> himself, who was only a little lower than the angels, but who drew from the holy and inexpressible fountain-like fullness of intelligence, with whose nectar the angels are intoxicated. We shall hear the venerable judge decreeing laws for us who dwell in the desert solitude of this body: Let those who are still defiled and in need of moral training dwell with the common people outside the tabernacle under the open sky, like <margin>Thessalian</margin> <margin>priests</margin> purifying themselves in the meantime. Those who have already composed their character, once received into the sanctuary, should not yet touch the sacred objects; rather, as diligent Levites in the service of dialectic <note>Dialectic refers to the art of logical argument and investigation of truth.</note>, let them first minister to the sacred rites of philosophy. 

Then, once admitted to these rites, they may contemplate now the multi-colored—that is, the starry <note>original: "sydereū"</note>—courtly ornament of the palace of the highest God, now the celestial candelabrum distinct with seven lights, now the "leathern elements" <note>This refers to the material world or "garments of skin" (Genesis 3:21) which some philosophers viewed as the physical shell of the soul.</note> in the priesthood of philosophy; so that finally, through the merits of theological sublimity, having been received into the inner recesses of the temple, they may enjoy the glory of divinity with no veil of images intervening. Indeed, Moses both commands these things of us and, in commanding, admonishes, excites, and exhorts us that, while we are able, we should prepare a way for ourselves through philosophy toward the future heavenly glory. 

Truly, it is not only the Mosaic or Christian mysteries, but also the theology of the ancients that shows us the benefits and dignity of these liberal arts and the matters <margin>of the Greeks</margin> <margin>mysteries</margin> about which I have come to dispute. For what else is intended by the stages of initiation observed in the Greek mysteries? Those who had been purified by those "cleansing" arts we mentioned—morality and dialectic—were then granted the reception of the mysteries. And what else can these mysteries be but the interpretation of nature's more secret things through philosophy? Then finally, for those thus prepared, there came that *epopteia* <note>original: "ἐποπτεία," a Greek term for the highest stage of initiation where the initiate "beholds" the truth directly.</note>, that is, the inspection of divine things through the light of Theology. 

Who would not seek to be initiated into such rites? Who would not desire to become a guest of the gods while still living on earth, neglecting the body and holding the goods of fortune in contempt, and, soaked in the nectar of eternity, to be gifted the prize of immortality though still a mortal animal? Who would not wish to be so inspired by those <margin>Socratic</margin> <margin>frenzies</margin> <margin>frenzies</margin> celebrated by Plato in the *Phaedrus*, that, by the rowing of wings and feet, he might fly away from here—that is, from this world "which is set in wickedness"—and be carried in a most rapid course to the celestial Jerusalem? 

We shall be driven, fathers, we shall be driven by Socratic frenzies, which so place us outside our own minds that they place our minds and ourselves in God. We shall be driven by them indeed, if we have first done what is in us. For if the forces of our emotions have been so tuned through moral power to the proper measures that they sound together in harmony, and if reason has moved itself forward according to number through dialectic, then, inspired by the frenzy of the Muses, we shall drink in the heavenly harmony with our innermost ears. 

Then <margin>Bacchus</margin>, the leader of the Muses, showing us the "invisible things of God" <note>A reference to Romans 1:20: "For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities... have been clearly seen."</note> through the visible signs of nature in his mysteries as we philosophize, will intoxicate us from the richness of the house of God; in which, if we are entirely faithful like Moses <margin>Moses</margin>, most holy Theology approaching will animate us with a double frenzy. For standing on her most eminent and sublime watchtower, measuring what is, what will be, and what has been in an unchangeable eternity, and looking upon primal beauty, we shall be the winged lovers <margin>prophets of Apollo</margin> of these things, like the prophets of Apollo; and finally, spurred by an inexpressible love like a gadfly <note>original: "æstro," referring to the divine sting or "frenzy" of inspiration.</note>, like burning Seraphim, set outside ourselves and full of the divine power, we shall no longer be ourselves, but we shall be He who made us. 

If one scrutinizes the sacred names of Apollo <margin>Ammonius</margin> and their hidden mysteries, they sufficiently show that God is no less a philosopher than a prophet. Since Ammonius <note>Likely referring to Ammonius Saccas or Ammonius Hermiae, Neoplatonic philosophers.</note> has followed this out sufficiently, there is no reason for me to treat it differently now. But let the <margin>three Delphic</margin> <margin>precepts</margin> <margin>precepts</margin> come to mind, fathers, which are essential for those who are about to enter the most holy and august temple of the true—not the fictitious—Apollo, who illuminates every soul coming into this world. You will see that they warn us of nothing else but that...

<meta>This page continues the speaker's exhortation on the pursuit of philosophy as a means of ascending toward the divine. Following the previous discussion on the stages of the soul’s purification, the author now draws upon a wide array of ancient traditions—Greek, Persian, and Hebrew—to illustrate how different branches of knowledge (ethics, logic, physics, and theology) work together to perfect the human spirit.</meta>

-># ORATION<-

Having divided the philosophy about which we are currently disputing, let us embrace it with all our strength. For that famous saying, **nothing in excess** <note>original: *mēden agan*</note>—which correctly prescribes the standard and rule for all virtues through the principle of the "golden mean" <term>the mean: the Aristotelian idea that virtue lies between two extremes, such as courage being the middle ground between cowardice and recklessness</term>—is the subject of moral philosophy. Likewise, that other saying, **know thyself** <note>original: *gnothi seauton*</note>, rouses and exhorts us to the knowledge of all nature, of which the nature of man is the connector and, as it were, the blending point. <margin>Zoroaster, Plato</margin> For he who knows himself, knows all things in himself, as Zoroaster first, and later Plato in his *Alcibiades*, have written. Finally, once we have been illuminated by this knowledge through natural philosophy, we will be so close to God that we may hail him with the theological salutation "Thou art" <note>original: *ei*</note>, and we shall call upon him as the true Apollo, familiarly and therefore happily.

Let us also consult Pythagoras, who was considered the wisest man, <margin>Pythagoras the wise</margin> chiefly because he never thought himself worthy of the name "wise." <margin>Explanation of Pythagoras's precepts</margin> He will first command us **not to sit upon a bushel** <note>The *modius* or bushel was a Roman unit of dry volume; here it represents idleness</note>—that is, we must not lose the rational part of our soul (which measures, judges, and examines all things) by letting it lapse into idle sluggishness. Instead, we must direct and stir it up constantly through the practice and rules of dialectic <term>dialectic: the art of logical argument and investigation of truth</term>. Then, he will point out two things we must especially avoid: **not to urinate against the sun**, and **not to trim our nails during a sacrifice**. But after we have "urinated away" our flowing appetites through moral philosophy and the rejection of excessive pleasures, and have trimmed the "parings of our nails"—that is, the sharp outbursts of anger and the stings of our spirits—only then may we begin to take part in the sacred mysteries of Bacchus (of which we have made mention) and devote ourselves to that contemplation of which the Sun is rightly called the father and leader.

Finally, Pythagoras will advise us to **nourish the cock**—that is, to feed the divine part of our soul with the knowledge of divine things as if with solid food and heavenly ambrosia. This is the cock at whose sight the lion—that is, all earthly power—trembles and shows respect. <margin>The Cock of Job and Socrates</margin> This is the cock to whom we read in the Book of Job that "understanding was given." At the crowing of this cock, straying man comes to his senses. This cock daily harmonizes with the morning stars as they praise God in the early dawn. It was this cock that the dying Socrates said he owed to Aesculapius <note>original: *Aesculapio*</note>, the physician of souls, when he hoped that the divinity of his soul would be joined to the divinity of the greater world, being now placed beyond all danger of sickness.

<margin>The Chaldeans</margin> Let us also review the monuments of the Chaldeans, and we shall see (if they are to be believed) that the path to happiness is open to mortals through these same arts. <margin>Chaldean interpreters, Zoroaster</margin> The Chaldean interpreters write that it was a saying of Zoroaster that the soul is winged, and that when the wings fall off, the soul is carried headlong into the body, but when they grow back, it flies back up to the heavens. When his disciples asked him how they might obtain souls with well-feathered wings, he replied: "Water your wings with the waters of life." When they asked again where they might seek these waters, he answered them (as was his custom) through a parable: "The paradise of God is washed and watered by four rivers. From there you may draw the waters of salvation." The name of the river from the North is **Pishon** <note>original: *pi*</note>, which denotes "Rightness." The one from the West is **Gihon** <note>original: *gi*</note>, which signifies "Expiation." The one from the East is **Tigris** <note>original: *ti*</note>, which sounds like "Light." The one from the South is **Euphrates** <note>original: *eu*</note>, which we can interpret as "Piety."

Pay attention and carefully consider, brothers, what these doctrines of Zoroaster mean: surely nothing else than that we should wash away the filth of our eyes by moral science, as if by the wintry waves of the West; then, by dialectic, as if by a Northern rule, we should align our vision toward what is right. Then, in natural contemplation, let us accustom ourselves to endure the still-weak light of truth, like the cradle of the rising sun; until at last, through theological piety and the most sacred worship of God, we may—like heavenly eagles—bravely endure the most brilliant radiance of the midday sun. <margin>David, Augustine, Ancient Abraham, Cabalists, Moors</margin> These are perhaps those "morning, midday, and evening" knowledges first sung of by David and later explained more broadly by Augustine. This is the midday light that inflames the Seraphim <term>Seraphim: the highest order of angels, associated with burning love and fire</term> and likewise illuminates the Cherubim <term>Cherubim: the second order of angels, associated with divine wisdom and light</term>. This is the region toward which the ancient father Abraham was always traveling. This is the place where, as the doctrines of both the Cabalists <term>Cabalists: followers of Jewish mysticism</term> and the Moors <term>Moors: likely a reference to Islamic philosophers like Averroes</term> have handed down, there is no place for unclean spirits. And if it is permitted to bring anything of the more secret mysteries into public view, even under a riddle:

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's "Oration on the Dignity of Man," specifically moving from the spiritual preparation of the soul to a defense of the study of philosophy against its contemporary critics.</meta>

# ->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...after the sudden fall of our humanity from heaven <note>A reference to the Fall of Man in Genesis, which Pico views as a descent into intellectual and spiritual confusion.</note> dizzied our heads, and—according to Jeremiah— <margin>Jeremiah</margin> death entered through the windows, affecting our hearts and minds. We must call upon Raphael, <margin>Raphael</margin> the celestial physician, so that he may liberate us through moral philosophy and dialectic <note>The art of logical argument and investigation.</note> as if using healthy medicines. Then, once we are restored to good health, the strength of God, Gabriel, <margin>Gabriel</margin> will dwell within us. He will lead us through the wonders of nature, pointing out the power and presence of God everywhere. <margin>Michael</margin> Finally, he will hand us over to the high priest Michael, who will distinguish those who have completed their service in philosophy with the priesthood of theology, as if with a crown of precious stones. These are the things, most venerable fathers, which have not only encouraged but actually compelled me to the study of philosophy. I certainly would not be speaking of these things if I did not have to answer those who are accustomed to condemn the study of philosophy—especially in princes, or in anyone who lives with even a moderate fortune. For it has now come to pass (such is the misfortune of our age) that philosophizing is held in contempt and insult rather than in honor and glory. This deadly and monstrous idea has invaded almost all minds: that one should philosophize little or not at all. As if having the causes of things, the ways of nature, the reason of the universe, the counsels of God, and the mysteries of heaven and earth explored before our eyes and in our hands were nothing at all—unless one could hunt for some favor or acquire some profit for oneself. It has come to the point that (alas!) none are considered wise except those who make the study of wisdom a mercenary trade. One sees the chaste Pallas <note>original: "pudicam palladem". Pallas Athena was the Greek goddess of wisdom, traditionally depicted as a virgin.</note>—who dwells among men as a gift from the gods—being rejected, exploded, and hissed at. She has no one to love or favor her unless she brings some poorly-acquired money to her lover’s chest, like a prostitute receiving a small fee for her surrendered virginity. I say all this with the greatest pain and indignation, not against the princes of this time, but against the philosophers, <margin>Note</margin> who both believe and preach that one should not philosophize because no rewards or prizes are established for philosophers—as if they do not show by this very fact that they are not actually philosophers! Since their whole life is centered on gain or ambition, <margin>Note</margin> they do not embrace the knowledge of truth for its own sake. I will say this for myself, and I will not blush to praise myself in this regard: I have never philosophized for any other reason than to be a philosopher; nor have I ever hoped for or sought any other reward or fruit from my studies and late-night labors than the cultivation of my soul and the knowledge of the truth I have always so greatly desired. I have always been so fond and desirous of this truth that, leaving aside all care for private and public affairs, I have given myself entirely to the leisure of contemplation. From this pursuit, no detractions of the envious nor any curses from the enemies of wisdom have been able—or will ever be able—to deter me. Philosophy itself has taught me <margin>What philosophy itself has taught him.</margin> to depend on my own conscience rather than on external judgments, and to always think not so much about how to avoid being spoken ill of, but rather how to avoid saying or doing anything evil myself. Indeed, I was not unaware, most venerable fathers, that this very disputation of mine—which I wanted to honor with your most majestic presence because you all favor the liberal arts—would be as heavy and annoying to many others as it is welcome and pleasant to you. I know there is no lack of those who have condemned my undertaking before now, and who continue to condemn it on many counts. For it is common for there to be no fewer—if not more—barkers <note>original: "oblatratores". Pico uses the image of dogs barking at something they don't understand.</note> at good deeds done for the sake of virtue than at those done wickedly and wrongly for the sake of vice. <margin>Note</margin> There are those who do not approve of this whole style of disputing and this institution of publicly debating literature, asserting that it is for the display of wit <margin>The age of the author</margin> and the showing off of learning rather than for the acquisition of erudition. There are others who do not disapprove of this kind of exercise, but in no way approve of it in me, because at my age—being only twenty-four years old—I have dared to propose a disputation on the sublime mysteries of Christian theology, the highest points of philosophy, and unknown disciplines, in this most celebrated city, before a most ample assembly of very learned men, and in the apostolic senate. Others, while granting me the right to dispute, do not grant...

**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

There are those who complain about my disputing nine hundred questions <note>original: "nongentis... quaestionibus"; Pico famously prepared 900 theses or "conclusions" to be debated in Rome in 1487, aiming to reconcile all schools of thought.</note>, slandering the act as being as superfluous and ambitious as it is beyond my strength. I would have surrendered to their objections on the spot if the philosophy I profess had taught me to do so. Even now, with philosophy as my teacher, I would not respond if I believed this discussion between us was intended for quarreling or wrangling. Therefore, let all intent to disparage or provoke, and that envy which <insert>Plato</insert> writes is "always absent from the divine choir" <note>original: "a divino semper abesse choro"; a reference to Plato's *Phaedrus* (247a), suggesting that there is no room for jealousy in the pursuit of divine truth.</note>, also depart from our minds. Let us instead inquire in a friendly manner whether I ought to debate, and whether I should do so on so many topics. 

First, to those who slander this custom of public disputation <note>Public debates were a central part of university life in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, where scholars proved their mastery of logic and texts.</note>, I will not say much. For if this is a fault—if it be judged a fault—it is a fault I share not only with all of you, most excellent teachers, who have so often performed this duty with the highest praise and glory, but also with Plato, Aristotle, and the most esteemed philosophers of every age. To whom...

# ORATION

It would be more worthy of pardon than of accusation if a man has failed in his efforts. Moreover, according to the poet <note>The Roman poet Propertius, in his Elegies 2.10.6.</note>, if one's strength fails, "boldness will certainly be praise in great things, and to have willed them is enough." For if, in our own age, many—imitating Gorgias of Leontini <margin>Gorgias of Leontini</margin> <note>A famous Greek Sophist known for claiming he could speak on any subject.</note>—have been accustomed, not without praise, to propose discussions not only regarding nine hundred questions, but regarding all questions of all the arts, why should I not be permitted—perhaps even without blame—to dispute about many things indeed, but nevertheless things that are certain and determined?

Yet they say this is "superfluous" and "ambitious." I, however, contend that this was done by me not only in a way that was not superfluous, but was actually necessary. If they would consider the method of practicing philosophy with me, they would clearly be forced to admit this, even against their will. For those who have devoted themselves to one of the schools <term>families: refers to philosophical "lineages" or schools of thought like the Thomists or Scotists</term> of philosophers—namely to Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> or Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus</note>, who are now most popular—they can indeed make a trial of their doctrine in a discussion of even a few questions. But I have so trained myself that, **sworn to the words of no single master**, I might pour myself through all the masters of philosophy, examine all pages, and recognize all schools. Therefore, since I had to speak about all of them—lest I should seem bound to a single one as a defender of a "private dogma" and thus neglect the rest—I could not propose only a few things about each without simultaneously asserting many things about all of them.

Nor let anyone condemn in me the fact that **"wherever the storm carries me, I am brought as a guest."** <note>A reference to Horace, Epistles 1.1.14, describing an eclectic philosopher who doesn't stick to one school.</note> For this was once the practice of all the ancients <margin>The practice of the ancients</margin>: that in unrolling every kind of writing, they passed over no commentaries they could find unread. This was especially true of Aristotle <margin>Aristotle</margin>, who for that reason was called *the reader* <note>original Greek: αναγνώστης (anagnōstēs)</note> <margin>Plato</margin> by Plato. And truly, it is the mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within one Porch or Academy <note>The "Porch" refers to the Stoics; the "Academy" refers to the Platonists.</note>. Nor can it be that from every single school there is not something remarkable that is not shared with the others.

And so, to begin with our own thinkers, to whom philosophy most recently arrived: <margin>John Scotus</margin> there is in **John Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus, a medieval Franciscan theologian.</note> something vigorous and analytical. <margin>Thomas</margin> In **Thomas** [Aquinas], something solid and balanced. <margin>Giles</margin> In **Giles** [of Rome], something polished and exact. <margin>Francis</margin> In **Francis** [Mayronnes], something sharp and acute. <margin>Albert</margin> In **Albert** [the Great], something ancient, ample, and grand. <margin>Henry</margin> In **Henry** [of Ghent], as it has always seemed to me, something sublime and venerable. <margin>Averroes</margin> Among the Arabs, there is in **Averroes** something firm and unshakable. In **Avempace** and **Al-Farabi** <margin>Avempace</margin> <margin>Al-Farabi</margin>, something serious and pondered. In **Avicenna** <margin>Avicenna</margin>, something divine and Platonic.

Among the Greeks, philosophy is, in general, especially clear and chaste. <margin>Simplicius</margin> In **Simplicius**, it is rich and copious. <margin>Themistius</margin> In **Themistius**, elegant and concise. <margin>Alexander</margin> In **Alexander** [of Aphrodisias], consistent and learned. In **Theophrastus**, weightily worked out. In **Ammonius**, lucid and graceful. And if you turn to the Platonists, to review a few: In **Porphyry**, you will be delighted by the abundance of matter and many-faceted religion. In **Iamblichus**, you will venerate a more secret philosophy and the mysteries of the "barbarians" <note>Referring to his work "On the Mysteries of the Egyptians."</note>. In **Plotinus**...

He provides a "who's who" of Scholastic, Arabic, Greek, and Neoplatonic thinkers, highlighting the unique intellectual strength of each.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of natural magic, distinguishing it from "goetic" or black magic. The previous section likely introduced the two types of magic, and here he describes the beneficial, "natural" variety as a way of connecting the earthly and divine realms.</meta>

->THE ORATION<-

This [natural magic], having more deeply scrutinized that universal consensus which the Greeks more expressively call *sympathy* <note>original: "sympatheian" ($\sigma\upsilon\mu\pi\alpha\theta\epsilon\iota\alpha\nu$); the concept that all parts of the universe are interconnected and influence one another</note>—and having gained a clear perspective on the mutual knowledge of different natures—applies to each thing its own native charms. These charms, which the magicians call *magic wheels* <note>original: "iynges" ($\iota\upsilon\gamma\gamma\epsilon\varsigma$); in ancient mystical traditions, these were symbolic charms or "spells" used to draw down divine powers</note>, are miracles lying hidden in the recesses of the world, in the lap of nature, and in the secret storehouses of God. As if she were the artisan herself, she brings these wonders into public view. And just as the farmer weds elms to vines, so the magus weds the earth to heaven—that is, he marries the lower things to the gifts and powers of the higher world. 

From this it follows that while that other kind of magic [sorcery] appears monstrous and harmful, this natural magic appears divine and brings salvation. This is primarily because the former, by enslaving man to the enemies of God, calls him away from God; whereas the latter stirs up an admiration for the works of God, which is most certainly followed by an outpouring of charity, faith, and hope. 

<margin>Note</margin> For neither to religion, nor to the worship of God... <note>The text breaks off here; Pico is beginning to argue that natural magic is the highest form of religious devotion because it honors God's creation.</note>

He contrasts this holy pursuit with black magic, arguing that natural magic leads the practitioner toward God through the study of His miracles.</summary>

# OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...it was revealed, it is called <term>Kabbalah</term><note>original: "Cabala"; from the Hebrew 'qabbalah', meaning 'reception' or 'tradition'.</note>, which is the same among the Hebrews as "reception" is among us. This is because they received that doctrine not through written records, but through a regular succession of revelations from one to another, as if by a right of inheritance. However, after the Hebrews were restored from the Babylonian captivity by Cyrus and, under Zerubbabel, the Temple was restored, they applied their minds to repairing the Law. 

Ezra, then the leader of the assembly, after amending the book of Moses, clearly recognized that due to the exiles, slaughters, flights, and captivity of the Israelite people, the custom instituted by the ancestors of handing down doctrine by hand <note>Meaning oral transmission from teacher to student.</note> could not be preserved. Fearing that the secrets of celestial doctrine divinely granted to them would perish—as they could not endure long in memory without the intervention of commentaries—he decided that, having called together the wise men who then remained, each should bring forward what he held in memory concerning the mysteries of the Law. With scribes employed, these were compiled into seventy volumes (for there were approximately that many wise men in the <term>Sanhedrin</term><note>The supreme council or court of justice in ancient Israel.</note>). 

Lest you believe me alone regarding this matter, listen to Ezra himself speaking thus: "After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: 'Put the first things you wrote in public; let the worthy and unworthy read them; but you shall preserve the last seventy books so that you may hand them over to the wise men of your people. For in these is the vein of understanding and the fountain of wisdom and the river of knowledge,' and so I did." <note>Pico is quoting from the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (4 Ezra) 14:44-47.</note> These are Ezra's words verbatim. 

These are the books of the science of Kabbalah. In these books, Ezra deservedly proclaimed with a clear voice that there is a "vein of understanding"—that is, an ineffable theology concerning the <term>supersubstantial deity</term><note>A Neoplatonic term referring to God as being "above" or "beyond" the category of mere 'substance' or 'being'.</note>; a "fountain of wisdom"—that is, an exact metaphysics concerning intelligible and angelic forms; and a "river of knowledge"—that is, a most firm philosophy concerning natural things. 

These books, Pope Sixtus IV <margin>Sixtus</margin> <margin>fourth</margin>—who immediately preceded the current Innocent VIII <margin>Inno. viii</margin> under whom we happily live—took the greatest care and zeal to ensure they were translated into Latin for the public benefit of our faith. By the time he passed away, three of them had reached the Latins. These books are revered among the Hebrews in this time with such religious devotion that no one is permitted to touch them unless they are forty years old. 

When I had procured these books for myself at no small expense, and had read them through with the highest diligence and tireless labor, I saw in them (God is my witness) a religion not so much Mosaic as Christian. There I found the mystery of the Trinity; there the incarnation of the Word; there the divinity of the Messiah; there doctrine concerning original sin, its expiation through Christ, the heavenly Jerusalem, the fall of the demons, the orders of angels, purgatory, and the punishments of hell. I read the same things there that we read daily in Paul and Dionysius, in Jerome and Augustine. 

In those matters which pertain to philosophy, you would truly hear Pythagoras and Plato, whose decrees are so akin to the Christian faith that our Augustine <margin>Augusti.</margin> gives immense thanks to God that the books of the Platonists came into his hands. In short, there is almost no subject of controversy between us and the Hebrews about which they cannot be so refuted and convinced through the books of the Kabbalists that not even a corner remains in which they might hide. I have a most serious witness of this fact, Antonio Cronico <margin>Antoni⁹ cronicus</margin><note>Antonio Vinciguerra, known as Cronico, a Venetian diplomat and man of letters.</note>, a most learned man, who with his own ears—when I was with him at a banquet—heard Dactylus the Hebrew <margin>Dactyl⁹ hebræus</margin><note>Likely a contemporary Jewish scholar or convert known to Pico's circle.</note>, an expert in this science, yield completely <note>original: "pedibus manibusque descendere" — a Latin idiom meaning to agree or surrender unconditionally, literally "to descend with hands and feet."</note> to the Christian opinion regarding the Trinity. 

But to return to reviewing the main points of my disputation: I have also brought forward my own opinion on interpreting the poems of Orpheus and Zoroaster <margin>Zoroaster</margin>. Orpheus <margin>Orpheus</margin> is read among the Greeks almost in his entirety; Zoroaster is fragmentary among them, but more complete among the Chaldeans. Both are believed to be the leaders and authors of ancient wisdom. For I will say nothing of Zoroaster, who is frequently mentioned among the Platonists always with the highest veneration. Iamblichus <margin>Iamblichus</margin> of Chalcis <margin>Calcide⁹</margin> writes that Pythagoras <margin>Pythago.</margin> held Orphic theology as a model, according to which he shaped and formed his own philosophy. Indeed, they say the sayings of Pythagoras are called "sacred" for the sole reason that they flowed from the teachings of Orpheus.

-> SPEECH <-

From there comes the secret doctrine concerning numbers and whatever Greek philosophy held as great and sublime, as it flowed from the primary source. But (as was the ancient custom of theologians) Orpheus so concealed the mysteries of his dogmas in the wrappings of fables and a poetic veil that if someone were to read his hymns, they would believe nothing lay beneath them except the most trivial stories and nonsense. I wanted to say this so that you might recognize the labor and the difficulty I faced: to pluck the meanings of a secret philosophy from the tangled thickets of intentional riddles and the hiding places of fables—especially in a matter so grave, so hidden, and so unexplored, without the help and diligent work of other interpreters. And yet, my dogs <note>Pico refers to his critics and detractors as barking dogs.</note> barked that I have accumulated certain trifles and light things merely for an ostentatious display of numbers. As if all these questions were not extremely ambiguous and highly controversial, in which the leading academies <note>Refers to the major philosophical schools of the time.</note> fight as if with swords; as if I did not bring many things to these very people who carp at me—people who believe themselves to be the leaders of philosophers—things that are entirely unknown and unattempted. Indeed, I am so far from that fault that I have taken care to compress my disputation into as few chapters as I could. If I had wished (as others are accustomed) to divide and cut it into its own members, it would surely have grown into an innumerable count. And to say nothing of the rest: who is there who does not know that one single dogma out of the nine hundred <note>original: "nongentis" — Pico is referring to his famous "900 Theses" which he offered to defend in public debate in Rome.</note>—namely, the one concerning the reconciliation of the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle—could have been led by me into six hundred chapters (not to say more) without any suspicion of forced numbering, by enumerating point by point all the places where others think they disagree but I think they agree? But certainly (for I shall say this, though neither modestly nor according to my nature) I will say it nonetheless because my envious rivals force me to. My detractors force me to wish to prove by this encounter of mine not so much how much I know, but that I know things which many do not know. So that this may now become openly clear to you in fact, most venerable Fathers, and so that my speech may no longer delay your desire, most excellent teachers—whom I see with great pleasure standing ready and girded for the fight—may it be happy and auspicious: let us now join hands as the trumpet sounds. <note>Pico uses a military metaphor ("classicum") to signal the start of the intellectual debate.</note>

THE END of the Speech of Giovanni [Pico] of Mirandola.

[Large decorative initial I with floral motifs]
Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Giovanni Francesco, his nephew through his brother: Greetings in Him who is true salvation. My son, there is no reason for you to wonder, nor for you to grieve or be terrified, that as you departed from me many occasions for evil were immediately presented to disturb you and to oppose your chosen purpose of living well. How much more of a miracle would it be if to you alone among mortals the path to heaven lay open without sweat? <note>Pico reminds his nephew that spiritual growth requires effort and struggle.</note> As if the deceitful world and the evil demon had now for the first time ceased to exist, or as if you were not still in the flesh, which lusts against the spirit; for unless we watchfully provide for our salvation, that seductive flesh deforms us with the cups of Circe <note>In Greek mythology, the enchantress Circe turned men into beasts with her potions; Pico uses this as an allegory for sensory vice.</note> into the monstrous shapes of beasts. But as James writes, he affirms that you ought to rejoice. <margin>James</margin> "Rejoice, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations." <note>James 1:2.</note> Nor is it without merit that he said this: for what hope is there of glory if there is no hope of victory? Or what place can there be for victory where there is no battle? He is called to the crown who is called to the battle, and especially to that battle in which no one can be conquered against his will; nor do we need other strengths in order to conquer, <margin>The great happiness of the Christian.</margin> except that we ourselves wish to conquer. Great is the happiness of the Christian: since victory is placed in his own choice, and the rewards will be greater than every wish of the victor and every expectation. Tell me, I ask you, my dearest son, is there anything in this life among those things for which the lust of earthly minds is driven, for the sake of attaining which many labors must not first be undergone, and many indignities and miseries tolerated? # LETTERS

...after a thousand inconveniences and a thousand dangers to life, he might have acquired for himself a somewhat more abundant estate. Concerning the service of the world <term>militia saeculi</term> <note>original: "militia saeculi"—a common Renaissance and medieval metaphor comparing the grueling life of a courtier or public official to military service</note>, there is nothing for me to write to you, for experience itself has taught you, and continues to teach you, more than enough of its miseries. 

In earning the favor of princes, in cultivating the friendships of equals, and in seeking after honors, what a mountain of troubles! How much anxiety! How much worry! I could learn these things from you rather than teach them to you; for I, content with my books and my humble leisure <note>original: "ociolo," a term of endearment for his private time spent in study and reflection</note>, have learned since childhood to live within my station. As far as I am able, I dwell within myself, longing for and seeking nothing outside of my own soul. 

Therefore, these earthly things—fleeting, uncertain, worthless, and shared even with the beasts—we barely attain even when sweating and gasping for them. Yet toward the heavenly and divine things, which *no eye has seen, nor ear has heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man* <note>a reference to 1 Corinthians 2:9</note>, we move sluggishly and sleepily, and are almost dragged by the gods against our will... <note>The Latin ends abruptly here with "tra," likely the beginning of "trahimur," meaning "we are dragged."</note>

<meta>The previous page established a correspondence between a mentor and a young man who has committed to a "holy purpose"—likely entering a religious order or a life of dedicated piety. This page continues the mentor's exhortations on the necessity of prayer and scripture study.</meta>

->LETTERS<-

<note>original: "EPISTOLAE"</note>

...should need anything. For it is far more becoming that they themselves begin to be [truly] men by living well with you, than for you to choose to become shamefully like the beasts with them by abandoning your good purpose. I call God to witness that a kind of ecstasy and stupor sometimes seizes me when I begin to think about the pursuits of men—or to put it more significantly, their extreme madness. I know not whether to think on it or to grieve; whether to marvel or to weep.

<margin>Note</margin> For it is indeed a great madness not to believe the Gospel, whose truth the blood of the martyrs cries out, the apostolic voices resound, miracles prove, reason confirms, the world testifies, and the elements speak; even the demons confess it. But it is a far greater madness if you do not doubt the truth of the Gospel, yet live as if you did not doubt its falsehood. For if those things are true—that it is very difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven—why do we gape at accumulating wealth daily? And if it is true that glory should be sought, not that which comes from men, but that which is from God, why do we always hang upon the judgments of men? No one cares to please God. And if the faith in us is firm that the Lord will one day say, "Go, you cursed ones, into eternal fire," <note>original: "Ite maledicti in ignem aeternum"</note> and again, "Come, you blessed ones, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world," <note>original: "venite benedicti possidete regnum paratum vobis a constitutione mundi"</note> why do we fear nothing less than Gehenna <note>term: Gehenna (the biblical term for the place of fiery suffering/hell)</note> or hope for nothing less than the kingdom of God? What else can we say but that many are Christians in name, but very few in reality?

You indeed, my son, strive to enter through the narrow gate, and do not attend to what the many do; but the law of nature itself, reason itself, and God Himself will show you what is to be done. For neither will your glory be less if you are happy with the few, nor your punishment lighter if you are miserable with the many. There will be two remedies especially present for you against the world and Satan, by which you may be lifted as if on two wings from the valley of tears to the heights: namely, almsgiving and prayer.

<margin>Two most healthy remedies</margin> For what can we do without the help of God? Or how will He help if He is not called upon? But He will certainly not hear you when you call if you did not previously hear the poor man when he called. For it is not fitting that God should not despise you, a man, when you, a man, first despised another man. It is written: "In the measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you," and elsewhere: "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy."

When I invite you to prayer, I do not invite you to that which consists of "much speaking," <note>A reference to Matthew 6:7, warning against empty repetitive prayer.</note> but to that which, in the secret recess of the mind, in the inner chambers of the soul, speaks to God with the heart's affection and presents the mind to the Father, not only in the brightest darkness of contemplation <note>A mystical concept where the mind, blinded by the overwhelming light of God, enters a "divine darkness."</note> but in certain ineffable words in ways which only those who have experienced them know. I do not care how long your prayer is, but how effective, how burning, interrupted by sighs rather than diffused in a perpetual series of words and rhythms. If your salvation is dear to your heart, if you wish to be safe from the devil's snares, from the world's storms, and from the ambushes of enemies; if you wish to be pleasing to God and finally to be happy: let no day pass in which you do not approach your God at least once through prayer.

<margin>Prayer</margin> Prostrate before Him with the humble affection of a pious mind, cry out—not from the top of the lips, but from the innermost bowels—with the Prophet: "The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember; but according to your mercy remember me for your goodness' sake, O Lord." <note>original: "Delicta iuventutis meae & ignorantias meas ne memineris...": Psalm 25:7.</note> The Spirit who intercedes for us will suggest to you, as will necessity itself every hour, what you should ask from your God. Sacred reading will also suggest it, which I ask you again and again to always have in your hands, leaving aside now the fables and trifles of the poets. Nothing is more pleasing to God, nothing more useful to you, than if you do not cease to turn the sacred letters <note>term: sacred letters (the Bible/Holy Scripture)</note> with your hand by night and by day. For there lies hidden in them a certain living and effective heavenly power which transforms the mind of the reader—provided he handles them purely and humbly—into divine love by a certain wonderful power.

But I have already exceeded the limits of a letter, the subject itself dragging me along, and a certain wonderful charity with which I have followed you, especially from that hour when I was informed of your most holy purpose. Finally, I would wish you warned of this, of which I also spoke with you often when you were here with me: that you never forget these two things: that the Son of God [was born/died] for you...

**A**ccepi... <note>The letter begins: "I have received..."</note> I have received from you, most learned Beroaldo, a letter that was as lovely as it was erudite, along with many verses that undoubtedly challenge antiquity itself. That gift was most welcome to me. For your sake, I have spent some good hours of leisure on this fine business; I could not have occupied myself more pleasantly or honorably in any other matter. Indeed, I would act like a thoroughly ungrateful man if I wished to repay your excellent works with my own, which are of the worst sort—exchanging the "poison" of Suffenus for Catullian wit. <note>Pico refers to a poem by Catullus where Suffenus is described as a man who thinks he is a great poet but is actually terrible. Pico is being modestly self-deprecating.</note> For in poetry I am no better than he, except perhaps in this one regard: I recognize that I am a Suffenus, and I see what is in the knapsack on my back. <note>An allusion to Aesop's fable: humans carry two bags; one in front for others' faults, and one behind for their own.</note> You, however, demand that I give you something of my own writings; and you demand it in such a way that you seem to be making a formal request, appearing as though you would not take a rejection lightly. Therefore, I must satisfy you, even at the cost of whatever reputation I have with you. You shall have, then, two letters: one to Lorenzo de' Medici, and the other to Ermolao <note>Ermolao Barbaro, a famous Venetian scholar</note> concerning the style of philosophers. To these I have added certain short verses which fell from me during these days while I was busy with other things. You will read these things remembering that in these "humane studies" <note>the *studia humanitatis*, or liberal arts</note> I have applied only hurried care and borrowed time, as one who has devoted his primary work and "serious lamps" <note>original: "seriosas... lucernas," meaning late-night study</note> to philosophy. In that field, I hope I have made the kind of progress that you have among the rhetoricians and poets—among whom (I speak from the heart) I see no reason why you should not rightly claim the first place. Your friend Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano, the renowned poet and scholar</note> is entirely yours; he loves you as much as anyone can. Regarding myself, there is nothing I can do that you cannot promise yourself. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Lorenzo de' Medici, Health and Best Greetings.<-

**L**egi... <note>The letter begins: "I have read..."</note> I have read, Lorenzo de' Medici, your "Rhythms" <note>Pico is referring to Lorenzo's poetry written in the Italian vernacular (Tuscan) rather than Latin</note> which the local muses suggested to you in your tender youth. I recognized the muses and the legitimate offspring of the Graces; but I did not recognize the "work of tender youth." <margin>Note.</margin> For who, in your rhythms and the rhythmic joining of verses, would not perceive the Graces dancing to the beat? Who would not hear the singing muses in your melodious and modulated style of speaking? Who would recognize a mere youth in such unforced charm, cheerful wit, honeyed jokes, fitting allurements, and marvelous clarity? Or in the prudent arrangement and the most profound thoughts drawn from the inner sanctuaries of philosophy? I know certainly that I am not "on the white list" <note>original: "in hoc albo," an idiom for being an expert or authorized judge</note>, nor am I one who has ascended so high as to judge such things. But I wish it could be said, without suspicion of flattery, what I truly feel about them: I would say, surely, that there is none of the ancient writers whom you have not surpassed by a long interval in this style of speaking. Lest you think this is said to curry favor, I will bring you my reasons for this opinion. There are among you two especially celebrated poets of the Florentine tongue, Francesco Petrarch and Dante Alighieri; concerning whom it is generally said by the learned that matter is lacking in Francesco, and words are lacking in Dante. <note>Pico summarizes the common 15th-century critique: Petrarch has beautiful style but thin content; Dante has profound content but lacks "elegant" Latinate polish.</note> In you, one who has both mind and ears will find neither lacking; in your work, one cannot see whether the subject matter is more illustrated by the speech, or the words by the thoughts. But let us weigh the merits of each one individually, as if on a scale. If Francesco [Petrarch] were to come back to life, who doubts that regarding the meaning of the thoughts, he would voluntarily yield the palm to you? <note>original: "herbam tibi daturum," a Roman idiom for admitting defeat</note> For you are always sharp, serious, and subtle; while he, mostly snatching at commonplaces, colors his thoughts with words and makes ordinary things seem extraordinary by his style of speaking—in which we might see what he provides to you, and what you to him. In some parts he might seem sweeter; but to me, his sweetness is, so to speak, "sweetly harsh" and "pleasantly austere."
