<meta>This page continues a literary critique comparing the writing styles of two individuals—likely the recipient of the letter and a classical or contemporary rival—before moving into a comparison with the poet Dante Alighieri. The tone is highly laudatory toward the recipient, identifying his style as "Laurentian," which suggests the recipient is Lorenzo de' Medici.</meta>

->LETTERS<-

He is diffuse and smoothly soothing. You, with majesty and a certain lively light of oratory, dazzle the mind. In him, there is an ambitious and excessive care; in you, a diligence that is neglected rather than affected. He is tender and soft; you are masculine and <term>muscular<note>original: "torosus." In rhetorical terms, this refers to a powerful, "brawny" prose style compared to a "soft" or "flabby" one.</note></term>. He is voluble and melodious; you are ready, full, firm, and rhythmic. He is perhaps more charming; you are certainly more ample and upright. He is more adorned, but you are more sinewy. In him, there is much that you might prune away; in you, nothing is redundant and nothing is cut short. 

But perhaps I have been a bit bold in saying that something should be removed from him. It is certainly so, or so it seems to many in whose judgment I trust. For in my own view, he often seems to "sin" in the same way the <term>Asiatics<note>The "Asiatic" style of rhetoric was criticized by classical purists for being overly florid, wordy, and rhythmic at the expense of substance.</note></term> sinned: namely, by inserting words as if to fill up cracks, and employing full and harmonious voices not to decorate the meaning, but to prop it up—much like a flute-player supports a song so it does not limp. In you, all words are no less necessary to the matter than they are pleasing in their ornament, so much so that anyone who takes away from you mutilates the work, whereas anyone who takes from him merely shears and cleans it. 

Even if we were to grant (which I never will) that the things he wrote are more charming and more elegant than yours, it was easy for a man to excel when he did not have to labor and struggle with the very meanings themselves. But those sharp, subtle, and (to use one word) **Laurentian** <note>This refers to the style of Lorenzo de' Medici, "The Magnificent."</note> thoughts of yours can scarcely be said to reject the <term>curling-irons<note>original: "calamistros." A metaphor for artificial or overly-refined rhetorical flourishes.</note></term>; they do not willingly admit those artificial dyes. If he had been given those same themes to handle—he whom we read as soft, shining, and pleasant—we would surely read him as thorny, squalid, and unpleasing. This is evident whenever he attempts something acute, intricate, or knotted: his style falls just as his sense rises. But when he displays that "furniture" of words—his ointments, curls, and flowers—he reminds me of what Castritius warned regarding Gracchus: that we should not be deceived by the rounded sound and the flow of the verses, <margin>Note in the margin</margin> but we should inspect what lies beneath: what is the seat, what is the foundation, what is the depth beneath the words. If you were to do that there, you would see <note>original: "epicuri qnq; uacuū"</note> something as empty as **Epicurus's void**; either no sense lies beneath, or it is cold and trivial. In that part where one is greatest, if you do not excel even him, I see no reason at all why he should excel you in the grace of speaking. For words cannot be more illustrious than they are with you, and their arrangement is so fit that they could not cohere better, nor flow more roundly, nor fall more rhythmically in any way. 

But now let us carefully weigh **Dante** with you, about whom perhaps more people will stir up a controversy. For there are many who, in comparing writers, do not so much weigh their merits as count their years; they command others to read the ancients with reverence, yet they themselves cannot read their contemporaries without envy. Certainly, as far as style is concerned, I think no one will deny you the prize. Dante is sometimes horrid, harsh, and scrawny; he is often unrefined and unpolished.

<meta>This page continues a letter addressed to Lorenzo de' Medici (the Magnificent), praising his literary talent and comparing his poetic style and philosophical depth to the great masters of the past, specifically Dante and Petrarch.</meta>

# **LETTERS**

...they seem to be born naturally, not brought in from outside; necessary, not collected; entirely genuine, not grafted on. This is exactly what I cannot admire enough: how you seem to me to have surpassed **Dante**. <note>Dante Alighieri (c. 1265–1321), author of the *Divine Comedy* and the father of the Italian language.</note> For even if he flies high, he is lifted by the wings of his subject matter; you, even as your subject resists and pulls you downward, are raised to the heights by the wings of your genius. And you rise in such a way that you do not depart from the subject, but rather lift it up with you. You have deserved as much from the subject itself as the subject once deserved from Dante. Now one may see what the difference is between you, **Francis**, and **Dante**. <note>Francis refers to Francesco Petrarch (1304–1374), the famous Italian scholar and poet.</note> Regarding them, I might add this: Francis sometimes does not live up to his promises; he has that which charms at first glance, but satisfies no further. Dante has that which sometimes offends upon first encounter, but delights more as one penetrates his inner meaning. Your works have no less in their depth to hold the reader than they have on their surface to capture them. Add to this that those men composed their poems in seclusion, in the shade, in the highest tranquility of their studies; you sang yours amidst the tumult, the noise of the court, the shouts of the forum, the greatest cares, and the most turbulent storms, while being extremely busy. For them, the Muses were their ordinary and principal business; for you, they were a game and a kind of relaxation from your cares. For them, it was their greatest exhaustion; for you, exhausted as you were, it was your leisure. Finally, by relaxing your mind, you reached a point which they, perhaps, did not reach even when straining every nerve of their souls.

But what shall I say of my paraphrase? <note>original: "paraphraſi"</note> Why should I not call it mine, or by what right do I use this name? Finally, why not mine? For even if I venerate it as yours, I nonetheless love it as my own. I truly admire it and you within it, through which union [I see] how far I was from a true appreciation of your verses. In them, I had not looked deeply enough with my "owl-like eyes" at those things which were greatest and most illustrious. I saw them later revealed through you, which you alone were able and bound to do—bound to yourself and to us—lest you defraud yourself of much glory and us of much pleasure. I read it (I call God to witness), most excellent Lorenzo, not so much for delight as for instruction.

For how many things are there from **Aristotle**: <margin>Aristotle</margin> namely, from the *Physics*, from the books *On the Soul*, *On Ethics*, *On the Heavens*, and from the *Problems*? How many from **Plato**: <margin>Plato</margin> from the *Protagoras*, the *Republic*, the *Laws*, and the *Symposium*? <note>These represent the core of the Renaissance curriculum: Aristotle for natural science and ethics, Plato for political philosophy and the nature of love.</note> All of these, although I have read them elsewhere in those authors, I nonetheless read in your work as if they were new: as if they were better and transformed by you into I-know-not-what new form, so that they seem to be yours and not theirs, and in reading, I seem to be learning something. This is the greatest proof that you know these things not so much from a commentary as from your own self.

For many are accustomed to display more **sophistry** <note>original: "σοφισΤεία" (sophisteia)</note> in letters than actual effort. <margin>Note</margin> When they are about to write, they treat philosophers like "pragmatic" assistants, suggesting certain dogmas to them which they may thrust into their little books so that they might appear to be philosophers. But you can easily catch these people. For you see those ideas are neither rightly arranged nor coherent, and they are not explained by the authors, but rather entangled. And men who are otherwise eloquent appear like infants when speaking of those things. But who would not see that you do not hold these ideas as a loan, but as things over which you have right and power to turn, act, and handle according to your will? These things you have attained (O happy genius!) in the heat of the Republic and in an active life—things which we, who are not the disciples of philosophers but merely their "tenants" in a shaded and sedentary life, follow rather than overtake.

But what shall I say of the most sweet style of your paraphrase? It seems to me to be exactly like that of **Caesar** in the Roman tongue. <margin>Caesar</margin> For it is a speech not "made by hand," <note>i.e., not artificial or over-labored.</note> not gilded, not twisted, but upright by its own genius, candid and well-built; neither running out recklessly nor losing its footing; neither luxuriant nor meager, neither wanton nor unpleasant. It is sweetly grave and gravely lovable. The words are chosen and not hunted for; they are illustrious but not painted; necessary and not far-fetched; not merely explaining the matter but placing it right before one's eyes. I pass over how you always remember your own character, and how the seeds and traces of your famous wisdom are sprinkled everywhere. These things I and many others [see], and each sees much better ones. But besides these, I have seen two principal things which perhaps not many, however sharp-eyed, might see. The first is that it hides its own riches; so that it may avoid envy, it keeps its flowers in its bosom and does not show them off...

V iii <note>Printer's signature mark for the gathering of pages.</note>

->Florence, on the Ides of July [July 15], 1484.<-
->**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola greets his friend Hermolao Barbaro.**<-

**I** indeed, my dear Hermolao, can neither remain silent about what I feel regarding you, nor fail to feel those things which I ought regarding a man in whom all virtues are found together just as they are individually at their peak. But would that my mind were capable of perceiving your merits as they deserve! Would that I had such power of speech that I might one day express what I always feel. I know that the concepts I have formed of you fall infinitely below the heights of your learning. You should know also that whatever we speak is far less than what we conceive; know that words fail the mind just as the mind fails the reality of the thing. And yet, believe me, I dare to hope that I might also be able to imitate your qualities, though I cannot even estimate their magnitude. All men can admire you; so few can imitate you that no one can find fault. And would that I had such happiness that what I write might reflect some image of my Hermolao. For even if I were silent about the rest, your **style**—which you favor so little—affects and delights me wonderfully. It is so learned, grave, composed, refined, and polished. It is ingenious, containing nothing common or trivial, whether you look at the words or the ideas. My friend **Poliziano** <note>Angelo Poliziano, the renowned poet and scholar</note> and I often read whatever letters of yours we have, whether to others or to us. The later ones always strive to match the earlier, and new charms bloom fruitfully as we read, so that we have no room to breathe between our perpetual cheers of acclaim.

But it is wonderful to say how persuasive you are, and how you drive the reader’s mind wherever you wish. I have experienced this many times, but most recently in this last letter of yours to me. In it, you attack these **"barbarous" philosophers,** <note>Pico is referring to the medieval Scholastic thinkers like Aquinas and Scotus, whom the Renaissance Humanists criticized for their "ugly" Latin.</note> whom you say are commonly held to be filthy, rude, and uncultured; men who you claim did not even truly live while they were alive, much less live on after death—and if they do live now, they live in punishment and disgrace. I was so moved by this, and so ashamed and weary of my own studies (for I have now spent six years among them), that I wished I had done nothing rather than have struggled so laboriously in such a worthless pursuit. I have "lost," I said to myself, my better years and such great night-watches among **Thomas,** <margin>Thomas Aquinas</margin> **John Scotus,** <margin>John Duns Scotus</margin> **Albert,** <margin>Albert the Great</margin> and **Averroes,** <margin>Averroes (Ibn Rushd)</margin> in which I might perhaps have become something in "good letters." <note>The "Studia Humanitatis" or classical literary studies.</note> I thought to myself, as a way of consoling me, that if any of them should now come back to life, they—being otherwise men of many arguments—would surely have some reason to defend their cause. Finally, it occurred to me that one of them, perhaps a little more eloquent than the rest, might defend his "barbarism" in a way that is not at all barbaric:

"We lived famously, O Hermolao, and we shall live hereafter, not in the schools of grammarians and pedants, but in the circles of philosophers and the assemblies of the wise. There, the talk is not about the mother of Andromache, nor the children of Niobe, <note>References to obscure mythological trivia favored by some literary scholars.</note> nor such light trifles, but rather the reasons for human and divine things are discussed and debated. In meditating, inquiring, and untying these knots, we were so subtle, sharp, and fierce that perhaps we might seem to have been too anxious and 'morose'—if indeed anyone can be too morose or curious in searching for the truth. If anyone should accuse us of dullness or slowness in these matters..."

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the relationship between philosophy and rhetoric, specifically defending the "barbarous" or plain style of medieval scholars against the criticisms of ornate Renaissance humanists.</meta>

# LETTERS

<note>The text begins mid-word, continuing a sentence about "inherited quality."</note> ...inheritance: come, I pray, whoever he is, let him step forward. Let him be satisfied that those "barbarians" <note>In this context, "barbarians" refers to the Scholastic philosophers of the Middle Ages, whom Renaissance writers often mocked for their unpolished Latin.</note> did not lack Mercury <note>The Roman god of eloquence and communication.</note> in their hearts, even if they lacked him on their tongues; that they did not lack wisdom, even if they lacked the eloquence which, since it is not joined with wisdom, is perhaps so far from being a fault that joining them might even be an impiety. For who would not condemn and detest curls and makeup on a virtuous virgin? So great is the conflict between the duty of the orator and the philosopher that they could not fight each other more fiercely. For what else is the duty of the rhetorician than to lie, to deceive, to circumvent, and to use trickery? Indeed, it is your claim—as you say—that you can turn white to black and black to white at your whim. By speaking, you can raise up, cast down, amplify, or diminish whatever you wish; finally, by the almost magical power of eloquence that you boast of, you can transform the very things themselves into whatever appearance and habit you please. Thus, things become not what they are by their own nature, but what you have willed them to be—not in reality, but so that they appear so to the listeners, even though they are not. Is all of this anything other than a pure lie, a pure imposture, and pure trickery? Since it always either exceeds the truth by exaggerating or falls short by diminishing, and by a deceptive harmony of words—as if holding out masks and phantoms—it mocks the minds of the listeners by flattering them. 

Will there be any affinity between this and the philosopher, whose entire study is occupied in learning and demonstrating the truth to others? Add to this that no one will trust us if we affect the elegance and charms of words, as if we lacked confidence in our subject and did not rely on the truth, seeking instead to draw men to our opinion with these "panderings." For this reason, it is better to read sacred matters written in a "rustic" <note>Plain or unrefined.</note> way rather than elegantly; for nothing is more unbecoming or harmful in any subject where one deals with learning the truth than this whole elaborate style of speaking. This belongs to legal questions in the courts, not to natural and heavenly matters. It does not belong to those in the Academy <note>The school of philosophy.</note> but to those involved in public affairs, where what is done and said is weighed on the popular scale, and where flowers far outweigh the fruit. 

Do you not know that "not all things suit all men with the same thread"? <note>A variation of a Latin proverb meaning different styles suit different people.</note> Eloquence—we admit—is an elegant thing, full of enticement and pleasure. But in a philosopher, it is neither decorous nor pleasing. Who does not approve of a soft gait, expressive hands, and playful eyes in an actor or a dancer? But who would not disapprove, rebuke, and abominate these in a citizen or a philosopher? If we see a young girl with charming and witty manners, we will praise and kiss her; in a matron, we would condemn and shun these same traits. Therefore, it is not we who are foolish, but those who celebrate the Bacchanalia <note>Raucous, drunken festivals.</note> at the feet of Vesta <note>The goddess of the hearth and virginity; the author means bringing wild rhetoric into the house of sober truth.</note>; those who dishonor the gravity and purity of philosophical matters with playthings and curling irons. Indeed, what Synesius <margin>Synesius</margin> <note>Synesius of Cyrene, a 4th-century philosopher-bishop.</note> could aptly say about a young man’s speech: "A well-groomed speech is always a lewd one." For this reason, we prefer our own speech to be shaggy-haired, solid, and unencumbered, rather than beautifully groomed with the mark or suspicion of impurity.

And even if nothing else remained, this is most true: nothing is more foreign to the purpose of a philosopher in any matter than that which tastes of luxury or pride. Socrates <margin>Socrates</margin> used to say that Sicyonian shoes <note>Sicyon was famous for its fine, luxury footwear.</note> were comfortable and fit the foot well, but they did not suit Socrates at all. There is not the same rule for the dress of a citizen and a philosopher, just as there is not for their table or their speech. The citizen uses these things for pleasure; the philosopher uses them only for necessity. If the citizen neglects grace, he is not "civil"; if the philosopher affects it, he will not be a philosopher. If Pythagoras <margin>Pythagoras</margin> could live without food and herbs, he would abstain; if he could explain his thoughts by his look, or at least with less effort than speech requires, he would not speak at all. So far is he from polishing and adorning his tongue; indeed, we must be careful lest a reader, enticed by the "painted skin," linger upon it and never reach the marrow and the blood. We have often seen a tainted soul beneath a face covered in white lead <note>A common white cosmetic in antiquity, used here as a metaphor for deceptive rhetoric.</note>. We have seen, I say, in all these people—where it has become the custom because there is nothing inside that is not empty and vain—that they detain the reader on the surface with various melodies and harmonies. If a philosopher does this, Musonius <margin>Musonius</margin> <note>Musonius Rufus, a Stoic philosopher known for his austere teachings.</note> will cry out that it is not a philosopher speaking, but a flute-player piping. Therefore, let it not be counted as a vice in us that we have not done that which...

...to have done so was a flaw. We ask ourselves what we should write; we do not ask "how"—or rather, we ask "how" in this way: namely, without any pomp or flowery speech. We do not wish for our writing to be merely delightful, charming, or witty; instead, we want it to be useful, serious, and revered. We want it to achieve majesty through a sense of awe <note>original: "ex horrore." In this context, it refers to a solemn, dread-inspiring dignity or "shiver" of sublime truth rather than "horror" in the modern sense.</note> rather than seeking favor through softness. We do not look for the applause of the theater, nor for a smooth or rhythmic concluding phrase to soothe the ears—where one part is false and another merely pleasant. 

Instead, we look for the silence of a few, born of admiration, as they gaze more deeply into something: whether it be unearthed from the inner sanctuaries <term>adytis: the most sacred, hidden parts of a temple, here used metaphorically for the deep secrets of the natural world</term> of nature or brought down to men from the court of heaven. Furthermore, we seek something so sharp in its logic that there is no room for defense, yet so well-defended that there is no room for argument. Let them admire us, moreover, as keen in inquiry, circumspect in exploration, subtle in contemplation, and grave in judgment; let us be intricate in binding our arguments and effortless in unravelling them. <meta>This page appears to be part of a philosophical or rhetorical letter discussing the nature of language and the validity of non-Latin tongues. It continues a debate on whether the "correctness" of speech is universal or determined by local convention.</meta>

->LETTERS<-

The argument is flawed: an Arab will say the same thing; an Egyptian will say it; they will not speak in Latin, but they will speak correctly nonetheless. For the names of things are established either by choice <note>Latin: *arbitrio*, referring to human convention</note> or by nature. If they are established by a chance assignment—for instance, by a community of men coming to a common agreement, by which they have ordained what each thing should be called—then among those people, it is called correctly. What prevents these philosophers whom you label "barbarians" from having agreed upon a single standard of speech, held no less sacred among them than the Roman <note>Meaning the Latin language</note> standard is held among you? There is no reason why you should not call their standard "correct" just as you call yours "correct," if this assignment of names is entirely arbitrary. But if you do not wish to honor their speech with the title of "Roman," you may call it "Gallic," "British," "Spanish," or what the common people are accustomed to call "Parisian." When they speak to you, it will happen that they are mostly laughed at and mostly misunderstood; the same will happen to you when speaking among them: "Anacharsis <note>A famous Scythian philosopher of the 6th century BCE known for his wisdom and his status as a "wise barbarian" in Athens</note> commits a <term>solecism</term> <note>original Greek: *soloikizei*, meaning to speak incorrectly or with a foreign accent</note> among the Athenians; [likewise] the Athenians [among the Scythians...]" <note>The text cuts off, but the Greek proverb implies that the Athenians are just as much "barbarians" to the Scythians as the Scythians are to them.</note>

<summary>This page argues for linguistic relativism, suggesting that "barbarian" languages are just as valid and "correct" as Latin because the names of things are determined by human convention rather than nature. It uses the figure of Anacharsis to show that being a "foreigner" is a matter of perspective.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, specifically concluding a famous 1485 letter to Ermolao Barbaro regarding the value of "barbarian" (medieval) philosophy versus humanist eloquence, followed by letters to a mentor and the printer Aldo Manuzio.</meta>

### LETTERS

...knows the things of God and nature; the latter <note>The "latter" refers to the elegant but shallow orator, while the "former" is the unpolished but wise philosopher.</note> is most infantile in speaking, yet he perceives those things which cannot be praised enough in speech; the former, in speaking, is most eloquent at expressing the ineffable. These things, my dearest Ermolao, they might perhaps bring forward in defense of their own "barbarism," or perhaps they have arguments that are much better in their subtlety. I do not entirely subscribe to their opinion, nor do I think any free-born or liberal mind should.

But I have exercised myself freely in this subject as if it were an infamous one—just as those who write "Praises of the Quartan Fever" <note>A "quartan fever" was a type of malaria; writing a mock-praise of a disease was a standard rhetorical exercise to prove one's skill.</note> to test their wits. I did this with the same intent as Glaucon in Plato’s *Republic*, who praises injustice—not from conviction, but to stimulate Socrates to praise justice. In the same way, I wanted to hear the cause of eloquence pleaded by you, and so I was carried away into a somewhat licentious opposition against my own feelings and nature. 

If I thought eloquence should be neglected or held in lower regard than the "barbarians," I would not have almost entirely defected from them to the pursuit of Greek letters, as I did recently, and to your never-sufficiently-praised Themistius <note>Themistius was a Greek philosopher and rhetorician; Pico had been studying his works.</note>. To speak freely what I feel: certain grammarians turn my stomach. When they have grasped the origins of two measly words, they show themselves off and boast so much that they think philosophers should be considered as nothing compared to themselves. "We do not want these philosophies of yours," they say. And what wonder? Even dogs do not want Falernian wine <note>Falernian was the most prized wine of ancient Rome; Pico implies these critics lack the refined "palate" to appreciate deep thought.</note>. 

But let us close this letter here. Whether those "barbarians" earned any honor or name for themselves through the knowledge of things alone is not easy to say. But as for you: what praises should you claim for yourself, you who are the most eloquent among philosophers, and among the eloquent—to say it in Greek—the **most philosophical**? <note>original: "Φιλοσοφωτατοσ" (philosophotatos)</note>

Florence, June 3, 1485.

**S**alutations, most beloved father. I feel nothing regarding Apollonius of Tyana <note>An ancient miracle-worker and philosopher; there was much debate among Renaissance scholars as to whether he was a holy man or a magician.</note> beyond what you feel yourself; I shall write more to you on this matter when there is leisure, which perhaps will not be unpleasing to you. 

Regarding the difference in our translation from the Hebrew text in the third chapter of the book of Genesis, where it treats Eve and the serpent: this is my opinion. In the Hebrew, as you write, it says "he himself [the seed] shall crush your head" <note>original: "ipsum conteret caput tuum"</note>, and it refers to the seed of Eve, about which it had been said, "I will put enmity between your seed and her seed." However, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> and Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> translated it as "she herself shall crush your head" <note>original: "ipsa conteret caput tuum"</note>. In both cases, the sense is the same. For when it is said "he himself shall crush," it looks not so much to the person of Eve as to her posterity. Since it says she will do it, it means she will do it through her seed. But as to why they preferred to translate "she" rather than "he," I think the reason was to signify that since from Eve both males and females were to be propagated, what was said about the "seed" should be referred to the female seed specifically. 

These are the things that come to mind at present on this matter. I am constantly working on the *Harmony of Plato and Aristotle* <note>Pico's ambitious project to prove that the two greatest Greek philosophers actually agreed on most points.</note>. I give to that work its due time every morning; the afternoon hours are given to friends, to health, and occasionally to poets and orators. If there are studies of lighter labor, the night is shared with you and the sound of the Sacred Letters <note>The Bible.</note>. Please, do not let me long for your letters for too much longer. Greet Beroaldo. Your Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano, the famous humanist poet and Pico’s close friend.</note> is entirely yours. Farewell, and pray to God for me. 

Florence, March 20, 1490.

To the Reverend Father in Christ, Brother Battista Mantovano <note>A famous Carmelite poet and philosopher known as the "Christian Virgil."</note> of the Carmelite Order, distinguished poet, philosopher, and theologian, etc. 
His son, Giovanni of Mirandola.

Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Aldo Manuzio <note>The famous printer and publisher Altomanutio.</note>, greetings.

**M**y friend, I am sending the Homers <note>Likely copies of Homer's works for Aldo to study or edit.</note> which you desired, though later than you wished and I ought to have. I am so deeply distracted by work, my dear Aldo, that there is no room even to breathe. I have long since bound myself (as you know) to the service of letters. They exact their tribute of reading and dictating so severely that I can scarcely ransom my own health. 

As for what you write you will do: gird yourself for philosophy, but on this condition: remember that there is no philosophy which calls us away from the truth of the Mysteries. Philosophy seeks the truth, Theology finds it, Religion possesses it. 

Farewell. Florence, the eleventh day of February, in the year of grace 1490.

# LETTERS

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola sends greetings to Ermolao Barbaro, Patriarch of Aquileia.**
<note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a celebrated philosopher and nobleman. Ermolao Barbaro was a prominent Venetian scholar and diplomat who was appointed Patriarch of Aquileia in 1491.</note>

<note>The following paragraph begins with a large red initial A decorated with flourishes.</note>
I hear that you have been elected Patriarch of Aquileia. I congratulate those people on receiving such an excellent shepherd, and the whole Church on gaining a most vigorous soldier. I also congratulate you on being given this opportunity to illustrate and expand upon your own virtue. There are generally three kinds of life: the Civic, the Contemplative, and the Religious. In the first, we require prudence; in the second, learning; and in the third—which is like the summit <term>fastigio: a peak or architectural pediment, used here to describe the religious life as the highest point of human existence</term> of a whole life—we demand both of those qualities along with holiness. Until now, your city has experienced your great diligence and wisdom in managing the republic and handling its great affairs. Furthermore, all scholars love and admire you as a patron and champion of the liberal arts <note>original: "bonarum artium," literally "the good arts," referring to the humanities and classical studies.</note>. We know beyond doubt that you will now fulfill what remained to be done. For this we truly rejoice, so that in the future, the Church should owe no less to you than your city and the world of letters have owed you until now.

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola sends greetings to his friend Ermolao.**

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, Greetings.
<note>Marsilio Ficino was the head of the Platonic Academy in Florence and a mentor to Pico.</note>

**Q**uote: Those who strive with many words to obtain what they desire from friends do an injustice to friendship, as if friendship itself could not achieve what the allure of speech can. Therefore, I will deal with you simply, as that benevolence which has long existed between us requires: at this time, the Platonist Iamblichus <note>Pico is asking to borrow a manuscript of the Neoplatonist philosopher Iamblichus</note> is greatly necessary for my studies. ### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings.
<note>Angelo Poliziano was a renowned poet and scholar, and a close friend of Pico.</note>

**E**ver did my *Loves* <note>original: *amores*; Pico refers to his own literary works or poems, personifying them as "Loves"</note> declare themselves more politely or cheerfully received than in these past days at your house. And indeed, how friendly they were "pierced" <note>original: *confossi*; Pico uses a metaphor of a duel or critical "stabs" to describe Poliziano’s scholarly edits or critiques of his work</note>; when they congratulate themselves, they then owe you the most. For who would not wish to die by that sword? Yet they grieve that it was done more indulgently than was proper, and they are at the point where they doubt that you, blinded by love itself, were blinded toward my *Loves*. And thus they doubt so much that they do not trust your judgment (otherwise very grave) enough in their own case. Yet they do trust, and now they assert that they are free from their chains; they do not know how to be at home, and they securely demand liberty and the public eye. 

But what shall I say of the liveliness of your *Epictetus*? <note>Poliziano had recently translated the *Enchiridion* (Handbook) of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus from Greek into Latin</note> Oh, what a humorous thing, worthy of a Catonian laugh! <note>original: *catoniano*; referring to Cato the Elder, a Roman symbol of sternness—implying the book is so witty even a hard man would laugh</note> He was barely at the threshold when, spreading his robes, he said: "Behold the daggers, behold the arrows <note>original: *obelos* (critical marks) and *sagittas*; a pun on editorial marks being like weapons</note> if you do not know Greek! Behold me, if any of you is bold enough, I am ready to strike back!" Who could have restrained their laughter when a Stoic man joked so charmingly? We certainly refrained from weapons, both because he threatened that he would return the injury and because his skin had grown so thick that it would not admit such light blows. 

Therefore, with what veneration we ought, we welcomed the old man. When he finally sat down with us, he began to philosophize about morals. And he did so in Latin, not so much because he was among Latins (for there were those in that assembly who knew Greek), but because he himself tasted more brilliantly in Latin by your benefit <note>Pico is praising the quality of Poliziano’s Latin translation</note>. But his effort was not wasted, since he did not stop speaking before he had made us Stoics out of Peripatetics <note>Aristotelians</note>. And we all approved of that *detachment* <note>original: *apathian*; the Stoic ideal of being unmoved by passion</note>. You could see men, who shortly before were delicate, now become the most tolerant of all things: that we can indeed be provoked by others, but harmed only by ourselves who struggle against fate. And those things which are not ours, we should wish to happen as God wills; we should never blame nor accuse them, grieve for nothing, demand nothing, and not know how to be conquered or enslaved. 

Let us philosophize in action, not just in speech; and since we are novices, let us watch ourselves as if we were adversaries. Let us neglect rather than reject the opinion of others about us and other things of that kind which are external. Let us take care that we have lodging for a day as travelers, but that we do not possess those things. Let us love silence, lest the stomach vomit up what it has not digested. Let us rarely provide laughter for others, and never for ourselves. And to embrace it in one word: we have abundantly learned the whole of Epictetus: both to "endure" adversity and to "abstain" from pleasures <note>original: *sustinere* and *abstinere*; the core Stoic maxim "Endure and Renounce"</note>. 

See how specifically we have shaped our life according to your *Epictetus*. See how quickly, too, lest in this part we should not be Stoics: for they want a man to be warned that he fails as long as he does not make progress. Which, although I have admired it in others, I have admired it most of all in myself. Although I have always spent my time in the Lyceum or the Academy <note>The schools of Aristotle and Plato</note> and never in the Stoa <note>The "porch" where the Stoics taught</note>, I was so conquered by the speech of the old man that I went over to his opinion not only with my feet, but with my hands and my whole body. The list of Greek books that are staying here with me, along with Manuel's letter, which your letter...

**[Large red initial I]** I would have spoken with you more often and at greater length by letter, my dearest Niccolò, if I had known where you were, either by messenger, letter, or rumor. Indeed, I have anxiously inquired about this from many people, but I received only uncertain answers from everyone. Finally, in recent days, a letter from Antonio of Faenza <note>Antonio Faventino, a philosopher and contemporary of Pico</note>, a most serious philosopher, to Thomas Frignano <note>A member of a prominent Modenese family</note> fell into my hands. From that letter, I learned you were in Florence, which was most pleasing to me. As soon as I understood this, I gave a letter to a courier to take to you in Florence. The journey was in vain, for he did not find you there. I was deeply grieved. Today, Thomas indicated that you had departed Florence and were in Bologna; I immediately ordered this letter to be delivered to you.

In this letter, I shall not strive to further reveal my benevolence toward you nor my singular love, for you should not have even the slightest doubt about my goodwill toward you—unless you thought I had forgotten your extraordinary virtue and your services to me, which is not my nature. I could not, however, help but wonder greatly that when you rescued yourself from the city's turmoils to seek a place where you might live both peacefully and pleasantly, you either forgot this little town of ours or certainly looked past it. You seemed, Niccolò, to distrust either my will or my resources; but just as the latter are less than your merits deserve, so is my will greater than you might think. It will be pleasing to me if you inform me of your plan, but most pleasing of all if you do not disdain to share my hearth and home with me, to enjoy leisure with me while others occupy themselves with war. <note>original: "cum marte negociabuntur" — a reference to the ongoing military conflicts in late 15th-century Italy.</note>

I am sending you the remainder of **John the Grammarian** <note>Johannes Philoponus, a 6th-century commentator on Aristotle whose works were highly prized by humanists.</note>, which was missing for many days but has now been found. I am yours, and I await you. Farewell. From Mirandola, July 20, 1482.

With all diligence, if you love me, take care to obtain an index of all the books found in the **Library of Saint Dominic** <note>The famous library of the Dominican convent in Bologna.</note>. Send it or bring it with you. Farewell again.

I have finished building a suburban villa, pleasant enough given the condition of the place and region. I have composed a long poem about it; the home will be sweet to you, and the poem not unpleasant. Farewell once more.

->**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his friend Angelo Poliziano. Greetings.**<-

**[Large red initial Q]** Because you praised me so greatly in your recent letter, I owe you as much as I am distant from actually deserving such praise. For that is owed to a person which is given freely, not what is paid as a debt. Therefore, I owe you everything you write about me, since there is nothing of the sort in me. Since you owed this to me in no way at all, it was entirely the result of your kindness and singular benevolence toward me. For the rest, if you examine me, you will find nothing but what is thin, humble, and narrow. We are <term>novices and beginners</term> <note>original: "Nouicii sumus atq; tirunculi" — "tirunculus" refers to a young recruit or an apprentice scholar.</note> who have only just moved a foot out of the darkness of ignorance, and have progressed almost nowhere. It is kind enough to us if we are even counted among the ranks of the studious. The name of "learned" belongs to something else entirely, something peculiar to you and those like you; such grand things do not suit me. Since of those things which are foremost in the study of letters, I have not only found nothing certain, but have not yet even seen them except through a lattice. <note>original: "per transennam" — an idiom meaning to see something only in passing or through a screen.</note>

I will indeed try (as I am doing now) to be one day the kind of man you now proclaim me to be, and judge me to be—or at least wish me to be. Meanwhile, I will imitate you, Angelo, you who excuse yourself to the Greeks because you are Latin, and to the Latins because you "Graecize." I shall use a similar refuge: so that I may be approved by poets and rhetoricians because I am said to "philosophize," and by philosophers because I play the rhetorician and cultivate the Muses. Although it happens quite differently for me than for you: for while I wish to sit on two stools (as they say), I am excluded from both. <note>Pico uses the metaphor of "sitting on two stools" (geminis sellis sedere) to express his fear of failing to master both philosophy and rhetoric simultaneously.</note>

and it happens finally (to put it briefly) that I am neither poet, nor rhetorician, nor philosopher. You, however, fulfill both so well that it is hardly certain which you are more; you embrace both Greek and our own learning <note>original: "nostram minervam" — literally 'our Minerva,' referring to Latin scholarship and Roman eloquence</note> so beautifully, like a swan of both languages, that it is not easy to discern which is acquired and which is innate. For to say nothing of Latin (a field in which you yield to no one), who would believe—as was said of Hadrian—that a Roman man could speak so much like a Greek? Our Emanuel <note>likely referring to a contemporary scholar or teacher</note> swore while reading your letters that Athens itself was not so Attic. This is who you are, my Angelo (let flattery be far from here), to whom only one or two of our men, if any at all, might be compared. If only there were more such men, these centuries would have no reason to envy antiquity. Press on, I pray, and rescue letters from decay as much as you can, lest that brilliance of the Roman language becomes utterly obsolete through the injustice of time; always forge something new that may assist and illuminate the Latin cause. And let what you have at home finally come out for the common benefit of students. I indeed love and desire all your works just as I love you yourself; all the more because I have proposed you to myself as a model to be imitated, even if you are one whom all ought to follow but few can catch. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his friend Paolo Cortese, greetings.<-

**B**ene <note>The letter begins with a large red initial B</note> you think, Paolo. Let us send letters frequently so that we, who are divided by the distance of locations, may certainly be joined by the exchange of letters. It usually lightens the longing for those who are absent if you perhaps have a statue or an image of them at home. Truly, to me, there seems to be this difference between an image and a letter: the former portrays the body, the latter the mind. The former outlines only the extremities; the latter clearly expresses and molds the innermost parts. One represents the friend's cloak and garment, as it were; the other represents the true friend to us. One emulates the colors and figure of the flesh as best it can; the other emulates thoughts, plans, sorrows, joys, cares—all the emotions, in short. And those secrets of the soul, which one hardly speaks to anyone even in person, are most faithfully transmitted to an absent friend. Finally, the latter is a living and effective likeness, while the former is a dead and mute image. Let us therefore exchange these images of our souls—you yours, which you can make of gold and silver, and I mine of bronze or clay. Thus we shall be beyond all injury of place and time, just as the power of the soul itself knows neither the distances of space nor the delays of time. But truly, how much I owe you, most dutiful Paolo, since you were the first to call me to this duty with such a letter—one which held and delighted me so much that I do not remember being more delighted by any reading for many days. For it is full of eloquence, full of grace, full of love and goodwill. Perhaps you expected me to say "full of my own praises." Indeed, I was going to say this too. For I am not so iron-hearted—or if you prefer it said this way, not so much a philosopher—that I am not delighted by the praises of friends. If they are true, they recommend me to myself; if false, they recommend to me the love and goodwill of the writers. I will easily obtain permission from my philosophy to read your letters both frequently and with pleasure, even the parts that praise me. But it is not so easy to appear civilized or not ungrateful in returning this favor of correspondence. For an imperious mistress <note>referring to Philosophy</note> so constrains me, so demands her daily task, and finally so occupies me entirely, that scarcely anything of myself is left even for me. But such is your humanity that you will welcome even bad letters when we write, and take silence in good part when we are silent. Poliziano, our shared delight, greets you. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Troilo Malvezzi, greetings.<-

**L**ibellus <note>The letter begins with a large red initial L</note> your little book concerning the brave <note>original: "de fortibus"</note> has affected me with as much pleasure as usually affects one to whom the best fortune has happened. I give you great thanks for making me a participant in your late-night labors <note>original: "lucubrationum" — scholarship produced by burning the midnight oil</note>, especially such as these, in which both the subtlety of argument and the manifold and varied knowledge of things easily appears. One of these deserves praise for talent, the other for diligence. Our trifles <note>original: "Nugas nostras" — a modest reference to his own writings</note> which you desire I will give to you very soon. It is uncertain, indeed, which would be more unworthy: to occupy your reading with them...

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Thadeo Ugolino, Greetings.

**G** I received your most welcome letter, full of love, loyalty, and charity, not only because you remembered me, but because in it you friendlily remind me that I should remember myself—that is, the study of good letters <note>original: "bonorū studioꝝ"; referring to the liberal arts and classical studies</note> and the need to uphold the expectations I have given. Indeed, being conscious of my own weakness, I would not dare to promise anything, even of a mediocre nature, concerning myself. But He from whom comes every good gift of light, most merciful, as He has granted until now that men might hope for something from us, so He will grant in the future that we do not hold such a well-conceived opinion in vain. I hasten to Rome, where we shall put our studies to the test, or rather, face the test along with danger. If we achieve anything, it is God’s gift: to Him be praise and thanks. If we fail in anything, it is our own weakness; let it be imputed to us. For the rest, I am yours, as one who, because of the integrity of both your life and your character, would hardly grant the first place in loving you even to our friend Girolamo <note>likely referring to Girolamo Savonarola, a close associate of Pico</note>. Farewell from Fratta <note>A villa or town near Ferrara</note>.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Tommaso Mezzo, Greetings.

**S** I do not remember being more solidly delighted than I was recently while I was reading your *Epyrota* <note>A Latin comedy written by Mezzo, a Venetian humanist</note>: a little play that is undoubtedly most witty, both in the festive nature of its subject and the erudition of its style, challenging even the comedies of old. For what shall I say of these modern ones—plainly inept and witless—which easily reveal the childishness of their authors? It was truly worthy of being dedicated to Hermolao Barbaro <note>A famous Venetian scholar and diplomat</note>—I know not whether more by your name or mine. I believe all learned men owe as much to him alone as they hardly owe to antiquity itself. That you did not deprive me of it was in keeping with your most excellent kindness toward me, already well-perceived before now. Nor is there anything of mine of such value that, if I were to send it to you as if in exchange, I would consider the favor fully repaid. As for the new comedy you promise me, I am already waiting for it with open mouth <note>original: "inhio"; meaning to gape or long for eagerly</note>. Nor is there anything I desire more than it, except for your arrival here to join us. If I did not have to depart from here within ten days, as I think you have learned from our Seta, I would certainly have obtained it from you by persistent asking. For it is possible to gather from what you have written what future pleasantness there will be in our social intercourse, what in our living together, and what in those living voices which truly possess a hidden energy <note>original: "energiā"; the Greek rhetorical concept of vivid, active presence</note> that affects the mind more deeply and delights it in wonderful ways, far outweighing all writings. But since this is not permitted, do not expect the subject matter for a comedy from me again. I prefer that you produce both from your own storehouse, so that the little play may taste not of "Middle" <note>original: "mediū"; a pun on the recipient's name, Tommaso Mezzo, whose surname means "middle" or "half"</note> but of the whole Tommaso Mezzo. For I fear that by following your request, the dullness of my talent would cause me loss, and the work would degenerate from its maker by what it admitted of mine. With me, there is nothing that is not exposed, tasteless, foolish, or common. But these comedies require I know not what more secret things: the false, the biting, the elegant, and the sharp—qualities peculiar to you and the delights of your genius. Therefore, hasten the matter for me, which will be most welcome, so that since it is not permitted to enjoy your presence in person, I may enjoy you in this way even while you are absent. If, as I said before, my departure from here had not been so swift, we would surely have cultivated both our spirits and our talents together for several days. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, Greetings.

**N** You could not have asked for your Latin Muhammad <note>original: "maumettē"; likely referring to a Latin translation of the Quran or a philosophical work attributed to a Muslim author</note> back at a more opportune time than now, when I hope soon to hear Muhammad himself speaking in his native tongue. For after I kept watch day and night for an entire month over the Hebrew language, I have turned myself entirely to the study of Arabic and Chaldean <note>Aramaic, often referred to as Chaldean in this period</note>, fearing not at all that I shall make less progress in them than I have in Hebrew. In Hebrew, I can already—not yet with praise, but certainly without fault—compose a letter. See what the impulse of the mind can do. See what labor and diligence can achieve even where the strengths are somewhat weak. Certain books in both languages have driven me, or rather compelled me with another force, while I was doing other things, to learn the letters of the Arabs and the Chaldeans...

# LETTERS

[These books] have come into my hands not by chance or accident, but by the counsel of God and the favor of a divine power toward my studies. Listen to the titles—you will surely be stunned <note>original: "vadimonium deferes," a legal metaphor suggesting one would "forfeit their bond" or be rendered speechless by the news</note>. These books are Chaldean <note>In the Renaissance, "Chaldean" often referred to Aramaic or Syriac texts, believed to hold the secrets of ancient magic and theology</note>. If they are indeed books and not rather treasures! 

First, there are the oracles of Ezra, Zoroaster, and Melchior the Magi <term>Magi: ancient Persian priest-sages</term>. In these volumes, those texts which are circulated among the Greeks in corrupt and mutilated forms can now be read in their complete and perfect state. There is also a brief and rugged <note>original: "salebrosa," meaning rough or uneven, like a rocky path</note> interpretation by those Chaldean sages, but it is one full of mysteries. 

Likewise, there is a small book on the dogmas of Chaldean theology, along with a divine and most rich explanation by several Greeks and Chaldeans. See, Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence</note>, what unexpected blessings have slipped into my lap. Why should I not feel as though I have obtained the Horn of Plenty <term>Cornucopia: a symbol of endless abundance and wealth</term>? 

But what shall I say of the Arabic works? Among them are the letters of Mohammed of Toledo and Abulgalé <note>likely referring to Abu al-Hajjaj</note>, who studied under Averroes <note>the famous 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain</note>. And—what will move you even more deeply—there are many investigations by a certain Adelard <note>Adelard of Bath, a 12th-century English scholar known for translating Arabic scientific works into Latin</note>, who was taught in Egypt under Ammonius, the teacher of Plotinus <note>the 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism</note>.

This discovery highlights the Renaissance obsession with finding the "original" sources of ancient wisdom and theology.</summary>

# LETTERS

Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his brother <note>Pico uses "brother" here as a term of respect and religious kinship, as Battista was a friar.</note> Battista Mantovano, Carmelite. Greetings, etc.

**S**alutations, best of fathers. I have not written to you for some time, but in the meanwhile, I have read those divine and most holy poems of yours; in which there is such kingly majesty and such splendor of eloquence that the words and the ideas <note>original: "sententiae," referring to the deep thoughts or moral maxims within the work</note> seem to compete with one another to claim the prize. Happy are you, who are able to achieve the very best things you desire. Happy are we, to whom it has been granted not only to read what you have written, but also to love you, to see you, and to speak with you. This is a rich subject for me, one that would fill not just a letter but a proper volume, if either my own weakness or your modesty would permit me to wander freely in the praise of your poems. I will say this one thing: I am so delighted by the reading of your verses <term>carmina: literally "songs," but here referring to Battista's poetic compositions</term> that almost every day, when either weariness or exhaustion takes hold of me, I am accustomed to retreat into them as if into a garden.

# LETTERS

I value a single one [of your letters] more than the entire library of either Sunnadius <note>Likely a reference to an ancient collector or scholar, though less famous than Ptolemy; it may also be a Renaissance Latinization of a Greek name like Synesius.</note> or Ptolemy <note>Referring to the Great Library of Alexandria, the most famous library of the ancient world, founded by the Ptolemaic dynasty.</note>. For I am so far from neglecting the friendships of learned men <term>learned men: literally "men of letters" (litteratorum hominum), the intellectual elite who defined themselves through their Latinity and study of the classics</term> that nothing is of greater concern or closer to my heart.

I know, however, what place you claim for yourself among learned men; indeed, your letter was the most evident proof to me of your teaching, erudition, and humanity <term>humanity: from the Latin *humanitas*, referring to the refined culture, kindness, and education expected of a true scholar</term>. Therefore, if I did not love you greatly, I would have truly forgotten myself and would act far differently than I am accustomed. 

I love you, therefore, uniquely, although I have never seen you; I love you so much from my heart <note>original: "ex animo," literally "from the soul"</note> that I love few others more deeply, so that while our familiarity might eventually increase, my love for you cannot. And if anything—that is, whatever can be added—it will all come through your arrival here. This visit you promised of your own accord in your letters; and I request it as ardently as I impatiently desire it. 

If you procure for me John the Grammarian <note>original: "Ioannem grammaticum," referring to John Philoponus (c. 490–570 AD), an influential Alexandrian commentator whose works on Aristotle were highly sought after by Renaissance scholars.</note> on the *Physics* and Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, I will be bound to you in perpetual service... <note>The text ends mid-word with "de-", likely "devinctum" or "debitorem," indicating the writer would be forever in the recipient's debt.</note>

-># LETTERS<-

...they arrive to be corrected and whipped: so that they may pay the price for their errors with both the fingernail and the obelisk <note>In ancient scholarship, the 'fingernail' referred to polishing a work until no rough edges could be felt, while the 'obelisk' (†) was a mark used by editors to indicate doubtful or forged text.</note>. Therefore, present yourself to them as a fair judge, not an unjust one—that is, be severe rather than indulgent. For what greater injustice is there than to deceive a friend who expects everything from you? I am not of such a delicate disposition that I would shrink from another's erasures; nor do I seem so beautiful to myself that I would either ignore or accuse a critic. Indeed, perhaps neither you nor anyone else would believe how much these works of mine fail to satisfy me, so that even in those parts which please me more, I fear lest I be like that fellow Suffenus <note>A character from the poet Catullus, known for being a charming man who unfortunately thought he was a great poet while actually writing terrible verse.</note>. We are all deceived too much, and we do not see the knapsack that is on our own back <note>A reference to Aesop's fable: humans carry two bags; one in front for others' faults, and one behind for their own.</note>. Therefore, do not deny your labor in this honorable and noble matter to a very dear friend, especially one who asks with such great zeal and from the heart. But if I were the sort of person who could return the favor to you in such a matter, I would not keep silent about that Greek proverb: that Lysippus used to use the work of Apelles, and Apelles that of Lysippus in turn <note>original: "Lisippum apellis & apellem lisippi"; Lysippus was a great sculptor and Apelles a great painter; the proverb refers to masters of different crafts assisting one another.</note>. Farewell.

->## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings.<-

**W**hen I was in Florence in previous years, I left four love elegies with you. I had fashioned them at that time—almost as a boy—for the sake of exercising my mind, as is often done. They were indeed insipid, unlearned, and trivial, easily revealing the age and ignorance of their author. You, however, approved of them—not because the work deserved it, but out of your own kindness or indulgence. And for that very reason, to prove you had approved them, you asked for copies. Surely you were not unaware that such things are very sharp incentives for the minds of youths toward virtue; enticed by the desire for praise, they soon strive more deeply to taste the little bit of glory they have sipped. For just as strength lies flat and cold in the face of despair, there is no one who doubts it is lifted up and set on fire by hope. But now, my age removes that legal defense; the errors that were previously signed off on will now be turned into a fault against me, because I have not yet, in my more mature years, either cleaned them up better or deleted them. Therefore, if you love me, either send back to me whatever poems of mine you have, or tear them up, or give them to the fire. All of those, more carefully worked, along with many others which I have composed at my leisure since I left that place, will soon be entrusted to your "file" <note>The "file" is a common Renaissance metaphor for the painstaking process of editing and smoothing out literary prose or poetry.</note>. In the meantime, those which cannot live without damage to a friend should be condemned by the "fatal pebble" <note>original: "capitali dānentur calculo"; in ancient courts, a black pebble was used to cast a vote for condemnation or death.</note>. Furthermore, I would very much like you to send me your *Epictetus*, and what you have translated from Homer up to this day; likewise what you composed about Giuliano de' Medici in the mother tongue <note>The "mother tongue" refers to Italian (vernacular), as opposed to the scholarly Latin of the rest of the letter.</note>, and whatever else you have composed in the Latin language. I ask this of you as one who asks most earnestly, for I desire them as one who is most impatient. There is no reason for you to refuse because they might not yet be "brought to the navel" <note>original: "ad umbilicum nundum deducta"; an ancient Roman expression meaning a book is not yet finished. It refers to the wooden rollers (umbilici) around which a scroll was wrapped when completed.</note>. Since, if this is your wish, I already announce and promise you that all these things will remain secret with me. Farewell.

->## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, Greetings.<-

**I**t has always been my judgment, most learned Marsilio, that one should labor in no matter more than this: that we should in no way degenerate through idleness or sluggishness from the nobility of the mind—by which, as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and philosophical works were attributed; a favorite source for Ficino and Pico's Neoplatonism.</note> testifies, we are reckoned next after Jupiter. This has always been my primary goal: to acquire for myself the cultivation of the mind and the disciplines of the noble arts from wherever I could. Although this purpose of mine has been most constant since my boyhood, your exhortations when I was with you in previous years greatly stirred and inflamed me; never more ardently than from that day to this have I given myself entirely to letters. For three years now, Marsilio, I have been occupied among the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for their rigorous logic and physical studies.</note>, nor have I omitted anything, as far as in me lay, so that I might be admitted into the Aristotelian house as one not unworthy of their family. Although I have not achieved this in great abundance—since I am scarcely in the entrance hall—I have nonetheless proceeded so far that I would not hesitate to claim for myself the name of a "student," if not that of the "learned and erudite" (which my age does not yet allow). But since...

# LETTERS

It has always been your opinion, and the opinion of the most learned men, that whoever combines the Academic <note>The 'Academic' refers to the school of Plato, named after the Academy in Athens.</note> with the Peripatetic <note>The 'Peripatetic' refers to the school of Aristotle, named after his habit of walking while teaching.</note>; that person
would hold both schools of thought more correctly and more richly. I have considered that I should take up this province <term>province: used here to mean a specific field of scholarly duty or mission</term> myself:
so that now, through the strength of my own natural talent, and with the greatest possible persistence and diligence,
I might compare Plato with Aristotle and, in turn, through alternating studies, compare Aristotle with Plato.

But just as I needed you as an advisor before, so now I have need of you as a helper. It will be a mark of your kindness and
your goodwill toward me not to fail my purpose—especially one so honorable and noble—which I believe would be
most abundantly fulfilled by you if you were to send me your book *On the Immortality of Souls* <note>original: "de immortalitate animorum". This likely refers to Ficino's masterwork, the *Platonic Theology*.</note>.

With this book as a kind of guide, I am confident that I will progress in the Platonic discipline just as I desire.
For who is greater than Ficino? In whom, if truth...

...or more honorable than that one: if only it is among those [desires] called the desire for name and glory <note>original: "cupiditas nominis & gloriae"</note>. Truly, this can be provided to me more abundantly by no one than by you yourself: in whom all the virtues, as if individually, claim the palm of victory <note>The "palm" refers to the ancient Roman symbol of triumph and excellence.</note> for themselves in competition; and certainly there is no one to whom I would more gladly be indebted. In mutual duties toward you, since he can offer nothing either great or worthy of Ermolao, he will indeed be unequal; but if you look at his spirit, he is certainly equal...

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Ermolao Barbaro, Greetings.**

<insert>M</insert><note>The letter opens with a large, decorative red initial 'M' containing a smaller 'm' and a flourish extending to the left.</note> I remember that when I was deliberating which of the universities <note>original: *gymnasiis*, referring to centers of higher learning</note> of Italy I should primarily choose as my home for the studies of philosophy <note>original: *phiæ*, an abbreviation for *philosophiae*</note>, and while many things were calling me to Padua, I sought that place quite willingly so that the love for you which I had long nourished in my soul might be made manifest to you through mutual companionship. I was in Padua for two years. Yet—who would believe it?—I neither saw Ermolao, nor did I know him except by the reputation I had heard long before. It so often happens that while we disregard an offered opportunity through a certain lazy procrastination, it slips from our hands as if it were a slippery thing. I have regretted this matter vehemently and continue to regret it, all the more because, whereas previously I had known your learning in all subjects only by rumor, I have now recognized it with these very eyes and these very ears, while I heard the Roman Themistius <note>This refers to Ermolao Barbaro’s famous Latin translations and paraphrases of the 4th-century Greek commentator Themistius, which were highly regarded for their elegant Latin style.</note> discoursing through your own voice concerning the nature of the soul, the first beginnings of things, and the <term>science of reasoning</term> <note>This refers to logic, the foundational tool of medieval and Renaissance philosophy.</note>. Good God, how much learning!

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of philosophy as a pursuit of internal truth rather than external gain. He is responding to critics or friends who suggest he should use his talents to serve a political ruler.</meta>

-># OF MIRANDOLA<-

Would it not be <term>illiberal</term><note>In this context, "illiberal" means "unfree" or "ignoble"—something beneath the dignity of a free, educated person.</note> or not at all becoming of a prince, to make the study of wisdom a <term>mercenary</term><note>Original: "mercenarium." Referring to practicing philosophy for money or status rather than for its own sake.</note> endeavor? Who could bear or even listen to such things with a calm mind? Certainly, he was never a philosopher who became one only so that he might later either be able to, or choose not to, practice philosophy. Such a man practiced trade, not philosophy.

You write that the time is approaching for me to devote myself to one of the great princes of Italy. You do not yet know the opinion that philosophers hold of themselves: following <note>original: "oratiū," referring to the Roman poet Horace</note> Horace, they consider themselves the kings of kings; they do not know how to endure the whims of others or how to serve. They live within themselves and, content with the tranquility of their own minds, they are sufficient unto themselves. They seek nothing outside themselves; those things which are held in honor by the common people are considered dishonorable among them. All things for which human desire thirsts or for which ambition sighs, they neglect and despise. 

This is a path that should doubtlessly be followed by all, but especially by those upon whom fortune has so smiled that they may live not only elegantly and comfortably, but...

->LETTERS<-

...he even fled against me and from me: But the elephant does not care for a gnat <note>original: "non curat culicem elephas." A variation of a common Latin proverb suggesting that a person of high status or great mind is not bothered by the attacks of the insignificant.</note>. And I wish to forgive you for whatever that frivolous man has done wrong before now; but let him not abuse my patience in the future, lest I be forced to eventually treat him exactly as he has deservedly treated me. As for your excusing that friend of yours—the one for whom matters of love turned out badly—before our friend Florianus, you acted out of duty. He has ways to clear himself of the mark of crime through history, poetry, and even philosophy itself; he has the precedents of great men like David and especially Solomon to protect him, to say nothing of Aristotle. For while Aristotle was often desperately in love with certain courtesans, he remembered nothing of the ethics of his own teachers, but performed sacrifices to his beloved woman as if to Eleusinian Ceres <note>A reference to the medieval legend of Aristotle being humiliated by his infatuation with a woman (often called Phyllis), illustrating that even the greatest intellects are vulnerable to passion.</note>. 

But your friend does not embrace these defenses and "fortifications" for his misdeed; he does not merely love now, but he hates, rejects, and refuses his past actions. He seeks his own loss and does not pray away his guilt; he grieves that he has sinned and does not defend it. And to me, he seems worthy of excuse for this very reason: that he does not excuse himself at all. Nothing is weaker than man, and nothing is more powerful than love. Even the invincible and unshaken mind of Jerome <note>St. Jerome, known for his extreme asceticism.</note>, while it clung entirely to heaven, felt itself present among choirs of girls. What plague could infest a man that love will not overcome? If love could do this in the desert, on the bare ground with broken limbs, amidst the fasting of the weeks—what can it not do among feathers and shade, in the total abundance of delights? 

Add to this that he has now fallen for the first time, being otherwise unaccustomed to and ignorant of such a ruin. He can complain of Neptune <note>The god of the sea; used here as a metaphor for the "storm" of passion or fate.</note> who has suffered shipwreck only once. If he should strike against the same stone a second time, let no one hold out a hand; let no one take pity. Now, however, he cannot rightly be denied excuse—he who so regrets the deed that he does not think himself worthy of the favor of being excused. But perhaps this is too much, since your friend desires that the memory of such a deed should not only be omitted from letters in any way but should be entirely blotted out by his subsequent life. Farewell. Christopher was not present when I received yours. Commend me in no ordinary way to your master and to the entire Borromeo family <note>A powerful and influential Italian noble family.</note>, whom I have always loved and now love very much. At Perugia. October 15, 1491, in the year of grace.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola sends fondest greetings <term>S.P.: Salutem Plurimam, a standard Latin epistolary greeting</term> to his nephew Giovanni Francesco.**

**G**reatly pleasing to me were your letters; not only because I had heard nothing of you for a long time, but also because they indicated things to me in which I am wonderfully delighted: that those same things are pleasing to you, and I do not doubt they are most pleasing to God. You also should have no doubt that if you only proceed on the path you have begun, your reward will be copious in heaven. I have not yet sufficiently explored whether I must go to Rome or not. And as far as I can gather by conjecture, I believe it is more likely that I must go there; you know the reason. As soon as I have a certainty of this, I will immediately inform you, lest if you happen to come here (which I would otherwise greatly desire), you either do not find me here, or find me departing immediately so that you must return to your own country. In the meantime, you can stay at home, unless you feel otherwise. 

But remember this also: you have a wife to whom you owe your body, no differently than you owe your soul to God. Her desire must be satisfied in some part; and you must consider what she might desire or be able to desire based on her physical condition and her age, and what she might not ask for out of shame or virtue. For why should I be ashamed to write these things which the Apostle Paul also writes? There is almost no matter in which I suspect you could be more prone to error. And indeed, our men are very much deceived who think their wives are bound and devoted to them, but they themselves owe nothing to their wives—as if they could decide whatever they please regarding themselves at their own whim. Finally, you cannot be entirely your own, since by once subjecting yourself to the laws of marriage, you willed to belong to a wife. Nevertheless, you can be entirely God’s, whom you deserve for yourself while you obey His law...
