### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his friend Jacopo Antiquario, Greetings.

**I**ntermingled with the pleasures I took most when I was in Florence from the companionship of Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant Renaissance humanist and poet</note>—a man, in my opinion, the most learned of our age—it was no small joy that he would immediately give me your letters to him to read, so grave and elegant as they always were, as soon as he received them. I was greatly delighted in them by both a certain singular wisdom, for which you are commended by the most prudent men even in handling great affairs and business, and by the refinement and sobriety of your speech. Moreover, because you made honorable mention of us in some of them, your letters not only pleased me, but I also pleased myself in them. To be sure, my conscience yielded to the testimony of such a great man, thinking you were perhaps hiding a bit of what you felt; yet if my conscience were to give itself away, it was not fighting much and was almost willingly letting itself be deceived. 

Thus, I was doubly bound to you: on one hand by your virtue, on the other by the service—or rather, the benefit—you so often bestowed upon me. I thought more than once of giving you thanks by letter, lest I seem ungrateful or perhaps <term>rustic</term> <note>meaning boorish or lacking in courtly/humanist manners</note> toward you. But since you and our Politian were carrying on such a beautiful exchange of letters between you, I did not wish for a troublesome **Magpie** <note>original: "Pica"; a pun on his own name, Pico</note> to squawk against the Muses, nor like a poorly voiced Goose, to disturb the swans singing to one another. Otherwise, I knew my mind was open to you through our Politian; and being conscious of my own <term>speechlessness</term> <note>original: "infantiæ"; in this context, it refers to his perceived lack of eloquence compared to Politian, not actual childhood</note>, I used him as my most eloquent interpreter. 

Now your letters have been sent to us by him, which you recently gave to Riccio, a youth of outstanding talent; in which you attribute so much to me as I would not dare to hope for, let alone believe I deserve. The magnitude of your kindness has broken my hitherto—I know not if uncivil, but certainly not proud—silence, nor could I fail to give you immortal thanks, not because you overwhelm me with immoderate praises which I do not recognize, but because you love me so much that your judgment, otherwise constant and robust, has wavered so much in my case under the weight of love. I owe you more, therefore, than I could pay back, or you could easily believe; nor is anything so arduous or difficult that I would not do it for your dignity as I would for my own safety. You who possessed me through Politian until now, will now—with the situation unchanged—unfold the name of Pico which lay beneath for your own reasons. Farewell. From the Ferrarese countryside. 28 June 1494.

->To the most excellent and learned man, Lord Jacopo Antiquario, as a father.<-

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Andrea Corneo, Health and Greetings.

**S**atisfaction has been clearly and abundantly given to my wishes, dearest Andrea. For I have learned from your letters to Christopher—certainly our dearest friend—that you are living there both comfortably and with dignity. For this is, and always has been, my greatest wish: that you be well and happy, and I have nothing greater to say than this according to your merits. I never doubted this outcome. And this one thing was always clear to me: as long as you have your tongue, wherever you go, you will be held in high esteem. I know (let it be said without flattery) the nobility of your spirit, which will suffer nothing humble or common. I know your virtues, learning, manners, and wisdom: all of which will easily lead you wherever you aim. Yet I fear for your health, oppressed by so many diseases from your youth, as you used to tell me, until this day—debilitated more than broken; so much has that spirit of yours moved it, that it knows not how to be defeated, but with a certain perpetual solidity of its own, it fights strenuously against the blows of fortune. Have what...

Y ii <note>signature mark for the book binder</note>

Whatever they may be, I have decided they must be sent so that I might satisfy you, even at the cost of my entire reputation. I would, however, ask that you regard all these things as minor; for if you eventually desire my real works, we have weightier matters in hand which have not yet been "brought to the navel." <note>original: "ad umbilicum... ducta"; a Roman metaphor for completing a book scroll, which was wound around a central stick called an umbilicus</note> Even these very things we have sent were demanding a more perfect polish. But both the times and my studies in philosophy, over which I keep a most vigilant watch, have diverted me from that labor. We shall return, however, to the Muses at some point; and if we forge anything worthy of your ears, we will see to it that it is brought to you immediately. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to the Most Reverend Lord Cardinal...<- <note>The abbreviation R.C.C.S. likely refers to a high-ranking ecclesiastical correspondent, possibly a Cardinal.</note>

**A**<note>Large red initial A</note>ttheus, our most dutiful friend, gave me many greetings in your name and most aptly declared the love and goodwill you feel for me. He promised, moreover, your zeal and assistance in your name, should it ever happen that I need to make use of them. Would that I were equal to this service, most kind Father. For I have always hoped and prayed to be taken into your protection and numbered among your friends. But that you should come to me of your own accord, so kindly, with such friendly and liberal promises—and calling me, as it were, into your friendship (if I may say so, and you allow it)—has surpassed all my hope and every prayer. For what is it, or how great a thing is it, to be invited by one from whom it would have been enough not to be excluded? Although you have done something worthy of yourself, if not of me. For I could have been denied admittance based on my own merits. Yet, by your kindness, I could not go uncalled. Therefore, how I might explain how much I rejoice for myself, or how much I owe to you, I cannot even conceive. Certainly, I owe you all the more because you owe me nothing at all. Nor are those things too great or too many which Matthew and my other friends have reported, estimating me out of affection rather than judgment. But whatever or however great I am, allow me also to be among all those who—to say nothing of the rest—cherish and admire your virtues, through which one may see in you both that which surpasses antiquity and that which cannot be surpassed by posterity. I might say this deservedly, since in you nothing is lacking that might be placed in honor, or prudence, or learning. This one thing ought to be desired by all: that through you, someday, according to Plato’s wish, supreme power might be joined with supreme wisdom. <note>A reference to Plato's *Republic*, which argues that the world will only be right when philosophers become kings or kings become philosophers.</note> But these things are from God; meanwhile, I ask and pray this of you: that you provide me an opportunity—not for returning thanks (for there is no room for that, either through your greatness or my insignificance)—but for testifying to my spirit toward you, and my loyalty and devotion. You will find Giovanni Pico a man dedicated and devoted to you beyond all opinion; you cannot promise yourself more from him, but you can use all those things, whatever they may be, which are in him, into which you yourself will bring some of your own splendor. They will become great when they begin to be yours, for while they are mine, they cannot be great. Farewell.

->John Pico of Mirandola to Domenico Benivieni. Greetings.<-

**G**reetings, my Domenico, chosen perhaps by lot in the Lord: your letters were pleasing to me, and it was even more pleasing that I learned both in person from your brother while he was here, and through letters from our Pietro Antonio, that you are of a firmer constitution of body and a better stomach. Take care of your health—if we, if letters are of any concern to you—about which I am certainly and always solicitous, not only because I love you (for I love you vehemently), but because I love letters, which I believe and certainly know are in danger along with you. If your brother told you anything of our goodwill toward you, have the fullest faith in it; if he said anything of our praises, believe him only as much as he loves me, which is a great deal. There is no reason for you to marvel at our *Little Commentary* <note>Pico refers here to his *Commento*, a philosophical commentary on a poem by Domenico’s brother, Girolamo Benivieni</note>; when we wished to be idle and do absolutely nothing, we did that, relaxing the mind rather than straining it. It is entirely a prelude to the commentaries which we are meditating upon for Plato’s *Symposium*. There will be something in those at least for you to love and praise, as you love and praise all our things. Concerning the council <note>Likely the planned debate in Rome for which Pico wrote his 900 Theses</note> and the questions, as I think your brother reported, you already know why I wrote that I am working for you. What you ask of me I will do most willingly when I understand that you have been restored to your first and desired health from that weakness of body from which you have suffered until now; which I pray and hope for you with the same spirit with which you pray and hope for the health of my soul. Farewell from Fratta. November 10, 1486.

->John Pico of Mirandola to Andrea Corneo. Greetings.<-

**E**ven if I have given you letters either rarely or never, I have nevertheless thought of you and your affairs either often or always. But I do not wish to sell you hope, nor will I write to you what I might do for your benefit until I am able to write what I have accomplished. If, by your misfortune or mine, that should never happen, I would prefer you to believe that I worked on your behalf in nothing rather than in vain. But perhaps fortune will be more joyful for you than either hope itself or fortune is accustomed to be. There is no reason for your Laura to wait for our poems: for they have been called back to the anvil <note>A metaphor for revising and refining literary work</note> to be more tightly shaped; nor do they dare to go out into public with the face they now have. However, an immediate and urgent reason for a new work which I have in my hands at the persuasion of Lorenzo de' Medici delays their correction: in which I not only illuminate the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms of King David</note> with a longer interpretation, but since those which the Church chants were translated by the "Seventy" <term>Septuagint: the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible made by 70 scholars</term> and the Hebrews prove that translation to be unfaithful in more than six hundred places, I—relying on the properties of Hebrew and Chaldean <note>Renaissance scholars used "Chaldean" to refer to Aramaic or Syriac</note> literature—both assert and defend them for the integrity of their meanings against all calumny of the Jews. There is nothing left for me to write, except that you should recommend me to Hermolao <note>Hermolao Barbaro, a prominent Venetian humanist</note> as often as you see the man, and in no common way. Likewise, see that the learned and grave man Jacopo Volaterrano understands that he is vehemently loved by me; if I ever obtain from him the letters of Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a 4th-century Roman statesman known for his oratory</note> for a few days until they can be transcribed, he will bind me to him by a perpetual favor. Farewell. 1489.

# MIRANDOLA

From here, he might well inaugurate our friendship. I wanted to indicate to you what I was feeling. I would certainly have done so far more richly if I had my books here with me—those friends of all men—whom I might consult. However, they have already preceded me to Rome, like advance guards going before their master. I myself, already wearing my traveling hat and boots <note>original: "pætasatus... & caligatus." These are classical idioms for being dressed and ready for a journey.</note> and standing ready for departure, have written these things to you as familiarly as I have hastily.

Regarding what you ask about Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works were central to Renaissance scholarship.</note>: you should know that the authentic Josephus is not found among the Hebrews. Instead, they have an <term>epitome</term> <note>a summary or condensed version of a larger work</note> of Josephus—that is, a certain brief compendium—in which many things are fabricated. Several of the Hebrews have confessed to me that the things read there concerning the Ten Tribes (who did not return by <term>right of recovery</term> <note>original: "postliminio." A Roman legal term referring to the restoration of rights and status to a person returning from exile or captivity.</note> after the Babylonian captivity) are spurious and forged. Therefore, no credit at all should be given to their version of Josephus. 

I know that in the Greek Josephus there are certain passages that mention Christ and the faith in an honorable way. But whether these are exactly the same as those read in the Latin manuscripts, I do not

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and theological exhortation regarding the Christian's relationship with a hostile world, likely part of a collection of Neo-Latin letters.</meta>

->**LETTERS**<-

...in heaven when men have spoken evil against us, and have said all manner of evil against us falsely <note>original: "mentientes"; literally "lying"</note> because of him. This, if you do not know it, is Apostolic dignity: to be held worthy to be defamed by the impious for the sake of the Gospel’s name. When we read in Luke <note>original: "apud Lucam"; the author refers to the Acts of the Apostles, traditionally attributed to Luke the Evangelist</note> that the Apostles departed with joy from the presence of the council because they were considered worthy to suffer insults for the Name of Jesus.

Let us therefore rejoice if we are worthy of such great glory before God, so that his glory may be made manifest in our disgrace. And if we suffer anything harsh or troublesome from the world, let that sweetest voice of the Lord console us: *If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you.* <note>original: "Si uos mundus odio habet scito te quia priorem me uobis odio habuit"; a quote from the Gospel of John 15:18</note> If the world hated him through whom the world was made, shall we—the most wretched of "little men"—be indignant if someone detracts from us or speaks evil, especially if we consider our own crimes, for which we are most deserving of every kind of reproach? Should we begin to act badly ourselves just so that someone else might not speak evil of us?

Let us rather receive these insults eagerly. And even if it is not our good fortune to endure lashes, chains, prisons, or swords for the sake of virtue and truth—as our heroes <note>the martyrs and saints of the early Church</note> once did—let us consider it a job well done if we at least suffer the taunts, slanders, and hatred of wicked men. Otherwise, if every opportunity for merit is taken away from us, no hope of a reward will remain.

If men praise you for living well, then this virtue of yours, insofar as it is virtue, makes you like Christ; but insofar as it is praised, it makes you unlike him—for he received from men the death of the cross as the reward for his virtue. Because of this, as the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> says, *God also has highly exalted him and given him a name which is above every name.* <note>Philippians 2:9</note> It is therefore more desirable to be crucified by the world so that you may be exalted by God, than to be exalted by the world so that you may be judged by God. For the former is crucified into life, while the latter is exalted into a fall; the former is exalted into glory, while the latter is judged into hell.

Finally, if the world applauds you, it can hardly happen that virtue—which, standing upright, ought to have only God to please—does not bow for a moment to the favor of the applauding crowd. And even if virtue does not lose its integrity, it nonetheless loses part of its reward; for when payment begins on earth where everything is small, the reward will be less in heaven where everything is immense. Blessed are the insults that keep us safe, so that the flower of righteousness does not wither by the pestilential breath of empty glory, nor the reward of eternity be diminished by the hollow payment of popular rumors.

Let us embrace these insults, my son, and with a most holy ambition let us be proud of the faithful service found in the disgrace of the Lord’s cross alone. Paul says, *We preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, but to us, the power and wisdom of God.* <note>1 Corinthians 1:23-24</note> That wisdom of the world is foolishness before God; and that "foolishness" of Christ is what conquers the world’s wisdom, through which it pleased God to save those who believe.

If you do not doubt that those who detract from your virtue are insane—calling the Christian life (which is true wisdom) "madness"—think how great your own madness would be to be moved from a rightly ordered life by the judgment of the insane. For every error should be removed by correction, not increased by imitation. Let them gape, howl, and bark; you continue the journey you have begun, undaunted. Consider how much you owe to God because of their wickedness and misery—He who enlightened you while you were sitting in the shadow of death and associated you with the children of light, having moved you from the assembly of those who rave here and there in the thickest darkness without a leader.

Let that sweetest voice of the Lord sound in your ears always: *Let the dead bury their own dead; you, follow me.* <note>Matthew 8:22</note> For they are dead who do not live for God; and in this span of temporary death, they most laboriously acquire eternal death for themselves. If you ask them where they are heading, or to what they direct their studies, works, and cares—or finally, what end they have set for themselves in the attainment of which they will be happy—they will either have nothing at all to answer, or they will speak words that conflict and contradict themselves, like the ravings of fanatics. For they do not know...

I urge you, turn back: turn this over in your mind day and night, reflecting on how great a name his is, who has enriched you to such an extent that you will never be able to repay him or even calculate the value of what you possess. Think how much he is capable of, he who willed that you possess these things; how much he loves you, he who chose you for himself out of so many thousands. You, who as almost a boy would surpass old men, and who, not yet a youth <term>ephebus</term> <note>original: "ephebus"; a Greek term for a young man, typically aged 18–20, transitioning into adulthood</note>, would turn the circles of learned men toward admiration of your own learning. Unless you see this, and unless you value it, I affirm to you right now and freely declare: you are not yet as great as you truly are. 

It is immense and infinite, what I long ago promised myself regarding you, and what I still promise; but neither speech nor public praise can reach the height of the opinion I have already formed. I act as people usually do: the more they admire someone and wish to explain what they feel, the less they achieve what they intend. Just as they conceive something grand in their mind, words fail them, and they seem to be struggling with the weight of the idea rather than being able to express it. 

Therefore, do not merely listen to these things which I write about you and publish abroad; but rather understand those things which I say of you alone and silently within myself—which are, by Hercules, so much greater than this speech, just as thought is greater than words. Greet Marsilio <note>Refers to Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the famous philosopher and head of the Platonic Academy in Florence</note> and your friend Salviati. Regarding Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the renowned poet and scholar</note>, there is no need for you to labor, because shortly (as I hear) he will be with me. Nothing more pleasant than this could have happened to me in this whole embassy. 

I am so glad that a library is being built up there <note>Likely referring to the Laurentian Library in Florence</note> day by day, becoming larger and more ornate, that nothing could please me more. Letters <note>Meaning literature and classical learning</note> owe a debt to the Florentines, and among the Florentines to the Medici, and among the Medici to Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), known as "the Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and a massive patron of the arts</note>, who fosters this hereditary glory of his family with no less care than he does the republic, which he has the right to administer and establish. ->Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico. Greetings.<-

**[E]** Your *Hexameron* <note>original: "Xameron"; likely referring to Pico's "Heptaplus," a treatise on the seven days of creation</note> was delivered to us the day before yesterday by the efforts of Salviati. I read it so greedily that I devoured the whole thing on the very first day, and not without a single breath. Three things in it delight me wonderfully: first, that your oratory teaches and moves; this is something well-established that the ancient theologians of Isis <note>Barbaro refers here to ancient Egyptian mystery traditions</note> observed in sacred matters, and the Pythagoreans and Platonists in natural philosophy, while more recent writers only sweat over the task of teaching. 

Second, that in such a great abundance of material and freedom to plunder from others, you have such chaste and innocent hands; in this style of writing, you seem to have followed yourself and no other. This is not common to either the ancients or the moderns, but is peculiar and your own. In this—to reveal my feelings to you—I am so affected that since those earlier men did not say what you have said, they seem to me to have said almost nothing. 

Third, that I see you have been initiated into the sacred mysteries not so much of Aristotle as of Plato and his followers; you have brought full drafts from there into this late-night study. I omit how many excellent things from Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher</note> you have touched upon cursorily and elegantly, so that whatever the fifty-four volumes of his, arranged into six "Enneads" <note>Groups of nine books</note> by Porphyry, contain, you seem not merely to have read but to have mastered. Nor can I pass over this: that you conduct yourself as a middle ground between the new and old theologians, such that you neither hate the simple majesty of the former nor are you carried away by the ambitious subtlety of the latter. Thus it happens that while you wish to imitate the one, you are able to imitate the other; you have gathered the best of both kinds. We hope you will do the same in your explanation of the poems of David <note>The Psalms</note>. Farewell. Venice, September 4, 1489.

->Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico of Mirandola. Greetings.<-

**[S]** Greetings, most kind Mirandola. Indeed, I proclaim your name everywhere so gladly that I do nothing with greater pleasure—not only because, as Plato says, nothing is more pleasant to hear than the truth, but also because, as Palemo <note>A reference to the philosopher Polemon</note> says, it is much more pleasant to speak truths than to hear them. It happens that with no labor—as is often found in Aeschylus, Menander, and Euripides <note>Famous Greek playwrights</note>—the truth comes forth even when not sought; even when most unwilling, it is often expressed by no questioning but by its own power alone. This is that "tyranny" <note>The compelling, undeniable power of genius or truth</note> which you, following your own candor, interpret as humanity and goodness. And by Hercules, you are now so great that anyone who does not praise you detracts from their own judgment and reputation. They are acting in their own interest, consulting their own reasons, and redeeming their own fame, those who favor and desire yours. There are many names in your diary which you do not know are your debtors; many follow the counsel of Prodicus...

<meta>This page continues a series of letters or introductory praises regarding the works of the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, specifically focusing on his "Heptaplus" (a seven-fold account of the creation of the world).</meta>

->LETTERS<-

...they are greater and worthy of even greater admiration. For, lifted up from the waters—whether by swan’s feathers, I know not, or by the wings of Daedalus and Pegasus—I traveled through all the air and the ether to the very summit of corruptible things. <note>The author uses these mythological wings to metaphorically describe an intellectual or spiritual ascent from the physical "elemental" world to the higher "celestial" realms.</note> Not by my own leading, but by being carried aloft, I arrived there. It is a matter truly worthy of extreme wonder to have traversed this lower and elemental world. But it is a far greater thing to have reached the celestial world: to have penetrated first the orb of the Moon, then Mercury and Venus; to have seen the rays of the Sun; to have felt the heat of Mars; and finally to have known the healing rays of Jupiter and the heavy rays of Saturn. Then, at last, I observed that eighth sphere <note>original: "octauā illā sperā"; in the ancient geocentric model, the eighth sphere contained the "fixed stars," beyond the seven known planets.</note> shining with burning stars, and I perceived that all these heavens are rotated not by a simple and uniform motion, but by a triple and threefold one—though who is ignorant that all these things fall within the reach of our senses?

But he <note>Pico della Mirandola</note> gave me a third world to fly through in such a way that, with all the senses lulled to sleep (for they hinder rather than help this kind of inspection), I might see and perceive it with the mind alone—for by the mind alone are such vast spaces traversed. But the sharp edge of the mind, like an owl’s eye blinking at the rays of the sun, could not endure such splendor. Therefore, whatever remained hidden from me or escaped my eyes in this journey—or, to speak more truly, in this return to the fatherland—the guide himself <note>Pico</note> is not to blame, but rather he to whom the guide was showing the way. For the divine genius of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola both promises and provides a demonstration of all things.

What is there, then, my dear Robert, <note>likely Robert Salviati, a friend of Pico</note> that I should not confess I owe to you, having been enriched by you with such a great gift? Indeed, as soon as I began to taste it, such a great greed was stirred within me, and such a love of feasting arose from the sweetness of this food, that, impatient of any delay, I did not wait to chew it properly, but like a most ravenous bullock, I devoured the whole solid mass. But when, through continued reading, I had finished the entire work, I began to ruminate on it more carefully, bringing it back from my stomach to my mouth like that same beast. Then truly did a wonderful sweetness appear; then did a wonder never felt before take hold of me. 

But you will say: "Did you not admire the man’s learning before?" I did indeed admire how he was so well-versed in all disciplines that he seemed to excel in each one. No topic in physics, no place in mathematics escaped him when he disputed; and as for metaphysics and every kind of theology—whether you seek that which was stirred up by Mercury <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus and the Hermetic tradition</note> and perfected by Plato, or our own Christian theology, the most excellent and true of all—these recent centuries and many before them have seen nothing more learned than he. 

But lest you think (a fault which many of our people have labored under) that he separated eloquence from wisdom, does he not describe everything with the greatest weight, abundance, and elegance? Indeed, he may now be justly numbered among those ancient orators. I have admired these things in him until now, thinking that nothing could be added to such an invention. But since reading his *Heptaplus*, <term>Heptaplus</term><note>From the Greek "hepta" (seven); Pico's 1489 work providing a seven-layered mystical interpretation of the Book of Genesis.</note> I have begun to admire these higher things even more than what came before. Therefore, I would believe—not rashly or by chance, but by God’s command—that this divine man has emerged distinguished by these three names. 

For "John" <note>original: "Ioannes"</note> is interpreted as "the grace of the Lord," or "he in whom there is grace," or "he to whom a gift was made by God." Who does not see that he could not have attained the learning he has reached without the special and greatest grace of God? In the name "Picus" <note>original: "Pico"; the author puns on the Latin word 'picus' meaning woodpecker.</note> moreover, we know there is such hardness of beak and such strength of head that you will find no wood—no matter how bony or stony, if I may say so—that this bird cannot bore through, skillfully carving out a hiding place to retreat into and a nest to build. In the same way, there is nothing in any discipline so difficult for human genius to know that he, by pounding against its hardest parts, has not penetrated it, built his nest there, hatched his young, and brought them forth. And since everything in that man is to be wondered at, who would not think he should be called "Mirandula"? <note>The author derives the name of Pico's hometown, Mirandola, from the Latin "miranda," meaning "wonderful things."</note> For this reason, just as I congratulate you for enjoying his constant friendship, so I congratulate myself...

<summary>In this letter, the author expresses profound awe for Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s intellectual and spiritual depth, particularly praising his work the *Heptaplus*. Through elaborate metaphors of flight and etymological puns on Pico’s name, the writer depicts the philosopher as a divinely graced genius who bridges ancient wisdom and Christian theology.</summary>

# LETTERS

"I grieve," I say to myself, "considering myself unfortunate in this: that because of my many and necessary obligations, I am not permitted to stay by his side day and night, as I most ardently desire. For if it were permitted, I would never depart from the side—I do not say of an old man, but of a young man; I mean that young man in whom all wisdom and all learning is elderly and grey-haired." <note>The writer is referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, who was famously dubbed the "Phoenix of Wits" for his vast knowledge at a young age.</note> But you, to whom fortune has offered far greater leisure and nature has granted an excellent intellect, which your subsequent long-term practice and frequent use in all the liberal arts has increased and polished—enjoy this good thing that has fallen to you from heaven. Drink from this most fertile fountain, or rather this immense ocean; and drink as much as can be enough to quench not only your present thirst, but all future thirst.

Reflect, therefore; count and debate with yourself how very few mortals have ever received so much good. The great Alexander boasted that he lived in the times of so great a philosopher as Aristotle. But to you, it has been given by your most happy fate to have lived familiarly with Aristotle and Plato at the same time—and such an Aristotle and Plato that in them, besides the ancient doctrine of the Academics and Peripatetics, we see our Pauls, Johns, Dionysii, Augustines, Jeromes, Thomases, and other lights of this kind shining forth. <note>The writer suggests that Pico has synthesized classical Greek philosophy with the teachings of the Church Fathers (Paul, Augustine, Jerome) and Scholastic theologians like Thomas Aquinas.</note> Therefore, conclude from these things how much you ought to love yourself, or love him for this, my best Robert; you whom fortune itself has favored, and you who by your own prudence have succeeded in making yourself especially familiar to this man. Farewell. November 22nd. <note>original: "x. Kalen. Decembris" — The 10th day before the Kalends of December.</note>

## Alexander Cortese to his Pico, Greetings.

**I** have received no greater pleasure in my whole life than recently from your letters; and although I had believed all the highest things about you, you have nevertheless (I confess) surpassed my opinion. And you have surpassed it so much that I now consider the boundaries of your glory, although it is spread far and wide, to be narrow. Let us speak more aptly and far from the flattery from which illustrious minds have always recoiled: What in you is not extraordinary? What is not worthy of admiration? Individual qualities could honor anyone, but in you, all have been brought together equally. From everyone (if I may say so) you alone have stolen away all the Graces. <note>original: "veneres" — literally 'Venuses', a classical metaphor for charms, beauty, or intellectual graces.</note> And although your ancestors reached a point where only those born of them could easily arrive: you, however, have emerged so great that you seem to return more grace to them than you received. 

And indeed, old age brings authority to others, but youth extols your dignity; and what others surpass by time, you have surpassed by unconquerable virtue. In my judgment, you are placed beyond all risk of genius, and though I search through Greek praises, I find no one to whom I may deservedly compare you; and in short, one might believe that someone equal to you once existed, but it is not possible to see such a person at this time. Let all the talented men forgive me: everyone is greatly surpassed by Pico alone. Whom the kindness of nature has so cherished that she herself must seem a man for such a great abundance of all praises to be crowded into one. 

Why do you blush? Do you think I am false? I will indeed yield if you attribute this to Love, who is painted blind. But I have witnesses more substantial than my dear Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a leading humanist scholar and close friend of Pico.</note>, who is deceived only regarding me—and if he, as I hear, increases his riches of gold daily no less than his riches of speech, I congratulate him as much as I thank him; would that he possessed the Horn of Plenty, since he is neither unmindful of a guest nor of our old friendship. About Puccio, that most affectionate of men, another time: Who would not want to be indebted to him? But I delay you too long while you are intent on higher studies. 

And I see Marsilio Ficino <note>The head of the Platonic Academy in Florence and a central figure of the Renaissance.</note>, the prince of philosophers of our age, laughing at these trifles. Why should he not laugh? He who values all mortal things no less than he despises them. Oh, that someone would place me in your Academy and cover me with the great shade of its branches! Especially because Mars alone holds this sky; there is no honor worthy of the plow; the fields are neglected because the farmers have been taken away, and curved sickles are turned into rigid swords. <note>Cortese quotes Virgil’s *Georgics* (1.506-508) to contrast the peaceful world of philosophy with the contemporary reality of war and social decay.</note> But we are content with this Cato. You, meanwhile, gather from these scraps the fruit of my love, and do not think it a small thing to be loved by me, but return the favor. For the longing for you...

# LETTERS

...you elegantly bring forth the feelings of your mind, so that to you alone the immortal gods seem to have granted what they have given to very few indeed: namely, to think the best thoughts and to speak the best words. This you encompass no less in verse than in prose speech. Livy and Homer write, as if by divine inspiration, that the gods did not grant all gifts to a single man. <note>The author is referencing a classical trope: that the gods distribute talents (like strength, wisdom, or art) separately among men rather than giving all to one person.</note> 

For this reason, we often read of men who flourished by excelling in eloquence, while others were gifted with great learning; yet very few have emerged who were both eloquent and learned at once. In this regard, two "peaks" of the Roman language are cited: Terentius Varro and Marcus Cicero. <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC) was Rome's greatest scholar, while Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC) was its greatest orator.</note> From the former, knowledge of "things" (facts and history) was sought; from the latter, the mastery of "words" (style and oratory). The first is called the most learned in every respect by Terentianus; <note>original: "a Terentiano." Likely referring to Terentianus Maurus, a writer on Latin meter and grammar.</note> the second is called the most eloquent by everyone. 

As Seneca excellently remarks, that "happiness of talent" deserted Virgil <note>The poet Virgil, author of the *Aeneid*.</note> when he turned to prose; conversely, Cicero frequently wrote poems that possessed no grace and no charm—clearly while the Muses were "unwilling and resistant." <note>original: "musis scilicet invitis atque repugnantibus." This is a classical idiom meaning to act against one's natural ability or without divine inspiration.</note> But you, indeed, are both most learned...

...indeed, through your kindness I have attained that which I most desired. I thank you for such a gift, and I heartily congratulate him for having published such a great work to be celebrated by all of Christendom. In this work, I am truly uncertain whether to admire more the discovery of so many and such great things, or the incredible order within such variety, or the great elegance of speech in such laborious descriptions. For why should I mention the <term>Heptaplus</term> <note>original: "heptaplo"; Pico's 1489 work providing a sevenfold interpretation of the creation story in Genesis.</note>, which most commends the author’s efforts? There is no wordiness, no swelling of pride, and in everything a singular modesty without any suspicion of spite. I truly wish I could have returned a similar gift for this most sweet and desired gift of yours, so that you might perceive my spirit toward you more clearly. But I have sent to you what I could: a speech I recently delivered at Buda to King Matthias Corvinus <note>Matthias Corvinus (1443–1490) was the King of Hungary and a famous patron of humanist learning.</note>, which is the very first copy I have sent. When you have read it yourself, you will give it to your friend Pico to read. I judge him to be the most outstanding in every kind of learning of all those whose writings of our age I have seen thus far. Farewell, and continue to love me as you do.

**N** <note>The letter 'N' is a large red initial in the original.</note> **Battista Guarini to the most learned prince, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, greetings.**

I do not yet concede that the dispute should be settled in your favor. For I can easily turn those clever arguments of yours **back upon you** <note>original Greek: "ἀντιστρέφοντα" (antistrephonta); a logical term for an argument that can be reversed against the speaker.</note>. If I am your teacher, why do you not obey me? If I am not, why do you call me teacher? Nor do I refuse this name because I scorn you as a student—you whom I assert to be my own teacher. Rather, it is because I both venerate and proclaim your learning. In this, I am aware that neither my own talents, nor the marks of a slanted pen, nor small wax tablets, nor finally an <term>obelisk or asterisk</term> <note>These were proofreading marks used by scholars to indicate text that should be deleted or noted.</note> have moved you very much. But we seem to have fallen into a new kind of legal case: while you strive to claim that "possession" <note>likely referring to the status of being the "master" or "teacher"</note> for me, I am trying to claim it for you. What orator’s case ever had a plaintiff or defendant of this kind? My dear Pico, I will never "hand over the herb" <note>An ancient Roman idiom (herbam porrigere) meaning to admit defeat.</note> to you in this fight unless we first settle it on good terms, so that since you will not yield otherwise, each of us may be judged to be both teacher and student to the other. 

But jokes aside, let us deal with serious matters. Both your *Heptaplus* and you yourself can rightly be pleased with your work. Since you have won the approval of all learned men, no trace of spite appears even in the hidden corners of the tablet. It is to be hoped that the same will be more easily granted to you in your remaining writings, especially since that "best master of writing," practice, will have been added. As for what concerns me, I rejoice greatly that I am "on the lips" <note>meaning "being spoken of"</note> of that man who is praised and should be praised by everyone and everywhere: Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the ruler of Florence and a major patron of the arts.</note>. Especially with the addition of the judgment of Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), one of the greatest humanist scholars and poets of the Renaissance.</note>, whose vast and secret reading of manifold disciplines I so embrace that I admire it, and so admire it that I do not cease to commend it. Thus it happens that I consider it a triumph to be placed by him outside the "risk of learning" <note>He feels his reputation is safe once validated by such a scholar.</note>. 

Regarding your request for a list of my books, that is laborious and useless for me. It will be enough if you serve my needs as time requires. Currently, I desire Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century author of an encyclopedia of the liberal arts.</note> and Seneca’s *Natural Questions*, provided they are corrected manuscripts; for the works of the Sibyl that we have here are in need of repair. If I can buy them in printed form, it will be more pleasing to me; if not, they will return to you after a short "right of return" <note>original: "postliminio"; a legal term for the restoration of rights to a person returning from captivity.</note>. Farewell, my hope and the hope of good disciplines, and continue to love me. Ferrara, the Nones of December, 1489.

**Q** <note>The letter 'Q' is a large red initial in the original.</note> **From a letter of Ermolao to Giovanni Pico.**

Although I love these letters of yours because they flow, because they are not affected, and because they do not just "not know" care but actually reject it—that is, they do not receive it by design and they exclude it when it approaches and desires to be brought in—so that there are indeed traces of diligence in them, but they are in a way suppressed and repudiated. I am not so skillful that I can look into your genius and estimate its magnitude and fruitfulness. This much seems clear—and perhaps I am not mistaken—where you are aiming and directing your efforts, as well as where you are likely to end up and what you will achieve shortly. Nothing is more noble than that talent of yours, nothing more delightful; and let it be said once and for all, it expresses nothing, however roughly...

**LETTERS**

...if such natural talent should be called thus, which has produced fruits that should not be despised even by those of mature age and practiced learning. Consider how great you are, as I hear, in poetry: what spirit, what success, what strength, and finally what nobility and splendor in every act, especially in literature. What of when you act the philosopher? What memory, what great subtlety, what speed of mind agreeing with the vigor of the entire body. But I am carried away into your praises against my will—or rather, most willingly—for everyone most desires that which turns them toward itself even when they are unwilling and reluctant. That ambition of being praised by learned peers will be granted to you. A time more suitable for this duty will certainly be given. Now I come to the rest. <space> From a letter of Hermolao to Giovanni Pico. <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493) was a Venetian scholar and diplomat who famously corresponded with Pico regarding the relationship between rhetoric and philosophy.</note>

**G**ratulated I have this age for a path of such great learning that it knows almost everything; with such great care that it seems to know nothing at all <note>original: "nihil omnino scire uideatur"—a compliment on Pico’s effortless mastery, or "sprezzatura."</note>. I see you are an excellent poet, and a most eminent orator either now or shortly to be. I observe that you have become first an Aristotelian philosopher, and now also a Platonic one. I see that Greek letters—which alone could be missed in you, and without which you were going to achieve nothing—you have not only learned but drunk in; and this with such ease and speed that you yourself do not remember ever being ignorant of Greek letters, nor could you persuade others of it. This I proclaim of my friend Girolamo Donato <note>Girolamo Donato (c. 1457–1511) was a Venetian humanist and diplomat known for his Greek scholarship.</note> no less gladly than truly. I would urge you and the rest. <space> From a letter of Jacopo Antiquari to Angelo Poliziano. <note>Jacopo Antiquari (1444–1512) was a high-ranking secretary in the Milanese court and a patron of the arts.</note>

**O**nce, therefore, the offspring of long incubation tortured us in expectation; but having accepted Pico as a sponsor for the security of your name—whose entire life is full of glories, and by whom I seek with all my prayers to be received into the flock of friends on your behalf, and whose footsteps I always adore—whatever is born at home from your flock of fattened birds <note>original: "altilium cohorte"—a metaphor for Poliziano's literary works.</note> that is worth seeing, reading, or building, you should send it out, intending to hold all those in your strings who are led by some image of virtue or harmony. Farewell.

Angelo Poliziano to his friend Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, greetings <note>original: "S." stands for "Salutem," the standard Roman greeting.</note>.
**H**eretofore almost always (too shamelessly perhaps), I burned with the desire for perpetual fame, such that I considered surviving glory as everything. But since what I was writing hardly promised even the antiquity of a name, you, Pico, emerged to provide what I could not. Specifically, by dedicating the commentary *On the One and the Being* <note>original: "de uno & ente"—Pico's famous treatise (1491) attempting to reconcile the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle.</note> (for so you titled it), in which you recall the streams flowing through the Lyceum <note>The school of Aristotle.</note> and the Academy <note>The school of Plato.</note> to a single head, and you join our theology with a philosophy that is more one than twin. Therefore, I now seek the grass of Glaucus <note>original: "glauci gramen"—referring to the sea-god Glaucus who became immortal after eating a magical herb; Poliziano suggests Pico's work gives him immortality.</note> to live eternally through you. But posterity will also one day tell of you and with you: that there was once a certain Poliziano whom the great Pico himself, the light of all learning, esteemed so much that he did not hesitate to dedicate to him even his most beautiful book on the highest matters. I thank you, therefore, for immortality—and these thanks are immortal. Farewell.

Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Germain de Ganay, President at Paris, gives greetings.
**Y**ou wish to be more certain about the death of Pico della Mirandola, which seems to you still uncertain; you certainly wish to grieve more heavily, Germain. For while you have grieved heavily until now over this ambiguous loss, once you are made certain, you will, I think, soon grieve most heavily. It was perhaps better to mourn a doubtful loss than to be tortured by a certain one. Alas, what do you ask, my most longed-for Germain? I would rather remain in doubt. Nor can I at present make you certain without tears. This past November, on the day when Charles, King of the French, entered our city of Florence <note>November 17, 1494. Charles VIII's invasion was a pivotal moment in Italian history.</note>, our Mirandola left us, affecting the learned with almost as much grief as the King meanwhile brought joy to the city. Thus the provident genius of the place compensated for the mourning of the scholars with the joy of the people; and...

# LETTERS

...for the extinguished light of philosophy, he meanwhile kindled a royal light. Perhaps so that Florence would not see a darker day: the light of Mirandola was extinguished on earth and returned to heaven. For indeed, **Pico** migrated from this shadow of life with such cheerful security that he seemed, without a doubt, to be returning from a kind of exile to his heavenly homeland. You desire, furthermore, to know what Pico once composed, or what he was recently composing: he wrote the *Hexameron* <note>original: "Exameron"; a treatise on the six days of Biblical creation</note>, the *Apology* <note>Pico's defense of his 900 controversial theses</note>, and *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de uno & ente"</note>, as well as several letters. Whatever he had composed regarding fervent love during his youth, he later condemned with a more mature judgment and wished to be utterly destroyed; it cannot be published without doing him an injustice. I certainly knew the final will of this pious man. For in age, Pico was a son to me; in familiarity, a brother; and in love, truly another self <note>original: "alter ego"</note>. He was daily laboring on three things: the harmony of **Aristotle** with **Plato**, commentaries on the sacred scriptures, and refutations of the <term>astrologers</term> <note>Pico’s famous work "Disputationes adversus astrologiam divinatricem," which argued against the idea that stars control human destiny</note>. All these were argued with as much eloquence as subtlety; yet, while they were brilliant in style, they were sketched in such strange and obscure characters that they could hardly be read by him. Therefore, they have neither been completed nor revised by him, nor can they be transcribed by others, unless perhaps by divination. For if they could be, we would not miss our Pico so much as if he were absent, nor would we suspect him to be dead. But his pious nephew, **Giovanni Francesco**, powerful in letters and intellect, strives daily to rescue them from darkness into light, and describes the life and deeds of his uncle. Receive, finally, this epigram of ours regarding him: "Priests rarely allow the more secret mysteries to be seen and immediately hide them away; so God showed to mortals the divine philosopher **Giovanni Pico of Mirandola**, mature in his thirtieth year." So that you may know the remaining loss of letters made this autumn in Florence: our **Angelo Poliziano** <note>A renowned poet and scholar, and close friend of Lorenzo de' Medici and Pico</note>, most learned in the Latin and Greek languages, migrated from this life this past September before the death of Pico, in his fortieth year. He had already published his *Miscellanies*, his *Silvae* <note>A collection of occasional poems</note>, and certain declamations and several letters—all composed with sharp insight and elegance. He also daily noted down many things necessary for elegance in uncertain characters, just like Pico, so that in both men, a very heavy loss of literature has occurred. 

March 23, 1494.

***

->**Marsilio Ficino the Florentine to Giovanni Francesco, Count of Mirandola, greetings.**<-

I sent a brief letter to France regarding the death and praises of Pico after your departure. However, one may gather long and singular praises of Pico from my many writings throughout, especially from the later books of my letters. There are now twelve of them printed: from the preface to **Plotinus**, from the book *On the Sun*, and from the commentaries on the *Timaeus* and *Parmenides* <note>Plato's dialogues, which Ficino famously translated and commented upon</note>. Accept this epitaph for him: "Priests rarely allow the more secret mysteries to be seen; they immediately hide them away. So God showed to mortals the divine philosopher Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, mature in his thirtieth year." Let the epitaph end here. God seems to have given all things to Giovanni Pico: the most abundant goods of soul, body, and fortune. If only He had granted a longer span of life. But it is not right to accuse Providence in this. For if God had led him to the summit in a very short time, beyond the powers of nature, perhaps he could not have progressed to anything better. Truly, the mobility of nature does not allow one to stand still in the same place; yet, perfected virtue does not permit a relapse into something worse. But these and other things of that kind you yourself have written better and more extensively in the *Life of Pico*—not so much to illuminate him (for who can add light to the sun?) but so that, by clearing away the clouds, you might bring his hidden but light-worthy works into the clear. Therefore, mortals will wonderfully commend your great piety toward your uncle, and God will judge it worthy of no small rewards.

November 1, 1495.

## Twelve rules of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, partly inciting and partly directing men in the spiritual battle.

<summary>This page features letters from Marsilio Ficino reflecting on the deaths of the brilliant scholars Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and Angelo Poliziano, emphasizing Pico's unfinished intellectual projects and his spiritual legacy.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Angelo Poliziano, Renaissance humanism, Aristotle, Plato, Astrology, Florence, Neo-Platonism</keywords>

--- Page 89 ---
<meta>This page continues a series of spiritual instructions, likely following an introductory letter or preface. The text focuses on practical "rules" for maintaining a virtuous life amidst worldly and spiritual struggles.</meta>

# LETTERS

->**The First Rule:**<- If the path of virtue seems harsh to a person—because we must continually fight against the flesh, the devil, and the world—let them remember that whatever life they choose, even according to the ways of the world, they will still have to endure many adversities, sorrows, inconveniences, and hardships.

->**The Second Rule:**<- Let them remember that in worldly matters, the struggle is longer, more laborious, and more fruitless; in those affairs, labor is the only end of labor, and the ultimate result is eternal punishment.

->**The Third Rule:**<- Let them remember that it is foolish to believe one can reach heaven except through this kind of struggle. Just as our head, Christ <note>The "head" refers to Christ as the leader of the "body" of the Church, a common metaphor in Christian theology.</note>, did not ascend into heaven except by the cross, the condition of the servant should not be better than the condition of the master.

->**The Fourth Rule:**<- Let them remember that this struggle is not only to be endured with difficulty, but to be desired—even if no reward were to come to us from it—simply so that we may be conformed to Christ our God and Lord. Every time you resist a temptation or do violence to one of your senses <note>This refers to "mortification of the senses," or intentionally denying physical pleasures to strengthen the spirit.</note>, think of which part of Christ's cross you are being made like. When you resist gluttony and afflict your sense of taste, remember that he was given gall and vinegar to drink. When you pull your hands back from stealing something that pleases you, think of his hands fixed to the wood of the cross for your sake. If you resist pride, remember him who, though he was in the form of God <note>original: "in forma dei"</note>, took the form of a servant for you and humbled himself even unto death on a cross. When you are tempted by anger, remember him who was God and the most just of all men; yet, when he saw himself treated like a thief, mocked, spat upon, scourged, afflicted with every insult, and counted among criminals, he never showed any sign of anger or indignation. Instead, bearing all things with great patience, he answered everyone with the utmost gentleness. By running through each example in this way, you will find that there is no suffering that does not, in some part, make you conformed to Christ.

->**The Fifth Rule:**<- Do not trust in those <term>twelve weapons</term> <note>This is likely a reference to the "Twelve Weapons of Spiritual Battle," a popular devotional work by the Italian humanist Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note>, nor in any other human remedy, but only in the power of Jesus Christ, who said: "Trust, for I have overcome the world." And elsewhere: "The prince of this world is cast out." Therefore, let us also trust in his power alone to be able to conquer the world and overcome the devil. For this reason, we must always seek his help through prayer and through the prayers of his saints.

->**The Sixth Rule:**<- Remember that when you have conquered one temptation, another is always to be expected, because the devil always circles around looking for someone to devour. Therefore, it is necessary to always serve in fear and to say with the prophet: "I will stand upon my watch."

->**The Seventh Rule:**<- Do not merely avoid being conquered by the devil when he tempts you, but conquer him yourself. This happens when you not only refrain from sinning, but take the very thing he used to tempt you as an opportunity for some good. For example, if he offers you some good work of yours so that you might fall into vanity, you should immediately think of it not as your own work, but as a gift from God. Humble yourself and judge yourself to be ungrateful to God for his many benefits.

->**The Eighth Rule:**<- When you fight, fight as if you are about to win and then enjoy perpetual peace; perhaps God will grant this to you by his grace, and the devil, shamed by your victory, will not return. But once you have won, conduct yourself as if you are about to fight again. In battle, always be mindful of victory; in victory, always be mindful of the battle.

->**The Ninth Rule:**<- Even if you feel well-fortified and prepared on all sides, always flee from occasions for sinning; for as the wise man says: "He who loves danger shall perish in it."

->**The Tenth Rule:**<- Always meet temptations at the very beginning, and "dash the little ones of Babylon against the rock." <note>This is an allegorical interpretation of Psalm 137:9. In medieval and Renaissance spirituality, the "little ones" or "infants" of Babylon represent the very first stirrings of sinful thoughts, which must be destroyed before they grow into full-blown sins.</note> The rock, moreover, is Christ, because a remedy is prepared too late <note>A paraphrase of the Roman poet Ovid: "principiis obsta," or "resist the beginnings."</note> if the evil has already grown strong.

& i i i <note>This is a signature mark, used by printers to help binders assemble the pages of a book in the correct order.</note>

It draws heavily on the idea that the spiritual life is a form of warfare that requires both divine grace and the redirection of sinful impulses into virtuous acts.</summary>

->LETTERS<-

The eleventh rule: remember that although in the very conflict of temptation the battle may seem bitter, it is nevertheless far sweeter to overcome the temptation than to give in to the sin toward which you incline. Many are deceived in this because they do not compare the sweetness of victory to the sweetness of sin. Instead, they compare the struggle itself to the pleasure of the sin. Yet a person who has experienced a thousand times what it is like to yield to temptation should, at least once, try to experience what it is like to overcome it.

The twelfth rule: when you are tempted, do not believe that you have been forsaken by God, or that you are somehow less pleasing to God, or less just and perfect. Remember that after Paul saw the divine essence, he suffered a temptation of the flesh. God permitted him to be tempted so that he would not be tempted by pride. In this, a person should notice that even Paul—who was a "chosen vessel" <note>original: "uas electionis," a traditional title for St. Paul</note> and was caught up even to the third heaven—was still in danger of becoming proud of his virtues. As he says of himself: "lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh <note>original: "stimulus carnis meae"</note> to buffet me." Therefore, above all other temptations, a person must especially fortify themselves against the temptation of pride; for pride is the root of all evils. Against this, the unique remedy is to always reflect on how God humbled himself for us even to the cross, and how death will humble us—even against our will—to the point that we become food for worms.

Twelve weapons of spiritual combat which ought to be kept ready at hand when the lust for sinning subdues the mind:

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Brief and meager pleasure. | Eternal reward; eternal punishment. |
| Companions: disgust and anxiety. | The dignity and nature of man. |
| The loss of a greater good. | Peace of a good mind. |
| Life is a sleep and a shadow. | God’s benefits. |
| Death is imminent and unforeseen. | The cross of Christ. |
| The suspicion of a lack of repentance. | The testimony of martyrs and examples of saints. |

Twelve conditions of a lover:
1. To love one only and to despise all things for their sake.
2. To consider anyone unhappy who is not with the beloved.
3. To suffer all things to be with the beloved, even death.
4. To adorn oneself to please the beloved.
5. To be with the beloved however one can; if not in reality, then at least in thought.
6. To love all things that belong to the beloved: all friends, their home, clothes, and images.
7. To desire praises for the beloved and to be unable to suffer any disgrace toward them.
8. To believe all the highest things of the beloved, and to desire that everyone else believes the same.
9. To wish even to suffer some discomfort for the beloved, and for that discomfort to be sweet.
10. To weep with the beloved often; if they are absent, out of sorrow; if present, out of joy.
11. To always languish and always burn with desire for the beloved.
12. To serve the beloved while thinking nothing of reward or payment. 

We are usually led to this kind of service <note>referring to the service of God</note> primarily by three causes. The first is when the service itself is desirable for its own sake. The second is when the one we serve is in himself truly good and lovable—as we are accustomed to say we serve someone because of their virtues. The third is when that person bestowed many benefits upon you before you even began to serve. 

All three of these are found in God. First, for His service, nothing is newly received that is not already good for us, both for the soul and for the body; for to serve Him is nothing other than to move toward Him—that is, toward the highest good. Similarly, He is the best, the most beautiful, and the wisest; He possesses all the conditions that usually move us to love someone and serve them freely. Finally, He has bestowed the highest benefits upon us, since He created us from nothing and redeemed us from hell through the blood of His son.

<meta>This page continues a theological commentary, likely on the Psalms (specifically Psalm 16, known as Psalm 15 in the Vulgate), focusing on the spiritual disposition of the believer.</meta>

# LETTERS

->**Preserve me, O Lord.**<-

If anyone who is perfected wishes to examine their own state, they face one particular danger: that they might become proud of their own virtue. Therefore, David <note>The traditional author of the Psalms.</note>, speaking in the character of a righteous man concerning his spiritual state, begins with this phrase: **preserve me**. This expression, when properly considered, removes every occasion for pride. For if a person could acquire something by their own power, they could also preserve it for themselves by their own power. Therefore, whoever asks to be preserved by God in a state of virtue signifies by this that they did not acquire that virtue by themselves from the beginning. Furthermore, one who remembers that they attained virtue not by their own power, but by the power of God, cannot be proud of it. Instead, they are more likely to be humbled before God, according to that saying of the Apostle <note>St. Paul, in 1 Corinthians 4:7.</note>: *What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?* <note>original: "Quid habes quod non accepisti? et si accepisti quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis?"</note> There are, therefore, two phrases that we ought always to have in our mouths: one is *Have mercy on me, O God* <note>original: "miserere mei deus"</note> when we remember our sins; the other is *Preserve me, O God* when we remember our virtues.

->**Because I have hoped in you.**<-

This is the one thing that allows us to obtain what we ask from God: namely, when we hope that we will obtain it. If we observe these two conditions—that we never ask anything from God unless it is for our own well-being <note>term: "salutary" — things that are beneficial for the soul's salvation.</note>, and that we ask for what we desire ardently, with a firm hope that God may hear us—our prayers will never be in vain. Therefore, when we do not obtain what we ask, it is either because that thing is harmful to us (for we do not always know what we should ask for, as Christ says), or because—as Jesus said—*whatever you ask in my name will be given to you.* <note>John 14:13.</note> This name, "Jesus," means "Savior"; therefore, nothing is truly asked in the name of Jesus unless it leads to the salvation of the one asking. Alternatively, He does not hear us because even if we ask for good things, we do not ask *well*—that is, we ask with little hope. For one who hopes timidly asks coldly. This is why James said: *let him ask in faith, with no doubting.* <note>James 1:6; original: "postulet autem in fide nihil haesitans."</note>

->**I said to the Lord: You are my God.**<-

After he has fortified himself against pride, he begins to describe his own state. Indeed, the entire state of the righteous person consists in this phrase: **I said to the Lord: You are my God.** Although this phrase seems common to almost everyone, there are nevertheless few who can truly say it.

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual necessity of humility and hope, arguing that recognizing God as the sole preserver of virtue prevents pride. It outlines the conditions for effective prayer, emphasizing that requests must be for one's salvation and made with unwavering faith.</summary>

...depending on Him: for God acquired nothing from this, that He created the world <note>The Latin transcription 'nundum' is likely a typographical or OCR error for 'mundum' (the world).</note>; and He would lose nothing if the whole world were annihilated. <note>original: "EPISTOLAE"; while this header typically means "Letters," the text here functions as a commentary on scripture.</note>

...who entered paradise and opened the way of life to us, and was the first who rose from the dead; and his resurrection is the cause of our own resurrection. Therefore, those things which we have said concerning the resurrection are to be understood principally as referring to Christ, just as Peter the Apostle declared <note>referring to Peter’s sermon in Acts 2, where he explains that King David was prophesying about Christ's resurrection, not his own</note>. Secondarily, these things can be understood as applying to us, insofar as we are members of the body of Christ, who alone did not see **corruption** <note>original: "corruptionem"; in this context, it refers to the physical decay or putrefaction of a corpse</note>, because his body did not rot within the tomb. **YOU HAVE MADE KNOWN TO ME THE PATHS OF LIFE.**

And because the total happiness of this life consists in the proper vision and enjoyment of God, he then adds:

**YOU WILL FILL ME WITH JOY WITH YOUR FACE.** <note>original: "vultu tuo"; commonly translated in Bibles as "presence" or "countenance"</note>

And because this happiness will endure for eternity, he adds:

**DELIGHTS AT YOUR RIGHT HAND UNTO THE END.**

He says "at your right hand" because our happiness is made complete in the vision and enjoyment of the humanity of Christ, who sits at the right hand of Majesty on high <note>a reference to the session of Christ in heaven as described in Hebrews 1:3</note>, according to that saying of John: "This is..."

**Likewise, from Chapter 94 of the same work.**

At one time, Pico of Mirandola—a man who can never be praised enough—and I spent our spare hours running through the ancient commentators on the sacred Old Testament; especially the Greeks: Diodorus, Philo, Gennadius, Aquila, Origen, Basil, Didymus, Isidore, Apollinaris, Severianus, and many others of that kind. Like all the opinions of the Latin writers, he [Pico] sifts and weighs everything most diligently, comparing them with the opinions of Jewish and Chaldean <note>original: "chaldæorum". From this, truth might be drawn out, obscurity removed, faith strengthened, or impiety refuted.

**From the book on ecclesiastical writers by Johannes, Abbot of Sponheim.** <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a famous German abbot and bibliographer.</note>

Giovanni Pico, Italian by birth, Count of Mirandola and Lord of Concordia: a man most devoted to all good literature. Just as he is most noble by his distinguished blood, so he is most renowned for his truly divine intellect. ->**The External Binding**<-

The manuscript is encased in a worn, reddish-brown leather cover that shows the signs of centuries of use. The binder decorated the surface using a technique known as <term>blind-stamping</term> <note>A method of decoration where heated metal tools are pressed directly into the leather to create a design in relief, without using gold leaf or pigments.</note>. The primary design consists of a grid of intersecting diagonal lines that form a series of diamond shapes.

Within these diamonds, and at the points where the lines cross, the artist stamped small, circular floral rosettes. Along the right-hand edge, there is a vertical border featuring repeating <term>foliate motifs</term> <note>Decorative designs intended to look like leaves or plant life.</note>. 

On the left side of the cover, one can see the remnants of two metal hinges or clasps. These would have originally been used to pull the covers tight, protecting the pages inside from dust and keeping the material from warping. The leather is scuffed and shows patches where the top layer has worn away, revealing the textured history of the book's preservation.

--- Page 113 ---
<meta>This is the opening dedication of a biographical work, likely the Life of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, written by his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola and addressed to Ludovico Sforza.</meta>

# Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola to Ludovico Maria Sforza Visconti, "the Anglus," <note>The title "Anglus" was used by the Sforza family to claim a legendary descent from the kings of England.</note> Duke of Milan. Many greetings.

Most illustrious prince, among those who have handed down the lives of famous men, recorded in writing for the study of future generations, some have done so because they were bound by ties of blood or indebted by the education they received. They acted so that the names of these men would not fade away through the ravages of time <note>original: "edaci uetustate," literally "devouring antiquity."</note>, but would instead be rescued entirely from the injustice of being forgotten. This was the kind of devotion that Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman lawyer and author.</note> showed to his uncle Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*.</note>, and which Porphyry showed to his teacher Plotinus. 

Others, however, achieved this same goal even more successfully. That is, they did not care so much for the eternal memory of the deceased as they did for providing a model for the lives of those who survive them. Therefore, we find that Jerome recorded the life of Hilarion, Athanasius that of Anthony, [Sulpicius] Severus that of Martin, and Paulinus that of Ambrose. They committed to paper their tireless studies, their most disciplined characters <note>original: "mores exactissimos."</note>, and their most excellent works. Through these writings, the glory of God spread throughout the world, and men were guided toward living well and blessedly.

<summary>In this introductory letter, Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola explains to the Duke of Milan that writing biographies serves two purposes: honoring the dead and providing moral guidance for the living.</summary>

<keywords>Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, Ludovico Sforza, biography, moral examples, Pliny the Elder, St. Jerome, St. Ambrose, Duke of Milan</keywords>

--- Page 114 ---
THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, A MAN MOST ACCOMPLISHED IN EVERY BRANCH OF LEARNING, PUBLISHED BY GIANFRANCESCO, SON OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE GALEOTTO PICO.

Beginning to write the life of Giovanni Pico, my uncle, I consider it paramount to state to my readers (lest it be suspected that as his nephew or his student, I might say something out of favor in the manner of flatterers) that nothing here is granted to friendship, nothing to family, and nothing of his great favors toward me—which were indeed very great—is repaid with fictitious praise. Indeed, my narrative is as far removed from adulation as the need for flattery was absent. I have taken great care that readers do not judge me to have lied or been excessive in my praise. 

If I were to commit to writing everything I have conceived about him, the danger might perhaps be that his own lofty virtues, or those who champion them, might accuse me of being too sparing. This can be seen from this very argument: many highly polished writings by the learned men of our age—and even the foremost among them—have provided the most abundant testimony, not only to what we are about to say, but also while he yet enjoyed this light and after he exchanged it for a better one <note>A common Renaissance euphemism for death</note>. They excelled in their proclamations of his character and learning. I have ordered several of these to be appended at the end of this book, following his own commentaries, so that a firmer trust might be placed in witnesses who are not of his own family. 

<margin>Paternal lineage</margin> Setting aside his paternal lineage (though it is handed down in memory that its origins were drawn from Emperor Constantine through his great-grandson Pico, from whom the surname of the entire family is derived), we shall take our beginning from the time of his birth itself. This is both because he perhaps conferred no less honor upon the family than he received from it, and because I have judged that his own natural gifts of mind and the remaining sequence of his whole life and death—which I have either drawn from my own ears and eyes or received from most serious witnesses—ought to be opened up. Thus, I have set aside the family tree and the famous deeds of his ancestors to be recounted elsewhere. 

In the year 1463 from the Virgin’s birth <note>original: "Anno a partu virginis," referring to the year 1463 AD</note>, while Pope Pius II presided over the Church and Frederick III held the reins of the Roman Empire, his mother Julia, of the noble Boiardo family <note>The same family that produced the famous poet Matteo Maria Boiardo</note>, bore him to his father Gianfrancesco as her final child. <margin>Mother Julia. Gianfrancesco. Father Galeotto. Antonio Maria, brothers. Albertus Pius.</margin> For she had already given birth to Galeotto the elder (from whom I was born) and Antonio Maria, as well as two sisters. One of these sisters had already born Alberto Pio, one of the princes of Carpi, to her husband Leonello; she is now the consort of Prince Rodolfo Gonzaga. The other, after her first husband Pino Ordelaffi, prince of Forlì, had died, granted a second marriage to the Count of Monteagnano. 

A portent of no small significance appeared before his birth. <margin>The omen of the flame</margin> Indeed, a circular flame was seen to stand over the wall of his mother's bedchamber, and soon after to vanish. This was perhaps suggesting to us that he would be most similar to a circular figure <note>In Renaissance philosophy, the circle was the most perfect shape, symbolizing completion and divinity</note> in the perfection of his intellect, he who was to come forth among mortals in that same hour and be celebrated throughout the entire globe for the excellence of his name. His mind was destined to always seek heavenly things like fire, and his fiery eloquence, in harmony with his inflamed mind, was at some point to celebrate our God (who is a consuming fire) with all its strength—yet, like that flame, it was to be hidden from the sight of men immediately after it vanished.
