# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...so that they might announce these things and raise the minds of men from the earth to the heavens. He was of distinguished and noble appearance: tall and stately in stature, with a soft complexion. His face was beautiful overall, pale in color but interspersed with a becoming blush. He had bluish-gray, watchful eyes, and blond, naturally styled hair; his teeth were also white and even. Under his mother's authority, he was sent to masters and schools of learning. He cultivated the study of the humanities with such an ardent spirit that, in a short time, he was rightfully placed among the preeminent poets and orators of that era. 

<margin>A swift intellect</margin> Indeed, he was extremely quick in learning, endowed with such a ready wit that he could recite poems heard only once—both in their proper and in reverse order—to the great wonder of all. He retained them with a most tenacious memory. This is usually the opposite for others; for it often happens by nature that those with quick minds do not have strong memories, while those who grasp things with labor prove to be more tenacious retainers of what they have learned. 

<margin>As a boy, he was skilled in Canon Law</margin> When he was in his fourteenth year, at the command of his mother—who vehemently desired him to be initiated into holy orders—he moved to Bologna for the purpose of learning Canon Law <note>original: "iuris pontificii", the law and regulations of the Church</note>. Having sampled this for two years, and finding it full of nothing but dry traditions, he turned his attention elsewhere. Yet this was not without producing good fruit; for even then, as a boy of tender age, he compiled a certain summary or breviary from the letters of the Supreme Pontiffs—which are called Decretals—in which he concluded all the meanings of those sanctions as concisely as possible. For seasoned professors, this would have been no small work. 

But as a hungry explorer of nature's secrets, leaving these worn paths behind, he devoted himself entirely to the speculation of the intellect and to philosophy, both human and divine. For the sake of attaining this, he traveled through the literary schools not only of Italy but also of France, seeking out the famous teachers of that time with the utmost care, in the manner of Plato and Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a famous wandering philosopher of antiquity</note>. He devoted such tireless effort to those studies that he was considered both a consummate theologian and a philosopher, even while he was still "in the blade" <note>original: "in herbis", a metaphor meaning he was still very young or in the early stages of his career</note>. 

He had spent seven years among them when, eager for human praise and glory (for he had not yet been warmed by divine love, as will become clear), he moved to Rome. There, wishing to show how much envy from back-biters awaited him in the future, 

<margin>Nine hundred disputes proposed in Rome</margin> he proposed nine hundred questions <note>The famous "900 Theses" covering all branches of knowledge</note> concerning logic, mathematics, and natural and divine matters. These were drawn not only from the cabinets of the Latins and the chests of the Greeks, but were also unearthed from the mysteries of the Hebrews, and tracked down from the secrets of the Chaldeans and Arabs. He also wove into those questions much concerning the ancient and obscure philosophy of Pythagoras, Hermes Trismegistus, and Orpheus; much too concerning the Kabbalah <note>The Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation of the Bible</note>—that is, the secret reception of Hebrew dogmas—which 

<margin>Origen and Hilary</margin> Origen and Hilary among our own authors primarily mention. He also included much concerning natural magic, which he taught was separated by no small distance from the impious and wicked kind; and he proved this most elegantly by the testimony of many. Nor were seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas lacking—his own inventions and meditations, adapted to elucidate any questions of philosophy. To these he added a new method of philosophizing through numbers. He posted all of these at once in public places so they might be more easily publicized, promising that he would pay the expenses of those who had traveled to Rome from remote lands for the sake of debating. 

But because of the hostility of detractors (which, like fire, always seeks the heights), he was never able to ensure that a day for the debate was set. For this reason, he remained in Rome for a year. During that time, those fault-finders did not dare to attack him openly or in free examination. Instead, corrupted by pestilential envy—as many indeed believed—they tried to insult him with tricks and schemes, and to undermine him with hidden weapons. It was thought that he had provoked this malice against himself chiefly because many who had long applied themselves to literary business out of ambition or perhaps greed believed that his success would be a mark against them.

-># **THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**<-

If that young man—overflowing with the accumulated wealth of his ancestors and with vast learning, like a fertile, luxuriant field—did not fear to put his learning and genius to the test in the world's foremost city <note>Rome</note> regarding natural and divine matters (many of which had not been approached by our people for several centuries); and when he realized that nothing could be moved against his learning with the engines of truth, his enemies brought forth the siege-engines of calumny. They shouted that thirteen of his nine hundred questions were suspect regarding the true faith. To these critics, some perhaps joined themselves who—because those questions were unusual to their ears—attacked them with more piety than perhaps erudition, under the pretext of religious zeal. Nevertheless, many and indeed celebrated doctors of theology had previously approved those same questions as pious and pure, and had signed their names to them. Among this group was numbered Bonfrancesco of Reggio <margin>Bonfrancesco</margin>, <margin>of Reggio</margin> <margin>Bishop</margin>, the Bishop: a man of all-encompassing learning, the sharpest judgment, and distinguished by the gravity of his character, who at that time was acting as the legate in Rome to the Supreme Pontiff on behalf of the Duke of Ferrara. However, those babblers attempted nothing against him, fearing perhaps that they could not undermine his reputation, since whatever he handled he submitted to the correction of Mother Church and the Pope. But Pico, not enduring this damage to his reputation, published an **Apology** <margin>The Apology</margin> <note>A formal written defense of his ideas, titled *Apologia*</note>. It is certainly a varied and elegant work, filled with knowledge of many things worth knowing, yet it was composed in only twenty nights of study. By this publication, it was made clearer than light that his conclusions could indeed receive Catholic interpretations, and that those who had previously barked against them should be convicted of insolence and ignorance. In the manner of a most Christian man, he committed the book itself and whatever he was to write in the future to the judgment of Mother Church and her most holy leader. For he was most firmly persuaded that this ought to be done either expressly or tacitly, as if he were offering that saying of Augustine: *I am able to err, but I cannot be a heretic* <note>original: "Errare possum hereticus esse non possum"</note>, since one is a human trait, while the other belongs to a perverse and obstinate will. 

But when the Supreme Pontiff Innocent VIII <margin>Innocent</margin> <margin>the Eighth</margin> <margin>Pope</margin> learned through the publication of the **Apology** that those conclusions, which had previously been harassed by slanders, were interpreted in a Catholic sense and relieved of the mark of crime; and since some to whom the examination of the conclusions had been entrusted reported that snares could be placed before the faithful if some of those questions (which lay about in a raw and unexplained manner of disputation) were to wander about everywhere, he forbade the reading of the little book <note>The original 900 Theses</note> in which they were contained. All these things are clearly seen through a Diploma (which they call a "Brief") of the Supreme Pontiff Alexander VI <margin>Alexander</margin> <margin>the Sixth</margin>, under whom we now live. We have thought it right to hand this over to the printers along with the **Apology** itself. 

Indeed, at the very end of the **Apology**, Pico had already done by whatever reasoning he could what the Pope later provided by his authority. He had specifically entreated friends and enemies, the learned and the unlearned <margin>Note</margin>, to read the **Apology** but to pass over the little book of unexplained conclusions without reading it. This was because it contained many things that were not meant to be spread in the streets, but which he had undertaken to be disputed in secret gatherings among a few learned men. Having intended a scholastic exercise in the manner of the academies, he had proposed many impious dogmas of the ancient philosophers—namely Alexander <margin>Alexander</margin> <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a commentator on Aristotle</note> and Averroes <margin>Averroes</margin> <note>A medieval Muslim philosopher whose interpretations of Aristotle were controversial in the Church</note> and many others—which he had always asserted, professed, and preached, both publicly and privately, to deviate no less from the paths of true and right philosophy than from the paths of faith. And in this manner, speaking about that little book of nine hundred conclusions, he concluded his apologetic work: "Therefore, let those who hate me not read those things because they are mine; let those who love me not read them because from those things which are mine, they might imagine many things which are not ours." Furthermore, by the immense goodness of God <margin>The goodness of God</margin>, which elicits good even from evil, he judged (as he reported to me) that it had been brought about that the calumny...

# **THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

<margin>Conversion to God</margin> All those false and malevolent accusations inflicted upon him served to correct his true errors. As he wandered in the darkness, a most brilliant light began to shine, allowing him to see how far he had strayed from the path of truth. Previously, he had been both hungry for glory and inflamed by vain love, moved by the charms of women. Indeed, many women—drawn by his physical beauty and the grace of his face, added to his vast learning, great wealth, and noble birth—burned with love for him. Not shrinking from their devotion, he had for a short time neglected the way of life and drifted into luxuries. But, awakened by that aforementioned conflict <note>original: "simultate illa"; likely referring to his legal and theological troubles with the Church over his 900 Theses</note>, he restrained his mind which had been dissolving in luxury and turned it toward Christ. He exchanged feminine blandishments for the joys of the heavenly fatherland. Neglecting the breeze of "little glory" <note>original: "gloriolæ"</note> which he had once sought, he began to seek the glory of God and the utility of the Church with his whole mind, composing his character so that henceforth he could be approved even by the judgment of an enemy.

When he learned that his glorious reputation had immediately begun to fly through both neighboring and remote lands, many of those held to be the most learned philosophers flocked to him as if to a "market of good arts" <margin>Cicero</margin> (as <term>Cicero<note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator whose style was the gold standard for Renaissance humanists.</note></term> says). They came either to engage in literary contests or, for those with a more upright disposition of mind, to hear and hold fast to the healthy doctrines of right living. These teachings were sought all the more because they flowed from a man who was both highly learned and equally noble, and who had once followed the devious, winding paths of voluptuous softness. Such things seem to have the greatest influence in instilling moral discipline in the minds of listeners: those things which are good by their own nature, and which proceed from a teacher who has turned to the paths of justice from the distorted and crooked path of lust.

<margin>Burned love poems</margin> He had toyed with loves in elegiac poetry; these, composed in five books, he committed to the flames for the sake of religion. He likewise toyed with many things in <term>Tuscan rhymes<note>original: "Rhithmis... hetrufcis"; referring to poetry written in the Italian vernacular (Tuscan), as opposed to Latin.</note></term>, which a similar fire consumed for the same reason. <margin>The study of sacred literature.</margin> Embracing sacred literature with the most burning zeal, he immediately offered to the temple of God—as if the first fruits of his harvest—a work on the six days of creation in Genesis and the day of rest, titled the <term>Heptaplus<note>From the Greek for "sevenfold"; Pico’s work offering seven layers of interpretation for the opening of Genesis.</note></term>. At that time, he was twenty-eight years old. This work was perfect in genius and elaborated with industry, filled with the sublime dogmas of the philosophers as well as the deepest mysteries of our Christian theology. It was woven together with a sevenfold variety of narration, with the number of chapters in each of the seven expositions fitting the title of the book perfectly.

<margin>What the Epistles of Paul declare about sacred literature.</margin> However, because it unearths things from the bosom of nature and contains difficult evolutions of divine questions—and due to the most hidden meanings of the Prophet <note>referring to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis</note> and the elegance of the language—it does not offer itself everywhere to those who are unrefined in philosophy and eloquence. Rather, the use of that precious and rare furniture is prepared for the few. He himself, noticing this, made a charming mention of the matter at the end of the same preface. When he first tasted sacred literature, he exulted with joy, finding there not only true wisdom but also true eloquence. To omit many of the praises he brought to the New Testament, he used to say that the <term>Epistles of Paul<note>The letters written by the Apostle Paul in the New Testament.</note></term> surpassed the writings of all orators in eloquence. He specifically cited the night-studies of <term>Cicero</term> and even <term>Demosthenes</term> (the primary master of the craft of speaking, as he called him). He did not mean that Paul's letters were like theirs—"singed with curling irons" <note>original: "calamistris inustae"; a classical metaphor for a style that is overly artificial or superficially decorated</note>, stuffed with dyes scraped from everywhere and crowded with curled locks—but rather that they breathed and tasted of a true, solid eloquence, supported by true sentiments and true art. They were, to put it briefly, not intentionally stuffed with the "riches of the Egyptians" <note>A common biblical metaphor used by Saint Augustine to describe using pagan learning (Egyptian gold) for Christian purposes.</note>. Furthermore, he proclaimed all the <margin>Eloquence of the Old Law.</margin> utterances of the Old Law to be full of the most consummate science and wisdom; <margin>Augustine</margin> as many others have done, and as <term>Augustine</term> showed brilliantly in his book *On Christian Doctrine*.

<margin>Music cultivated</margin> ...interpretation only of the Lord’s Prayer, and approximately fifty Rules for Living Well—which were certainly too brief and undeveloped, as he had intended to expand them into many chapters if he had lived longer. He also composed two prayers to God: one in Italian <note>original: "rhithmis hetruſcis" — literally "Etruscan rhythms," a common humanist way to refer to the Tuscan/Italian vernacular.</note> verse and the other in elegiac meter, so that when he was worn out by weightier studies, he could soothe his mind by singing to the lyre. Indeed, in his earliest years of youth, he had so cultivated every kind of musical art that the melodies he devised and the harmonies he noted with proper arrangements became famous. We also saw many things in his desk, though they were disorganized; nevertheless, I thought something useful could be compiled from them, especially an explanation of the Psalms.

<margin>Letters of many forms</margin> But also about fifty letters written at various times—some personal, some doctrinal, some exhortatory—emerged along with the oration <note>This refers to the famous *Oration on the Dignity of Man*.</note> which he would have delivered at Rome if the disputation had taken place. This oration breathes the spirit of a most perceptive mind and the richest learning, remarkable for a young man not yet twenty-four years old—as do all his writings, which provide us with the wealthiest testimony of his most fertile eloquence.

<margin>An approved style of speaking</margin> He always used a style that was highly commendable—not borrowed, but natural and multifaceted, according to the variety of subjects. Even if he had (as they say) exhausted the entire "perfume-cabinet" of Isocrates <note>original: "myrothecion" — a Greek term for a collection of rhetorical ornaments or "scents."</note>, he nevertheless maintained a purity and the ornaments of a dignified grace.

<margin>Genres of speaking</margin> For those celebrated genres of speaking—of which Aulus Gellius lists three and Macrobius four—can be gathered from his writings without much effort.
<margin>Copious, Brief, Dry, Flowery, and Rich</margin> There one finds the **copious** style, in which Cicero is almost the master; the **brief** style attributed to Sallust; the **dry** style given to Fronto; and the **rich and flowery** style in which they say Pliny and Symmachus delighted. But perhaps Brutus would not have called this "copiousness" weak, nor Sallust "immoderate." An orator with sound judgment will easily detect that Fronto's "dryness" has been moistened, Sallust's "brevity" extended, and Pliny’s "flowery richness" carried out into a broader field. Add to these the "milky fountain" of Livy—perhaps without the "Paduanism" <note>original: "patauinitate" — a famous ancient linguistic critique of the historian Livy, suggesting his Latin had a regional Paduan accent.</note> he was accused of—along with many "little flowers" <note>stylistic flourishes</note> added from Apuleius.

Yet he did not exercise himself here merely in philosophy borrowed from the Greeks, nor in "Attic Nights" <note>A reference to the miscellany by Aulus Gellius.</note>, nor in fictional "Saturnalia" <note>A reference to the work by Macrobius.</note> constructed almost solely to praise Virgil's *Aeneid*, nor in Roman history, nor in a mere natural history void of the highest and most difficult speculations. Instead, he labored over that wonderful fabric of the world, struggled against the enemies of the most holy Catholic Church, and exhausted himself in banishing the astrologers. He worked at examining theological questions, labored on the harmony between Aristotle and Plato, devoted himself to explaining the sacred scriptures, and spent his efforts in advising and encouraging his friends.

But he was so far from affecting this eloquence of which we speak that he instead condemned those who, searching too scrupulously for "painted enticements" <note>original: "pigmētata lenocinia" — referring to overly ornate or artificial rhetoric.</note>, devoted all the powers of their intellect to investigating the origins of words. All of which turned many people all the more toward admiration of him, because he had spent a long and most diligent time among the writings of those who did not profess Latin literature to be filled with the "flowers of eloquence." Let the excessive lovers of antiquity endure this with a calm mind; for though this may be said concisely and briefly, it is perhaps all the truer for having been proclaimed by men more learned than I: Hermolao Barbaro, Battista the Carmelite <note>The poet Battista Spagnoli Mantovano.</note>, Marsilio Ficino, Matteo Bosso, and many other most learned and eloquent men.

<margin>Speed of reading</margin> He both read through and made excerpts from vast libraries of both Latin and Greek authors with incredible speed; he passed over no commentaries unread, provided the opportunity was given. He had attained such a degree of knowledge concerning the ancient Doctors of the Church that it is difficult to believe even of one who had spent his entire life solely in studying them. Regarding the "modern" <note>original: "neotericis"</note> theologians who used that style commonly called "Parisian" <note>The Scholastic style associated with the University of Paris, often criticized by Humanists for being "unpolished."</note>, he possessed such judgment that if someone had unexpectedly asked him to unravel some abstruse and poorly explained question from one of them, he would open it up with such fertility of mind and unlock it with such skill that...

# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA.

He held the entire body of sayings and teachings of those doctors <note>The "doctors" here refers to the great Scholastic and classical teachers of the Middle Ages and Antiquity.</note> before his eyes and ready for use, and in the same way, he had become acquainted with all their intellectual "families." He had examined every manuscript; nor should you believe him to be so devoted to only one of them (as is the custom among our men) that he would despise the others. For he had been so instructed from his youth—and so disposed in spirit—that he sought the truth in them all. He venerated the truth with equal honor wherever it shone forth, having stripped himself of private bias. What he thought of each of them, at least those who are considered the most famous throughout the world, can be seen in the preface to his *Apology* <note>original: "in Apologiæ pœmio"; Pico's *Apologia* was a defense of his 900 theses written in 1487 after they were challenged by a papal commission.</note>. There, when he recounts the properties and peculiar praises of the Barbarian, Greek, and Latin philosophers, his views are clear. However, whenever mention was made of those philosophers or theologians who wrote in the "French style" of debating <note>The "French style" refers to the Scholastic method of the University of Paris, which relied on rigorous logic and the "disputation" of specific points.</note>, he was accustomed to praise **Thomas Aquinas** <margin>Thomas Aquinas.</margin> above all others, as one who rested more solidly than the rest upon the foundation of truth. He even calls him "the splendor of our theology" in his *Heptaplus* <note>The *Heptaplus* (1489) was Pico's seven-fold explanation of the first chapters of Genesis.</note>. Having been asked about this very frequently, and by me personally, he gave the same answer. Nor should anyone be persuaded to the contrary by certain points contained in his *Apology* that were to be debated—points which might seem openly opposed to Thomas's opinions. For he was then a very young man, eager for glory, and in that most celebrated city <note>Rome, where he intended to hold his great debate.</note>, he sought the fame of his party by defending whatever side he could, in the manner of **Gorgias of Leontini** <margin>Gorgias of Leontini</margin> <note>Gorgias was a famous Greek Sophist known for claiming he could speak on any subject with equal eloquence.</note>. To this I add that out of ten thousand propositions, failing to agree with—or even opposing—three or four of them does not prove a lack of respect. Furthermore, he was most skilled in the art of debating, and he applied himself with frequent and very intense effort to these literary contests while his passion for them was burning. When he was arguing, you could easily perceive the sharpness and vigilance of **Scotus** <margin>The sharpness of Scotus</margin>, the vigor of **Francis** <note>Likely Francis of Meyronnes, a 14th-century follower of Duns Scotus.</note>, and the abundance and multitude of **Aureolus** <margin>Aureolus</margin> <note>Peter Aureolus, a Franciscan philosopher known for his vast commentaries.</note>. Nor were those "nodes" of logic missing—the complex twists and turns—which were supported not so much by tickling subtleties as by genuine weight. When he was responding, you would have seen the strength and power of **Thomas** and the breadth of **Albert** <note>Albert the Great, the teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note>. 

Truly, however, he had long ago sent a "parting message" to these conflicts <note>A polite way of saying he had retired from them.</note>, and day by day he grew more and more to loathe that duty. Indeed, he turned it down even when **Ercole d'Este**, the Duke of Ferrara <margin>Ercole d'Este</margin>, and his messengers most earnestly requested it—even when he personally asked. While the General Synod of the Preaching Friars <note>The Dominicans.</note> was being celebrated in Ferrara, the Duke asked him not to be reluctant to debate. Though he resisted complying for a long time, he finally yielded to the many requests of that Prince, whose love for him was no small thing, and performed the duty. From this, it was debated whether he appeared more skillful or more eloquent, more learned or more kind. From the mouth of the debater, such an alacrity of spirit always shone forth that he seemed to be discussing a pleasant and peaceful matter rather than a sharp and difficult one. Therefore, those who hung on his every word were stirred to a wonderful love for him. 

But he had a frequent adage: <margin>Adage</margin> that such a task was the "duty of a logician, not a philosopher." He also said that those disputations were beneficial which were practiced in a peaceful spirit to track down and search out the truth in private places, without outside judges. But he believed those public ones were most harmful, which were done in the open to show off learning or to catch the "breeze of the common folk" and the applause of the unlearned. He judged it almost impossible for the desire for honor—which agitates those "front-wandering" <note>An unusual term for those who seek the spotlight.</note> debaters—not to be joined by an inseparable bond to a desire for the shame and confusion of the person with whom they are debating. He called this a lethal wound to the soul and a deadly poison to charity. He decided that he would have nothing at all to do with the "traps" <margin>Sophists' little traps, Suiseth.</margin> and quibbles of the sophists and those "Swineshead trifles" <note>original: "Suiſſeticas quilquilias"; This refers to the works of Richard Swineshead, an English mathematician nicknamed "The Calculator." His work was notoriously complex and criticized by humanists as being intellectually empty.</note> which are called "calculations." These are mathematical commentaries applied to natural things with more subtle—or should I say more troublesome—inventions. Truly, even if he were learned in them and had read such writings (which perhaps Italy did not fully know, for no path of literature could be found so pathless or inaccessible that he had not explored it thoroughly by his own footstep), he nevertheless seemed to hate and detest them. In my judgment, the value of those...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, written by his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico. It transitions from discussing his intellectual methods to his personal character, his massive library, and his eventual renunciation of worldly wealth.</meta>

-># THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...observing common practice, <note>Gianfrancesco is critiquing the academic style of the day, which often favored winning an argument over finding the truth.</note> he noticed that in debating, people focused more on bringing infamy to their colleagues and undermining their memories than on discovering the truth. He believed that such efforts contributed little or nothing to the tireless work required to find the truth. But, so as not to wander further and delay the reader, I will summarize briefly. Some men have shone with eloquence but were disgraced by their ignorance of the secrets of nature. Another might know foreign languages but remain unskilled in the universal decrees of the philosophers. One might have read through the discoveries of the ancients but composed no new doctrines of his own. For another, knowledge was sought only for the sake of human fame and glory, rather than for the benefit of the Christian commonweal, both divine and human. 

But Pico had embraced all these fields with such equal passion that they seemed to flow into him in great heaps and crowds. He was not like many who, lacking excellence in any one thing, merely dabble in everything. Rather, he had advanced so far in all the sciences that, whichever one you considered in him, you would have judged that he had chosen that specific one as his own particular specialty. These things were all the more admirable because he attained them through the power of his own genius and a love for truth, almost without a teacher. Regarding him, we might apply what Epicurus said of himself: <note>original: "Se sibi ipsum fuisse magistrum"</note> that he was his own teacher.

<margin>Five causes of such wonderful effects.</margin> I have found that five causes combined to produce these wonderful effects in such a short span of time: incredible talent, a most tenacious memory, ample resources (which helped him purchase books in our own language, as well as in Greek and the <term>barbaric languages</term> <note>In the Renaissance, "barbaric" usually referred to non-Classical languages, specifically Hebrew, Aramaic, and Arabic, which Pico studied extensively.</note>), tireless and indefatigable study, and finally, a contempt for earthly things. 

<margin>Seven thousand gold coins spent on acquiring books.</margin> If he had been born in that ancient age of the Spartans, I recall my memory telling me that he spent seven thousand gold coins <note>A staggering sum in the 15th century, equivalent to millions of dollars today.</note> up to that day on acquiring volumes of every kind of literature. If we believe Aristotle, he would have called him a "divine man." But I think it is time to leave behind the virtues of his intellect; now we must follow the noble parts of his soul regarding his actions, and his most exacting character must be brought into public view. This is so that his soul’s fire for God may become known, his wealth bestowed upon the needy may be praised, and so that those who have finally devoted themselves to divine law may find an abundant occasion to give thanks to the Author of all good things. 

Therefore, three years before he passed away, so that he might live in deep peace and be secure in wherever the scepter of power might fall after setting aside the cares of ruling, he handed over all the ancestral lands he possessed in Mirandola and Concordia—that is, a third part of them—to me, whether by gift or by sale I do not know. This act was later confirmed with imperial liberality by the August Maximilian <note>Emperor Maximilian I (1459–1519).</note>, who is our King and, I might say, our immediate Lord (for we have recognized no other over the many centuries since Mirandola and Concordia were built, except for whoever sits successively on the Royal or Imperial throne of the Romans). 

<margin>Giving to the poor.</margin> Whatever money he received from this business, he distributed part to the poor and spent part on buying lands from which he and his household might be supported. Specifically, he had purchased for himself the <term>corbulas</term> <note>Likely referring to the "Corbola" estate or specific agricultural plots.</note> in the territory of Ferrara for many thousands of gold coins. 

<margin>A modest table.</margin> He likewise distributed many silver vessels and precious pieces of furniture for the use of the poor. He was content with a modest table, though it still retained something of his former elegance regarding the dishes and the silver vessels. Each day, he poured out prayers to God at the appointed hours. He always gave money to any poor people he encountered. Not content with that, he gave a great deal of authority to Girolamo Benivieni <note>A famous Florentine poet and close friend of Pico.</note>—a learned citizen of Florence whom he loved dearly for his great charity and integrity of character—instructing him to always help the needy with Pico's own money. He also provided dowries for young women to be married, and he commanded that as soon as Benivieni had spent the money, he should ask for more immediately.

...had shaken off the burden from the shoulders of the entire **Christian commonwealth** <note>original: *totius christianæ rei publicæ* — a term referring to the collective body of the Christian world</note>. It was a burden, truly, for which a very great reward is prepared for those who undergo it—at least for those who, being unwilling, embrace it only for the sake of obedience and providing help. 

It was his firmest conviction: that for a philosopher, it is no source of praise to have accumulated wealth, nor to have sought honors, but rather to have refused them. And by refusing shadowy glory, he sought to attain the true glory which always follows virtues like an inseparable and devoted companion. 

He held human glory as next to nothing. He often said that fame might be of some use to the living, but it profited the dead not at all. In the year that he was completing the works he had begun and was hastening their publication—but in the year 1494 of our redemption <note>original: "M. cccclxxxxiiii. anno... redemptionis nostrae"</note>—while he was finishing his thirty-second year of life and staying in Florence, he was seized by a most insidious fever. The most benevolent spirit of the high-minded King <note>original: "magnanimi regis"; referring to King Charles VIII of France, who had a great interest in Pico.</note> and the distinguished virtues of the sick man demanded it. Indeed, Pico was very well known to the King by reputation then, and was also joined to him by a certain familiarity; for he had been honorably received by the King in Gaul <note>The Latin "galliis" refers to France.</note> while he was visiting Paris. Truly, just as he presented a marvel to the whole world and to many ages while he lived, so it was decreed that his death should be celebrated as no less remarkable and unheard of. Concerning this, I think those things ought to be related here which I heard with my own ears while I was in Florence—whither I had traveled, though not in time, upon hearing of his illness—in the sacred temple which is called Santa Reparata. <note>Santa Reparata was the ancient cathedral of Florence, over which the current Duomo (Santa Maria del Fiore) was built.</note> There I heard Girolamo Savonarola of Ferrara, of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note>, a man most skilled in theology, most distinguished in fame, and most renowned for holiness, delivering sacred sermons to the Florentine people.

But first, it is my counsel to warn those ignorant of sacred letters with the words of Apuleius: <margin>Words of Apuleius quoted by Brother Girolamo</margin> "Lest with dull ears and an obstinate heart they think these things are lies, which may seem new to the hearing, or strange to the sight, or certainly difficult beyond the reach of thought; yet if they investigate a little more deeply, they will find them not only evident to the understanding, but also very easy to perform." He, therefore, declaiming from the pulpit, insinuated to all who were present what I am about to say: 

"A secret must be revealed to you, O Florence, which is indeed as true as that Gospel of John so frequent among you. I would have remained silent, certainly, but I am compelled to speak; and He who has the power to command me has ordered that I make these things public. Furthermore, I think there was none among you who did not know Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. He had been heaped with great benefits from God and great graces, and was endowed with manifold learning; perhaps no mortal ever possessed so celebrated a genius. The Church suffered a great loss in him. I believe that if a longer span of life had been granted to him, he would have excelled all who have died these last eight hundred years because of the monuments of writing he would have left behind. He was accustomed to frequent my company and reveal his secrets, from which I knew that he was summoned to the religious life by God through internal voices. Desiring to comply with these inspirations, he had proposed to obey them more than once. 

But, ungrateful for divine benefits—either called away by his senses, he drew back from the labors (for he was of a delicate temperament), or perhaps thinking that the religious life had need of his works—he deferred it until this time. I say this not as a certainty, but as something conjectured and presumed by me. For this reason, I threatened him with a scourge for two years if he should neglect the work God had proposed for him to perform. I confess I prayed to God repeatedly that he might be struck just enough so that he might finally take the path shown to him from on high. I did not seek this by which he was struck down; I had not thought that this was decreed by God: that he should leave this life and lose a part of the distinguished crown prepared for him in heaven, and that he should not fully attain the fame and celebrity of name which he would have held at its highest peak had he lived. 

Truly, the most kind Judge behaved most mercifully toward him. And because of the alms bestowed with a large and most lavish hand upon the poor, <margin>Almsgiving</margin> and the prayers which were most insistently poured out to God, it has been brought about that—although his soul does not yet exult in the bosom of the Father above the heavens— <margin>The state of the soul</margin> neither is it consigned to the lower regions to be tortured by perpetual torments. Instead, assigned to the fire of Purgatory for a time, he must pay temporary penalties. I say this most gladly in this place so that those who knew him, and especially those who were heaped with his benefits, may aid him with their prayers."

The man of God [Savonarola] affirmed these and many other things with a clear voice. He added that it was not hidden from him that preachers of the word of God become worthy of eternal punishment if they mingle lies with such things. He further added that for several days these things had been known to him in their entirety. But because of words which the sick man affirmed a Virgin had spoken to him, Savonarola had stood wavering and fearful for a long time, lest that had been an illusion produced by demons, since the Virgin's promise seemed frustrated by his death. <margin>The double death</margin> Nevertheless, it became known to him that the deceased had been deceived by the ambiguity of 'death.' <meta>This page continues a defense of a specific individual—likely Pico della Mirandola—whose prophetic insights and character were under scrutiny. It transitions from a theological justification for his revelations into an epitaph for him and a poem regarding the symbolism of the Cross.</meta>

...to receive, for it is beneficial to reveal these most holy laws of divinity to the multitude of men: as we are taught by that same Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century, famous for his works on celestial hierarchies.</note> in his book *The Celestial Hierarchy*, so that the ignorant might be raised up by these first steps toward the most venerable light. Those who doubt are, without question, ignorant of divine literature and are of an insolent and stubborn disposition; for in those writings, it is shown that future divine mysteries are revealed not only through good men, but sometimes even through wicked men and false prophets. This prevents one from withholding faith from this man, who excels in both learning and so many virtues, and who has already predicted many future things that have now come to pass. And he testified to this not in a dream-like way, but by affirming it with great constancy. Add to this that the philosophy of Aristotle does not cry out against these things, and the Platonic schools support them—though I would not accept such testimony as weighty unless it were by the authority of the divine Scriptures. However, it is not absurd to occasionally cite these outside sources, so that the arrows of the malevolent may be turned back with greater force upon those who sent them. 

But we must now return to our own concerns: we ought not to mourn so much that we have lost such a man, but rather give thanks to the King to whom all things live for having had him at all. Indeed, having completed the duty of this mortal life, and having long dwelt among the inhabitants of Kedar <note>original: "cedar." A reference to Psalm 120:5, often used to signify living in a state of exile or among those who do not know peace/light.</note>—upon whom he poured no small amount of light—he is even now entering the inaccessible and infinite light of the heavenly homeland. There, he will enjoy the ineffable divinity without end, bringing help to us also in the days to come.

**THE END.**

**Epitaph of Mirandola.** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance philosopher.</note>

John of Mirandola lies here. The rest is known 
By the Tagus, the Ganges, and perhaps even the Antipodes. <note>The Tagus is a river in the Iberian Peninsula and the Ganges is in India; the "Antipodes" refers to people on the opposite side of the earth. This suggests his fame reached the known and unknown ends of the world.</note>

**A poem by Caecilius Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, concerning the wood of the Cross:** <note>This poem, "De Ligno Crucis," was historically attributed to St. Cyprian, though modern scholars often attribute it to a later "Pseudo-Cyprian."</note>

There is a place at the center of the whole world, as we believe,
Which the Jews call Golgotha in their native tongue:
Here I remember that wood, cut from a sterile oak,
Was planted and brought forth most healthful fruits.
Yet it did not offer these to those who settled there as farmers;
Rather, foreigners possessed the blessed fruits
Of the tree. This sight rises up from a single trunk,
And soon extends its arms into twin branches,
Just as the yardarms of a ship stretch out the heavy, full sails;
Or like the yoke when the young oxen are uncoupled from the plow.
The earth conceived what this tree bore, fallen from that first mature seed;
Soon after—miraculous to tell—
The third light <note>The third day, referring to the Resurrection.</note> raised the branch up again, fearsome to the earth 
And the heavens above, blessed with the fruit of life.
But for twice twenty days <note>The forty days between the Resurrection and the Ascension.</note> that branch was strengthened;
It grew immensely and touched the high heavens with its peak,
And at last added its holy head to the heights.
Meanwhile, it brought forth great branches of twelve-fold weight, <note>A reference to the twelve Apostles.</note>
Spreading them out and reaching across the entire world,
To provide food and everlasting life for all nations.

<meta>This is the opening page of the Prooemium (Preface) to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's *Heptaplus*, dedicated to Lorenzo "the Magnificent" de' Medici. It establishes the author's intent to reveal the hidden philosophical depths within the Book of Genesis.</meta>

-># THE HEPTAPLVS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-
->## ON THE SEVENFOLD NARRATION OF THE SIX DAYS OF GENESIS<-
->### TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI. PREFACE.<-

**[Decorative Initial M]** It was the emulation of your studies, Lorenzo de’ Medici, that moved me to review the secret volumes of Moses. Last winter, I noticed that in whatever leisure time the Republic <note>Lorenzo was the de facto ruler of the Florentine Republic; Pico refers to Lorenzo's heavy political duties.</note> afforded you, you applied yourself nowhere more greatly or willingly than to that reading. At the same time, a private reason also invited me: for another work of mine—already begun under your auspices but growing in your name—in which I have attempted not only to defend the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms.</note> translated by the Seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and continually sung in the Church from all suspicion and slander, but also to illuminate them with the torches of interpretation, I found no treatment more useful, none more fruitful, and none more consistent (or to speak more truly, necessary) than the study of those books. <margin>The mysteries of all nature are contained in the Genesis of Moses.</margin>

It happened during these days that I was diligently occupied with those celebrated works of the six days in the creation of the world. Great reasons present themselves to make us believe that the secrets of all nature are contained within them. For even if I omit the fact that our prophet <note>Moses.</note>, full of God and the heavenly spirit, received all these things from the master of all truth, <margin>The most learned Moses</margin> have not the testimonies of our own people, his own people, and finally even the Gentiles, proclaimed him to be most deeply learned in human wisdom, all doctrines, and literature? There exists among the Hebrews a book by that most wise man surnamed Solomon, titled *Wisdom*—not the one now in the hands of Philo <note>Pico distinguishes between the canonical *Book of Wisdom* and a more esoteric Hebrew text.</note>, but another composed in the more secret language they call "Jerusalemite"—in which that man, an interpreter of the nature of things as is believed, confesses that he received all such discipline from the inner sanctuaries of the Mosaic law. <margin>Why Moses appears crude and common</margin> Likewise, as far as our own authors are concerned, both Luke <note>In Acts 7:22, Luke writes that Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.</note> and Philo, most weighty authorities, state that he was most highly educated in the universal doctrine of the Egyptians. Moreover, all those Greeks who are considered more divine—Pythagoras, Plato, Empedocles, and Democritus—employed Egyptian teachers. <margin>Mysteries of the Gymnosophists, Egyptians, and Pythagoras</margin> It is a well-known saying of the philosopher Numenius that Plato is nothing other than an "Attic Moses" <note>An "Athenian Moses"; Pico is arguing that Greek philosophy is derived from Hebrew revelation.</note>. Furthermore, Hermippus the Pythagorean attests that Pythagoras transferred many things from the Mosaic law into his own philosophy.

But if Moses appears meanwhile to be crude and common in his books, rather than a philosopher, a theologian, or a master of some great wisdom, let us recall that it was a celebrated practice of the ancient sages either not to write of divine matters at all, or to write of them in a disguised manner. <margin>Philolaus of the Pythagoreans</margin> Hence they were called "mysteries," for they were not mysteries if they were not hidden. This was observed by the Indians, by the Ethiopians (who are named for their nakedness <note>The <term>Gymnosophists</term>, or "naked philosophers," of India and Ethiopia.</note>), and by the Egyptians. This is what those Sphinxes in front of their temples suggested. Taught by them, Pythagoras became a master of silence; <margin>Lysis and Hipparchus</margin> nor did he himself commit anything to writing, except for a very few things which he commended to his daughter Dama as he was dying. For the "Golden Verses" that are circulated are not by Pythagoras, as is commonly believed even by the more learned, but by Philolaus. Thereafter, the Pythagoreans most religiously guarded that law. <margin>Ammonius, Origen, Plotinus, Herennius, Porphyry</margin> Lysis complained that this law was violated by Hipparchus. Finally, Porphyry is the authority that the disciples of Ammonius—Origen, Plotinus, and Herennius—were sworn to it. Our Plato so concealed his dogmas under the veil of winged enigmas, fables, mathematical images, and the obscure signs of receding meanings, that he himself said in his letters that no one would openly understand his opinion on divine matters from what he had written, and he proved it to those who were less believing. Therefore, if for this reason we think the reading of Moses is, as it were, worn out, because it contains nothing in the [first appearance...]

He explains that Moses deliberately hid profound secrets beneath a simple literal narrative, following the ancient tradition of keeping "mysteries" veiled from the uninitiated.</summary>

<meta>This page appears to be an introductory section of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s *Heptaplus* (15th century), a discourse on the seven days of creation. The text establishes the necessity of esoteric interpretation—the idea that divine truths are hidden beneath a "veil" of simple language to protect them from the uninitiated.</meta>

-># HEPTAPLVS<-
->(The Sevenfold Account)<-

<margin>Jesus Christ wrote the Gospel:</margin> ...not condemn them for a surface appearance that is uncommon or unrefined, lest by that same example we condemn all the ancient philosophers for a lack of cultivation and ignorance—those very men whom we revere as the masters of all wisdom. We see this same practice observed in the Church. Jesus Christ, the image of the substance of God, did not write the Gospel, but preached it. He preached to the crowds in parables, but privately to a few disciples, to whom it was given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, speaking plainly and without figures. Yet he did not tell everything even to those few, because they were not capable of receiving everything; there were many things they could not carry until the coming Spirit taught them all truth. If those few chosen from so many thousands could not carry much, how could the whole Israelite crowd—tailors, cooks, butchers, shepherds, male and female servants—to whom the Law was given to be read, have carried the weight of the whole Mosaic, or rather divine, wisdom? 

<margin>Why Moses had a veiled face.</margin> Moses, indeed, on the height of the mountain—certainly that same mountain on which the Lord often spoke to his disciples—was illuminated by the light of the divine sun; his whole face shone in a marvelous way. But because the people, with their blinking, "night-owl" eyes <note>original: *noctuinis*. Pico uses this term to describe those whose spiritual vision is too weak for the "sun" of divine truth.</note>, could not bear the light, he spoke to them with a veiled face. 

<margin>Matthew first wrote the Gospel. John.</margin> Let us return to our own writers. Matthew was the first to write the Gospel, and as the prophet says, "hiding the words of God in his heart" <note>A reference to Psalm 119:11.</note> so that he might not sin, he followed the history of only those things which pertained to the humanity of Christ, so that the memory of his deeds might not perish through forgetfulness. For this reason, in the mystic spectacle of Ezekiel, we understand him to be represented by the figure of the Man. <note>The "four living creatures" in the vision of Ezekiel (man, lion, ox, eagle) were traditionally used as symbols for the four Evangelists.</note> John, who revealed the secrets of divinity more than all the others, was finally compelled to speak of the eternal generation of the Son—things he had long kept silent—many years after the cross of the Lord, in order to abolish the heresy of the Ebionites <note>An early Jewish-Christian sect that taught Jesus was a mortal man and not the divine Son of God.</note>, who asserted that Christ was a man but not also God. He pronounced these things to a few, and obscurely, beginning thus: "In the beginning was the Word." <note>John 1:1.</note> 

<margin>Ebionites, Paul, Dionysius.</margin> Paul denies "solid food" to the Corinthians for the reason that they still live by the laws of the flesh and not by the Spirit; he speaks wisdom only among the "perfect." <note>1 Corinthians 2:6 and 3:2.</note> Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century mystical theologian believed in Pico’s time to be the direct disciple of St. Paul mentioned in Acts 17:34.</note>, the disciple of Paul, writes that it was a holy and established practice in the churches not to communicate the more secret dogmas through letters, but only by word of mouth to those who were rightly initiated. 

<margin>Jerome.</margin> I have pursued these matters at length because there are many who, judging by the "rough bark" <term>cortex</term> <note>The literal or external meaning of a text, often contrasted by Renaissance thinkers with the "pith" or "marrow" of its hidden spiritual meaning.</note> of the words, despise and scorn the book of Moses as something common and trivial. To such people, nothing is less credible than that he holds in his depths something more divine than what he promises on the surface. 

<margin>Why he dared to write after so many interpreters.</margin> If that error has been sufficiently refuted, it should now be easy to believe that he has treated the nature of the entire creation of the world—that is, if in some part of his work, like a farmer, he has buried the treasures of all true philosophy. This was done primarily in this section, where he philosophizes most deeply, either explicitly or implicitly, concerning the emanation of all things from God: their degree, their number, and the order of the parts of the world. For this reason, it was a decree of the ancient Hebrews (which Jerome also mentions) that no one should touch this account of the creation of the world until they had reached a mature age. 

Therefore, I will perhaps be seen to have done something worthwhile if, having lingered longer with more exact care and more laborious study (as far as my weakness allowed), I have searched out the understanding of the Mosaic reading. In explaining this, although I saw that many Latins and Greeks had labored over it—and furthermore, ancient and modern Chaldean <note>Referring to Aramaic paraphrases of the Bible (Targums).</note> and Hebrew interpreters almost beyond number—I did not even dare to think of writing or commenting on anything new regarding this matter. However, I remembered that the Mosaic Law warned that no one should harvest their field entirely and completely, but should leave an untouched portion of it for the poor and needy, who might take bundles and handfuls from there to sustain their hunger. <note>Leviticus 19:9-10.</note> When this came to mind, I began to survey the vast fields of the Prophet <note>Moses.</note> with sharp eyes, to investigate whether the most learned interpreters—who were no less cultivators of the Law than its interpreters—had, according to the edict of the Law, left some part untouched for us, who are weaker, to harvest. From which I also...

<summary>Pico argues that Moses hid profound philosophical truths beneath the literal surface of the Genesis creation story to protect them from the unlearned. He justifies his new commentary by suggesting that, like a field being gleaned, earlier scholars left behind "handfuls" of divine mystery for him to discover.</summary>

**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...or to gather at least a few stalks of grain to place upon the altars of the church as if they were the first fruits of the harvest, so that I might not be cast out from the privileges of the temple like a false Israelite or one who contributes nothing <term>asymbolus</term> <note>original: "asymbolus", from the Greek 'asymbolos', referring to someone who attends a banquet without bringing their share or contribution.</note>. Matters have proceeded according to my wishes; not that I can achieve anything they could not, but because they, following the law's command, did not wish to block the path for the diligence of those who came after. Indeed, such is the vastness and fertility of this field that no number of grain-harvests could equal it. Although infinite and most powerful efforts have been spent upon it with all their strength, we can still say that Gospel saying: *The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few.* <note>A reference to Matthew 9:37.</note>

Therefore, what the most holy men—Ambrose and Augustine, as well as Strabo, Bede, and Remigius, and from the more recent ones <margin>Latin interpreters</margin>, Giles and Albert—have written on this book; likewise among the Greeks <margin>Greek interpreters</margin>—Philo, Origen, Basil, Theodoret, Apollinaris, Didymus, Diodorus, Severus, Eusebius, Josephus, Gennadius, and Chrysostom—all this we shall leave entirely untouched by us. For it would be both reckless and superfluous for a weak man to exert himself in that part of the field where the most robust minds have long since labored. Likewise, of those things which either Jonathan, Onkelos, or Simeon the Elder passed down in Chaldean <margin>Chaldean interpreters</margin> <note>original: "Chaldaice". Pico is referring to Aramaic translations and paraphrases of the Bible known as Targums.</note>, or what the Hebrews—whether the ancients <margin>Hebrew interpreters</margin> like Eleazar, Abba, Joannes, Neonias, Isaac, and Joseph, or the more recent ones like Gersonides, Saadia, both the Abrahams <note>Likely referring to Abraham ibn Ezra and Abraham ben David.</note>, both the Moseses <note>Likely referring to Moses Maimonides and Moses Nahmanides.</note>, Solomon <note>Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki).</note>, and Menahem—have written, we shall make no mention for the present.

We shall, however, bring forward in addition to all these seven other expositions of our own invention and meditation <margin>Seven new expositions</margin>. In these, we shall first take care to overcome, if we can, three difficulties with which it seems all those who have undertaken to explain this book have had a great and difficult struggle.

The **first** difficulty <margin>First</margin> is lest anything said by Moses should seem either insufficiently or insufficiently learnedly and wisely spoken. Some have freed themselves from this in this way: that he neither spoke of everything nor brought forward grand and sublime matters because he was speaking to an unrefined people who were not fit for the understanding of all things. We can believe that the unrefined listeners were satisfied if he covered the light of knowledge—which the wise might look into—with thick words, as if surrounded by a <term>horn-lantern</term> <note>original: "cornea testa". Truth is compared to a candle flame protected by a translucent horn casing; it provides light but prevents the flame from being extinguished or blinding the viewer.</note>, lest eyes that were duller might be dazzled. He brought the light so that it might benefit healthy eyes, yet he brought it enclosed and veiled so that it might not hurt those with weak vision. For he neither ought to, nor could, nor wanted to help the learned any less than the unlearned.

The **second** difficulty <margin>Second difficulty</margin> is that the tenor of the interpretation should be consistent with itself, fitting together from its own parts, and that the whole series, as if by a single stroke, should be brought back to the same sense from which it first set out, as if mindful of its purpose. We should not, perhaps, introduce him speaking of <term>Ideas</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, the eternal forms or blueprints of things.</note> here, only to have him deal with the elements or man in the next clause. This is an arbitrary and violent kind of exposition. Yet, to avoid this in the explanation of this book has seemed to many—I will not say difficult—certainly laborious for all. Such is the complexity, such the ambiguity, such the variety of the entire text. See how much labor it is <margin>How difficult a task he approaches</margin>, and how not easily done, what we have conceived in our mind (may we achieve it!): that from the beginning, having started a new work always with not just one, but a sevenfold sense, we might interpret this entire creation of the world in a continuous and unmixed order of exposition, using none of the works of those who came before.

The **third** difficulty <margin>Third difficulty</margin> lies in this: that we do not make the Prophet—or rather the Divine Spirit through the Prophet—assert anything foreign or monstrous or alien to the nature of things as they are now seen, and to the truth which our own people have also accepted as found by the better philosophers. But as to why seven expositions are brought forward by us, by what reasoning they were undertaken <margin>The reason for the commentary</margin>, what our plan is, and what necessity drove us to them, and what is entirely new in what we are attempting to bring forth, we shall make clear in the following chapter. In that chapter, the writing of him who has written most perfectly on this matter—that is, on the creation of the world—in imitation of nature itself...

<summary>In this preface to the Heptaplus, Pico della Mirandola outlines his plan to provide seven new layers of interpretation for the creation story in Genesis, distinct from the many Latin, Greek, and Hebrew commentators who preceded him. He identifies three main challenges: ensuring Moses's words appear wise to both the simple and the learned, maintaining a consistent internal logic for each interpretation, and ensuring the text aligns with natural philosophy.</summary>

->ANOTHER PREFACE TO THE WHOLE WORK.<-

[Marginal notes:]
The levels and differences of the three worlds
The Angelic world
The Celestial [world]
The Sublunary [world]

[Main text:]
**T**hree worlds are depicted by antiquity. The highest of all is the ultra-mundane, which theologians call the angelic and philosophers call the intellectual; Plato says in the *Phaedrus* that no one has sung of it enough according to its dignity. The next to this is the celestial; the last of all is the sublunary, this [world] which we inhabit. This is the world of darkness; that one, however, is of light. The heavens are tempered from both light and darkness. This [world] is noted for its flowing and unstable substance, like water; that one by the fire of the brightness of light and the sublimity of its place. The heavens are of a middle nature and are therefore called <term>Shamaim</term> <note>original: "asciamaim"; Pico uses a common but philologically creative etymology</note> by the Hebrews, as if from *esh* and *maim*, that is, from fire and water, of which we said it is composed. Here there is a vicissitude of life and death; there, perpetual life and stable operation. In the heavens, there is stability of life but a change of operations and places. This [world] is from the decaying substance of bodies; those from the nature of the divine mind. The heavens are constituted of body, but incorruptible; of mind, but bound to the body. The third is moved by the second; the second is ruled by the first. Furthermore, there are many differences between them, which it is not my intention to narrate here, where we are flowing past these things rather than flooding them. Yet I should not omit that these three worlds were most clearly figured 
<margin>In the tabernacle of Moses, the three worlds are represented</margin> 
by Moses in the construction of that admirable tabernacle of his. For he divided the tabernacle into three parts, each of which could not more expressly represent the individual worlds we have mentioned. For the first part, defended by no roof or shade, was open and vulnerable to rains, snows, suns, heat, and cold; it was a most clear image of our sublunary world. Not only clean and unclean, sacred and profane men inhabited it, but also animals of every kind; and in it, because of the sacrifices and constant slaughters, there was a perpetual vicissitude of life and death. The remaining two parts were both covered and free from every foreign injury on all sides, just as both the celestial and super-celestial worlds are incapable of injury or insult. Both were also honored with the name of holiness, yet so that the one which was more secret was called the Holy of Holies, while the other was decorated only with the title of Holy. Similarly, although both the celestial and angelic worlds are each holy, since above the moon, after the fall of Lucifer, no evil...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s exploration of the "Heptaplus," specifically his theory of the three worlds: the Super-celestial (angelic), the Celestial (planetary), and the Terrestrial (elemental).</meta>

**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...nor is it or can it be a small thing; however, the angelic world is held to be far holier and more divine than the celestial. But why do we pursue these more remote similarities? For if the final part of the tabernacle was common to both men and beasts, and the second part—which shone entirely with the splendor of gold—was illuminated by a candelabrum distinguished by seven lamps, which <margin>What the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew interpreters mean</margin> as all Latin, Greek, and Hebrew interpreters say, signifies the seven planets; and in the third part, the most sacred of all, there were winged cherubim—do they not set before our eyes the three worlds? This one which both beasts and men inhabit, the celestial in which the planets flash, and the super-celestial dwelling of the angels. 

We are also reminded here of a higher Gospel mystery <note>original: *sacri* — a sacred rite or mystery</note>. For since the way to the super-celestial world and the company of angels has been opened to us through the cross and blood of Christ, therefore, <margin>The meaning of the tearing of the veil at the death of Christ</margin> when he died, the veil of the temple was torn, by which the Holy of Holies <note>the innermost sanctum of the Tabernacle</note> (by which we said the angelic world is signified) was separated from the other parts. This was a sign that the way is now open for man to the kingdom of God—to God himself who flies above the cherubim—an entrance that had been closed from the beginning by the laws of justice due to the sin of our first parent <note>Adam</note>. 

This is enough regarding the three worlds, in which this must be observed first of all (as almost our entire intention depends upon it): these three worlds are one world. <margin>Three reasons why the world is one</margin> This is not only because they are all traced back to one principle and to the same end, or because they are tempered by appropriate numbers and bound together by a certain harmonic kinship of nature and an orderly series of steps; but because whatever exists in all the worlds together is also contained in each individual one. There is not one among them in which everything does not exist that is in the others. I believe this was the opinion of <margin>Anaxagoras</margin> Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who taught that "everything is in everything."</note>, if we consider his view correctly explained, and it was later followed by the <margin>Pythagoreans</margin> Pythagoreans and <margin>Platonists</margin> Platonists. 

Truly, those things which are in the lower world are also in the higher ones, but in a better condition <note>original: *meliore nota* — of a better mark or quality</note>; likewise, those in the higher worlds are seen in the lowest, but in a degenerate condition and a "corrupted" nature, so to speak. <margin>An example of the proposed truth</margin> Among us, heat is an elemental quality; in the heavens, it is a heating power; in the angelic minds, it is the *Idea* of heat. Let me say something more specific. Among us, there is the element of fire. The Sun is fire in the heavens. In the region beyond the world, there is the Seraphic fire of the intellect <note>referring to the Seraphim, the highest order of angels, whose name means "the burning ones."</note>. But see how they differ: the elemental fire burns, the celestial fire gives life, and the super-celestial fire loves. 

There is water among us; there is water in the heavens (the mover and mistress of our water, namely the Moon, the threshold of the heavens); and there are waters above the heavens, the seats of the Cherubim. But see the disparity of condition in the same nature: the elemental moisture overwhelms the heat of life; the celestial moisture feeds it; the super-celestial moisture understands it. 

In the first world, God—the primal Unity—presides over the nine orders of angels as if over so many spheres, <margin>The ten spheres of the intellectual world</margin> and being himself immovable, he moves them all toward himself. In the middle world (that is, the celestial), the Empyrean heaven <note>the highest, most spiritual heaven</note> similarly presides over the nine celestial spheres like a general over an army; <margin>The ten spheres of the celestial world</margin> while each of those spheres revolves in unceasing motion, the Empyrean, mimicking God, remains still. 

In the elemental world, after the primary matter which is its foundation, there are also nine spheres of corruptible forms. <margin>The ten spheres of the elemental world</margin> First, three spheres of bodies lacking life: the elements, the mixtures of elements, and those intermediate "imperfect" mixtures such as the "impressions" <note>atmospheric phenomena like meteors or rainbows</note> that occur in the heights. Next, three spheres <margin>Body, Nature, Soul</margin> of vegetable nature, divided into three primary types: herbs, shrubs, and trees. Finally, three spheres of the sensual soul: that which is "imperfect" (like the zoophytes <note>organisms like sea anemones or sponges that seem to be part animal, part plant</note>), that which is "perfect" but remains within the limits of irrational imagination (beasts), and that which—the highest in beasts—is even capable of human training, which is a middle ground between man and beast, just as the zoophyte is a middle ground between beast and plant. 

But I have said more on these things than is necessary. I will only add that the mutual containment of the worlds is also indicated in the <margin>Testimony from the sacred letters</margin> Sacred Scriptures. For it is written in the Psalms, "He who creates the heavens in intellect," and we read that the angels of God are "spirits" and his ministers are a "flame of burning fire." For this reason, celestial names are often given to divine things, and even earthly names; sometimes through stars...

Sometimes they represent them by wheels and living creatures; <note>A reference to the "wheels" and "living creatures" in the vision of the prophet Ezekiel.</note> sometimes by the elements. From this, heavenly names are often given to earthly things. This is because all these worlds, bound by the chains of concord, trade their natures and their titles with one another in mutual generosity. From this principle—if perhaps someone has not yet noticed—flowed the entire discipline of allegorical meaning. Nor could the ancient fathers have fittingly represented some things by others, unless they had been taught the hidden friendships and affinities, so to speak, of all nature. Otherwise, there would be no reason why they should represent one thing by this image rather than another. But being knowledgeable of all things and driven by that Spirit <note>The Holy Spirit</note> who not only knew these things but made them, they most aptly represented the natures of one world through those things they knew corresponded to them in the other worlds. Therefore, the same knowledge is necessary—unless that same Spirit is present—for those who wish to rightly interpret their images and allegorical meanings.

<margin>The Fourth World</margin>
But besides the three worlds we have described, <note>In previous sections, Pico describes the Intellectual (Angelic), Celestial (Planetary), and Sublunary (Elemental) worlds.</note> there is a fourth world in which all those things found in the others are also discovered. This is man himself. For this reason, as the universal teachers say in the Gospel, he is designated by the name "every creature." For while the Gospel is to be preached to men, and not to brutes or angels, the command from Christ is nonetheless to "preach to every creature." <note>Mark 16:15. Pico argues that "every creature" refers to man because man contains all levels of creation within himself.</note> It is a common saying in the schools that 
<margin>In what way man is a microcosm</margin>
man is a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "minor mundus"; literally "smaller world." A central Renaissance idea that the human body and soul mirror the structure of the entire universe.</note> in whom are seen a body mixed from the elements, a heavenly spirit, the vegetative soul of plants, the senses of brutes, reason, an angelic mind, and the likeness of God. 

<margin>That Moses treated all these worlds</margin>
If we establish these four worlds, it is credible that Moses, in order to speak sufficiently about the world, discussed all of them. Since a writer portrays nature—if he is as skilled in nature as we believe this man to have been—it is

credible that his teaching about them was arranged no differently than the Almighty Creator arranged them within themselves. First, then—which is the greatest point of all—as we have 
<margin>The root of the [fourth] exposition</margin>
shown that the things in all worlds are contained in each individual one, Moses, as an emulator of this dual nature, should never treat any one of those worlds without treating all of them together at the same time under the same words and context. From this, a fourfold exposition of the entire Mosaic reading immediately arises: in the first place, we explain whatever is written there concerning the angelic and invisible world, making no mention of the others. In the second place, likewise, all things concerning the celestial world; then concerning this sublunary and corruptible world; fourth, concerning the nature of man. For if the intelligible world <note>The world of pure thought/angels</note> is never treated without the scripture also reminding us of the other worlds—just as that world contains all the lower natures within itself—then we certainly can, and indeed must, interpret every small part concerning all of them. 

Furthermore, just as the various natures are contained within each other promiscuously, yet have obtained distinct and proper seats and certain peculiar laws, so it is here. <margin>The root of the fifth exposition</margin>
deals with the first nature specifically, and then in the same order through the rest. From this, the necessity of a fifth exposition arises. 

Added to this is the reason why these things are distinct: 
<margin>The root of the sixth exposition</margin>
because there is no multitude which is not "one," they are bound together by a certain discordant concord and are tied by multiform links as if by chains. Since it is likely that Moses deals with this in the whole work, it calls us, even if we are unwilling, to a sixth interpretation. Thus far we have undertaken to set forth the words of Moses. I have divided the entire exposition into seven books or treatises, rather to imitate **Basil** and **Augustine** <note>St. Basil the Great and St. Augustine of Hippo both wrote famous commentaries on the creation account in Genesis</note> than because the reader's attention is refreshed by this frequent distinction, as if taking a break. It happens that since there are seven expositions arranged in seven books, and each book is divided into seven chapters, all things correspond to the seven days of creation. Likewise, it was done by us for a most fitting reason: that just as the seventh day with Moses is the Sabbath and a day of rest, so every seventh chapter of our exposition is always directed toward **Christ**, who is both the end of the Law and our Sabbath, our rest, and our happiness.

## THE FIRST EXPOSITION: ON THE ELEMENTARY WORLD.
### Chapter One of the First Book.

<margin>On the principles of corruptible things</margin> **N**atural Philosophers <note>In the Renaissance, "Natural Philosophy" was the study of the physical world, similar to what we call "science" today.</note> who discourse on the nature of <term>corruptible things</term> <note>Things that are subject to change, decay, and death in the physical world.</note> establish these principles for the universe: that there is a crude **Matter**, void of forms, indeed fit for receiving all forms, but by its own nature deprived of all of them. By its power, matter is handled, so that what is in <term>potentiality</term> <note>The capacity to become something.</note> might at some time become an <term>actuality</term> <note>The state of being something in reality.</note>, just as soft and undefined wax...
