...is transformed into various figures by the guidance and touch of the hand, according to the will of the one handling it. 

Since, however, nature does nothing at random but always for the sake of achieving some good, the <margin>Efficient cause</margin> final cause immediately introduces itself. <margin>The End</margin> And indeed, the closest end of the acting cause is the "form," which it draws out from the lap of matter. <margin>Form</margin> For nature acts and moves with this plan: to lead that matter toward the perfect state of form; hence, form is the third principle established by Aristotle. <margin>Dispositions of matter</margin> This form, however, cannot be drawn out from the bosom of matter unless it is first affected and prepared with suitable qualities. The entire labor of the craftsman and the entire duration of the action is spent on these preparations, while the specific form itself shines forth instantly in a single moment, like the reward for the labor. The <term>Peripatetics<note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, named after the covered walkways (peripatoi) where they studied.</note></term> call the craftsman himself a cause rather than a principle. 

<margin>Natural causes are instruments of the divine</margin> However, the <term>Platonists<note>Followers of Plato, who often sought a more spiritual or mystical interpretation of the physical world.</note></term>, always mindful of divine things, want us to be reminded that natural acting causes—even if they seem to be the only ones to us that move, form, and transmute bodies—are by no means the primary causes of what happens. Instead, they are the instruments of the divine art, which they obey and serve. Just as the hand of a builder might assemble, arrange, and transform all the material of a house—the wood, stones, and mortar—and although nothing else seems responsible for the building besides those hands, we nonetheless know they are merely an <margin>Organic and Exemplary cause</margin> instrument. They serve and obey the art residing in the mind of the architect, who, having conceived of the house as a whole, then arranges and unfolds it piece by piece in the physical material. 

From this, the Platonists add two more causes: the "organic" and the "exemplary." The Peripatetics do not deny this; indeed, they confirm it with that well-worn saying: *Every work of nature is a work of intelligence.* <margin>Explanation of the words of Moses</margin> These are the things said in common regarding perishable things; Moses so encompassed all of them in the work of the first day that the most esteemed philosophers have said nothing more certain or more fitting about them.

### Chapter Two <margin>Heaven, Earth, Stoics</margin>

In the beginning, therefore, he established two causes: the agent and the matter—that is, the cause which is in <term>act<note>actualized or fully realized being</note></term> and the cause which is in <term>potential<note>the capacity to become something else</note></term>. He calls the former "Heaven" and the latter "Earth." This interpretation of ours is first supported by the authority of the <term>Stoics<note>A school of philosophy that taught that the universe is governed by divine reason; they often identified the active principle with the heavens.</note></term>, who called the acting cause "heaven" and the material cause "earth," as Varro writes (not to mention the Greeks). 

Reason also supports this. For matter is the most lowly of all natures, just as the earth is among the elements; they correspond in exactly the same proportion. As the <margin>Peripatetics</margin> Peripatetics prove, the "agent" is to "matter" as heaven is to earth. 

<margin>The earth was void and empty</margin> Moreover, this "Earth"—that is, matter—is "void and empty," as <term>Hieronymus<note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note></term> translated it, or as the <term>Septuagint<note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note></term> says, "invisible and uncomposed." All these terms suit raw and formless matter; since it lacks all forms, it is rightly called "void and empty," and it is entirely uncomposed and invisible. 

<margin>Hebrew: Tohu and Bohu</margin> Truly, the Hebrew words <term>Tohu<note>original: "tou"</note></term> and <term>Bohu<note>original: "bou"</note></term>, which are read in this passage, are explained differently by many Hebrews. They interpret *Tohu* as a brute thing, stunning and astonishing. This refers to the dark and deformed appearance of matter, because when we fix our attention on trying to know it, it leaves us <margin>Aristotle, Plato</margin> astonished. For this reason, Aristotle said it is known to us by "analogy," and Plato said it is known by "bastard reasoning." 

<margin>The beginning of form</margin> Many explain *Bohu*, however, by the force of the word itself, as the "inchoation" or the first rudiment of form. Indeed, if we translate the word literally, *Bohu* is as if we said "in it is" or "something is in it." If we follow this, we understand that in addition to the potential of the subject, there is an <margin>Albert, Ancient Simeon</margin> incipient form within it. This was believed not only by <term>Albertus<note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who synthesized Aristotelianism with Christian thought.</note></term> and many Peripatetics, but also by the ancient Hebrews, as we clearly gather from the records of the ancient Simeon. 

But in what way this "beginning of form" is to be understood is declared by what follows: <margin>Darkness, Abyss</margin> "and darkness was upon the face of the abyss." He calls the earth "Abyss"—that is, matter extended in three dimensions into the deepest depths. Upon this is "Darkness"—that is, <term>privation<note>the absence or lack of a form that a thing should naturally possess; a key concept in Aristotelian physics.</note></term>. This is a particularly celebrated principle among the Peripatetics, and no name fits it better than "darkness." There is, however, a "privation" by which it differs from a mere "negation," as the great Albertus most firmly maintains...

<margin>Of matter.</margin> You will arrange these things concerning the beginning of form of which we speak, a matter about which the same philosopher <note>Pico refers here to Aristotle, whom Renaissance scholars often called "The Philosopher."</note> has discussed copiously and subtly. And immediately, as that spirit worked the waters and permeated the subject at the command of God the craftsman, **light** arose—that is, the beauty and splendor of form.

### Chapter Three.

Since we descend in the correct order from common and general things to special things, as Aristotle proves, Moses, intending to do the same, after speaking of those things which are common to all elemental things, divides the entire elemental substance into three parts on the second day. <margin>What we should understand by "waters" on the second day.</margin> First, however, it must be understood that all **material forms** are designated by him here under the name of "waters," than which no term could be more fitting. That title of "substance" is legitimately claimed only by those things which stand by themselves, leaning upon themselves, and are true by reason of what they are, unmixed with foreign things and not at all adulterated. <margin>Heraclitus; Poets.</margin> **Heraclitus** called the substance of sensible things a "sea," and among the poets...

...that those things are according to their own more divine nature, or that they similarly show themselves to men as shining and equally sparkling; and that some of them follow another star in heaven as their prince and leader. ## Chapter Six

<margin>The Pythagoreans</margin>
What follows concerning the production of animals and finally of man is now manifest. For after plants, those "mixed" things follow which can feel and move, even though the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras.</note> ascribe a "dull sense" to plants—a matter we shall discuss in the harmony we are producing with the help of a more extensive study. These animals, however, which participate in motion and sense beyond any controversy, are distinguished here by Moses—as they also are in the **Timaeus** <note>original: "Timeo"; a reference to Plato’s dialogue regarding the creation of the physical world.</note>—into those that fly, those that live in the water, and those that dwell on the land. Man is the supreme and prince of all; here, the nature of the corruptible world <note>The "corruptible world" refers to the earthly realm where things are born, change, and die, as opposed to the eternal heavens.</note> reaches its furthest point and **sounds the retreat.** <note>original: "receptui canit"; a military metaphor meaning that nature has completed its march and now rests at its peak.</note>

## Chapter Seven

<margin>Christ our happiness</margin>
Just as man is the absolute completion of all lower things, so **Christ** is the absolute completion of all men. For if, as the philosophers say, all perfection is derived from that which is most perfect in any given class <note>term: "genus" — Pico is using the Aristotelian logic that within any category, there is one supreme example that defines and empowers all others.</note> as if from a fountain, there is no doubt that the perfection of all goodness is derived from Christ the man into all other men. To him alone was the **spirit given without measure** <note>A reference to John 3:34.</note> so that we might all receive from his fullness. See how this prerogative is undoubtedly owed to him as God and man; it belongs to him by a peculiar and legitimate privilege even insofar as he is man.

# SECOND EXPOSITION CONCERNING THE CELESTIAL WORLD

## PROLOGUE

<margin>Three reasons why Moses wrote figuratively</margin>

**S**hould we rise from the elements to heaven—from corruptible to incorruptible bodies—it will be clear to everyone that by the same words with which the nature of the elements was shown to us, the highest doctrines regarding the celestial beings were also encompassed by the prophet. When we revolve this in our minds, there will be another reason ready at hand beyond those we mentioned in the prefaces. For example, when Moses was about to speak of the **agent cause** and of **matter**, <note>term: "agent cause and matter" — The 'agent cause' is the force that acts to create something, while 'matter' is the underlying substance. These are technical terms from Aristotelian physics.</note> why did he not call them by those express words, but instead called them "heaven and earth"? And why did he call the dispositions of matter "waters" rather than "qualities" (as the philosophers do)? Why did he call comets and lightnings and other things of that sort "stars" and "constellations" rather than by their proper names, and so on with the rest?

In the beginning, we proposed that it was the ancient custom to write of great physical and divine matters in a hidden and figurative way. Furthermore, because of the "rudeness" of the listeners <note>Moses's original audience was considered by Renaissance scholars to be uneducated and unable to grasp abstract philosophy.</note> who could not bear the splendor of the Mosaic teaching, it was necessary for him to speak to them with a "veiled face" lest those who were to be enlightened be blinded by too much light. 

Now we have the opportunity for a **third reason**: namely, that if he had named "matter," "form," "qualities," and "agent cause," those terms might indeed serve in a treatise on the corruptible world, but not for the others. <margin>The wonderful craftsmanship of Moses; the most perfect style of writing</margin> Wherefore, it is the unthought-of and wonderful craftsmanship of Moses—a truly divine rather than human industry—to use such words and to arrange his discourse so that the same words, the same context, and the same sequence of the entire scripture should aptly suit the secrets of all the worlds and of all nature. This is where the book of Moses surpasses all the learning, eloquence, and genius of the nations. This is the new and as-yet-untouched thing that we have attempted to bring forward: to prove by the thing itself that this was indeed done by Moses. This is the idea, this is the model of the most perfect writer; not only because this kind of writing portrays and emulates nature, as we demonstrated above...

### Chapter One.

Whatever exists as a number after the Unity is made perfect and complete by that Unity. 

<margin>Unity</margin> 
Unity alone is entirely simple and perfect in itself; it does not go out of itself, but clings to itself with an indivisible and solitary simplicity. This is because it is self-sufficient, needing nothing, and full of its own riches. 

<margin>Number</margin> 
Number, since by its nature it is a multitude, becomes simple through the benefit of Unity, insofar as it is capable of simplicity. However, the further any given number is from Unity, the more it always falls into a greater multitude; in such a number, there is more dissimilarity, more parts, and more composition. Yet no number is so close to Unity that it is not still a multitude, possessing a "unity" that is added to it rather than being its natural essence—being one not by nature, but by composition. 

<margin>The ascent of the mathematicians to divine things</margin> 
Let us transfer these principles to divine matters in the Pythagorean manner <note>Pythagoras was a Greek philosopher who believed that the universe was built upon mathematical principles and that numbers held mystical significance</note>. 

God alone, who is from no one else but from whom all things come, is the most simple and indivisible essence. Whatever He has, He has from Himself: by the same reality through which He *is*, He also knows, He wills, He is good, and He is just. We cannot understand Him as being anything other than the very act of "Being" <term>Being: the original Latin "esse" refers to the pure act of existing, which Pico distinguishes from "essence" (what a thing is)</term> which He is. Other things are not "Being" itself; rather, they exist *through* it. 

Therefore, an angel is not Unity itself; otherwise, he would be God—or there would be many Gods, which is a concept that cannot even be imagined. For what will be "one" if Unity itself is not one? It remains, then, that an angel is a "number." And if he is a number, he is a multitude made one in some part of himself. 

Every number is imperfect insofar as it is a multitude, but perfect insofar as it is one. Therefore, whatever is imperfect in an angel, let us ascribe to the "angelic multitude"—which he possesses because he is a number, that is, a creature. Whatever is perfect, let us ascribe to the "added unity"—which he possesses because he is joined to God. 

We find a double imperfection in an angel: First, because he is not "Being" itself, but an essence that participates in Being so that it may exist. Second, because he is not "Understanding" itself, but understanding comes to him so that he may perceive; for although his nature is intellect, he is only a vessel for intelligence. The second imperfection depends on the first, since that which does not exist of itself certainly does not understand of itself, for nothing can act where the very act of Being is not present. 

Both of these imperfections happen to the angel because he is a multitude. It remains that his completion and perfection must come from the Unity that descends from above. But God is that Unity, from whom "Being," "Life," and every perfection are derived for the angel. 

Just as there is a double imperfection—a double multitude, so to speak—so let us understand a double arrival of Unity to perfect both. The first is that where the essence is raw, unformed, and devoid of life and "Being"; this is the <note>original: "Terra inanis & uacua"</note> "formless and empty earth" <margin>Formless earth</margin> which God created. 

You might not believe, as some have believed, that the *forming* of the essence belongs to the Creator but the *creation* does not. At the same time as the earth, He also created the "heaven"—that is, the act of that essence and the shared unity within the multitude, which is "Being" itself. Thus, the creation of heaven and earth is, as it were, the same act, since it is a shared embrace of two natures coming together toward the same thing through a similar bond. 

Nor do we speak out of harmony with the ancients when we call "Being" (the participation in divinity) "heaven." For <margin>Xenophanes</margin> Xenophanes <note>original: "Zenophanes"</note> called the archetypal world a "sphere," and the Saracens <note>A term used by medieval and Renaissance writers to refer to Muslims; Pico is likely referencing Islamic philosophers like Avicenna</note>—indeed, even our own people—call God a "circle."

...to become children of God through grace. One must not understand this "son" to be the person we see, who is fleeting and fragile, but rather the one who rules this very person whom we see. In the history of the Kingdom, we read according to the Hebrew literature <note>Pico often references "Hebrew literature" to signal his use of Kabbalistic or Rabbinic sources alongside Christian ones.</note> that Solomon prayed with these words: "Hear, O heaven." <margin>History of the Kings</margin> In that context, "heaven" does not mean the literal sky; rather, he calls upon God, the ruler and lord of heaven and earth. Therefore, the "lower waters" purge our "earth," which is why it comes into view as something bright; the "celestial" ones illuminate what has been purged. Finally, the "super-celestial" ones perfect and fertilize it with a certain fiery and life-giving dew, leading to such great happiness that the soul no longer sprouts merely medicinal herbs, but germinates the Savior himself. Thus, not just a single virtue, but Christ—the fullness of all virtues—is formed within us. <margin>Christ is the fullness of all virtues.</margin>

**Chapter Six.**

Next follows the creation of a multitude of inhabitants from the elements: fish, birds, and beasts. Here, I would have been held in great distress—more so than anywhere else in this entire work of ours—if I did not have at hand Isaiah, in whose writing we read of the winged Seraphim, and Ezekiel. <margin>Isaiah, Ezekiel, the ancient Hebrews, and the unities of the angelic legions.</margin> If we believe the Hebrews, Ezekiel's "birds" and "beasts" also indicate spiritual substances to us. The ancient Hebrews run to my aid, for they want the entire angelic multitude to be hinted at in this place by Moses. Let us say, then, following in their footsteps, that the prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis, as "the prophet."</note> here refutes the error of the philosophers. Those philosophers believed that there were indeed some primary intellectual substances, but they denied what the theologians say: that these individuals preside over a numerous multitude, just as commanders lead legions. When we think of the nine angelic orders, and each order has been assigned its own leader, let us imagine in our minds that leader and prince as a "great sphere." Then, let us imagine the following army as the inhabitants and ornament of that sphere, just as we think of fish in the water, birds in the air, beasts on the earth, and stars in the eighth sphere. Thus, that saying of Daniel will be true: "ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him, and a thousand thousands ministered to him." <margin>Daniel</margin>

**Chapter Seven.**

Finally, he mentions man—not because man is an angel, but because he is the end and boundary of the angelic world. Just as when he was dealing with corruptible nature, he brought man into that nature not as a part, but as the principle and head. It follows that the study of man belongs to three worlds: to the world that is his own, and to each extreme—the incorporeal <note>the spiritual/angelic realm</note> and the elementary <note>the physical/material realm</note>. He is the middle point between them, positioned so that he is the "end" of one and the "beginning" of the other. 

But I see a "snare" prepared for our explanation, since it is added that man "rules over" the fish of the sea, the birds, and the beasts. If those animals signify the angelic nature to us, how can it be true that man rules over them, when both philosophers know and the prophet testifies that man was made "lower than the angels"? <margin>Jesus Christ, the firstborn of every creature; Dionysius; Paul</margin> May He be with us and break the snare—He who also crushed Satan under our feet—Jesus Christ, the firstborn of every creature. He truly breaks the snare and unties and breaks every knot. For not only was human nature so highly exalted in Him (in whom the whole divinity dwelt bodily) that the man Christ, as man, teaches, illuminates, and perfects the angels (if we believe Dionysius), having been "made so much better than the angels," as Paul says, as he inherited a more excellent name than they. But also all of us, to whom power was given to become "sons of God" through the grace of which Christ is the giver, can be raised above angelic dignity.

<summary>Pico explains that the "fish, birds, and beasts" of Genesis represent the vast legions of angels, and argues that through Christ, humanity can transcend even these angelic heights.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the Fourth Book of the Heptaplus. In the previous three books, Pico della Mirandola interpreted the first chapters of Genesis as descriptions of the three cosmic realms: the angelic (intellectual), the celestial (planetary), and the sublunary (corruptible nature). Here, he begins his fourth "exposition," arguing that the same text also describes a fourth world: the "human world" or the nature of man.</meta>

-># HEPTAPLUS<-

->### THE FOURTH EXPOSITION CONCERNING THE WORLD, THAT IS, THE HUMAN WORLD, AND CONCERNING THE NATURE OF MAN. THE PREFACE TO THE FOURTH BOOK.<-

**[Decorated P]** After we have shown that the prophet <note>original: "propheta"; Pico refers to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis.</note> has sufficiently treated all parts of the world and all celestial, angelic, and corruptible nature, it remains (if we are mindful of our promise) to interpret the entire reading once again concerning man. We shall prove this through the work itself: that there is no statement in this entire work which—just as it dealt with the three worlds discussed above—does not also encompass hidden meanings and the deepest truths concerning the nature of man. Nor shall we have done a less worthy service if we are diligent in explaining this fourth narration than we were in the previous ones. For how useful and necessary self-knowledge is to man (to set aside the **Delphic inscription** <margin>The Delphic inscription. Plato.</margin> <note>original: "littera delphica"; the famous Greek maxim "Know Thyself" (Gnothi Seauton) inscribed at the Temple of Apollo in Delphi.</note>) has been so demonstrated by Plato in the first *Alcibiades* that he left nothing for later writers to attempt to bring as anything new to the subject. And indeed, the zeal of one who, still ignorant of himself and still not knowing whether he can know anything at all, yet so boldly affects a knowledge of things that are so far from him, is wicked and rash.

Let us return, therefore, into ourselves, and let us see (as the prophet says) what great goods God has done for our soul. For if, by chance, one is less diligent in recognizing things within oneself, one might hear the Father saying in the *Song of Songs*: "If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go forth and depart, following the tracks of your flocks." <note>Song of Songs 1:8. Pico interprets this biblical verse allegorically as a warning about the consequences of lacking self-knowledge.</note> You see what punishment for our ignorance awaits us. For we must "depart"—that is, from the Father—which departure is followed by disinheritance; what could be more unhappy? We must also "go forth": namely, out of ourselves. For the mind <margin>The triple punishment for self-ignorance: Above oneself, From oneself, Behind oneself.</margin> that does not see itself is not at home with itself. But he who "goes out" is torn away from himself; what could be more bitter? Third, we must go "after the tracks of our flocks," that is, after the tracks of the brutes <note>The "brutes" refers to animals or the irrational, animalistic instincts within human nature.</note> which are within us—about which we shall say enough in the exposition—and what could be more miserable? What more despicable and contemptible? To become, in effect, the foot-servants of beasts, over whom nature had appointed us the leaders. Therefore, proceeding not after the tracks of the brutes but after the tracks of Moses, let us enter into ourselves; let us enter the inner chambers of the mind, with the prophet himself unbarring the entrance for us, so that within ourselves we may happily recognize both all the worlds and also our Father and our homeland.

### Chapter One.

Before we arrange the exposition more accurately according to the words and order of the prophet, it is necessary to say something in passing about the nature of man and to explain certain terms, so that the understanding of the entire meaning may then be more fitting. Man consists of a body and a rational soul. The rational soul <margin>The rational soul. Aristotle. The Platonists. Plotinus.</margin> <note>original: "Animus rationalis."</note> is called "heaven." For Aristotle calls heaven a living being moved by itself, and our mind (as the Platonists prove) is a substance moving itself. Heaven is a circle, and the mind likewise is a circle; indeed, as Plotinus writes, heaven is a circle precisely because its soul is a circle. Heaven is moved in an orbit; the rational mind, transferring itself from causes to effects and again returning from effects to causes, revolves in a circle of reasoning. If these points were to be explained individually to those who have not read them elsewhere, we would no longer be interpreters of Moses, but of Aristotle and Plato. The body <margin>Body. Spirit. Aristotle.</margin> is called "earth," since it is of an earthy and heavy substance. Wherefore, being made from the soil <note>original: "humo"; a wordplay on "homo" (man) and "humus" (soil/ground).</note> (as Moses writes), it gave the name to "man." But between the earthly body and the celestial substance of the mind, there was a need for a middle link <note>original: "medio vinculo".</note> which would join such distant natures together. Assigned to this duty is that thin and spiritual little body <note>original: "spiritale corpusculum"; Pico refers to the "pneuma" or "spiritus," a quasi-physical substance thought to carry signals between the soul and the physical organs.</note> which both doctors and philosophers call the <term>spirit</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirit" was a subtle vapor that mediated between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note>. Aristotle writes that this is of a more divine nature than the elements and corresponds proportionately to the heaven. Here it is called "light," a title that could not more aptly agree with the opinion of the philosophers and doctors, for it is the common consensus of them all that this is a most luminous substance, and it delights in nothing more than in light.

<summary>Pico introduces the Fourth Exposition, arguing that the Book of Genesis describes human nature as a microcosm. He defines man as a composite of a rational soul (associated with heaven), a physical body (associated with earth), and a mediating "spirit" or "light."</summary>

...to be nourished and restored. It follows that just as all the power of the heavens (as Avicenna <margin>Avicenna</margin> <note>original: "Auicenna"; Pico refers to the Persian polymath Ibn Sina, whose medical and philosophical works were foundational in Renaissance thought.</note> writes) is transferred to the earth by the vehicle of light: so too every power of the soul—which we have called "heaven"—and all vital power—namely, motion and sense—flows and is poured into this earthly body (which we have called "earth") through the mediation of the <term>shining spirit</term> <note>original: "lucido spiritu"; in Renaissance medicine and philosophy, "spirit" was a subtle, vaporous substance that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh.</note>.

Let us now descend to the words of the Prophet <note>original: "prophetæ"; Pico refers to Moses, the traditional author of Genesis.</note>: in whose writings we first see the creation of heaven and earth as the extremes—namely, the rational power of our substance and the earthly body. Since light—that is, the shining spirit—is added last, they are united in such a way that from evening and morning—that is, from the nocturnal nature of the body and the morning nature of the soul—one human being is formed. # HEPTAPLUS

<note>Pico della Mirandola’s *Heptaplus* (1489) is a seven-fold explanation of the seven days of Genesis. In this section, he allegorically links the creation of the physical world to the internal workings of the human body and soul.</note>

Aristotle, we call "common" <note>original: *communē*. The "common sense" (*sensus communis*) in medieval and Renaissance philosophy was not "good judgment," but a specific internal faculty that unified the data from the five individual senses into a single perception.</note>; this, however, if we follow Aristotle, is located in the heart: just as rivers flow together into the sea. Nor would we speak absurdly if we said that from that sea, the five senses of the body—which we see as hearing, sight, taste, touch, and smell—enter the continent of the body like five Mediterranean seas spread out. <margin>Plato</margin> This was clearly the opinion of Plato in the *Theaetetus* <note>A Platonic dialogue concerning the nature of knowledge; here Pico refers to the idea that senses must converge in a single soul or faculty to be processed.</note>. For the senses were provided by nature to all mortals to procure life and health for the body: so that through them they may recognize what is harmful and what is beneficial to them; then, once these are known through the appetite attached to the senses, they may reject the former and desire the latter; and finally, through the coupled power of movement, they may flee from evils and pursue what is useful.

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

Let us consider, therefore, whether of the emotions by which we are moved, some pertain more to the body and others to the internal sense which the philosophers call "phantasia" <note>This refers to the "imagination" or the faculty of forming mental images.</note>. Those which impel us toward food or toward sexual desire <note>original: "venerem"</note> seem to me to pertain to the body. For these were given to us by God both for the protection of the body which we nourish, and for the procreation of children in whom we might survive when we ourselves pass away. Yet we abuse these very things, attracted more than is proper by the lure of pleasure; through gluttony and through lust, "making provision for the flesh," as Paul says, "in its desires" [Romans 13:14]. <margin>Paul</margin> In his words, it should be noted that he did not say "do not care for the flesh," but "do not do so in its desires"; because, namely, we must use those things for necessity, not for pleasure—much less should our happiness be placed in them. Let us therefore understand these emotions through the beasts of burden and the wild animals, which are called the offspring of the earth rather than of the waters. This is because they are both fulfilled and excited through the members of this coarse body, and were provided for us by God for its well-being—though they become a means of destruction for those who wither from excessive drinking <note>original: "crapulis"</note> and are dissolved by lust. 

But let us refer to the "waters"—that is, the sense of imagination—those affections which are more spiritual and can be called the offspring of our thought rather than of the flesh. Of this kind are those which call us to honors, to anger, to vengeance, and the remaining affections related to these. These are necessary and useful to those who use them in moderation. For one must be angry, but within limit; and vengeance is often a work of justice; and each person must protect their own dignity; nor should honors be refused which are obtained through honorable arts. I say this so that, since God created these "brutes" which indicate our sensory appetites and blessed them once created, we do not believe them to be evil by their own nature (as the Manichaeans <note>An ancient religious movement that taught a strict dualism between good/spirit and evil/matter.</note> do), or created by an evil principle rather than by the good God. <margin>Manichaeans</margin> Therefore, all those things are good and necessary to man; but we ourselves, by exceeding into ambition, fury, burning rage, and pride, make those things evil through our own fault, which that Best [God] had established as the best things. 

### Chapter Six

<margin>The Chaldean King</margin> But see how perfectly it agrees with what we have said, that man was subsequently made by God in His own image to rule over the fish, the birds, and the beasts which both the water and the earth had produced. This is what we were already discussing above regarding man; but now for the first time we understand the "image of God" within him. From this comes his dominion and command over the brute creatures. For man was so established by nature that reason should rule over the senses, and that every fury and appetite of both anger and lust should be restrained by its law. But having blotted out the image of God through the stain of sin, we wretches and unhappy ones have begun to serve our own beasts; and to dwell with the Chaldean king <note>A reference to Nebuchadnezzar, who in the Book of Daniel was humbled by God and lived like a beast in the fields.</note> among them, lying upon the ground, greedy for earthly things, forgetful of our fatherland, forgetful of our father, forgetful of our kingdom, and of the privilege of our former dignity given to us. "Indeed, man, when he was in honor, did not understand: but was compared to the foolish beasts of burden and made like unto them" [Psalm 49:20]. 

### Chapter Seven

<margin>Jesus Christ</margin> <margin>The Newest Adam</margin> Truly, just as all in the first Adam—who obeyed Satan rather than God—degenerate from man into beast, being deformed according to the flesh; so in the newest Adam, Jesus Christ—who fulfilled the will of the Father and by his blood overcame spiritual wickednesses—all who are his sons according to the spirit are regenerated through grace. We are reformed from being merely human into the adoption of the sons of God; provided that, just as in him, so in us the prince of darkness and of this world finds nothing of his own.

## FIFTH EXPOSITION CONCERNING ALL THE WORLDS SEPARATELY IN SUCCESSIVE ORDER. 

### PROLOGUE TO THE FIFTH BOOK.

Just as Moses, as we have shown, discussed all the worlds together—the intellectual, the celestial, the elementary, and the human—in the individual parts of his narrative, imitating nature (or rather God, the craftsman of nature, who is contained within all the individual worlds), so too our prophet, following the example of nature itself—which distributed proper seats, proper rights, and peculiar laws to each one—by a wonderful and perfect mastery of divine art, has written the Scripture...

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Pico della Mirandola's *Heptaplus*, a 1489 work that provides a sevenfold interpretation of the first chapters of Genesis. Having established his method of looking for multiple layers of reality within the biblical text, he now transitions into the first specific exposition: the Angelic World.</meta>

->### THE SEVENFOLD EXPOSITION<-

He has arranged his work in such a way that he might everywhere discuss all things with the same appearance and under the same veil of words, yet specifically assign individual parts of his work to individual worlds in a sequential order. To demonstrate this, we shall begin to interpret the first part concerning the first world—that is, the angelic <note>The "angelic world" refers to the realm of pure spirits and intellectual beings, the highest level of creation in Pico’s Neoplatonic hierarchy.</note> world; then subsequently the remaining parts concerning the others, shrewdly observing in the words of Moses that golden **Homeric chain** and the **Platonic rings** <margin>Homer’s chain; Platonic rings</margin> <note>The "Homeric chain" is a classical metaphor for the hierarchical link between heaven and earth; the "Platonic rings" refer to the series of magnetic or divine inspirations described in Plato's *Ion*.</note> suspended from the living power of the Creator as if from the true stone of the unconquered Hercules.

### Chapter One.

When we are about to speak concerning the angelic nature, which is pure intellect, let us first conceive in our minds that minds are like eyes. For what the eye is in physical things, the mind is in the spiritual genus. Even if the eye possesses some light within the mixture of its own innermost substance, it nevertheless requires external light to perform the duty of vision, in which it observes the colors and differences of things. Nor should it be said for that reason that it is not "sight" by its own nature, even if it does not see except by the benefit of light. For even the ears—not to mention inanimate things—and all other parts of the body are illuminated by light, yet they do not see. Therefore, that thing has obtained the nature of seeing and is "sight" by the very reason of its essence which, having received light, is able to see. 

Let us consider these same things in intellects: Intellects are the eyes, intelligible truth is the light, and since the intellect itself is something of an innermost light, it can see itself, but it cannot see the rest. Truly, it requires the forms and ideas of things, which it uses like certain rays of invisible light to clearly perceive intelligible truth. Nor should it be said for that reason (as we demonstrated by the example of the eye) that they are not "intelligent" by nature, or that they obtained their intellectual property by accident, sharing the same condition as our own minds. 

This is the source of the opinion of those who judge the title of "intellect" to be unworthy of God. Because if we understand the intellect as an eye which sees not from itself but by participation in light—since God is Light (for truth is light)—and vision is the action by which the eye reaches the light, then God does not need this operation, for He is Light itself. He is as much further removed from ignorance of all things than the angels are, as the nature of light is further from darkness than the eye is. 

But let us return to the angels. The eye—that is, the intellectual substance—is not entirely simple; <margin>Angels consist of act and potency; Averroes the Arab</margin> <note>In medieval philosophy, "simple" means a thing is not made of parts. Only God was considered truly simple; angels, though spirit, were thought to be composed of "being" and "potential."</note> otherwise, it would not be open to the composition of incoming light. From this comes the common axiom that angels consist of **act** and **potency** <term>Act and Potency: Aristotelian terms where "act" is the completed reality and "potency" is the capacity to become or receive something</term>, however anxious the dispute may be as to what that "act" is and what that "potency" is, and what the reason for their composition might be. Likewise, consider what the Arab **Averroes** <note>original: "Auerrois arabs"; Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Western university debates.</note> intended when he said that both the intellect which is in act and that which is in potency exist in all intellects below God. But it is enough for us, as far as this passage is concerned, however the common opinion is accepted. 

Moses reveals all these things we have said to us on the first day. For he divides the substance of the angel into "heaven" and "earth"—namely, the nature of act and the nature of potency. Moreover, just as the same thing has different properties, so it has different names. Therefore, this same **act**, while it is accepted as the power granting sight to the eye and as the fulfillment of potency, is called "heaven," because it stands in the same relationship to potency as heaven does to earth. Conversely, because it is in need of light and cannot perform its own duty of intelligence by itself, it is represented by the "waters"—a body capable of light, yet by its own nature shining very little. 

There is also another reason for the comparison: because this act of potency (which he calls "earth") is nearest to the earth, just as water is. But let us now meet the words of the Prophet: *God created heaven and earth*—the nature of act and the nature of potency, from which He fashioned the angel. And the earth—that is, potency—is *empty and void*: empty of act and void of light, which it does not receive except through the mediation of the waters. And since opposites happen regarding the same thing, and it pertains to the same thing to host both light and darkness, he added: *and darkness was upon the face of the abyss.* <margin>What the abyss is</margin> Nor did he say "upon the earth." For the **abyss** is nothing other (unless we misuse the word) than the depth of the waters. Upon these waters the Spirit of the Lord was carried—that spirit, certainly, which from the beginning...

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

The Apostle James calls Him the **"Father of Lights,"** <note>original: "pater luminum"; a reference to James 1:17</note> from whom, James says, the light of <term>intelligible forms</term> <note>The "blueprints" or abstract ideas that exist in the mind of God or the angels before they become physical things.</note> soon rises above those angelic minds. Perhaps the <margin>Saracens</margin> <note>The "Saracens" refers to medieval Muslim philosophers and theologians, whom Pico often cited to show a universal agreement among different faiths.</note> also understood this when they spoke of the angels being led out by God from darkness into light and filled with eternal joy. For pleasure follows understanding, and no pleasure is greater, truer, or more lasting than this.

->Chapter Two<-

The celestial world is closest to this world of ours. Its primary characteristic is that it serves as the interval between both worlds: the <term>intelligible world</term>—which we have just discussed—and this <term>sensible world</term> <note>The world we can perceive with our five senses.</note> which we inhabit. We cannot more clearly indicate the essence of any middle nature than by expressing the extremes which it connects, since a middle nature always tempers the qualities of the extremes. Therefore, Moses opens up a great science of the heavens for us when he describes the heaven as being placed between "the waters and the waters"—that is, between the angelic and the corruptible substances—placed there not so much by physical location as by its very nature. We have already said that by "waters," we should understand the "forms" which are present in potential, like those near the earth, and which perfect an essence. However, just as there is one "earth" of angels and another of the elements (because their potential power is different), so too is there a different reasoning for the "waters" (the forms) in each place. Truly, between these two, the middle heaven has been allotted its place by the providence of the Creator, possessing on one side divine life and on the other physical embodiment; here incorruptible substance, there visible substance; here the firmness of essence, there the changing of location; here whatever is simple and uniform, and there whatever is varied, mixed, and dissimilar.

->Chapter Three<-

After this, he briefly reminds us of the integrity, position, and order of the elements through the gathering of the waters into one place and the laws prescribed for the sea so that it does not overwhelm the earth. There is nothing that more clearly indicates that there are laws placed within the elements—beyond their mere blunt, physical inclination—by an intelligent Cause, by which they are governed and held in their places, than these barriers of the waters. These boundaries restrain the ocean, whose force would otherwise carry it over the entire circuit of the earth; just as fire rests entirely upon the air, the ocean draws back its foot as if warned by a <term>pedagogue's rod</term> <note>A "pedagogue" was a tutor or guardian; Pico uses this metaphor to show nature following a strict, guided discipline.</note> and does not advance further than our safety and the life of all living creatures requires. This cannot be attributed to the "necessity of matter" (which would instead incline all elements equally toward a spherical shape), nor to a "fortuitous collision of atoms" as <margin>Epicurus</margin> <note>The Greek philosopher Epicurus, who argued the world was formed by random atoms rather than divine plan.</note> dreams, nor to the "seminal force of a mute nature" as <margin>Strato</margin> <note>Strato of Lampsacus, a philosopher who believed nature functioned automatically without a conscious God.</note> says, which is ignorant of its own purpose. Instead, it must be referred solely to the **Final Cause**, which only a Mind and intellectual Providence can direct. For this reason, it happened that when Moses treated the order of the elements, he remembered only this fact; and the prophets so often bring this forward as the most powerful argument for divine power and wisdom. Hence in the Proverbs: "When He fortified the depths with a certain law and circle." And again: "He who surrounded the sea with its boundary." And in <margin>Jeremiah</margin>: "Will you not fear me? says the Lord, who placed the sand as a boundary for the sea." And that other verse: "You set a boundary which they shall not pass over, nor shall they cover the earth." Furthermore, because the entire constitution of the elements is organized so that things may be mixed, especially those which are alive, immediately after the ordering of the earth and waters and the firmament, he added the command for the earth to bring forth plants—a work which otherwise would have belonged to the fifth day.

->Chapter Four<-

After he dealt with the celestial and elementary spheres, and thus with the whole integrity of the physical universe, there remained to be discussed the inhabitants and "citizens" (so to speak) of this worldly city. He deals first with the celestial beings, as if they were the senate and officials of the city, and then the terrestrial beings, as if they were the common people. He mentions the celestial beings first, which God placed in the firmament to be for signs and seasons, and to shine in the sky and illuminate the earth...

<summary>Pico interprets the creation of the heavens and the containment of the seas as evidence of divine providence rather than random chance, arguing that the universe is a structured hierarchy connecting the angelic and human realms.</summary>

-># HEPTAPLVS<-
->*(The Sevenfold Account)*<-

...they might signify. I mean the sun, the moon, and the stars. At this point, very deep questions would need to be discussed, each of which would require a full volume of its own to explain: in what way are these stars in the firmament? Are they there as its more noble parts, as the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, so named because they often walked while discussing ideas</term> believe? Or are they like living creatures in their own spheres—just as fish are in the water or beasts are on the land—as Eusebius Medus and Diodorus maintain? 

This passage also demands a confrontation with the "genethliacs" <term>genethliacs: Astrologers who predict a person's fate or character by the position of the stars at their birth</term>. They seek to use this text to support the science of divining by the stars and foretelling future events, arguing from the fact that Moses said the stars were placed by God "for signs." 

This is a science criticized not only by our own Christian authors like Basil—who rightly called it "a most busy vanity"—and sharply censured by Apollinarius, Cyril, and Diodorus; it is also a science which the good Peripatetics reject and which Aristotle himself despised. Even more significantly, as the author Theodoret <note>original: "Theodoritus," referring to Theodoret of Cyrus, a 5th-century theologian</note> records, it was repudiated by Pythagoras, by Plato, and by all the Stoics. One should also inquire here into the nature of the stars, their motion, and their governance...

<meta>This text appears to be from the writings of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), likely his "Heptaplus" (a mystical account of the seven days of creation), rather than his more famous "Oration." It explores the theological definition of man's "dignity" and his status as the "image of God."</meta>

Clearly, for our sake the Son of God both becomes man and is fixed to the cross. For it was also fitting that he who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature in whom all things were founded, should be coupled with him by an ineffable union—he who was made in the image of God, who is the bond of every creature, in whom all things are concluded. Nor was it right, if the whole of nature was in danger along with man, that its loss should either be neglected or repaired by anyone other than him through whom all nature had been established.

### SIXTH EXPOSITION ON THE KINSHIP OF THE WORLDS WITH EACH OTHER AND OF ALL THINGS. PREFACE TO THE SIXTH BOOK.

<margin>Vestige of the Trinity. Triple unity in things.</margin> **G**od is unity so distinguished by a trinity that he does not depart from the simplicity of unity. <margin>Father, Son, Spirit. The root of all ordered charity.</margin> For first, there is that unity in things by which each thing is one in itself and consists and co-exists with itself. Second is that by which one creature is united to another, and by which finally all parts of the world are one world. The third and most principal of all is that by which the whole universe with its maker is one, just as an army with its leader. This threefold union is present in each thing through its own one simple unity, derived from that One which is both the first One and Trinity at the same time as being One: I mean from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. 

For the power of the Father, producing all things, bestows his unity upon all; and the wisdom of the Son, rightly disposing all things, unites and couples all things in turn; and the love of the Spirit, converting all things to God, joins the whole work to the maker by the bond of love. ### Chapter One.

The nature capable of this supreme happiness is twofold (as we have shown): angelic and human. <margin>Angelic and human nature are capable of celestial happiness.</margin> The former is called "heaven," the latter "earth," because angels inhabit heaven and we inhabit the earth. And of heaven there is nothing more to be said, because he <note>Moses, the presumed author of Genesis.</note> was going to write a law not for angels, but for men. Descending, therefore, to men, he says: *The earth was formless and empty, and darkness was over the face of the deep.* <note>original: "Terra erat inanis & uacua: & tenebræ erāt super faciē abyssi." A quote from Genesis 1:2.</note> God does not create emptiness; He does not create darkness. But the earth (he says) *was* empty and there *was* darkness. He does not say these were created, but that they existed. Why this was said will become clear as soon as we learn what this emptiness and this darkness are.

Human nature, which is called "earth" when compared to the angels, was formless and empty of its original justice right from the beginning—because it sinned immediately—and its "face," that is, its reason, was veiled by the darkness of sin. God did not make these things, but rather the malice of man, who by his own will deprived himself of those goods with which God had enriched him. Thus the state of corrupted nature is described by the prophet. How it was later restored to its pristine dignity and prepared for supreme happiness—first through Abraham, then through Moses, then the prophets, and finally through his only-begotten Son—will be shown in what follows. 

But even at the time when the waters were veiled in darkness, stained as they were by the ancient filth of the mark of original sin, the Spirit of the Lord nevertheless fostered them. This is to be understood in two ways: first, that men were guided by the light of the divine countenance which is sealed upon us—that is, by the light of natural intelligence; and second, that the human race was not abandoned by the care of divine providence. Instead, the Spirit of the Lord fostered the waters—that Spirit who (as the Apostle says) <margin>The Apostle.</margin> *intercedes for us with unutterable groanings* <note>original: "intercedit pro nobis gemitibus inenarrabilibus." A reference to Romans 8:26.</note> and who even then was constantly considering how to purge those waters of the poisons with which the ancient serpent had infected them.

He was the first to complete the law of nature and meditate upon the divine law; the first to persuade men to the worship of the one God against idols and the nations; the first who attempted to dispel the darkness of error and declare war on the evil demons who are called the "princes of darkness." For this reason, he is deservedly named "Light." Because all the disciples of the Lord did the same, they were all called by the Lord "the light of the world." This is the first light that shone upon the world, distinguishing between the religion of the demons and that of the true God, as if between light and darkness.

public oracles of Elijah circulating among them, without any figure of speech or veil, saying expressly that the Messiah would come in the fourth millennium of the world. These words are in the section titled *Avodah Zarah* <note>original: "Anodazara"; a tractate of the Talmud concerning "Strange Worship" or idolatry.</note> in the chapter *Lifnei Ideihen*: "The school of Elijah taught: The world is to exist six thousand years. Two thousand years of chaos; two thousand years of the Law; and two thousand years of the days of the Messiah. But because of our sins, which are many, there have passed of them [the Messianic years] those that have passed." <note>Pico is quoting the Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 97a/b, though he cites Avodah Zarah. The Hebrew text he transliterates is: "Shesh alafim shana havé haolam: shné alafim tohu, ushné alafim torah, ushné alafim yemot hamashiach..."</note> These are their words. Come now, with these very words placed before everyone's eyes, since I have brought nothing invented or arbitrary...

-># HEPTAPLUS<-

Let us discuss and examine the words of the prophecy, and we will immediately grasp the matter at hand. "The world," he says, "is six thousand years." <note>This refers to the "House of Elijah" prophecy found in the Talmud, which divides world history into three 2,000-year epochs.</note> We might interpret this to mean that after a circuit of six thousand years, the end of the world will occur as a future "Sabbath," as many of our own people have believed. Or, if we take the truer view that "no one knows that day," <note>A reference to Matthew 24:36 regarding the end of the age.</note> we may understand it in this sense: that there is no further prophecy in the Law beyond that time. But this does not pertain to the question at hand. Let us see what follows:

<margin>Hebrew interpreters.</margin> **Two thousand years of emptiness; two thousand years of the Law; then the Messiah.** All the Hebrew interpreters call the time before any law was given by God to men "emptiness." But I see the Jew mocking and saying: "If there are two thousand years before the Law and two thousand years of the Law, then the Messiah should not come on the fourth day—that is, while the fourth millennium is passing—but rather on the fifth day, because it says *after* the fourth millennium."

However, the response is easy, supplied by the courageous truth. For when it is said by Elijah, "Two thousand emptiness, two thousand Law," it should not be understood as if the world would be without law for a full span of two thousand years, and similarly that the Law would endure for exactly two thousand years. Rather, it means that the time of the Law of Nature <note>The "Law of Nature" refers to the moral code inherent in humanity before the written commandments of Moses.</note> would reach into the second millennium, and the time of the Written Law would reach up to the fourth. But even before the second millennium is finished, the Law begins; and before the fourth is over, the Messiah arrives.

I do not make up or dream this exposition for myself; <margin>Elijah the Talmudist</margin> Elijah himself teaches it to me, and the <term>Talmudists</term> <note>Scholars and compilers of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> teach it as well. This will soon be manifest to you, you Judean "asp"—unless you close your ears. <note>A harsh rhetorical flourish common in Renaissance polemics, comparing the listener to the "deaf adder" of Psalm 58:4.</note> Elijah says: "Two thousand emptiness and two thousand Law." Let us see in what sense the statement about "emptiness" was true; from that, let us learn the method for explaining what is said about the "Law."

<margin>How the beginning of the Law should be understood.</margin> We must take the beginning of the Law either from Moses or from Abraham. It cannot be taken from Moses, for then the "emptiness" would have lasted for over two thousand three hundred years or thereabouts—for that is roughly the time from Adam to Moses. Therefore, the beginning of the Law must be taken from Abraham, to whom was given the covenant of circumcision, which is the root and foundation of the entire ancient Law. But from Adam to Abraham, if you consult the histories, they find that a full span of two thousand years had not passed, but only one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight years. <note>Pico is using a specific Hebrew chronology here to show the Law started "early," within the second millennium.</note> Thus, the fullness of the Law succeeded the emptiness not *after* the second millennium, but *within* its boundaries.

By the same logic, the fullness of the Gospel ought to succeed the emptiness of the Law not *after* the fourth millennium, but while the fourth millennium was still passing. If they impudently and stubbornly try to deny this, <margin>Talmudists</margin> let them hear their own Talmudists, who strongly support our opinion. For they themselves admit that even at the time they were writing, the time predicted by Elijah for the coming of the Messiah had already passed; they attribute this delay to their own sins. But if Elijah's words were understood to mean that Christ would come *after* the fourth millennium and not *within* the limits of that fourth, the Talmudists would not have said, nor could they have said, that the time promised by the prophets for the Messiah had passed. For at the time when the Talmudic doctrine we have cited was written, four thousand years had not yet passed since the beginning of the world.

As we showed above, Jesus appeared three thousand five hundred and eight years after the beginning of the world, according to the Hebrew reckoning. <margin>The Jerusalem Talmud</margin> Moreover, they themselves record that the Jerusalem Talmud was written three hundred years after the death of Christ, <margin>The Babylonian Talmud</margin> and the Babylonian Talmud one hundred years after the Jerusalem one. Therefore, both were composed within the boundaries of the fourth millennium, and yet they both admit and complain that the time spoken of by Elijah for the coming of Christ had already passed.

Where will they hide themselves now, or what lurking-holes will they seek, to escape or ignore our Sun <note>The "Sun" here refers to Christ or the "light" of the Christian truth.</note> shining throughout the whole world, even against their will? The Talmudists admit (even if they do not believe the ancient writers) that the times predicted by the prophets for the arrival of Christ have passed. They admit the prophets believed he would come during the very times when we maintain Jesus arrived. Nor are their teachers entirely untruthful when they say the Messiah did not come because of their sins. For indeed, he did not "come" to those who did not recognize him. Nor is he a Messiah—that is, a redeemer and avenger of the most wretched captivity—to those...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of the Genesis creation account, specifically focusing on the fourth and fifth days, comparing the physical creation of plants and animals to the spiritual history of the Jews and Gentiles.</meta>

# THE SEVENFOLD EXPLANATION

...namely the fruits of vegetables and herbs. After the sun was created, the waters produced two kinds of living creatures—birds and fish—with even greater fertility than the earth. The earth, no longer content only with trees and shrubs, produced both great cattle and beasts of burden. Do you not see <margin>Simeon</margin>—even if I were to remain silent—that the word of the good Simeon is fulfilled: that this sun of ours should be **a light for the revelation of the nations and the glory of your people Israel**? <note>original: "lumen ad reuelationem gentium & gloriam plebis tuæ israel." This is the "Nunc Dimittis" from the Gospel of Luke (2:32), a song of praise often used in Christian liturgy.</note> Do we not have clearly before our eyes—if we interpret it no other way—both the calling of the nations and the transformation of the earthly Jerusalem and the shadowy synagogue into the true church and the perpetual, heavenly city of God? 

Before the rising of the sun, the waters produce nothing. The earth produces something, but it is thin and meager. For before the coming of Christ, there was no sign of life among the nations <note>In this context, "the nations" (Gentiles) refers to the non-Jewish world.</note> and no fruit of true religion. <margin>The Israelites practiced the true religion</margin> Among the Israelites, there was indeed some hope of life; they knew the way of light in part and practiced the true religion, but it was inchoate and imperfect until He should come who is **the way, the truth, and the life.** <note>A reference to Jesus’s description of himself in John 14:6.</note> 

And unless we return to this mystery, let someone offer me a reason why He divided the adornment and offspring of the earth in such a way that it produced some things before the sun, but others after the sun. Why, likewise, do the waters produce nothing before the sun, while the earth produces something? Why are two kinds of living creatures produced from the waters, while only one kind is produced from the earth? Why is the bird, an animal of the air, ascribed to the waters? 

For—to address the first point—it is not sufficient to say, as some have, that herbs and plants were brought forth from the earth before the making of the sun so that they would not seem to be created by its power. For by that same reasoning, it would be much more necessary for the fish, the birds, and all the adornment of the elements to be made before the sun, so they would not be believed to be made by its power. Moses would have thus left us with a suspicion: even if the light of the sun had not been necessary to produce plants (as they are more "imperfect"), it might have been necessary to produce animals, which are more "perfect." For it follows that if the more perfect things could come into the light without the sun's help, then the less perfect things could certainly be made without it. However, the logic does not work in reverse: just because the lowlier things were made without it—such as plants, the most humble class of living things—it does not follow that the entire nature of animals could be produced without the sun's intervention. 

Therefore, the intention of the Author is more truly investigated from what we have said. Similarly, if someone says the creatures related to the waters are those that live in the waters, he will see that one kind should have been assigned to the waters, but two kinds to the earth, because the home of birds is the earth rather than the water. And beyond all controversy, if we consider the nature of the animal, a bird is either a creature of the land or of the air; <margin>The deepest reasons</margin> it is in no way an aquatic creature. 

But hear the deepest reasons of all, which pull us—even against our will—toward the mysteries of Christ and the church. And certainly, if all things (as Aristotle says) <margin>Aristotle</margin> are in harmony with the truth, then all things must especially harmonize with Christ, who is Truth itself. It was not for nothing or for no reason that He said so often to the Hebrews: **Search the scriptures: for they are they which testify of me** <note>original: "Scrutamini scripturas: ipsæ sunt quæ testimoniū perhibent de me" from John 5:39.</note>; indeed, He asserted that many things—rather, all things—in the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets were predicted concerning Him. 

But we are often blind in the face of such great light; we cannot consider the wonders of His law unless He reveals them to our eyes. Let us proceed, with Him bringing us aid, to the revelation of these mysteries and figures. Two animals are produced from the waters, and one from the earth, because there was a greater fullness of believers from the nations than from the Jews. However, even if the earth produced fewer, it produced more "perfect" living creatures than those which the waters produce: namely, cattle and all four-footed beasts. For although more of the heathens believed than the Hebrews, those from the Hebrews were more perfect: from them came the Apostles, the founders of the entire religion. Likewise, the waters produced two different kinds and a double nature...

...brings forth [from the earth] only land animals; whereas of birds and fish [the water brings forth many]: because among the Gentiles, some are transferred to Christ from the service of demons, and others from the law of nature. Every Hebrew is a Hebrew only <note>Pico argues that the Jewish people are defined solely by their unique Covenant, whereas Gentiles are defined by their diverse backgrounds—either paganism or natural philosophy</note>, because it was not permitted for them to live within the boundaries of nature alone; to them was given the specific law of God, which is not common to other nations. "For He has not dealt so with every nation, and His judgments He has not made manifest to them" <note>A quote from Psalm 147:20, emphasizing the exclusivity of the Mosaic Law before the coming of Christ</note>. Therefore, the fish signify to us those who came to us from the cult of demons, not only because the waters (as we showed above) represent the impiety of the nations, but because Jonathan the Chaldean <margin>Jonathan the Chaldean</margin> <note>original: "Ionethes caldæus." This refers to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible</note> testifies that in the sacred scriptures, wicked demons are often signified by these animals that live in the waters.

The birds signify those who were translated from the institutions of nature to grace. The clear reason for this comes from what we wrote abundantly in the preface of this book concerning natural and supernatural happiness. For we showed that the sky is the most expressive image of supernatural happiness, and that natural happiness is a certain secondary and imaginary thing rather than true happiness. Therefore, those who achieve this [natural happiness] by using the laws of nature are most fittingly denoted by birds, inhabitants not of the first and true heaven, but of the air; which, by a certain secondary and imaginary reason, also claims the name of "heaven" for itself. Hence "winged creatures of the sky" and "birds of heaven" are so frequently called in divine scripture. See, however, how it was done with deep counsel: that the birds are referred not to the air, but to the water. This is because those who lived according to nature were still counted as the "people of the nations" <note>the Gentiles</note>. Indeed, they both called themselves nations and lived among the nations—such as, perhaps, Socrates and many of the philosophers. For this reason, both types [the impious and the natural philosophers] are commonly referred to the waters. 

But it is easy to show how well this explanation fits with Evangelical and Apostolic doctrine. For the Apostles converted from the Hebrews were figured as "oxen"—terrestrial animals—by Paul <margin>Paul</margin>, and by our doctors in the commentary on the Gospel <margin>The Gospel</margin> where the sellers are cast out of the temple <note>Refers to the Cleansing of the Temple; Pico is linking land animals to those already within the "structure" of God's Law</note>; and Christ <margin>Christ</margin> calls the Israelites "sheep." However, the Apostles, to whom the conversion of the Gentiles was commanded, were called "fishermen" by the Lord. Their leader was Peter, who at Rome—the mistress of the nations—was to be a fisherman, as it were, of the ocean and of the great sea creatures. Moreover, Christ—who said He was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel—claimed for Himself the name not of a fisherman, but rather of a shepherd.

### Chapter Six.

From this, the solution to the question that has long troubled the interpreters of this book is also manifest: Why on the second day was it not said: "And God saw that it was good"? <margin>Why it was not said on the second day "that it was good"</margin> If we say what is usually said—that it was done because the work of the waters was not finished on that day, but on the third, when the waters under the heavens flowed together into one place—it will not seem fully satisfactory. For the proper work of the second day is not the arrangement of the waters, but the arrangement of the firmament, which was fixed in the middle place between the waters. On that day, there was both the making of the firmament, when God said "let there be a firmament," and the distinction of the waters, when He said "and let it divide the waters from the waters"—all of which was sufficiently completed. However, the collection of the waters (which is called the sea), the revelation of the dry land, and the production of plants belong entirely to the character of another work; thus, they were finished on another day, that is, the third, to which they pertained. Therefore, the reason must be sought from a deeper mystery. The firmament (as we showed above) represents the Law. And the firmament, just as it was unformed, was also not simply perfect until it was furnished with the sun, moon, and stars. In the same way, the Law was not indeed evil (as the Manicheans <margin>Manicheans</margin> <note>Followers of a dualistic religion who believed the Old Testament God was evil; Pico is defending the dignity of the Hebrew Law while still calling it "incomplete"</note> say), but it was also not simply "good"—that is, perfect—until...

<meta>This page concludes the seventh chapter of the seventh book of the Heptaplus, where Pico della Mirandola discusses the relationship between the Law and the Gospel, and the transformative power of baptism. It then transitions into a specialized exposition of the very first word of the Bible, "Bereshit" (In the beginning).</meta>

->HEPTAPLUS<-

<margin>Christ fulfilled the law</margin>
Christ came: he who fulfilled the law. If the firmament <note>original: "firmamentum"; here Pico uses the sky/heavens as an analogy for the Old Testament Law.</note> had been evil, it would not have received the sun. If it had been perfectly good, it would not have needed the sun. But the firmament was good only insofar as it was capable of holding the sun and the other stars; just as the Law was good insofar as it was our guardian <note>original: "pedagogus"; a reference to Galatians 3:24, where the Law is a tutor leading to Christ.</note> leading us toward Christ. Moses permitted many things because of the hardness of the people's hearts which the Gospel later did not permit. However, we cannot call the Law evil, as Mani <margin>Mani</margin> <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD) was the founder of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that often rejected the Old Testament as the work of an evil deity.</note> believed; yet we can most clearly call it "not good," as the prophet teaches. Among his writings, God, speaking of the Hebrews, says: "I gave them precepts that were not good." <note>Ezekiel 20:25.</note> He did not say "evil precepts," but "not good precepts"—that is, not perfect, not absolute, not completed. The <margin>Ancient Hebrews</margin> ancient Hebrew doctors confirm this; interpreting that passage of Ecclesiastes, *Vanity of vanities and all is vanity* <note>original: "Vanitas uanitatū & oīa uanitas"</note>, they say: "Even the Law is vanity until the Messiah comes." And concerning these matters, enough has been said.

### Chapter Seven.
<margin>What the power of baptism effects</margin>
Now, since the supreme benefit of the Word made flesh <note>The Incarnation of Christ.</note> was that through the sacrament of baptism—through which the power of Christ is poured into us—we might be reborn as children of God, born not of blood but of God; Moses finally indicates this to us. After the rising of the sun and its demonstration to the world, and after the fertility of the waters and the earth, he makes man in the image of God—not a transitionary man, but a celestial one. For once the <margin>Paul</margin> Jews and Gentiles had turned to Christ, this one thing remained: that through the most holy washing <term>laver</term> <note>original: "lauacrum"; a ceremonial bath or the baptismal font.</note>, conforming themselves to the cross of the Lord, they might be reformed into the image of God. For if baptism makes us children of God, and the Son is the image of the Father, is it not the power of the entire Trinity working in baptism which says: *Let us make man in our image*? If, therefore, we are in the image of God, we are also children. If we are children and heirs, we are heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. But who are the children? It was written by Paul that we cry out "Abba, Father" <note>original: "abba pater"; Abba is Aramaic for Father.</note> in the Holy Spirit. Those, therefore, who live by the Spirit, these are the children of God; these are the brothers of Christ; these are destined for the eternal inheritance, which reward—both of faith and of a well-lived life—they shall happily possess in the heavenly Jerusalem.

->**EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST WORD, THAT IS, "IN THE BEGINNING."**<-

<margin>A paradoxical doctrine of the ancient Hebrews</margin>
**N**ow we have come to the end of the work, having run through the sevenfold exposition of the context of the entire universe. But I recognize that something still remains untouched and undiscussed by us, which it seemed ought to have been explained in the first place: namely, what the first word of the Law means, which is: *In the beginning* <note>original: "In principio"; in Hebrew, "Bereshit".</note>. It was not by chance or without cause that I wished to speak of this "beginning" at the end of the whole work. I am not going to dispute here concerning the Son of God (who is the "Beginning" through whom all things were made, for he is the Wisdom of the Father), nor am I going to prove that the ancient Hebrews felt the same as our people on this point—though we shall do that elsewhere. Instead, we intend to give the readers a taste of Mosaic depth through another method of interpretation. We shall not do this, however, until we have touched briefly upon a certain doctrine of the older Jewish discipline which is truly a paradox. It is the firm opinion of all the ancients, which they confirm with one voice as an indubitable fact, that the complete knowledge of all arts and all wisdom, both divine and human, is included in the five books of the Mosaic Law. It is, however, concealed and hidden in the very letters <note>original: "litteris"; Pico is referring to the mystical tradition of the Kabbalah, where the letters of the Torah are seen as building blocks of creation.</note> by which the words of the Law are woven together, in the manner we shall now declare. Let us take, for example, the first small section of the book of Genesis, namely from the commencement up to the place where it is written: *And God saw the light, that it was good.* All that scripture is joined together from one hundred and three elements <note>letters</note>, which in that way...
