<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s "Heptaplus" (15th century), a mystical sevenfold explanation of the creation story in Genesis. Here, Pico applies Kabbalistic techniques to the very first word of the Bible to extract hidden theological meanings.</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...expounded: wherein the words as they are arranged constitute what we read, showing nothing but what is common and trivial. This literal order of the letters forms the outer shell; this text holds the marrow of hidden mysteries within. But if we take those same elements, broken apart into words, and correctly join together the words that can be formed from them according to the rules they <note>Pico is referring to the Kabbalists, Jewish mystics who used letter permutations to find hidden meanings.</note> hand down, they say it will happen that—if we are capable of receiving this shut-away wisdom—wondrous and most secret dogmas about many things will shine forth for us. And if this is done throughout the whole Law <note>The Torah/Pentateuch.</note>, then at last, from this arrangement and connection of elements correctly established, all the doctrine and secrets of every liberal discipline will come to light. 

I said, however: *if we are capable of receiving this shut-away wisdom*. For it can happen that while we are handling, dissolving, and composing various words, many terms and a complex series of speech may be born from them which teach great things and signify great things; yet unless someone has obtained the teaching on that matter elsewhere, they cannot help but look down upon those things as useless and accidental, because they do not understand what they signify. For we cannot learn the dogmas and doctrines there; we can only recognize them. I neither approve of these things by asserting them, nor do I attest to them—since I have not tested them, nor do I trust that I am able to do so—yet I neither deny nor despise them. This is partly because this opinion has great authors, and partly because concerning Moses—who was faithful in all the house of God—even greater things can easily be believed. <margin>Moses faithful in all the house of God</margin> 

However, even though I am not entering those deep abysses, but merely skimming the shore of this sea, I have encountered such riches of gems—which the poets say neither the Hermus nor the Pactolus <note>original: "Hermus... pactolus" — two rivers in ancient Lydia (modern Turkey) famous in Greek mythology for being filled with gold.</note> carry—that I thought it would not be unwelcome to our people if I published them. <margin>Hermus, Pactolus</margin> I chose to take a risk with the first word of the work, which among the Hebrews is *Bereshit*, and which we read as *In the beginning*. <margin>In the first word, the rational order of the entire world is contained</margin> Could I also, by using the rules of the ancients, bring to light anything from it worthy of being known? Therefore, beyond my hope and beyond my expectation, I found—what I myself could hardly believe when I found it, nor could others easily believe—the entire rational order of the creation of the world and of all things opened and explained in that one single word. I say a thing that is marvelous, unheard of, and incredible. But soon you will believe it if you pay attention, and the matter itself will prove me true. That word among the Hebrews is written in this way:

-> [Hebrew: בראשית] <note>Transliterated as: B-R-A-Sh-Y-T (Bereshit).</note> <-

From this, therefore, if we join the third letter to the first, it makes the word **Ab** <note>Hebrew: אב (Father).</note>. If we add the second to the first doubled, it becomes **Bebar** <note>Hebrew: בבר (In/by the son).</note>. If we read all letters except the first, it becomes **Reshit** <note>Hebrew: ראשית (Beginning).</note>. If we connect the fourth to the first and the last, it becomes **Sciabat** <note>Likely referring to Shabbat (Rest/Sabbath).</note>. If we set the first three in the order they lie, it makes **Bara** <note>Hebrew: ברא (He created).</note>. If, omitting the first, we take the next three, it makes **Ros** <note>Hebrew: ראש (Head).</note>. If, omitting the first and second, we take the two following, it makes **Es** <note>Hebrew: אש (Fire).</note>. If, omitting the first three, we couple the fourth to the last, it makes **Seth** <note>Hebrew: שית (Foundation).</note>. Again, if the second is joined to the first, it makes **Rab** <note>Hebrew: רב (Great).</note>. If we set the third, then the fifth, then the fourth, it makes **Hisc** <note>Likely referring to Ish (Man).</note>. If we join the first two to the last two, it makes **Berit** <note>Hebrew: ברית (Covenant).</note>. If we join the last to the first, it makes the last and twelfth word, which is **Thob** <note>Hebrew: טוב (Good).</note>, by turning the letter *Tav* into the element *Tet*, which is very common among the Hebrews. 

Let us see, however, what these first signify in English; then, what mysteries of all nature are revealed through them to those not ignorant of philosophy. **Ab** signifies *Father*. **Bbar** signifies *in the Son and through the Son* (for the preposition *Beth* signifies both). **Reshit** signifies *beginning*. **Sabath** signifies *rest and end*. **Bara** signifies *he created*. **Ros** signifies *head*. **Es** signifies *fire*. **Seth** signifies *foundation*. **Rab** signifies *of the great*. **Hisc** signifies *of man*. **Berit** signifies *by a covenant*. **Tob** signifies *with the good*. And if we weave the whole speech together in a following order, it will be of this sort:

**The Father, in the Son and through the Son, created the beginning and the end, or rest, the head, the fire, and the foundation of the great man by a good covenant.**

<summary>Pico della Mirandola uses Kabbalistic letter permutation on the first word of Genesis ("Bereshit") to reveal a hidden sentence that summarizes the Christian and philosophical structure of the universe.</summary>

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...[returning] to the good: <note original="dere bono">This is the conclusion of a sentence from the previous page, likely discussing all things returning to God as the "Supreme Good."</note> this entire discourse springs from the analysis and recombination of that first word. <note>Pico is referring to the Hebrew word *Bereshit* ("In the beginning"). In this section of the *Heptaplus*, he famously rearranges the letters of this one word to derive several other Hebrew words, such as *Rosh* (Head), *Esh* (Fire), and *Berit* (Covenant), to show that the entire secrets of creation are hidden in the very first word of Genesis.</note> How deep and how full of every kind of learning its meaning is cannot be obvious to everyone. However, some things—though not all—are immediately clear through the terms that are signaled to us. It is known to all Christians that the Father created in the Son and through the Son. Likewise, it is known that the Son is the beginning and the end of all things: for he is the <margin>John</margin> **Alpha and Omega** <note>original: "alpha & ω". These are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet.</note> (as John writes), and he called himself the "Beginning." We have also shown that he is the end of all things, <note original="regz">The OCR "regz" is a standard abbreviation for "rerum" (things). Pico is arguing that Christ is both the source and the final destination of the universe.</note> so that they might be restored to their source.

Other matters are a little more obscure: specifically, what is meant by "head," "fire," and the "foundation of the great man"; what that "covenant" is, and for what reason it is called "good." For it is not immediately obvious to everyone that the entire system of the **four worlds** <note>Pico’s philosophy posits four interconnected layers of reality: the Angelic/Intellectual, the Celestial (the stars and planets), the Corruptible (the Earthly realm of change), and the Human world (the "Microcosm").</note> we have discussed is explained here, as well as their kinship and happiness, which we debated last.

First, then, it must be noted that Moses calls the world a "**Great Man**." <note>The concept of the *Macrocosm*: the idea that the universe itself is structured like a giant human being.</note> For if man is a "small world," then the world is surely a "Great Man." Taking this opportunity, he very aptly represents the three worlds—the intellectual, the celestial, and the corruptible—through the three parts of man. At the same time, he uses this figure to show not only that all worlds are contained within man, but <margin>Which part of man corresponds to which world</margin> briefly declares which part of man corresponds to which world.

Let us therefore consider three parts in man: first, the supreme part, the **head**; then, that which extends from the neck to the umbilicus; and third, that which extends from the umbilicus to the feet. For these are distinguished and separated in the human form by a certain variety. But it is wonderful how beautifully and precisely, through an exact logic, they correspond in proportion to the three parts of the world. In the head is the brain, the <margin>Knowledge, Motion, Generation</margin> source of **knowledge**. In the chest is the heart, the source of **life, motion, and heat**. In the final part are the genital members, the principle of **generation**. 

In the same way, in the world, the highest part—which is the angelic or intellectual world—is the source of knowledge, for that nature was made for understanding. The middle part—which is the heavens—is the source of life, motion, and heat, in which the Sun rules like the heart in the chest. Below the Moon is that which is known to all...

<meta>This page contains a Latin poem titled "Deprecatoria ad Deum" (Prayer of Entreaty to God) by the famous Renaissance philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494). The poem is written in elegiac couplets, a classical meter often used for personal or mournful themes.</meta>

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's Prayer of Entreaty to God. <margin>9</margin>

Gracious God, who is to be revered in the highest majesty,
Who truly holds one divinity in a threefold power: <note>original: "triplici numine." A reference to the Christian Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—as a single Godhead.</note>
Whom the blessed crowd of the angelic choir serves
Above the flaming walls of the high world;
Whose omnipotent right hand once created this
Immense work, visible to our eyes:
You who turn the heavens, who direct the world with a nod,
By whose command the sent lightnings fall:
Spare us, I pray, you wretched ones; wash away our filth, I pray,
Lest the just punishment of your fury drive us.
But if our debts were weighed in an equal scale,
And if the standard of your judgment were severe,
Who could bear the horrendous whip of the living Avenger,
And who could endure his heavy blows?
The <term>Fabric of the Universe</term> itself would not withstand your angry right hand— <note>original: "Machina." Pico uses "Machina mundi" (the machine or fabric of the world) to describe the physical cosmos as a complex, designed structure.</note>
That Fabric which is not destined to perish until the final day.
What mind is not condemned by the origin of the first fault? <note>A reference to "Original Sin," the theological belief that all humans inherit a fallen state from the first ancestors.</note>
Or what mind has not been made guilty by its own crime?
Or surely you are that very one whose nature is always to spare,
And who holds justice with an equal measure of mercy:
You who repay rewards far greater than what is earned,
Just as you grant punishments lighter than the sins committed.
For your mercy is greater than our faults,
And to give to the unworthy is a thing more worthy of God.
And they are made sufficiently worthy, if he deigns to love them—
He who himself creates worth in those he found unworthy.
Therefore, pitying us, I pray, look upon your people with a peaceful face,
Whether you prefer to call us your servants or, rather, the accused.
Certainly, we are the accused, if you look at the crimes of our life—
The work of a far too ungrateful mind.
But if instead you discern your own gifts within us—
Gifts ennobled by your extraordinary blessings—
We are the very ones whom nature once made your servants,
And whom holy grace soon after made your children.
But (alas!) the indulgence of such a great destiny weighs upon the wretched:
Those whom grace made children, sin has made the accused.
Sin made us the accused, but let grace conquer sin,
So that your honor may grow through our transgression.
For although your wisdom or your power might otherwise
Be known for revealing their riches to the world,
The glory of your goodness is greater when found in our errors,
And that love shines out, to be loved above all things.

He who was able to bring down the Lord from high heaven
And to lift the limbs of the highest God onto the cross:
So that the blood and water from your side
Might wash away the foul filth contracted from our ancestral seed <note>original: "patrio de semine sordes"; a reference to the theological concept of Original Sin inherited from Adam</note>
Thus your love and piety, most mild King,
Allows such evils to provide the material for such great goods.
O love, o piety, so well provided for our affairs!
O goodness, made the servant of your servant!
O love, o piety, poorly known in our ages!
O goodness, now nearly conquered by our evils:
Grant, I pray, that there may be a passion in our hearts
Equal to this great love, which may always preserve us:
Grant that we may lay down the empire of Satan—
Whom we repent having served for so many years—by shaking off his yoke:
Grant, I pray, that the fires of a mad mind be extinguished,
And let your love live in our breast:
So that when the spirit, having finished the duty of mortal life,
Shall be led before its Lord,
Having obtained the promised kingdom by a happy lot,
It may feel that you are not a Master, but a Father.

THE END.

### Roberto Salviati sends greetings to Lorenzo de' Medici

Since I was born with such a disposition, most illustrious Lorenzo, and so fashioned by nature that nothing is more important to me than to love, cherish, and venerate those who are either excellent in talent or singular in learning: I could not help but love your Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a brilliant philosopher and nobleman famous for his "Oration on the Dignity of Man."</note> above all others and admire a man truly most worthy of all admiration. Since he recently dedicated to you a book on the **sevenfold explanation of the six days of Genesis** <note>This refers to the *Heptaplus* (1489), Pico's complex, mystical commentary on the creation story in the Bible</note> as the first-fruits of his studies—a work most excellent not only in my judgment but in the judgment of all—I wished to take care that it should be published at my expense in a corrected edition. I have no doubt that I will simultaneously satisfy my love for him and the public benefit of scholars. I also hoped that I would be doing something not unwelcome to you if those physical and divine mysteries which he shared with you should finally, through me, become common to all. Farewell.

<meta>This page begins the "Apology," Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's defense of his 900 theses, which had been suppressed by the Church. It follows his famous "Oration on the Dignity of Man," which was intended as the preface to the debate that never happened.</meta>

# THE APOLOGY OF MIRANDOLA

## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI:

I have dedicated our **Apology** to you, Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent," the de facto ruler of Florence and Pico's primary patron and protector.</note>, not because (God is my witness) I see the work as worthy of such a great man, but because it is owed to you by that right through which I realize I have long owed you all my things. For you should be most firmly persuaded that whatever I am, or whatever I am to be, is yours, Lorenzo, and shall remain yours forever. I say less than I would wish, and these words are all too cold to sufficiently express what I feel: with what love, what loyalty, and what respect I follow you, and have followed you for many years now. 

I am moved by the many favors you have bestowed upon me, which clearly testify to your most loving spirit, as well as by those rare goods of yours—not so much of fortune as of the mind—which your own modesty does not permit me to recount at present. I return to the **Apology**: I ask that you look upon it with a cheerful face. It is surely a small gift, but a significant testimony of my loyalty and respect toward you for all time. 

If it should happen that you touch upon this work amidst the great affairs with which you are always most busily occupied, remember that this is a rushed <note>original: "properatum"</note> work rather than an elaborate one, and that the subject matter of the work had to be taken from the judgment of others rather than my own. I have not dedicated it to you so that you might recognize in me some excellence of talent or learning (which is not in me), but so that you may know—for I shall say it again—that whatever I am, I am most devoted to your Greatness.

# THE APOLOGY OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA.

When I had recently come to Rome <margin>Innocent VIII, Supreme Pontiff</margin> to kiss the feet of the Supreme Pontiff Innocent VIII—a name most well-deserved for his innocence of life <note>Pico is using a wordplay on the Pope's name, "Innocent."</note>—according to the custom, I did so with the intent not to depart from my usual practice of always composing or treating some literary matter. I wished to do something, according to my strength, worthy of the city of Rome, pleasing to a Christian prince, and useful to myself and to scholars. 

I proposed **nine hundred questions** <note>The famous "900 Theses," covering everything from logic and physics to Kabbalah and magic.</note> on divine and natural matters, to which I was prepared to respond in a public assembly of the most learned men. Hardly had they appeared in public when a multi-faceted crowd of detractors rose up against me—even among some who, if they did not approve of my talent or learning, might at least have approved of my devotion to the liberal arts. One could see the varied fastidiousness, the turned-up noses, the censures, and the diverse judgments of every single person, as always happens when we attempt something new and non-trivial. 

There were about five principal points upon which these "flowers of wisdom" <note>An ironic or sarcastic reference to his critics.</note> condemned me. Some, for instance, carped at philosophy and letters altogether, even so that they might appear knowledgeable; sometimes they added that Adam was cast out of paradise because he wanted to make himself equal to the gods through the knowledge of good and evil. They argued that those who wish to know more than is proper should be driven out of Christ’s court by a similar example. 

Others did not so much disapprove of philosophy as of this very kind of disputing and this practice of publicly debating about literature, barking <note>original: "oblatrantes"</note> that it was intended for a parade of talent and a display of learning rather than for the acquisition of erudition. 

<margin>The age of the author</margin> Several called me bold and rash. They wondered how I, at this age—having not yet completed my **twenty-fourth year**—would not hesitate to propose a disputation in the most celebrated city, in the most ample assembly of learned men, concerning the highest points of philosophy, the sublime mysteries of Christian theology, and unknown disciplines. 

Many accused me not so much for being in Rome, or for being a youth, but for the sheer number of questions—that is, that I was going to dispute about nine hundred points—calumniating that this was done superfluously, ambitiously, and beyond my strength. 

Among those, however, who professed the study of wisdom (that is, theology), there were some who, perhaps not content with lighter insults, no longer called me merely bold, or rash, or boastful, but a **magician**, an **impious man**, and a **new [heretic]** in the Church of Christ...

<meta>This page begins Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's "Apologia" (1487), his formal defense against the papal commission that condemned several of his "900 Theses." It follows his attempt to hold a grand public debate in Rome, which was cancelled when he was accused of heresy.</meta>

->**A DEFENSE**<-

...proclaimed me a heresiarch <note>A "heresiarch" is a leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note>. I call God to witness that I have long been in doubt whether I should wash away these charges or rather pass over them in silence. Two things especially moved me to keep silent. First, because I have always been a man who shrinks from contention and brawls, and I have always loved the peace of mind and the tranquility of a most gentle life which my studies have provided me. Nor do I hate any task of writing more than that which is based on dispute and acrimonious altercation of any kind—for I have never considered it the part of a good man or a philosopher to return an injury or an insult, any more than to inflict one. The second reason was that I was content with the judgment of the Supreme Pontiff <note>Pope Innocent VIII, who initially allowed the debate but then formed the commission that condemned Pico’s work.</note>—whose memory I must always worthily celebrate—and with the judgment of many from the most holy apostolic senate <note>The College of Cardinals.</note>, whose kindness and most benevolent spirit toward me I neither can nor should ever forget. It seemed to me that I could easily ignore the hatred and the insults of wicked men; indeed, regarding all other matters, I was of the opinion that they were unworthy of any eventual response.

But regarding the one charge of the crime of heresy brought against me, I feared that if I did this—that is, if I did not refute it—I might seem to acknowledge the crime. 

<margin>Rufinus</margin> Furthermore, Rufinus <note>Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 345–411), a monk and translator known for his controversy with St. Jerome.</note> writes most wisely that it is indeed glorious to suffer injuries patiently after the example of Christ, but he who bears or ignores a mark of heresy is not a Christian. 

<margin>Jerome</margin> And our Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), the scholar and Bible translator.</note> exclaims with a most clear voice and with the greatest possible intensity of spirit: <note>original: "Nolo in suspitione haereseos quenquam esse patientem."</note> *“I do not wish anyone to be patient under the suspicion of heresy.”* Therefore, Jerome does not wish me to be silent; by his authority, he draws and impels me—a man who is otherwise unwilling and fond of leisure—to write. 

Wherefore, if there are any who perhaps wish I would remain silent, let them know that their controversy is not with me, but with Jerome, who does not wish me to stay silent. Who can fail to listen to Jerome without disgrace? Therefore, at his persuasion—indeed, even at his compulsion—I have set about writing a brief defense. I do this not to tear down or accuse anyone, but so that I may rightly excuse myself from the greatest crime of impiety which has been unjustly charged against me. I pray that my detractors might endure this with the same spirit with which I have always endured their unfair offense. 

Let them endure it, I say, so that I—who am a Christian born of Christian parents, who bear the banner of Jesus Christ on my forehead, and who would gladly die for the faith of Christ—may exclaim with a steady mind (as if with Paul's own voice): <note>original: "Non magus non iudaeus sum: non ysmaelita non haereticus."</note> **I am no sorcerer, no Jew, no Ishmaelite <note>The term "Ishmaelite" was commonly used in this period to refer to Muslims.</note>, no heretic.** But I worship Jesus, and I carry the cross of Jesus in my body, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world. 

<margin>Paul</margin> Finally, while I neither claim for myself titles of "holiness" or "wisdom" and such excellent labels, nor do I take them away from others, I pray they do not take this one thing from me, for the protection of which I would even willingly shed my blood: namely, that I may call myself a Christian. If they grant this, I am not writing for them, from whom I have already obtained what our entire defense strives for. I write for others, who believe or suspect that I am, or once was, a heretic. 

However, although the principal purpose of this is to show that it is not I, but those who slander me as a heretic, who deviate from the orthodox and Catholic path, nevertheless, since I must write, we shall also say something about those things which were first charged against us. I do this so that our detractors cannot abuse my silence as if it were a confession of guilt. 

The first thing that many turned into a fault was my habit of "philosophizing." To these people, I will say nothing in this place, because it is my plan to plead the cause of philosophy separately in a specific work <note>Likely referring to his "Oration on the Dignity of Man," originally intended as the introduction to his 900 Theses.</note>. Altogether, if it is a disgrace to devote oneself to letters and to cultivate the good arts and disciplines, I would rather acknowledge this fault than pray for forgiveness. Even to those who detest this kind of disputation and this custom of publicly debating about God, nature, and morals: I shall not say much, since this "crime"—if it is a crime—is common to me and great men, indeed to the most approved philosophers of almost all ages. For them, it was most certain that nothing was more useful for achieving the knowledge of truth which they sought than to be frequently engaged in the exercise of disputation.

<summary>Pico della Mirandola defends his decision to write this "Apologia," arguing that while he prefers peace, he cannot remain silent under the charge of heresy without appearing to admit guilt. He asserts his identity as a devoted Christian and justifies his use of public philosophical debate as a traditional path to truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his public disputation (the 900 Theses). He is addressing critics who find his youth or the sheer number of his propositions to be arrogant.</meta>

->BY GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...most frequent through practice. For just as the powers of the body are made stronger through gymnastics <margin>Gymnastics makes the powers of the body stronger.</margin>, so in this literary arena, as it were, the powers of the soul emerge far stronger and more vigorous. Nor would I believe that the poets meant anything else by the "arms of Pallas" <note>Pallas refers to Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and war, often depicted in armor to symbolize that wisdom requires a defensive and active intellect.</note>, or the Hebrews when they say that "iron" is the symbol of the wise, than to show us that these most honorable kinds of contests are absolutely necessary for attaining wisdom. 

Thus it happens that the Chaldeans <margin>The Chaldeans</margin> <note>Ancient Mesopotamian people often associated in the Renaissance with astrology and hidden wisdom.</note> require this in the horoscope of one who is to be a philosopher: that Mars behold Mercury in a trine aspect. <note>An astrological configuration where two planets are 120 degrees apart; here, it suggests a harmonious blending of Mars (conflict/energy) and Mercury (intellect/speech).</note> It is as if to say that if you take away these encounters and these "wars," all philosophy would become drowsy and sleepy. 

But as for these matters, as I said, I prefer to defend myself with the authorities and precedents of great men rather than with abstract reasons. It seems a greater task to satisfy those who say that I am unequal in age, talent, and learning to such a great undertaking, and that I have not—following Horace <margin>Horace</margin> <note>The Roman poet Horace famously advised writers to "consult their shoulders" to ensure they didn't take on a subject too heavy for their talent.</note>—consulted my shoulders as to what they can bear and what they refuse. 

Truly, this is a difficult line of defense for me; for if I call myself equal to the task, I seem to incur the mark of a conceited man who thinks too much of himself; if I confess myself unequal, I seem to be marked as reckless and ill-advised. I have fallen into a serious dilemma, where I cannot without fault promise what I cannot do, and yet I cannot without fault fail to provide it. And indeed I could cite that passage from Job <margin>Job</margin> that "the spirit is in all men," and perhaps hear with Timothy <margin>Timothy</margin> <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 4:12: "Let no one despise your youth."</note>, "Let no one despise your youth." 

But I will say this more truly from my own conscience: there is nothing great or singular in me. I do not deny that I am perhaps studious and eager for the liberal arts; yet I neither claim nor assume for myself the name of a "learned man." For as my friend Hermolao <margin>Hermolao</margin> <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a famous Venetian scholar and friend of Pico.</note> once wrote—that delight of the Latin tongue, the splendor and glory of our age—"he cannot be other than unlearned who believes himself learned." 

Therefore, why I have placed so great a burden on my shoulders was not because I was unaware of my own weakness; but because I knew that this kind of fight (that is, a literary one) is peculiar in that there is profit in being defeated. Thus it follows that even the weakest person not only should not shrink from them but can and should rightfully seek them out. For he who falls receives a benefit from the victor, not an injury; for through the victor he returns home richer (that is, more learned) and better equipped for future battles. 

Animated by this hope, I, a weak soldier, have not feared to settle upon so serious a battle with the strongest and most strenuous of all. Whether this was done rashly or not, one could certainly judge more correctly from the outcome of the battle than from my age. 

It remains for me to answer those who are offended by the large number of propositions I have put forward, as if this burden sat upon their shoulders and not rather that I alone must endure whatever labor there is. It is surely unbecoming and too peevish to wish to set a limit on another's diligence and—as Cicero <margin>Cicero</margin> says—to desire "moderation" in a matter which is the better the larger it is. In such grand daring, it was altogether necessary for me either to succumb or to satisfy the challenge. 

If I were to satisfy it, I do not see why what is praiseworthy to perform in ten questions should be considered blameworthy to have performed in nine hundred. If I were to succumb, my enemies would have reason to accuse me, and my friends reason to excuse me. Since in a matter so serious and so great, that a young man with slender talent and small learning should fail, he would be worthy of pardon rather than accusation; for according to the poet <note>Propertius, a Roman elegiac poet.</note>, "if strength fails, boldness will surely be praised, and in great things it is enough to have willed." 

And if in our own time many, imitating Gorgias of Leontini <margin>Gorgias of Leontini</margin> <note>A Greek Sophist famous for his claim that he could speak on any subject proposed to him.</note>, have been accustomed—not without praise—to propose a debate not only on nine hundred but on every single question of all the arts, why should I not be allowed, without blame, to dispute about many questions, which are nevertheless certain and determined? 

But they say this is "superfluous and ambitious." I, however, contend that this was done by me not only in a non-superfluous way, but in a necessary one; which they themselves, if they consider my method of philosophizing, must clearly admit even against their will. For those who have devoted themselves to any one of the "families" of philosophers—to Thomas <margin>Thomas</margin> <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the leader of the Thomist school of Scholasticism.</note> for instance, or to Scotus <margin>Scotus</margin> <note>John Duns Scotus, the leader of the Scotist school of Scholasticism.</note>, who are now most often in people's hands—they can indeed make a test of their learning even in the discussion of a few questions. But I have so trained myself that...

F ii <note>Printer's signature mark for the gathering of pages.</note>

He dismisses accusations of arrogance by citing the precedents of ancient philosophers and the value of intellectual ambition.</summary>

<meta>This page appears to be a section from a defense of intellectual syncretism, likely from Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s "Apologia." It continues the theme of justifying why the author draws from so many diverse philosophical schools rather than sticking to one orthodox tradition.</meta>

# APOLOGY

Bound to the words of no single master <note>This is a famous allusion to the Roman poet Horace: "nullius addictus iurare in verba magistri." It was a common motto for Renaissance humanists claiming intellectual independence.</note>, I poured myself through all the masters of philosophy, examined every manuscript, and became acquainted with every school of thought. Therefore, since I had to speak regarding all of them, I did so lest—if I had been a defender of a private dogma and neglected the rest—I should seem beholden to any one school. Even if they proposed only a few points regarding each individual school, it was impossible that there would not be many points when those from all schools were brought together. 

Nor should anyone condemn this in me—that "wherever the storm carries me, I am brought as a guest" <note>Another Horace reference: "Quocumque me tempestas deferat, deferor hospes." It suggests the author is a traveler through ideas, staying temporarily with different philosophies to learn from them without becoming a partisan slave to any.</note>. For it was once observed by all the ancients that, in unrolling every kind of writing, they would pass over no commentaries unread if they could help it. This was especially true of Aristotle, who for that reason was called "the Reader" <note>original: αναγνωστης (*anagnostēs*)</note> by Plato. And indeed, it is the mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within a single portico <note>A reference to the "Stoa," the porch where Stoic philosophers taught.</note> or a single Academy. Nor can one have rightly chosen a path for oneself from among them all, who has not first become familiarly acquainted with them all...

There are many who, just as dogs always bark at strangers, so they themselves often condemn and hate what they do not understand. Not only famous Hebrew teachers write of this, but also from our own: Ezra <margin>Ezra</margin>, Hilary <margin>Hilary</margin>, and Origen <margin>Origen</margin> <note>Ezra is the biblical scribe; Hilary of Poitiers and Origen were early Christian Church Fathers who integrated Greek and Hebrew thought into Christianity.</note> write that Moses on the mountain received from God not only the Law, which he left to posterity written in five books, but also a more secret and true explanation of the Law. Instead, he himself should reveal it only to Joshua <note>original: "Iesu naue," referring to Joshua son of Nun, Moses's successor.</note>, and then Joshua to the other succeeding heads of the priests under a great religious obligation of silence. And rightly so. For it was enough for the common people to recognize through simple history now the power of God, now His wrath against the wicked, His mercy toward the good, and His justice toward all, and to be instructed through divine and saving precepts for living well and happily and for the worship of true religion. But to make public to the common people the more secret mysteries and the secrets of the highest divinity, which lie hidden under the shell of the Law and the rough cover of words—what else was that but to "give what is holy to dogs and to scatter pearls among swine"? <note>A reference to Matthew 7:6.</note> Therefore, to keep these things hidden from the common crowd and to communicate them only to the perfect <note>The "perfect" (perfectis) refers to a high level of spiritual or intellectual initiation.</note>, among whom Paul says he speaks wisdom, was a matter not of human counsel but of divine command. Pythagoras wrote nothing except a few small things, which he entrusted to his daughter Dama <margin>Pythagoras</margin> <margin>Dama</margin> as he was dying. The Sphinxes carved on Egyptian temples <margin>Sphinxes</margin> warned of this: that mystical doctrines should be kept inviolate from the profane multitude by means of the knots of riddles. Plato <margin>Plato</margin>, writing to Dion about the highest substances, said: "I must speak through riddles, so that if the letter should happen to reach the hands of others, what we write to you may not be understood by them." Aristotle <margin>Aristotle</margin> used to say that his books on "First Philosophy" <note>This refers to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>, in which he treats of divine matters, were "published and not published." What more? Origen asserts that Jesus Christ <margin>Jesus Christ</margin> <margin>Origen</margin>, the teacher of life, revealed many things to his disciples which they were unwilling to write down lest they become common to the crowd. He saw that it would happen that the secrets of celestial doctrine divinely granted to him would perish, for their memory could not long endure without the intervention of written commentaries. He decreed that the wise men who then survived should be called together, and each should bring into the open what he remembered regarding the mysteries of the Law; and with scribes employed, these were reduced into seventy volumes (for there were approximately that many wise men in the Sanhedrin)...

<meta>This page continues the author's theological defense regarding the specific nature of Christ’s descent into Hell, a controversial point in his 13 Theses. He is navigating the fine line between "real presence" and "presence by influence" (effect), citing major Church authorities to show his views are within the bounds of orthodox debate.</meta>

# THE DEFENSE

...the certain and determined manner of Christ’s descent. Whence there has been no lack of some <term>doctor</term><note>A "Doctor of the Church," a title given to influential saints and theologians.</note>—whose condemnation I have never read on this point—to whom it seemed probable and, alongside the truth of the <term>Article of Faith</term><note>A fundamental point of Christian doctrine.</note>, defensible that the soul of Christ was not <term>presentially</term><note>Physically or locally located in a specific spot.</note> in hell. <margin>Francis</margin> All the authorities which **Francis** cites in the fourth book and other theologians cite in the third, it may seem to someone that they could be explained as a descent by "effect" just as much as by "real presence." This follows the same method of interpreting Scripture used by the very doctors who hold the opposite view. For we read in **Ecclesiasticus, chapter 24**: *I will penetrate all the lower parts of the earth.* <note>original: "Penetrabo omnes inferiores partes terrae." This quote is from the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 24:45 in the Latin Vulgate.</note> <margin>Thomas</margin> Explaining this, **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, the most influential medieval theologian.</note> says in the third part of the *Summa* that this is to be understood as being accomplished "by effect." Therefore, someone might perhaps say by analogy that the authorities who state He "penetrated" into <term>Limbo</term><note>The place where the souls of the righteous stayed before Christ's resurrection.</note> or the **Bosom of Abraham** <note>A biblical term for the place of rest for the dead.</note> could be explained in the same way. For "to penetrate" is the same as "to enter deep within," which is even more than simply "to descend." Therefore, if He is said not only to have entered, but to have entered deep within the lower parts of the earth—not because He was really present there, but only because He was there by His effect—then it could also be said that He was in the Bosom of Abraham and entered the Bosom of Abraham only by effect and not by real presence.

However, I do not say these things because I ever believed that Christ, while existing presentially elsewhere, was said to be in hell only because He performed some work there—just as a King, while staying in his palace, is said to be in another part of his province where he effectively accomplishes something by the authority of his power and command. That was never my opinion, as will soon be clear in the declaration of my views. On the contrary, I firmly hold and have held, and have always said both publicly and privately, that if the soul of Christ was anywhere during those **three days** <note>The time between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection.</note>, it was in hell, and that it was truly present there. But I wished to say these things for a fuller examination of this matter, so that we might see the truth of what **Augustine** said in his book *On Heresies*: that nothing is more difficult than to define what is or is not heretical. <margin>Augustine, Note on Epiphanius and Filastrius</margin> For this reason, he says it happened that when two very famous writers, **Epiphanius** and **Filastrius**, wrote about heresies, they disagreed greatly in their counting of them, for no other reason than that what seemed heretical to one did not seem so to the other.

But now I come to reveal my own opinion on the manner of Christ’s descent and to perfectly declare my conclusion. First, I will set out its meaning in summary. Second, I will explain and prove it more broadly. <margin>Summary sense of the conclusion</margin> The summary sense of my conclusion is this: because Christ descended to the lower regions according to His soul only, and because it seems that being located or moved locally does not apply to a soul—just as it does not apply to any <term>separate substance</term><note>A "separate substance" is a being that exists without a physical body, such as an angel or a human soul after death.</note>—except by reason of its operation <note>Its action or influence.</note>. Therefore, I say that to have descended to hell, or to have been in hell locally, does not seem to have applied to Christ except by reason of His operation; thus, although the soul of Christ was truly present in hell, His substance itself was not the reason for that presence, but only His operation.

So that these words may be more fully understood, it should be noted that there is a twofold opinion among those who posit that <margin>Twofold opinion of those who posit that separate substances exist in a place through a passing operation. First: Gregory of Nyssa</margin> separate substances are in a place only through a "passing operation" <note>An action that starts in the spirit but takes effect in the physical world.</note>. For some say that no place is owed to incorporeal substances by reason of their own substance, just as a soul is never truly white or black. And so, according to them, it can be said not irrationally that the soul is not in a place and is "nowhere," just as it is truly said to be neither hot nor cold. As for the authorities of Scripture which seem to give a place to angels when they say they are in heaven or are sent to this place or that, these must be understood as follows: not that they are actually here or there (since they are not properly in a place), but that they "operate" here or there, or begin to operate where they were not operating before. These thinkers rely heavily on the words of **Gregory of Nyssa**, who says that while we ought to say a spirit "acts here," we say it "is here" only by an improper use of language. And so this opinion holds that the substance of an angel or a separate soul can never be said to be present to this place or that, except in a negative sense...

<summary>Pico explores the theological debate over whether Christ's soul was "physically" present in Hell or present through His power (effect). He argues that for spirits and souls, "being in a place" is defined by where they act rather than physical location.</summary>
<keywords>Descent into Hell, Limbo, Thomas Aquinas, Francis of Meyronnes, separate substances, presence by effect, local presence, Gregory of Nyssa, heresy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his theses, specifically concerning the nature of how incorporeal beings (like angels or the human soul) exist in a physical location. This follows a discussion on whether the soul is "everywhere" or "nowhere."</meta>

**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

[not] distant. But if it is ever said to be or to have been somewhere: it is the same as if it were said to be <term>operating</term> <note>original: "operari"; acting or exerting influence</note> or to have operated there. And they add that this way of speaking is borrowed from bodily things: because we see that they cannot act unless they are present—at least according to common opinion. Therefore, believing the same regarding incorporeal things, we conclude that where they operate and where the influence of their operation is found, there also their substance is locally present. They conclude, finally, that it is a crudeness of the intellect and a failure of the imagination to be unable to understand that something can be a "being" and yet not be in a location; and they argue that the reasoning of those who say that "being" presupposes "operating" is frivolous. For that proposition is true only in the sense that a non-being cannot operate. For an agent must be "in act" <note>A philosophical term meaning "actually existing" or "currently active" rather than just having the potential to exist.</note> according to the principle that some moving species will always exist. However, it is not true in the sense that operating in a place presupposes being in that place, since it remains possible for the operator to be of such a nature that local presence or distance is no more owed to it than whiteness or blackness. Those holding this opinion would therefore say that the soul of Christ, when separated from his body, according to its substance, was neither in <term>hell</term> <note>The "Descensus ad Inferos" or Descent into Hell, referring to the period between Christ's death and resurrection.</note> nor outside of hell: but was truly nowhere. It is said, however, to have been in hell because it operated in hell. And it is said to have been most principally in that part of hell where it most principally operated. However, although many doctors <note>Church scholars or university professors.</note> hold this opinion regarding the manner of being presentially in a place, I nevertheless do not hold it, nor did I follow it in my conclusion; rather, I held that which I will immediately subjoin. 

There is, therefore, another opinion which says <margin>Second opinion which the author held</margin> that a separated substance, such as an angel or a soul not united to a body, is indeed truly in a place. And thus it is as truly <term>definitively</term> <note>To be "definitively" in a place means the soul is "there" in its entirety at every point of that space, rather than taking up volume.</note> present locally as a bodily thing is <term>commensuratively</term> <note>To be "commensuratively" in a place means the object matches the dimensions of the space it occupies (like water in a glass).</note> present locally. And in this, this way of thinking agrees with the common path, which is the path of Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a highly influential Franciscan philosopher.</note> and all the Scotists. But they differ in this: that the Scotists say that the definition and limitation of the essence—and ultimately the intrinsic determination of its substance—is the reason for a separated substance being in a place. 

But this opinion, which I have followed in my conclusion, says that just as a bodily substance is commensuratively in a place, yet the reason for its being so in that place is not its "substantiality" but its quantity (which is extrinsic and foreign to the definition of its substance); so also, although an incorporeal substance is truly definitively in a place and locally present, nevertheless the reason for its being in that place is not its substance, but its operation passing from it to the outside. <margin>Clarification of the opinion</margin> I judge this opinion, when understood in this way, to be not only non-heretical, but even more probable than its opposite. And it is this: even if the finitude or limitation of a separated nature is the reason why it is not *everywhere*, or the reason why if it is in one place it is not simultaneously in another as a whole (and both by its nature), it is nonetheless not the reason for the substance itself being simply in that place. Rather, it is its effect or operation—taking "operation" to mean every relationship to a body or a place, whether acting or being acted upon—other than the mere state of being present in a location. And this is understood as a matter of fact, not denying another possible mode of descent or placement of the separated soul (as I say in the following conclusion), though that mode is unknown to us. Following this opinion in my conclusion, I say that Christ was in hell only through [his] effect...

<summary>Pico discusses the philosophical problem of how a non-physical soul or angel can "be" in a physical place, specifically addressing the soul of Christ during the Descent into Hell. He rejects the idea that spirits are "nowhere" and instead argues that their location is defined by their "operation" or actions within that space.</summary>

->**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**<-

...there is a manifest contradiction in the articles <note>original: "articulis"; this likely refers to the Condemnations of 1277, a list of forbidden theological and philosophical propositions in Paris</note>. <meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his philosophical theses, specifically addressing the nature of incorporeal substances (like angels or souls) and their relationship to physical space. Incorporeal things are entirely abstracted from location; and indeed, it is a great lack of refinement to imagine otherwise. The same holds true for the indivisibility of an incorporeal thing and the indivisibility of a point, which I shall make clearer <margin>It is argued</margin> for this master. Let him tell me, I pray: if there were a "separated unity" <note>original: "unitas sepata"; a Pythagorean or Platonic concept of number existing independently of physical objects</note>, would it have a determined <margin>against the opponent</margin> location? Certainly, it is clear that it would not, since a unity is distinguished from a point by the fact that a point has position, while a unity does not. But it is manifest that an angel and any incorporeal substance <margin>The proponent</margin> is even more abstracted than any quantity, whether continuous <note>like a line or solid</note> or discrete <note>like a number</note>. For Metaphysics, <margin>Point</margin> as is clear to everyone, deals with more abstract things than arithmetic, which is one of the <margin>Unity</margin> mathematical sciences; therefore, it can be said even less of an angel that it has a location. If this master <margin>Henry</margin> cannot imagine the abstraction of an angel, let him at least consider the abstraction of a unity. Let him hear what should be said concerning this according to Henry <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a major scholastic philosopher</note>. For he, in the place cited above when speaking of this matter, says: "Those, therefore, who cannot understand an angel according to the nature of its substance—as a unity without the character of a point—are those of whom the Commentator <note>referring to Averroes, the influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher</note> speaks regarding the second book of the *Metaphysics*, in whom the imaginative faculty dominates the cogitative <note>rational</note> faculty. And therefore, as he says, we see that such men do not believe in demonstrations unless their imagination accompanies them. Whatever they think of, they imagine as a quantity having position, as a point; hence such men are melancholic <note>In medieval medicine, the 'melancholic' temperament was associated with deep focus but also a tendency to get stuck in sensory mental images</note> and become the best mathematicians, but they are naturally inept at science." These are Henry’s words, verbatim. From which it follows that, according to Henry, this master is ill-disposed toward the study of natural philosophy, worse for the study of metaphysics, and worst of all for the study of theology, which also deals with the most abstract things. There remains for him only an aptitude for mathematics; and since he has not exercised himself in those, let him judge for himself what judgment should be made of him.

After resolving the arguments that are commonly brought against the foundations of the position I followed in my conclusion regarding the manner of Christ’s descent <note>Pico is referring to his controversial thesis on how Christ descended into Hell</note>, I wish also to bring forward the words of our Albert <margin>The Great</margin>—not less great in learning than in his surname <margin>Albertus</margin>—which I remember reading in his works on this matter, specifically in his book on *Physics*. For we know from logic that it is not a valid argument to move from the destruction of the antecedent to the destruction of the consequent <note>a logical fallacy where one assumes that if 'If A, then B' is true, then 'If not A, then not B' must also be true</note>. And therefore, although it is true that 'that which does not exist is nowhere,' it does not follow from this that 'that which exists is somewhere.' And although this does not follow from the words, yet there are many who say that everything that exists is in some place, using this reason: 'Everything that exists is a particular thing. A particular thing is here and now; and what is here and now is somewhere. Therefore, everything that exists is somewhere.' Furthermore: 'Everything that is of a defined essence exists because it is confined within its own limits; and what is of a defined essence is defined in a place; and what is defined in a place is in some place.'"

But these men distinguish, according to John of Damascus <margin>John of Damascus</margin>, saying that a thing is said to be in a place in two ways. For a thing is there <term>circumscriptively</term> <note>occupying space such that its boundaries match the boundaries of the space, like water in a cup</note> when a beginning, middle, and end are assigned to it <margin>Being in a place in two ways</margin> in that place; and in this way, they say bodies are in a place. Again, a thing is in a place <term>definitively</term> <note>present in a location without occupying physical dimensions, like a soul in a body or an angel in a room</note> when its essence is so finitely enclosed in one place that nothing of it is found outside that place; and in this way, they say indivisible things are in a place, and similarly intelligences <note>angels</note> and souls, etc. "But we do not believe these things," says Albert, "for even the highest heaven is neither defined nor circumscribed by place, because everything that is in a place is enclosed and contained by the place in which it is; and an intelligence, by its nature, is not in a place nor in any spatial difference." These are Albert’s words to the letter. He does not approve of that common distinction of being in a place "definitively" and not "circumscriptively," even though some masters thought it a total sin to deny that distinction in any way. Now, finally, it remains for me to show how they are in...

->APOLOGY<-

<margin>A defense among the Thomists</margin> <note>Thomists were followers of the philosophy and theology of St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note>
But whatever the case may be regarding the opinion of Thomas, it has nothing to do with the matter at hand: because to err concerning the opinion of Thomas is not to err in faith. Indeed, there is often a variety of opinions among the Thomists regarding his actual views. It is enough that this much is clearly evident: that when I proposed my conclusion, I believed this to be the opinion of Thomas. Furthermore, I am not now twisting the proposition into a sense <margin>Note.</margin> different from the one I held then. That I believed this from the beginning, and that this was my judgment regarding Thomas’s opinion when I published my conclusions, is most clearly proven by this: I proposed the conclusion that Thomas and <term>Scotus</term> <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major rival philosopher to Aquinas.</note> do not differ regarding the way angels exist in a place. Now, it is well known that Scotus explicitly states that even if all <term>operation</term> <note>In this context, "operation" refers to an angel or spirit performing an action or exerting power in a specific location.</note> were set aside, a place is still owed to incorporeal substances. Therefore, it follows that I must have believed Thomas held this same view. And for that reason—although I firmly held that Christ was truly and presently in hell, and in this I agreed with Thomas and all Catholics—nonetheless, because I thought Thomas believed his own substance was the reason for his being locatable, rather than his operation, I stated in my conclusion: "not in the way that Thomas and the common path propose."

<margin>That Saint Thomas sometimes held different views.</margin>
Nor should it seem strange to anyone that Thomas follows one opinion in one place and another elsewhere. For in his first commentary on the *Sentences*, he follows the opinion of the <term>Commentator</term> <note>Averroes (1126–1198), the influential Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> regarding beings generated from putrefaction <note>The medieval belief that some life forms, like insects, were created spontaneously from decaying matter.</note>; yet he later rejects this in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics* and elsewhere. Likewise, in the second book of the *Sentences*, he follows the Commentator’s opinion regarding the matter of the heavens, which he later rejects in his commentary on *The Heavens* and in his *Summa*. Furthermore, in the fourth book and in his questions on Boethius's *On the Trinity*, he holds the Commentator's view on "unbounded dimensions," yet he does not hold it in his own later treatise (as is believed) and in many other places. Also, in the first book of the *Sentences*, he says that the same action understands both the intelligible object and the act of understanding itself. However, in the first part of the *Summa* and the third book of the *Sentences*, he holds that reflexive action differs from direct action. Likewise, in his writings, he holds that the soul of Christ, insofar as it was joinable to a body, was like the soul of a <term>wayfarer</term> <note>A "wayfarer" (viator) is a person still living on earth, traveling toward God.</note>; but insofar as it was joinable to the Word, it was like the soul of a <term>comprehensor</term> <note>A "comprehensor" is one who has reached the end of the journey and sees God directly in heaven.</note>. Yet in the *Summa*, he holds that the soul of Christ was entirely and in all respects like that of a "comprehensor," and that it was only by divine dispensation that the gifts of clarity and impassibility <note>The state of being unable to suffer or feel pain.</note> did not flow into his body. He also thinks differently about the knowledge of Christ in his writings than he does in the *Summa*, and so it is with many other matters where one can see that he followed different opinions in different places.

If these men insist that the opinion regarding being in a place through operation is also Thomas’s view, they will have nothing more against me than this: that my opinion regarding the manner of Christ's descent <margin>Note.</margin> is even more probable and less to be judged heretical, insofar as it is true even according to the opinion of Saint Thomas. For this reason, I am all the more surprised that these masters condemned my conclusion; for before they judged that conclusion heretical, I had not only explained my intention to them in these words but had even dictated them to be written down and noted, saying: "Let no one understand me to say by this conclusion that the soul of Christ did not descend to the underworld, or that the soul of Christ was not in hell during those three days; on the contrary, I confess both. But I say that neither local motion nor being located in a place belongs to any separated substance, such as the soul of Christ was, except by reason of its operation." These precise words and no others, word for word, I pronounced for them to note as a brief declaration of this conclusion. How they could still judge it heretical after this—when they could have held it as Catholic—I do not see.

<margin>He argues against his opponents.</margin>
And so, to show briefly by way of argument, recapitulating that those who believe my proposition cannot be defended from heresy are themselves erring in the faith, I argue as follows: one who poses a conclusion that is heretical in itself can be accused of heresy only insofar as that heresy exists in the intellect. But one who poses my aforementioned conclusion cannot, by the act of posing it, be accused of heresy...

->**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**<-

If, therefore, the aforementioned conclusion is not in itself heretical—and they <note>Referring to his critics or the papal commission</note> hold the major premise as granted—I prove the minor premise <term>minor premise: the second step in a logical argument or syllogism</term> thus: Whenever, by positing everything from which proposition "A" necessarily follows, one cannot be accused of heresy, then he who posits proposition "A" itself likewise cannot be accused. 

But he who posits everything from which the positing of my conclusion follows—in the manner I have posited it—cannot be accused of heresy; therefore, he who posits the proposition itself as I have posited it cannot be accused. 

I prove the minor premise thus: the contradictory of this statement—"the reason for being in a place (that is, here or there) in the manner declared above regarding separate substances <note>original: "separatis substantiis." and the contradictory of this statement—"it is not permitted to argue from a whole conjunction to one of its parts"—is not a matter of faith; 

and the contradictory of this statement: "If anyone, having posited a certain negative or affirmative assertion, adds the authority of some Doctor <note>A "Doctor" refers to a recognized teacher of the Church, such as Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus.</note> with the word 'as' <note>original: "ut"</note>, the word 'as' can be taken just as well determinatively as relatively." 

Because it can just as well be equivalent to the phrase "in the manner which" as to the word "that" <note>original: "quod"</note>...

-># APOLOGY<-

He defends the conclusion without applying any abuse or distortion of either the terms or the speech. <margin>Durandus; the words of Durandus</margin>

Concerning the third, it proceeds thus and it seems—

--- Page 200 ---
GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

Also, by appropriation <note>In theology, "appropriation" is the practice of attributing a specific quality—like wisdom or power—to one person of the Trinity or to a specific nature of Christ, even if it applies to the whole.</note>, just as Christ was blessed according to his soul, so it is attributed to him according to that soul to have been the cause of blessedness in others. For it is fitting that a being in potentiality <note>A state of being where something could happen, but hasn't yet.</note> be brought into actuality by that which is already in act. According to some, another effect towards which the soul of Christ directed itself was as an agent: namely, to illuminate the souls of the fathers <note>The "Holy Fathers" refers to the Old Testament patriarchs and prophets.</note> who were in limbo and regarding the mysteries that fall under revelation. For according to Dionysius in the seventh [book] of the *Celestial Hierarchy*: Christ, according to his soul, has the task of teaching the <margin>Dionysius 9</margin> angels; and by reason of this double effect, the soul of Christ can be said to have descended into hell.

This is confirmed by a threefold reason. The first is because moving or descending belongs to a <margin>First reason</margin> separated soul not in the manner of the movement of bodies, but in the manner in which movement belongs to a spiritual substance. However, for other spiritual substances, such as God or an angel, it is not fitting to move from place to place by a movement that exists within them as subjects, but rather through the effect they have on other things; therefore, in a similar way, it belongs to a separated soul and belonged to the soul of Christ. The second reason is as follows: Christ is said to have descended into hell <margin>Second</margin> so that he might illuminate the souls of the holy fathers to see God. At the very same instant in which Christ died, the holy fathers saw God. In that same instant, the soul of Christ could not be in hell by physical movement; therefore, he did not descend there by a movement within himself, but by the effect he had on others. Also, just as in those three days <note>The three days between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection.</note> the soul of Christ is said to have been in hell <margin>Third</margin> with the souls of the holy fathers, so in those three days (or part of them) he is said to have been in paradise with the soul of the thief. To whom it was said in Luke 23: "Today you will be with me in paradise." But this cannot be understood as a location acquired through movement; since those who posit that a spirit is in a place "definitively" <note>A scholastic term meaning the spirit is where its power is operating, rather than occupying physical space like a body.</note> and moves from place to place, hold that the same spirit cannot be in multiple places nor be moved simultaneously by several movements tending toward several places. Therefore, it must be understood according to the effect.

For if anyone says that "paradise" is spoken of in <margin>Paradise</margin> two ways: In one way as a physical place, namely the <margin>spoken of in two ways</margin> empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most "fiery" heaven in medieval cosmology, where God dwells.</note>—and in this way Christ's soul was not in paradise except after the Ascension. In another way, paradise is called the vision of the divine essence—and in this way the soul of Christ was in paradise from the instant of his conception, and the soul of the thief on the very day of the Passion. In this way, it is not contradictory for the soul of Christ to have been simultaneously in paradise—meaning he saw God—and to have been locally in hell. If it is argued in this way, it is not valid because just as paradise is <margin>Hell</margin> spoken of in two ways, so is hell. In one way, hell is called a place corresponding to <margin>spoken of in two ways</margin> beneath the earth. In another way, it is the lack of the divine vision. Therefore, just as the soul of the thief is only said to have been with the soul of Christ in paradise because, by the merit of Christ's Passion, the thief's soul saw God, so Christ's soul is only said to have been with the souls of the chosen fathers in hell because their souls—which lacked the divine vision and were thus said to be in hell—were purged of this lack by the merit of this Passion. 

Therefore, both should be understood equally regarding the effect, not regarding the location or local movement within the soul itself. However, although this may be said with probability and seems to sufficiently preserve the article [of faith] and the words of scripture, yet because divine power is not grasped by human reason, it must not be stubbornly asserted that Christ’s soul could not have descended to hell by some other way unknown to us. To the first argument, it must be said that the same finite thing cannot be in several places at once "definitively" or "circumscriptively" <note>Ways of being in a place: "definitively" (occupying a space) or "circumscriptively" (having boundaries matching the space).</note>, nor is the soul of Christ posited to have been in paradise and hell simultaneously in that way. But according to the effect, nothing prohibits the same finite thing from being said to be in several places when the effects are compatible and are simultaneously subject to the power of the same agent. Thus, Christ's soul is said to have been in paradise and in hell at the same time, because by his merit the soul of the thief saw God (which is to be in paradise), and the souls of the fathers lacked the divine vision and because of this were said to be in hell...

<summary>This page discusses the theological nature of Christ's "Harrowing of Hell," arguing that his descent was an "effect" (bringing the vision of God to the Patriarchs) rather than a physical movement of the soul through space. Pico explores the definitions of Paradise and Hell as both physical locations and spiritual states.</summary>
<keywords>Harrowing of Hell, Limbo, Holy Fathers, Christology, Pseudo-Dionysius, scholasticism, Empyrean, soul, divine vision</keywords>

# APOLOGIA
(A Defense)

...were liberated from this lack and consequently from hell. Indeed, according to one and the same effect—namely, according to the liberation of the Fathers—Christ’s soul could be said to be simultaneously in paradise and in hell, considering the starting point and the ending point of that effect. <note>The author is discussing the "Harrowing of Hell," the theological belief that Christ descended into the realm of the dead between his death and resurrection to free the souls of the righteous.</note> For by reason of the lack of the divine vision from which they were liberated through Christ’s passion, it could be said that Christ’s soul had been in hell; but by reason of the divine vision to which they were admitted, it could be said to be in paradise. Regarding the second point, it must be said that by the very fact that through Christ’s passion we are liberated from fault and from punishment, Christ is said to have descended into hell, because by the merit of his passion some were rescued from the punishments of hell. That descent is not considered according to a local movement existing in the soul, but according to the effect he had in saving people. These are the words of Durandus, verbatim. <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334) was a Dominican theologian known as the "Modern Doctor" for his willingness to challenge established views, including those of Thomas Aquinas.</note> Seeing as such an opinion is never found to have been retracted, if it were simply heretical and consequently against what has already been determined by the Church, it follows that Durandus died a heretic.

<margin>Exclamation / The Order of Preachers / Thomas</margin> O distinguished Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note> and the greatest splendor of our religion, can you endure this: that your teacher—perhaps the first after Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> or without doubt among the first—whose books are held, read, and honored daily in your schools, in your cloisters, and in your libraries, is now pronounced a heretic? You should plead the cause of your teacher; I have pleaded mine. Indeed, O Church, you should plead your own cause, you who have permitted Durandus to be read publicly for so many years and still permit it. Either through ignorance you never recognized such a foul heresy (according to these masters) or through negligence and contempt for divine matters, you did not condemn it once recognized.

If they say there was no need for a new condemnation, since this opinion is among those already condemned: First, it follows from this (as I said above) that Durandus died a heretic.

<margin>Durandus / Capreolus / Durandellus</margin> Second, it follows that Capreolus, Durandellus, and many other doctors <note>John Capreolus was a major defender of Thomism; Durandellus was a critic of Durandus.</note> who recite the opinion of Durandus and yet do not charge it with heresy, were ignorant and unrefined in the faith, not knowing how to discern a heretic from a non-heretic. Third, let these fathers tell me where they themselves have read the condemnation of this opinion. As for myself, I confess I do not remember having read it anywhere. They certainly cannot bring forward any determination of the Councils against Durandus. Not only was this opinion never condemned in the Councils, but no mention was even made of it in any of them.

Likewise, I do not know how they will be able to cite the words of Holy Scripture against him,

<margin>Scotus</margin> if Scotus <note>Duns Scotus, a hugely influential Franciscan theologian.</note> does not lie when he says (on the testimony of Franciscus) that regarding the soul of Christ—not to mention the manner of the descent—there is no express mention in the Gospel doctrine, as is clear from the premises we laid out at the beginning. This is evident regarding the manner which Durandus would perhaps use to explain the authorities of Scripture that might seem to be against him. Regarding the authorities of the Saints <note>The "Saints" here refers to the Church Fathers.</note>, they could perhaps bring forward many who say that Christ’s soul was in hell during those three days just as his body was in the tomb, and similar things. Whatever may be said of Durandus's "fantasy"—namely, the manner in which he would explain the aforementioned authorities, perhaps by saying this is said of the soul and not of the whole composite person, because he worked those things principally through the soul—whatever, I say, he himself may say (whose opinion I neither hold nor have ever held), I say this and firmly assert: this consequence is not valid: "This opinion is against the sayings of Augustine, or Jerome, or Gregory <note>The primary Latin Church Fathers.</note>, and so on for the other doctors of the Church; therefore it is heretical."

<margin>Note / On the authority of the doctors, namely Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, and others</margin> The truth of this statement, just as it is believed by all good and subtle theologians, will also be evidently proved by me. For although the writings of the holy doctors placed outside the biblical canon are to be handed down and read and received with due reverence, their sayings are not of such firm and immovable authority that one is not permitted to contradict them or doubt them, unless they are otherwise proven evidently and expressly through Holy Scripture, or have been firmly determined by the Church itself authorizing them as containing firm and indubitable truth. Therefore, an opinion cannot be precisely and manifesty convicted as heretical through the sayings of the saints outside the biblical canon. For where there is no infallible truth, there is no faith.

<summary>The author defends the theologian Durandus against charges of heresy, arguing that disagreeing with Church Fathers like Augustine does not constitute heresy unless the point is settled by Scripture or a Church Council.</summary>
