<meta>This page continues a theological argument regarding the nature of certainty in faith, contrasting the absolute authority of Holy Scripture with the fallible writings of Church Doctors and Saints.</meta>

->## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...certain and indubitable. Since faith rests on infallible truth—indeed, concerning such matters, there is no infallible reason for assent nor firm adherence <note>The author argues that faith requires a foundation that cannot fail, unlike human logic which can be mistaken.</note>. From this, it follows that where there is no certain truth and indubitable faith, one is always assenting with doubt and with the fear of what is false. For, as **Augustine** <margin>Augustine</margin> says in his letter to **Jerome**, and in the eleventh book of *Against Faustus* (chapter 8) and the sixteenth book against the same Faustus: if the Scripture does not contain infallible truth and if any part of it is found to be false, there remains in it no certain faith by which it may be firmly believed; and because of a falsehood found in one part, the whole is held suspect, and thus faith would stumble. For as **Augustine** says in *On Christian Faith* (chapter 7), faith stumbles if the authority of the Holy Scriptures wavers.

That there is no infallible truth in the sayings of the Saints <note>In this context, "Saints" refers to the "Church Fathers" or "Doctors of the Church"—authoritative Christian teachers like Augustine or Jerome.</note> outside the biblical canon, three proofs occur to me for the present purpose. <margin>First proof that the sayings of the saints outside the Bible are not infallible truth</margin>

**The first proof** is because the Doctors themselves doubt their own sayings, wondering whether they have erred in them or not. Hence **Augustine**, in the first book of *On the Trinity* (chapter 1), says: "Let it not trouble me to seek where I hesitate, nor will I be ashamed to correct myself where I err." And in chapter 2: "Therefore, whoever reads this where he is equally certain, let him walk with me; where he equally hesitates, let him seek with me; where he recognizes his error, let him return to me; where he recognizes mine, let him call me back." From this comes Augustine's book of *Retractions*, in which many things from his earlier sayings are condemned and retracted. Hence, in the second book of *On the Trinity*, he says: "I would rather be rebuked by anyone than be praised by one who is either in error or a flatterer." For a person in error confirms the error by praising it, while a flatterer entices one into error. "But the just man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head" <note>This is a reference to Psalm 141:5.</note>.

And as **Guido the Carmelite** <margin>Guido the Carmelite</margin> says in his *Book on Heresies*: although **Augustine** <margin>Augustine</margin> speaks humbly in these sayings, he nonetheless speaks truly. Hence Augustine himself says to Vincent: "I cannot, nor ought I, deny that just as in the works of my elders, so in my own many small works there are many things which can be rebuked by a just judgment and without any rashness." And in the book *On True Religion*, he says: "Whatever error shall be found in my books, this alone is to be attributed to me; but whatever is true or well-explained, let that be attributed to God, the one rewarder and giver to all." Therefore, the sayings of Augustine—that distinguished and divine Doctor—may not always contain indubitable truth in all things, since he himself doubts whether he has erred or not. And what has been said of Augustine should be understood similarly for the other Doctors.

**The second proof** <margin>Second proof</margin> is taken from the discord <note>original: "discordia"; meaning disagreement or inconsistency.</note> that exists among the authors themselves. For discord among writers is a testimony of falsehood, since it is necessary that at least one of those disagreeing says what is false; for necessarily one side of a contradiction is false. Therefore, **Augustine** <margin>Augustine</margin> in the sixteenth book of *The City of God* proves the truth of Holy Scripture from the mutual harmony of its writers, in which all agree and none disagrees with another—which testifies to the indubitable and infallible truth of Holy Scripture. For to the true and to truth, as **The Philosopher** <note>The "Philosopher" is the traditional title for Aristotle.</note> says in the first book of the *Ethics*, all things are in harmony—which does not happen in other writings. For how great the discord is in the sayings of the Saints outside the canonical Scriptures, no one is ignorant unless he has not read their books. 

**Augustine** disagrees with the other holy Doctors <margin>Augustine</margin> regarding the understanding of the **Six Days of Creation** <margin>On the works of the six days</margin>. For others posit that God made those works of the six days according to a succession of time; from these Augustine disagrees, for he posits that all things were made at once, according to that text: "He who lives forever created all things together" <note>Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 18:1.</note>. Hence, moved by this, Augustine enumerates those six days not according to a succession of times, but according to the distinction of the angelic knowledge of things in their own kind and in the Word. Yet neither these nor those are called heretics, even though it is certain that one of the opinions is false, and consequently their sayings do not rest upon infallible truth.

Similarly, **Jerome** and **Augustine** disagree. For Augustine makes David the author of all the **Psalms** <margin>On the author of the Psalms</margin>, which Jerome denies. They disagree similarly over the **rebuke of Peter by Paul**—whether it was concerning <term>mortal sin</term> <note>A grave sin that separates the soul from God's grace.</note> or his own <term>venial sin</term> <note>A lesser sin that does not break the soul's relationship with God.</note>...

<summary>This page argues that while the Bible is infallible, the writings of Church Fathers like Augustine and Jerome are not, proven by their own self-corrections and their frequent disagreements on matters like the timeline of Creation.</summary>

...this. **Mortal sin is in itself a finite evil.** The second is this: **for a mortal sin of finite time, etc.** A certain Master, <note>Likely one of the papal commission members who condemned Pico's theses.</note> having a dispute with me over this conclusion, said: "What other testimony do we seek that your conclusion is heretical, since you yourself clearly say it is against the sayings of the Saints?" <note>By "Saints," he refers to the Church Fathers and established theological authorities like Augustine or Thomas Aquinas.</note> For the logic holds: it is against the sayings of the Saints, therefore it is heretical. I showed him then—as I will also show below—how my conclusion in no way opposed the opinions of the Saints, and how my words were to be understood. But even if it were the case that the conclusion was against the sayings of the Saints, how much his logic would be worth—and how unworthy it is of a theologian, as he boasts himself to be—can be clear to anyone from what was said above in the first conclusion. I know what I might say here about this Master. For he is the one who so often sent letters back to his home country about me, promising a "trophy" and a "triumph" as if he had already defeated me. But I wish, as I promised from the beginning, to plead my case with reasons, not insults. I come now to the conclusion. And because these Masters judged both the conclusion itself and the responses I gave them when they questioned me about it to be false, erroneous, and heretical, I wish first to declare the conclusion itself to be Catholic <note>Meaning "orthodox" or in line with universal Church teaching.</note> and in harmony with the sayings of almost all doctors. I say "mine," because if you take it in a sense other than the one I intend, it is no longer my conclusion which I proposed. <margin>A proposition with multiple meanings</margin> For a proposition is manifold—it can be many propositions. Therefore, I want to declare it and my responses to be such [orthodox]. Regarding both the conclusion and the responses, I will always declare the meanings I intend for them, which the force of the words allows.

<margin>First thing to note regarding sin: Turning toward and Turning away</margin> For the explanation of the conclusion, five things are to be noted. First, it must be noted that in sin, two things can be considered: the **turning toward** a created good <note>i.e., choosing a worldly pleasure or object over God.</note> and the **turning away** from the immutable and uncreated good <note>i.e., God.</note>. In the first way, sin is a finite evil, even according to all the doctors. In the second way, sin is a finite evil according to the common path of reasoning. And because the turning toward a created good—which the sinner misuses by sinning—is part of the intrinsic nature of sin itself, <margin>Second thing to note</margin> it is therefore said that sin is **intrinsically a finite evil**. However, the turning away from the uncreated good makes it **extrinsically infinite**, because it is called an "infinite evil" only insofar as it is a turning away from an infinite good. Therefore, it remains that it is only an infinite evil extrinsically and objectively. 

Second, note that by "time" we can understand only the "time of the way" <note>Original: "tempus viae." In Scholastic theology, the "way" refers to our mortal life on earth before reaching the "goal" of the afterlife.</note>; and in this way, it is certain that neither sin nor anything else pertaining to man can be infinite according to the "time of the way" of any traveler <note>A "viator" or traveler is a living human being on their spiritual journey.</note>, which is not only finite in duration but also short. In another way we can understand "time" as the time of both the "way" and the "goal" <note>Life and the eternal state following it.</note>; and this is how it is taken in the conclusion. And thus, something in a man can last for an infinite time, as is evident. 

<margin>Third: Mortal sin can be understood as an Act or as Guilt</margin> Third, note that **mortal sin** can be understood in two ways. In one way, for the forbidden act or the omission of an act commanded by God. In another way, for the **guilt** <term>Reatus: the legal or moral debt of punishment that remains even after the act of sin is finished.</term> left behind from the aforementioned forbidden act or omission. This guilt, in many places in Holy Scripture, is called "sin." And by such "sin," someone is called a "sinner" even when the act of sinning has ceased or passed. From this third note, it is clear that it is reasonable to say that although in one who is damned for mortal sin, the sin itself for which he is damned eventually ends in terms of the "intrinsic entity" of the act, it does not end regarding the **guilt**. Indeed, if it ended, eternal punishment would not be owed to him. And so, the sin to which infinite punishment is owed is "infinite according to time" in regards to the guilt. 

<margin>Fourth: "To be owed" can be understood in two ways</margin> Fourth, it must be noted that "to be owed" is understood in two ways, or can be understood in two ways when we say some punishment is "owed" to a sin. In one way, that is said to be "owed" to someone which will at some point be paid back to them; and thus it is said reasonably and orthdoxly that for a sin of finite time—regarding both its intrinsic entity and its guilt—infinite punishment is **not** owed according to time. And in this way the present conclusion is understood: that to a sin of finite time [punishment] is not owed, etc. For every...

**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...in that sin in the manner mentioned above; and this is what Gregory <note>original: "Gregorius"; referring to Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD), a foundational theologian for the medieval Church</note> intends to say when he states that the <margin>Gregory</margin> sinner is punished with eternal punishment because he sinned in his own "eternity"—that is, without end. Thomas <note>original: "Thomas"; referring to St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential Scholastic philosopher</note> also agrees in the fourth book of the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* of Peter Lombard was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages; Aquinas wrote a famous commentary on it</note>, saying that for this reason the punishment of the damned lasts <margin>Thomas</margin> forever: because the guilt lasts forever. I say, therefore, that in every person who is damned there is one sin of infinite duration, speaking both of the "time of the way" <note>original: "tempore uiae"; a technical theological term referring to human life on earth as a journey toward God</note> and of the "time of the end" <note>original: "termini"; referring to the fixed state of the soul after death</note>, namely the failure to repent, which in the damned person never has an end. And so it is clear that the infinity of the duration of the sin in the person who is damned—I say infinity in terms of the legal guilt, or the stain, and the lack of repentance or the failure to repent—is the reason why eternal punishment is owed to him and will eventually be paid. This is sufficient regarding that conclusion.

The other is the "improper" <note>Meaning figurative or indirect.</note> sense of the stated proposition: and it is that the cross of Christ is adored—that is, Christ is adored *in* it as in a memorial of Him—just as if He were present in Himself. This was to be understood by reason of that which is primarily brought to our memory, <margin>First point</margin> which is the humanity of Christ; I said this briefly because I was referring to those authors whom I considered to have been read and re-read ten times over by these masters, as they are seasoned scholars.

Secondly, it is clear that they spoke falsely when they said I deny every mode of adoration of **latria** <term>latria: the highest form of worship, which the Catholic Church teaches is reserved for God alone</term>. For I expressly say in my conclusion that I deny the "mode of Thomas." Even if I had not said this, but the proposition simply stood as "neither the cross nor any image is to be adored with **latria**," still, by the power of the words, that proposition would not deny every mode of adoration of **latria**. For it is clear according to good <margin>Second point</margin> logic that the negation or distribution of a "multiple term" <note>A term with more than one meaning.</note> does not negate or distribute it for every possible instance of every meaning. Otherwise, this proposition—"every dog is a star"—would have to be simply granted or simply denied. Just as one does not say collectively that every "celestial dog" <note>The constellation Canis Major</note> and every "sea dog" <note>A shark</note> and every "barking dog" is a star (although it says so of all of them individually), so in this negative "the cross is not adored with the adoration of **latria**"—where the word "adored" is ambiguous, referring to adoration as an end-point and to adoration by way of a memorial—it does not deny every mode of adoration collectively.

Thirdly, it is clear that this proposition could be stated thus absolutely and without distinction: "The Cross is not to be adored with the adoration of **latria**." This is because in the proper <margin>Third point</margin> sense, it is true, or at least more probable than its opposite; and the proper sense is to be more closely observed by the rigor of speech than the improper sense, in which it is false. For just as an analogical term placed by itself stands for its most famous meaning, so a word having both a proper and an improper sense, if spoken without specification, is to be understood according to its proper sense rather than the improper one. Therefore, as I said, I could have put it forth without distinction, intending to declare the sense in which I understood it during the debate. From this I infer that although in a <margin>Note</margin> multifaceted proposition it is perhaps better to do as I did—that is, to determine the sense in which it is posed—rather than to pose it without distinction, yet there is a greater defect in condemning a proposition as simply and indistinctly false when it is true in its proper sense, just because of the falsity of its improper sense. I wanted to note this here not only for this conclusion—in which I specifically deny the "mode of Thomas"—but also because of many other conclusions which, although they have a Catholic meaning which I always promised I would declare (as I am declaring now), were nevertheless condemned simply and without distinction. But however it may be regarding my conclusion, they cannot excuse their condemnation of it from error. I clearly declare it thus: this was formally their determination: "Because he denies every mode of adoration of **latria** toward the cross, according to the way of Catholic doctors and the prayer which the universal Church makes to the cross, therefore we say the aforementioned conclusion is scandalous, offensive to pious ears, and against the custom of the universal Church." This was precisely their judgment. First, let them say...

->### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

<meta>This page continues a theological debate concerning the "assumptibility" of natures—specifically whether God could take on a non-human or irrational nature (like that of an animal or an object) in the same way He took on human nature in the person of Jesus Christ.</meta>

->APOLOGIA<-

...it seems that He can provide substance and a personal foundation <term>supposit<note>In scholastic theology, to "supposit" a nature means to provide the underlying personal existence (hypostasis) for that nature. Here, the author asks if God's personhood could "own" any kind of physical nature.</note></term> to any nature. The second reason is because during the three days <note>The "triduum," or the three days between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection.</note> God provided a personal foundation for the body that was in the tomb, even though it was not then a rational being. And just as He provided that foundation for three days, He could have done so for as long a time as He willed. These are the two primary foundations for the opposing opinion. And these same points, as was seen in the recitation of his opinion, <margin>Solution to the first reason</margin> Henry <note>Likely Henry of Ghent, a prominent 13th-century theologian.</note> brings up against himself. To the first reason, as we have seen, he responds that it is true that the fullness of all being is in God, and every principle of providing substance and personal foundation is found most fully in Him. However, this is not the *total* cause of why a nature can be assumed [by God]; rather, it is a contributing cause. Indeed, unless the one assuming was God, He could not assume a nature. But beyond this, something is required in the thing being assumed by which it is "assumptible": and this is the principle of being an **image** [of God] and, finally, a fitness for supernatural elevation toward a **blessed operation** <note>Meaning the ability to know and love God in heaven.</note>. Since this is found only in an intellectual nature, it seems appropriate that only such a nature can be assumed. For it seems reasonable that a nature which cannot be elevated to the "second act" <note>The "second act" refers to the functioning or operation of a thing—in this case, the use of intellect and will.</note> cannot be elevated to the "first act" either. From this response, Henry seems to want to preserve the idea that nothing is taken away from divine omnipotence. For while others claim that God *could* provide a personal foundation in this way, Henry also attributes all that power to God. He does not deny that, from the perspective of the one assuming, God has the fullest power to assume any nature. Rather, he says that an irrational nature itself is not "assumptible"—not because of a defect in divine omnipotence, but rather because of the excellence of the divine nature and the deformed deficiency of the irrational nature. 

<margin>A manifold solution to the second reason. First part.</margin> Regarding the second reason, it seems many things can be said. First is the response of Henry, who says that He assumed the nature of that body insofar as it was ordered toward the intellectual soul; by reason of that ordering, even the body itself can be called "intellectual" in a ministerial and preparatory sense. To respond more completely, it must be said that when it is stated that nothing but an intellectual nature can be assumed by God, it is understood that nothing else can be assumed as the *primary* thing assumed, or as the complete and adequate object of the assumption. The body during the three days in the tomb was not assumed in that way, as is clear, but only as a part of the rational nature, which was the total and primary thing assumed. Furthermore, someone might perhaps say <margin>Second part.</margin> that it was not properly said to be "supposited" <note>Meaning given a personal foundation.</note> during those three days, because a body is not a nature that can be supposited by its own personal foundation. Hence, it could consequently be said, not improbably, that to terminate the dependence of the nature of that body is not the same as providing it a "supposit" [personal foundation]. Otherwise, everything that terminates the dependence or leaning of a part would "supposit" it, which is not said. And so, although the Word <note>The Logos, or the second person of the Trinity.</note> during the three days terminated the dependence of the body—just as the whole humanity would have terminated it—and by virtue of this, the body in the tomb communicated to Christ the property of "lying in the sepulcher," yet He did not properly provide a personal foundation for the body in the same way He would for a whole human nature. The most evident sign of this is that the nature of that body did not communicate the property of "being a body" to Christ during those three days in a "concrete" way, in the same way the human nature had communicated, and still communicates, the identity of being "man." Thus the response to the aforementioned objections against Henry's opinion is clear. Regarding other irrational natures, Henry seems to say that the Word could not assume them through <term>circumincession<note>A technical term (perichoresis) for the mutual indwelling of the divine and human natures.</note></term> or provide a personal foundation, especially one having a final purpose. For he says himself: no purpose could exist for the assumption of any nature other than an intellectual one, because assumption exists only for the promotion of the nature assumed—a promotion which only an intellectual nature can have. <margin>Augustine</margin> Hence, Augustine says in his commentary on John: "the Word willed to be born of man, so that you might safely be born of God." <note>original: "verbum voluit nasci ex homine: ut tu securus naſcereris ex deo"</note> From this it appears that concerning any other nature which is not "born of God" through grace, it would be in vain for God to be born as that nature. From these points, it can be seen that it is not irrational...

<summary>This page addresses whether God's omnipotence allows Him to assume any physical nature, concluding that only intellectual natures (like humans) are "assumptible" because they are made in God's image and capable of salvation. It specifically refutes the argument that Christ's dead body in the tomb proves God can assume irrational things, arguing the body was only assumed as part of a larger human whole.</summary>

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...therefore I can not have an explicit act of contradicting this opinion in particular. And because these masters <note>The papal commission of theologians appointed to examine Pico's 900 theses.</note> also insisted particularly on this: that such conclusions at least should not be disputed because they might cause a scandal among the faithful. I wish to say this regarding that conclusion: even if the opposite view were truer and more in line with the common path, yet if it were publicly disputed, it would be more scandalous to common people and offensive to pious ears. 

For what unrefined and simple person would not be offended if they heard someone saying it is possible that these propositions are true: **"God is a donkey"** or **"God is a piece of wood"**? What if they heard those things which many who follow the aforementioned opinion concede: **"God can be damned to hell,"** or **"God could be tortured by the devil in hell,"** or even **"The devil can be God"**? 

Although these statements cause no scandal among many learned men when speaking of God's *absolute power* <term>potētia abſoluta: a technical term in medieval theology referring to what God could theoretically do by His power, regardless of the laws He actually established</term>, the common and simple folk would certainly be much more offended by them than if they heard that a donkey cannot be united to the divine nature in the unity of a *suppositum* <term>suppositum: the individual person or substance; in this context, the act of God taking on a physical nature, as in the Incarnation</term>. 

Yet these fathers <note>The inquisitors/theologians judging him.</note> have said that, by the very force of the words, my conclusion detracts from divine omnipotence and therefore "smacks of heresy." I do not know what logic—or rather, what theology—they are relying on. For let them tell me, I pray, whether a person who says they do not *assent* to a certain proposition is saying, by the strict rigor of the words, the exact opposite of that conclusion? 

Let them say whether this logic holds up: "I do not assent to" or "I have no opinion on this conclusion: *The Pope is sitting*"; "Therefore, I believe this: *The Pope is not sitting*." Would not the first part be true of a person who is sleeping? A sleeping man has no active thought at all, yet the second part could be false. 

Furthermore, if the present conclusion really did detract from divine omnipotence according to true theology, it would not merely "smack of heresy" but should be judged as fully heretical. Indeed, even a sleeping Catholic or a small child who does not yet have the use of reason—and thus does not have an active "assent" to the proposition "God can assume any created nature"—would be a heretic, or at least would err in faith. No one would ever say such a thing. From this, it is clear that their condemnation of me is not right.

Their formal determination was based on my response and the opinions and reasons of Henry <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a major scholastic philosopher whose work Pico drew upon.</note>, upon whose opinion I relied when proposing the conclusion. Their verdict was:

> "It seemed to us that the aforesaid conclusion, by the force of the words, detracts from divine omnipotence; and through this, it smacks of heresy."

First, they were deceived because when I said I followed Henry in *this*, they did not understand that by the word *this* I was referring to the conclusion itself which they asked me to explain. In "this" therefore—that is, in the conclusion itself, in not assenting to the idea that "God can assume any nature etc."—I said I followed Henry. I did not mean by "this" the specific opinion which says "God *cannot* assume any nature." 

But perhaps they believed there was no difference between one statement and the other. However, if they are learned theologians, they ought to know the difference between *not explicitly believing* something is possible by the power of God, and *explicitly disbelieving* it. 

<margin>Henry, the Solemn Doctor</margin> 

Second, they ought to remember that from their words it follows that the famous Henry—who is called the "Solemn Doctor" <note>original: "doctor ſolēnis"</note> due to the excellence of his teaching—died a heretic. As seen above, in his old age, Henry turned to this opinion and remained in it: that not every nature can be assumed by God. 

Third, just as in their condemnation of my previous conclusion, they are entirely in error here as well. If it were true, as they say, that the conclusion is against the omnipotence of God, then the conclusion would be simply heretical, and not merely "smacking of heresy" as they claim. 

Fourth and last, they erred because even if Henry’s opinion were entirely heretical, my conclusion would not be heretical by the force of its words. As I have explained at great length, the words themselves do not imply that opinion. And yet, they specifically condemned it based on the "force of the words."

I ii

# APOLOGY
## FIFTH QUESTION CONCERNING NATURAL MAGIC AND THE CABALA OF THE HEBREWS

**V** <note>The original text uses a decorative "V" for "Varta," an archaic or decorative spelling for *Quarta* (Fourth).</note> **The fourth conclusion** condemned by those men was this: **"There is no science that more greatly confirms for us the divinity of Christ than magic and the Cabala."**

In explaining this conclusion, I stated that among the sciences—those which are "sciences" in such a way that they do not rely on divine revelation in their method of proceeding, nor in their principles, nor in their conclusions—there is none that confirms the divinity of Christ more effectively (in the manner that sciences discovered by human effort can provide such certainty) than that <term>Natural Magic|The study of the hidden properties and "sympathies" of the natural world, which Pico distinguished from forbidden demonic magic.</term> about which my conclusions were proposed, and that part of the <term>Cabala|A Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation. Pico believed that when applied correctly, it proved Christian doctrines.</term> which is considered a science and is not revealed theology. 

These masters <note>Referring to the ecclesiastical commission appointed by Pope Innocent VIII to examine Pico's 900 Theses.</note> claimed that my explanation did not match the intent of the words of the aforementioned conclusion. They further asserted that the conclusion itself, according to the literal meaning of the words <note>original: "de virtute sermonis"</note>, was false, erroneous, and heretical. Regarding this condemnation of theirs, <margin>First</margin> I ask that we examine individually how many points are to be condemned. First, let them tell me how it can be...

-># APOLOGY<-

Our doctors <note>Latin: "doctores nostros," referring to the established academic and theological authorities of the Church</note> say that all magic is prohibited. If, therefore, all magic is prohibited, it follows that none is permitted.
But you say that some magic is not prohibited; therefore, you stand in contradiction to the doctors of the Church.
Indeed, the ignorance of those who speak this way is truly marvelous. For first, the assignment of names is not done by us now; rather, we use names and their meanings based on the custom of the ancients. If, therefore, they <margin>The Great [Magus]</margin> <margin>Persian Magus</margin> <margin>Pythagoras</margin> <margin>Druids</margin> <margin>Prophets</margin> <margin>Sanhedrin</margin> <margin>Pharisees</margin> wished to call this branch of <term>natural science</term> <note>The study of the hidden, active powers within the physical world, distinct from "black magic" or demonic intervention</note> "magic," why do you want me to innovate the names? And should what they named "magic" be called "geometry" or "arithmetic" by me?
I am neither the first nor a newcomer in calling this science "magic"; many holy and learned men came before me. Let them be brought to judgment; let them be condemned, if it is a damnable thing for this science to be called by this name. I maintain, however, that this naming was rightly established:

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his "900 Theses," specifically focusing on the distinction between prohibited (diabolical) magic and "natural magic," which he views as a legitimate branch of science.</meta>

->### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...[that I have] superstitiously and diabolically approved this natural [magic] can be not only no cause for scandal, but even a source of edification for simple people. For I have seen many who, hearing that the Magi <margin>Note</margin> <note>The "Magi" are the Wise Men or Three Kings from the Biblical nativity story.</note> came to adore Christ, believe that this name "Magi" signifies nothing other than necromancers. From this, they take the argument that magic is not prohibited, nor contrary to the faith of Christ, since the practitioners of magic were the first to adore Christ himself. It is useful, therefore, to have taught the faithful that when they hear the word "Magus," they should not always understand it to mean a worshiper of demons. And when they hear that among the Persians the Magi were held in the highest honor and reverence because of their learning and wisdom, they should know that those men were philosophers, not necromancers—whom all nations have always pursued and detested as deadly and harmful, or rather as a plague, casting them out and treating them poorly. 

Similarly, when they read that Albert <margin>Albertus</margin> <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a renowned medieval scholar and theologian who wrote extensively on the natural sciences.</note> spent much time among the experiments of magic, they should understand this as natural magic, not the prohibited kind. This prevents people from giving themselves over to what they presume was permitted to such a great man, using his example as an excuse for themselves. Therefore, our "Magical Conclusions" remove scandals from the minds of the faithful rather than generating them. For if they ever read in the works of the Doctors <note>The "Doctors" refers to the established authorities of the Church, like St. Augustine or Thomas Aquinas.</note> that all magic is prohibited, they will immediately understand from the reasons for that prohibition that those authors are speaking only of that magic which involves commerce with demons, and that they intend nothing regarding natural magic. 

However, as Hilary <margin>Hilary</margin> says, the understanding of sayings is to be taken from the reasons for the speaking. <note>original: "intelligentia dictorum ex causis assumenda dicendi." This is a legal and theological principle: to understand a statement, you must look at why it was said.</note> If they wish to return to the force of the words, they can know from logic <term>dialectica; the art of logical argument and classification</term> that the negation or distribution of a "multiple term" <note>An "equivocal" or "multiple" term is a word with more than one meaning.</note> does not negate or distribute it for every underlying meaning joined together. Therefore, since this term "magic" is equivocal—referring both to the superstitious and the natural—a distribution added to it will not apply to every possible meaning. But from the statements that "all magic is prohibited," it will be understood only that all types of *superstitious* magic are meant, which are all called by one name and one reasoning. 

For many things are prohibited, and all these matters are clear and lucid even to the moderately learned. In no way, therefore, should my "Magical Conclusions" have been suspect to these masters. For, as I said in my first conclusion, I refute all magic prohibited by the Church, damning and detesting it, and protesting that I speak only of natural magic. I declared this even more expressly through a special conclusion, stating that by this magic we perform nothing except by activating or uniting natural virtues. For thus says the eleventh of the Magical Conclusions: 

*"The wonders of the magical art exist only through the union and activation of those things which are found in nature, sown as seeds and separated."*

And it is the same as what I said in the thirteenth conclusion: that to perform magic is nothing other than **to marry the world.** <note>original: "maritare mundum." This is one of Pico's most famous metaphors, suggesting that the natural magician acts as a "matchmaker," bringing together different forces of nature to produce amazing effects.</note> I intend for the aforementioned specification and restriction of my intention in the Magical Conclusions toward natural magic to be applied to every particular conclusion. And so, when I speak of the activity of characters and figures in a magical work, I am speaking of their true and natural activity. For it is clear that they possess such activity according to all philosophers, both in acting and in the manner of acting and receiving. 

And although, according to the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>, they are of far less activity and power than material qualities, nevertheless the Pythagoreans <margin>Pythagoreans</margin> would say—whose philosophy I call "more secret philosophy" in my twenty-fourth conclusion because it is less known and less in use—that just as mathematical things are more "formal" than physical things, so they are also more "actual." And just as they are less dependent in their being, so too are they in their operation. And so, regarding what I said about their greater power: although the disagreement between the Pythagoreans and the Peripatetics is indifferent to the Faith, I did not say it as something true in itself and absolutely, but as a consequence of the "secret philosophy" of the Pythagoreans, to be understood in the manner aforesaid. Among them, the opinion is that among all mathematical things, numbers are the most formal, and thus also the most actual; and among odd numbers, the number three <note>original: "ternarium"</note> is the most so. Because it is the first odd number, and the first in every genus is the most perfect in that genus...

<margin>Jerome</margin> These are the words of Hilary, verbatim. Secondly, it is argued that since, according to Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430), writing to Volusianus</note> in his letter to Volusianus, <margin>Second argument.</margin> "in miraculous things the whole reason for the deed is the power of the doer," to thus restrict this miraculous sacrament to a determined mode of defense—which is not found expressed in the canon of Scripture or by the determination of the Church—is to restrict divine power to the capacity of our intellect. This is dangerous and contrary to Augustine, who says there: "If a reason is sought, it will not be miraculous; if an example is provided, it will not be unique. Let us grant that God can do something that we confess we cannot investigate."

Thirdly, it is argued that if the opposite of a thing <margin>Third argument.</margin> (regarding its "being so") is not evidently held from the sayings of the saints, it can much more easily be held as a "possibility." In that other opinion, it is not verified that the bread *is* the body of Christ since there are two persons. In this one, however, it is verified because of the unity of the person, who is one in two natures. ->APOLOGIA<-

...the gift would not be a fast, and there would not only be spiritual food there, but also physical food; this is contrary to the dignity of the sacrament. Furthermore, Christ would be setting something aside after he had assumed it into the unity of his person <term>suppositum; the distinct individual existence of the Word</term>, because he would be assuming "breadness" <note>original: "paneitatem"; the essential quality of being bread</note> which he would then set aside once the bread was converted into his limbs.

<margin>Response</margin>
To these points, one might perhaps say first—while still upholding the statement—that even without the conversion of the bread into Christ's body, it is possible for Christ’s body to be on the altar in the aforementioned way: through the "sustaining of the breadness" in the Word, together with the humanity long ago assumed. This refers to the body as a category of being <note>original: "ut est genus"; referring to "body" as a general type of substance</note>, not merely as a physical part. Thus, it refers to the body that is Christ, derived from "corporeity" which is a nature, and it can be spoken of directly. 

<margin>To the second point in opposition</margin>
And when it is argued that the "body as a category" should not be called the Body of Christ, the answer is that it indeed should. Just as we speak of the "creature of salt" (meaning that which is salt) and the "Word of God" (meaning the Word which is God); and as it is said, "By the word of the Lord"—meaning the Word which is God—"the heavens were made." We also say that the substance of matter remains throughout a total natural transformation—that is, the substance which is matter. Similarly, our opponents say that the substance of the bread is converted into Christ's body—certainly the substance which *is* bread, not just a part of the bread.

<margin>John of Damascus</margin>
In this same way, John of Damascus, in Book III, Chapter 17, accepts the "flesh of Christ"—meaning the flesh which is Christ—as a category, saying that the flesh of the Lord is said to be "deified" and consubstantial with God. 

And when it is argued that the form of the words would not be fitting—that "This is my body" would mean "This is the body of my part"—the answer is that perhaps it would not be accomplished through such a form of words. Perhaps a sacramental power would be divinely given to any word whatsoever; for God could give to this word—"This is my body"—any power He chose to give. He could even give it to a word that is not meaningful, out of His absolute power, because God’s power is not restricted to the linguistic meaning of words. 

<margin>Response to the third point in opposition</margin>
And when it is argued that even if bread were the body and vice versa, it does not follow that "where the bread is, there the body is on the altar," the answer is that yes, it does follow. For whatever is said of the predicate is also said of the subject. For instance: because God is man and God is everywhere, it follows that the man Christ is everywhere just as God is. It follows that God is enclosed in the cradle, is the son of the Virgin, and sucks at the breast just as the man Christ does. Likewise, it follows that if the man Christ is bread and vice versa, then if the bread is on the altar, Christ the man is also there—and not only by reason of Him being everywhere as God, but because the bread is on the altar. For the properties <term>idiomata; the specific attributes of the divine and human natures</term> of the assumed natures are shared on the part of the subject, especially because in the subject, the term stands for the person <note>supposito</note>. 

However, it is said "on the part of the subject" because perhaps on the part of the predicate, the properties are not necessarily shared, because there the term stands for the nature. Hence, perhaps it is not necessary that Christ-as-man be everywhere, even though Christ-as-God is everywhere, even though on the part of the subject the "man Christ" is everywhere. Nor is the argument about the soul and body during the three days <note>the "Triduum" between the Crucifixion and Resurrection</note> valid; for they were not united in the person in such a way that they were predicated of the person or of each other, since they were united as parts of a single nature. Therefore, it is not necessary for them to share properties with each other in the way that those natures do which are spoken of in relation to each other. It is certain, however, that even if it does not follow by necessity, it follows at least as a possibility. 

<margin>First response to the fourth point</margin>
As for the claim that if there is a "sustaining of the breadness," it must end at the same point where we say "conversion" ends—namely, at the body—the response is that this is not a necessity. 

<margin>Second response</margin>
Rather, we can say that the sustaining occurs in the person <note>supposito</note> simply, even if those who propose "conversion" say it ends at the "body" as a part. It could also perhaps be said (as will be discussed below) that this sustaining can end at the body, not as "human" but as "united." For if the Divine Person has another nature to sustain within itself—insofar as He draws it into His own being—then to whomever He communicates His infinite being, He could also communicate the power to sustain another nature united to Himself within that being. More on this below.

<margin>Response to the fifth point</margin>
When it is objected that, according to this second way, the body of Christ would not "begin to be" on the altar, but rather something would "begin to be" the body of Christ or the body would "become" Christ: it would be said that just as if breadness were added to Christ (who was already man), Christ-as-man would begin to be bread, so he begins to be on the altar in a new way "by accident" <note>philosophically: a non-essential or external change</note> because it is appropriate to the bread itself. Christ, that is, will begin...

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...[Christ] as man to be visibly on the altar; and that he is the food of the faithful by reason of the <term>breadness</term> <note>original: "paneitas"; a technical Scholastic term for the essence or "being-ness" of bread</note> assumed, just as Christ as God began to be in the lap or womb of his mother in a new way by reason of the humanity he assumed. To that which is said concerning the assumption of a pre-existing "breadness" into its own <term>individual substance</term> <note>original: "supposito"; in Scholastic philosophy, a "suppositum" is an individual, complete substance that subsists by itself, such as a person</note>: <margin>Response to the sixth [argument].</margin> It is answered that God can assume every assumable nature pre-existing in its own individual substance and, in the act of assuming it, deprive it of its own individual existence and draw it into His own being. For it is well known that the Word <note>The "Word" (Verbum) refers to the Second Person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ</note> could set aside his human nature, which would immediately then have its own personal subsistence and the character of an individual substance and person—even though it does not have this while united to the Word—and it would be, as to its essence, the same humanity that was previously united. Therefore, in a similar way, He could assume a humanity previously existing in its own individual substance in the manner already described; and it would be the same nature now assumed that was previously not assumed.

But when it is argued that power cannot be conferred to the Word for this purpose: <margin>Response to the seventh [argument].</margin> perhaps it can and perhaps it cannot. And if an *inherent* power cannot be given—because such a power would be a created thing—perhaps an *assistant* power can be given, because such a power would be uncreated and not created. And in this way, there would be an assumption of "breadness" sacramentally by the power of the Word, just as great men <note>Likely referring to major Scholastic theologians like Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus</note> also propose that power is conferred upon the sacraments of the New Law. And perhaps if an inherent power can be conferred upon the sacramental word to convert the whole [of the bread] into the whole [of Christ], and especially into what already exists without increasing it, it can also be conferred for the aforementioned effect; for perhaps it will seem to someone that this is of the same level of difficulty as that.

To that which is said concerning the breaking of the fast: <margin>First response to the eighth [argument].</margin> one might answer that the rule about not breaking the "natural fast" <note>The "natural fast" required total abstinence from food and drink before receiving the Eucharist</note> follows the commonly held view: namely, that the substance of the bread does not remain. For if we propose that the substance *does* remain, we shall say something else. Or perhaps it will be said <margin>Second response</margin> that the priest is not called "fasting" after consuming [the host] because the substance of bread is not there; for however much the substance of bread might not be there, if a Jew or a Christian were to consume the sacramental <term>species</term> <note>The outward appearances of bread and wine (sight, taste, texture) that remain after the substance has changed</note> as bodily food and with the intention of eating, he would break his fast. But because the priest does not consume it as bodily food, but as a sacrament, the fast is therefore not broken. And it would be similar if the substance of the bread remained: he would still not break the natural fast, provided it was not consumed as bodily food.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that Christ does not set aside what he once assumed: <margin>First response to the ninth [argument].</margin> this is said by presupposing that he is held to have assumed only human nature, just as in fact he assumed only that. Nevertheless, he could assume another nature and set it aside. <margin>Second response.</margin> It can also be said that if "breadness" were assumed by the Word, it would never be set aside by the Word through himself or on his own part, but "by accident" due to the condition of the nature assumed. <margin>Another question.</margin> With its natural defects, he would set it aside because of the corruption of the assumed nature, just as he "left" his humanity during the three days [in the tomb].

But again, by way of disputation, let us inquire whether the body (which is a part) can be truly saved as being on the altar without the conversion of the bread into it. <margin>Argument for the affirmative side.</margin> And it seems so: because just as color is sustained in a substance as in a subject through the mediation of another "accident"—for example, the surface—this does not mean the surface is the subject of the color (for one accident is not the subject of another, because as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says, there is no "quality of a quality"). Rather, it is because color does not exist in a subject except in relation to the surface. In this way, "breadness" can be sustained in the Word through the mediation of the body; not indeed that the body is the immediate sustainer and giver-of-being to the assumed "breadness" and the Word is primary. Rather, "breadness" is not given being in the individual substance of the Word except in relation to the body of Christ as a part. For God can place this order between assumable natures, even if that order does not exist in their own nature; just as he can take away from some things the natural order they have among themselves—as he did between the heat and the act of heating in the furnace of the Chaldeans <note>A reference to the Biblical story of the three youths in the fiery furnace (Daniel 3), where the fire existed but did not burn them</note> and in many other cases. Therefore, just as color—because it exists in a substance in relation to a surface—is spoken of in relation to the surface in a concrete way as an accidental quality...

<meta>This page continues a theological "Apologia" (Defense), likely from the late medieval or early Reformation period, debating the mechanics of the Eucharist. The author is arguing for the theory of "Assumption" or "Impanation" as a more logical alternative to "Transubstantiation."</meta>

->APOLOGIA<-

**Fourth** [arguments] are maintained without a multiplication of miracles. **Fourth**, because Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10: *The bread which we break, is it not the participation in the body of the Lord?* <note>original: "Panis quem frangimus nonne participatio corporis domini est."</note>
**Fifth** **Fifth**, because Christ is present sacramentally wherever he is present directly by the power of the sacrament. But Christ is made present on the altar more directly through **assumption** than through **conversion**: because the form of this sacrament, which brings about what it signifies, more directly brings about that which it more properly signifies. And this is a union by **assumption**, in which the <term>properties are shared</term> <note>original: "communicantur idiomata." This is a technical theological term meaning that the attributes of the divine and human (or here, the bread) are attributed to the same person/subject.</note> so that "this" truly is "that" which the formal words sound like: *This is my body.* It is not, however, a union of **conversion**: because through conversion the bread is not Christ, nor vice versa; rather, the bread "becomes" Christ or is "converted" into Christ. 
<margin>Sixth</margin> **Sixth**, because that mode of **conversion** is intricate and contains many difficulties; this mode [assumption], however, is clear and efficient. For we already believe in **assumption** through another Article of Faith <note>Referring to the Incarnation, where the Word "assumed" human nature.</note>. Whatever things are identical in their <term>underlying subject</term> <note>original: "supposito." The 'suppositum' is the individual substance or person that "holds" the traits.</note> are limited such that wherever one is, the other is also. Just as wherever there is "loud music," there is also the "whiteness" of the musician <note>A classic scholastic example: if the person playing music is white, the 'subject' (the person) contains both attributes in one place.</note>. I say "limited" because if one were limited and the other unlimited, where the limited one was, the unlimited would be, but not necessarily vice versa. But if the bread were **assumed**, the human body of Christ and the body of the bread would be one in their **underlying subject**, and both would be limited. Therefore, since the **assumed** bread would be on the altar, the body of Christ would consequently be there as well. Likewise, the "middle" is closer than the "extreme." But if Christ were to assume the bread or the "breadness," he would do so by means of his own corporeality: because a less worthy thing is capable of being assumed by means of a more worthy thing, according to the fitness of **assumption**. Therefore, since the subject of Christ doing the assuming would be on the altar with the **assumed** bread, much more so would the body of Christ be there, which would be the "medium" of the **assumption**. 
<margin>Lastly</margin> **Lastly**, it seems that the authorities of the Saints regarding **conversion** can nonetheless be preserved while holding to **assumption**. For since *being* <note>original: "esse" (the act of existing)</note> differs from *essence* <note>original: "essentia" (the nature of what a thing is)</note>, one can be assumed while the other is not. Hence, the Word was not "incarnated" in the same way it is <term>impanated</term> <note>original: "impaneatum." The theory that Christ becomes present "in the bread" rather than replacing it.</note> in the bread; for in that [Incarnation] assumption, the essence was assumed before it had its own being. Thus, it never had a being other than the divine being communicated to it, which is why it was an **assumption** without any **conversion** of the assumed into the assumer or vice versa. This is why the Church says: "not by the conversion of the divinity into flesh," and nor—supplementary—the reverse, "but by the **assumption** of the humanity into God." Pre-existing bread has both *being* and *essence*, and the **assumption** into the humanity of the <term>subject</term> consumes its individual "subsistence"—not by annihilation, but by the **assumption** of the substantial essence, this mystery is perfected. And so all the authorities speaking of **transubstantiation** and **conversion** can be referred to the *being* and not to the *essence*. And the authorities saying that after the consecration "bread does not remain, but was," are true regarding its *being*: because it remains only according to its *essence*. From these points, it appears that the body of Christ can be just as truly present sacramentally on the altar through the **assumption** of the "breadness" without **conversion**, as is now commonly proposed through **conversion**.

<margin>Assumption</margin> Indeed, a good distinction between these three terms—**assumption**, **conversion**, and **annihilation**—cannot be understood except by presupposing the manner of this opinion. We say that:
1. That which is **Assumed** is that which, prior to having any existence of its own capable of being a subject, is taken up into the new being of a subject.
<margin>Annihilation</margin> 2. That which is **Annihilated** is that which simply ceases to be, so that its reproduction would be a [new] creation. It is entirely irrelevant to this whether something succeeds it or nothing succeeds it, because that is entirely external to the thing which ceases to be. 
<margin>Conversion</margin> 3. That which is **Converted** is that which, remaining according to its **essence** but having lost its own being as a subject, passes into the *being* of another subject and truly becomes that subject. 
<margin>Reason for conversion</margin> And this is the true reasoning of **conversion**, in which two things are understood: first, that it remains in its **essence** (which distinguishes it from the **annihilated**); and second, that it becomes something else by reason of the subject (which distinguishes it from the non-converted). And while it becomes something else by reason of its own subject, it lets go [of its former state], which distinguishes it from the **assumed**. However, if one holds the common way of **conversion** [transubstantiation], the bread is not "converted" but is actually **annihilated**; and those who wish...

The author provides technical definitions to show that Transubstantiation actually implies the total destruction (annihilation) of the bread, which he finds problematic.</summary>

->APOLOGY<-

Coal and fire are not the same thing in their underlying reality <note>original: "supposito"; a technical term in scholastic philosophy referring to the individual substance or "personhood" of a thing</note>, yet one, through its own corruption, passes into the other. In this same way, the bread of communion is not one with divinity in its underlying reality; rather, by its own ceasing-to-be, it passes into the body of Christ, which is united to divinity.
<margin>Against</margin>
But against this, it is argued that then the bread of communion would be comparable to the fire into which the coal has passed through its own destruction, and not to the coal itself, in which the nature of fire is found simultaneously alongside the preservation of the nature of the wood. Seek a response,
<margin>Response</margin>
and perhaps it is this: that the likeness does not hold true in all respects. Perhaps it would have been better if John of Damascus <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749) was a Syrian monk and Church Father whose writings on the Eucharist were central to medieval debates.</note> had not proposed that comparison. And when the same Damascene says that God "yoked" divinity to the bread,
<margin>Solution</margin>
it must be said that this was not through "assumption" <note>original: "assumptionem"; the author is distinguishing between the Incarnation (where God assumed human nature) and the Eucharist</note>, even though it is joined like food is to the one eating it, because it is converted into him. Let that likeness which can apply there be accepted between this conversion and that one.
<margin>of the objection</margin>
<margin>Saint Thomas</margin>
Saint Thomas Aquinas, in the fourth book [of the *Sentences*], distinction 11, question 1, says that the word of Damascene is to be understood regarding the "species" <note>original: "species"; the outward appearances of bread (color, taste, texture) that remain after the substance has changed</note> by which the body of Christ, united to divinity, is joined in an unspeakable manner. This is what he says; and since this manner is unspeakable, one ought not to seek further concerning it. In the third part of the *Summa* <note>The *Summa Theologiae*, Aquinas's most famous work</note>, question 75, he says God "yoked" his divinity—that is, his divine power—to the bread and wine, not so that they remain in this sacrament, but so that he might make his body and blood from them.
<margin>Regarding the authority of the Apostle.</margin>
To the authority of the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note>, it is said that his speech is figurative, both on the part of the subject and the predicate. For "bread," on the part of the subject, stands for the sensible sacrament—namely, the outward appearances of the bread. The "Body of Christ" is also taken figuratively. Hence, according to the Gloss <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard medieval commentary on the Bible</note>, through that speech it is not meant to be understood that the substance of the bread or the appearance of the bread is truly and actually Christ, or the body of Christ; nor that the body of Christ is predicated directly of the substance of the bread or its appearance.
<margin>The Gloss</margin>
Rather, the sense is: the bread which we break in the sacrament—that is, the participation in the bread broken on the altar—is the participation in the divine body; that is, it makes us be one with Christ. Let those Masters who were condemning my views remember: if the words of Damascene and Paul in this matter were taken as they seem to sound on the surface and at face value, they could produce an erroneous sense of the faith for many.
<margin>To the other point</margin>
When, however, it is said that fewer difficulties follow from this position regarding "assumption," it must be said that in those matters which belong to faith, one should not always choose that which leads to fewer difficulties, but rather that which is more in harmony with apostolic traditions and church dogma, even if more difficulties arise.
<margin>First solution.</margin>
For it is necessary to "take the intellect captive" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 10:5</note> in service to the faith, and to commit oneself with humility to the traditions of the Fathers,
<margin>Plato.</margin>
as even Plato says well and most religiously in the *Timaeus*.
<margin>Second</margin>
Furthermore, someone might say that although that "assumption" theory would better preserve the appearance to the senses, conversion <note>transubstantiation</note> better preserves the appearance to the intellect—that is, the words of the Gospel, which it is better to preserve because they cannot lie, whereas the senses can be deceived.
<margin>Again it is argued for the opposing side.</margin>
But it is argued further for the opposite side: that if this does not happen through "assumption" (so that it would be included in the Article of the Incarnation), then since the belief would be the same, there ought to be a special Article [in the Creed] for this conversion, yet it is not in the Creed.
<margin>The first response</margin>
Some say, like Peter of Palude <note>A 14th-century Dominican theologian and Bishop</note>, that the article concerning the Eucharist is perhaps specifically under that phrase, "the communion of saints," etc.
<margin>Peter of Palude.</margin>
Saint Thomas, in the *Secunda Secundae* <note>The second part of the second part of the *Summa Theologiae*</note>, says that in the sacrament of the Eucharist two things can be considered: one, that it is a sacrament, and this has the same rationale as other effects of sanctifying grace.
<margin>Saint Thomas</margin>

In the third book of the *Sentences*, however, he says that faith concerning the body of Christ, and all sacraments, the "keys," and all such things, is included in the Article regarding the effect of grace, which is "the holy Catholic Church," etc.

<meta>This page concludes Pico's defense of his views on the Eucharist (Question 6) and begins his famous, controversial defense of the early Church Father, Origen (Question 7).</meta>

Regarding the statement by Peter of la Palud <note>original: "Petrus de palude"; Peter of la Palud (c. 1275–1342) was a prominent Dominican theologian and Bishop of Jerusalem</note> that when it is said "the body of Christ is broken," it must be interpreted to mean that the body remains under the <margin>Peter of la Palud</margin> **outward appearances** <term>species: the physical qualities of the bread and wine—like taste and color—that remain after the substance has changed</term> which are broken as long as it remains in any part whatsoever. Furthermore, Peter adds these <margin>Note.</margin> words: "Thus I say that God could **assume** the bread and wine just as he could **convert** them, and that he could institute words at the speaking of which an **assumption** <note>This refers to 'impanation,' the idea that Christ's body could coexist with the bread, as opposed to 'transubstantiation' where the bread's substance is replaced</note> would follow, just as now a **conversion** follows the speaking of these words; however, he did not give this power to these words, nor could the meaning of the modern doctors be preserved if an assumption occurred instead of a conversion." These are his words. These words are most effective for the truth of my conclusion, which is entirely about what is **possible** and not about how things actually are, etc. <margin>To the other point</margin> Regarding the point that whenever there are two things that are the same in their **underlying subject** <term>supposito: the individual person or thing in which properties exist</term>, wherever one is, the other is also: it is said that this reasoning holds only for those things that are in a place by **accident**. It is otherwise for those <margin>To the last point.</margin> things which are in a place **by their own nature**. Moreover, when it is said that "the bread is the body of Christ" or "the body of Christ is the bread" cannot be verified unless the bread remains: it must be said that this is to be interpreted as "where the bread was, there the body of Christ is made." And let this suffice for the disputation of this question; from all of which I hold those things that are in harmony with the declaration of my conclusion explained above. However, those things I judge to be discordant, I consider rejected and condemned.

->SEVENTH QUESTION CONCERNING THE SALVATION OF ORIGEN.<-

[A large decorative initial R containing a figure of a man, possibly a scholar or saint, in a landscape] It is more reasonable to believe that **Origen is saved** than to believe that he is **damned**.
These masters <note>The papal commission of theologians who examined Pico's 900 theses</note> said that this conclusion is rash, deserving of rebuke, and "savors of heresy," and is against the determination of the universal Church. I, however—to speak of them more modestly—wish to show that their judgment is not correct, and that this conclusion is not against the determination of the Church; and what is more, even if everything they bring against me were true, it still cannot be said that this conclusion is heretical or "savors of heresy." For a fuller declaration of this matter, there will be **seven articles**. In the first, it will be seen whether Origen ever wrote or believed any heretical opinion <margin>Seven articles: how the declaration of the conclusion should proceed.</margin> regarding matters of faith. In the second, granted that he did write them, whether he transcribed them **dogmatically**, or as a **believer**, or merely as an **inquirer**. In the third, granted he wrote as a believer, whether he believed in such a way that by writing those things he sinned mortally and could be called a heretic. In the fourth, granted that he wrote and wrote in such a way that he erred in writing: whether he ever repented for such things. In the fifth, granted that neither his repentance nor his lack of repentance is certain: whether it is more reasonable to believe him damned or saved. In the sixth, what must be judged from the words of the decrees regarding what the Church has determined about Origen. In the seventh, to what extent the determination of the Church binds our belief in this matter. Regarding the matter of the first article, there was a bitter <margin>For the first article.</margin> contention between **Rufinus** and **Jerome**. <margin>Rufinus</margin> <margin>Jerome</margin> To them (as **Augustine** says, who deplores the dissension that arose between them), <margin>Augustine</margin> God had granted that, as the closest and most intimate friends, they might together lick the **honey of the Holy Scriptures**. Rufinus is of the opinion that the heretical dogmas found in Origen's books were falsely inserted by heretics who corrupted his books, and that they were not from the mind of Origen. Jerome feels the opposite. But let us see what probability each opinion holds, and <margin>Concerning the controversy of Jerome and Rufinus over the first article.</margin> it will perhaps appear that—preserving the faith and fully satisfying all those things which we are bound to believe of necessity for salvation—it can still be freely and probably believed that those principal heresies for which Origen’s sin is proved (and consequently his damnation) were not from the mind of Origen, but were falsely attributed to him by treacherous heretics corrupting his books. Moreover, <margin>Pamphilus the martyr.</margin> on this side, there is first the authority of **Pamphilus the Martyr**, whose book is offered in defense of Origen, in which that most glorious martyr, using the words of Origen himself from his books recited there, shows that he thought in a Catholic manner regarding those things in which he is accused of being a heretic. For, according to you, O Jerome, Eusebius tries in his books to prove that Origen was an Arian. But in the book of Pamphilus, nothing else is attempted but to prove that Origen was *not* an Arian, and that whatever things are found in his books confirming the heresy of Arius were inserted by the Arians themselves (of which kind Eusebius himself and many others were). Therefore, it is necessary that this book be entirely different from that one, since it argues a completely different—indeed, a contrary—case.

Nor is it enough if someone says that those things pertaining to the Arian heresy were changed from Eusebius’s book. For Jerome cannot say that Eusebius showed Origen’s books were corrupted in those parts pertaining to other heresies. Because Jerome himself, in his second book against Rufinus, says that apart from what pertains to the Son and the Holy Spirit, in other dogmas Eusebius and **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a prolific theologian who also defended Origen.</note> most aptly agree with Origen’s sect. Therefore, it cannot be well understood how the same things read in the book of Pamphilus could be read in the first book of Eusebius, unless perhaps some common points about Origen that do not pertain to the point of this conclusion being discussed. Nor does it seem so marvelous as Jerome wonders, if Pamphilus and Eusebius wrote some similar things, since—as Jerome himself says—they were companions. Eusebius could have either recounted things read in Pamphilus’s work in his own books, or, as happens every day, discovered and thought them up for himself by a similar movement of the mind.

And so much for the first book of Eusebius. As for Jerome’s claim that Eusebius wrote in the *Life of Pamphilus* that because of his humility, Pamphilus wrote nothing of his own work except for letters—and he adds that Eusebius, a defender of Origen and a praiser of Pamphilus, says this—Rufinus would perhaps respond that this does not do much against him. First, because even that little treatise of Pamphilus leans toward the brevity of a letter rather than the magnitude of a full book. <margin>First</margin> Second, because that brief defense <note>original: "apologia"</note> for Origen perhaps cannot correctly be called an "original work," since Pamphilus does not dogmatize <note>set forth formal doctrines</note> there; indeed, no question of a matter is treated there in general, but it deals briefly only with a particular man: that is, Origen. <margin>Second</margin> Whether his books were corrupted or not is not the same as establishing an "original work." Nor is it for a man of humility to raise himself up by avoiding the name of a "dogmatist" or "author." Third, it is possible that this book did not even come to the knowledge of Eusebius, both because of the smallness of the book and because of the author’s humility (which Eusebius himself mentions), as he wrote nothing great and was one who hid rather than showed off even those thin and tiny things he did write. <margin>Third</margin> Fourth, Rufinus will say it is even possible that Eusebius—as a defender of the Arian treachery <note>original: "perfidiae"</note>—wanted not only to hide the book of the martyr which deprived his sect of Origen's testimony, but also to act through this indirect testimony of his so that future generations would not believe the work belonged to Pamphilus. <margin>Fourth</margin> Therefore, what Jerome says (as if to strengthen his argument) that a "defender of Origen" says Pamphilus wrote nothing, is actually against him rather than for him. For since Eusebius defended Origen not as a Catholic but as an Arian, he could rightly be suspected in this matter, as I have said. But why is it necessary to labor over these points? <margin>Hilary, the Synod of Ariminum</margin> <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a leading opponent of Arianism. The Synod of Ariminum (359 AD) was a council where many bishops were pressured into accepting an Arian creed.</note> Rufinus also relates that the book of Hilary the Confessor was falsified by heretics after the Synod of Ariminum. He notes that for this reason, when a question was raised against Hilary in a council of bishops, he ordered the book to be brought from his house—a book which, unknown to him, a heretic was keeping in his own chests. Rufinus says that when it was presented and judged heretical by everyone, the author of the book, Hilary, left the council excommunicated. Jerome claims this is false and a fiction created to slander Hilary, though he offers nothing else to prove it. But whether it was true or not cannot be well known, nor does it pertain much to the defense of Origen. What is true is that Rufinus, being about to recount this concerning Hilary, prefaced it with these words: "And lest anything be lacking for easy belief, I will re-examine matters still within our memory, so that the truth of the testimony may be hidden from no one." Therefore, either it was true, or great was the impudence of Rufinus to weave an open lie and a new fable about a matter so recent in memory. But whether it be true or false, it does not seem to have been invented or recounted to slander Hilary; for it slanders those who corrupted Hilary's book rather than Hilary himself, whom Rufinus attests was innocent of heresy and was unjustly excommunicated because he was craftily deceived.

After this, <margin>Tertullian, Cyprian</margin> Rufinus recounts that a book by Tertullian, titled *On the Trinity*, was being read in Constantinople under the name of Cyprian the Martyr by heretics of the Macedonian party <note>A group that denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>. # DEFENSE

We read that Methodius <note>Methodius of Olympus (died c. 311 AD) was an early Christian bishop who was initially a fierce critic of Origen’s allegorical interpretations but later came to respect his work.</note> repented for having condemned Origen.
