But for him who is said to have "fallen from heaven," there will be no conversion, even at the end of the age. These are Origen's words. Also, that heresy which is imposed upon him—that the Spirit does not understand the Son and the Son does not understand the Father—is falsely attributed to him. This is clear from what he himself says regarding that passage of Paul: "O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God" <note>Romans 11:33</note>. For he says that while this depth of God is "unsearchable" to every creature, he could not say such things regarding the Son and the Holy Spirit, because the Son says to the Father in the Gospel: "Father, all mine are thine, and thine are mine." And regarding the Holy Spirit, Paul himself proclaims, saying: "No man knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him; so also the things that are in God no one has known except the Spirit of God" <note>1 Corinthians 2:11</note>. Therefore, when Paul says, "Who has known the mind of the Lord?" <note>Romans 11:34</note> he is speaking of creatures, but he excepts the nature of the Trinity. These are Origen's words.

One heresy attributed to Origen seems to remain: namely, his opinions concerning the soul <margin>Defense offered</margin>—that souls were created from eternity and "slid down" from heaven into bodies. Regarding the soul, <margin>against the charge of heresy</margin> Origen himself writes in his commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to Titus that he can determine <margin>regarding the creation</margin> nothing from Church dogma except that all souls are of the same species, that they possess <margin>of souls.</margin> free will, that they are rational, that they are immortal, that they were created by God, and that they will have punishments for evil and rewards for good. These things alone he says he affirms regarding the soul because there is evident testimony for them in the Scriptures. But in other questions concerning the soul, he says he states what seems more probable to him, proceeding by way of inquiry rather than by way of determination, because nothing regarding those matters is held as determined in Church dogma. However, that which seemed more likely to Origen—that souls were created in the heavens and living there before they entered bodies—is something that all <note>early writers</note> concordantly agree upon. And Rufinus, <margin>Rufinus</margin> in his *Apology to Anastasius*, Bishop of the city of Rome, after relating three opinions concerning the soul, concludes in this way: "I, for my part, having read these individual views, call God to witness that even to the present I hold nothing certain or defined regarding this question, but I leave it to God to know what is the truth; and if He shall deign to reveal it to anyone, I nevertheless do not deny that I have read these individual views, and I confess I am still ignorant of them, except for that which the Church clearly hands down: that God is the creator of both souls and bodies." Also, in the book of Pamphilus, it is not denied that Origen adhered to that opinion, but his defense is written thus: <margin>The book of Pamphilus</margin> "Now, since there is diversity among Churchmen, and some feel one way about the soul and others another, and all differ, why is this man to be accused more than the rest?" Then, after these words, the opinions concerning the soul that existed at that time are recited—among which is the one now held by Catholics. And when it is shown that manifest proofs from the Holy Scriptures cannot be applied to them, and that great difficulties befall their authors, it is concluded thus at the end: "But what we wish to show from all these things is that, just as those who think any one of these opinions we have set forth above is true are not rightly called heretics by anyone—for the reason that nothing certain or manifest seems to have been said about them in the Divine Scriptures, nor is it thought to be contained in the preaching of the Church—so it is not just to blame this man for discussing what seemed more likely to him." That is what is said there. I, however, from all the above, infer two propositions. The first is: <margin>First proposition</margin> if Origen felt as a Catholic regarding both the Trinity and the salvation of demons (as seems more fully proven by the testimonies), we cannot convict him as a heretic because of an erroneous opinion regarding the soul.

Indeed, not only in the time of Origen but also in the time of Augustine—who <margin>Augustine lived about 200 years later</margin> lived about 200 years after Origen—there was still a question among Catholics (that is, the universal Church) regarding his letter to Jerome: namely, whether individual souls are created for individual persons, as <term>orthodox tradition</term><note>Meaning the officially accepted teaching of the Church.</note> now holds. # GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

and I would say, preserving the faith of the Fathers, that he <note>Referring to the early Christian scholar Origen</note> did not write these things at all, but they were maliciously invented and written by heretics to obscure his famous name and titled with his name. These are his words, verbatim. These things were said concerning the first article to be examined and investigated: whether those two opinions of Origen were heretical or not. In this matter, as in all others, I always prefer the judgment of the Church over the judgment and reasons of all others.

For the second article, it seems more reasonable that Origen should be excused <margin>For the second article</margin> because if he wrote anything that is not accepted by Catholics, he proceeded in those writings neither dogmatically nor assertively, but always doubtingly and inquiringly. Therefore, just as there are many things in Augustine’s books on Genesis <note>Augustine’s *De Genesi ad litteram*</note> which are not accepted, they are nevertheless excused by us because, as he himself says in his book of *Retractions*, more things were sought after in that book than were found. Likewise, there may be many things in Origen's books to be rejected and condemned, but because he spoke not by determining them but by inquiring, he should not therefore be called a heretic. For heresy is properly called an assertion <margin>Heresy properly defined</margin> of a dogma against the express truth of either Scripture or the determination of the Church. That Origen always spoke in this way is evident from many places. For even after a disputation on the soul, he says: <margin>Note the words of Origen</margin> "let these not be dogmas according to our opinion, but only things inquired into and put forward so they do not seem entirely unaddressed." <note>original: "haec iuxta nostrā sniam nō sint dogmata sed quaesita tantum atq, proiecta ne penitus intractata uiderent"</note> And elsewhere, speaking of the resurrection, he says: "If these things are not contrary to the faith," etc. And further down: "a triple suspicion suggests itself to us concerning the end, from which the reader may investigate which is true and better." Then he joins three opinions on the resurrection. And in the preface to his books on Genesis, he says: "If something profound occurs, it must indeed be spoken of, but not however affirmatively." And further: "concerning great things which are above us, we are not ignorant of our own ignorance." And on the *Letter to the Romans*, book II: "let these things be said by us on the condition that if any have spoken better and more reasonably, they should hold those things rather than these of ours." And in book IV: "these things, as best we could, were set forth in places so arduous and difficult; if someone perhaps considers the zeal of our mind, they will be able to embrace them. If, however, they wish to note the weakness of our perception, we ask for pardon; and we freely yield to him who can discourse or explain these things better." And elsewhere: "let he who reads prove which of these is more suited to the apostolic sense and hold that." And in the fifth book: "these things meanwhile were able to occur to us in the present place. If anyone, however, has perceived something better, let it not be a burden to look back at those things while omitting these." And he who <margin>The book *Periarchon* for the third article</margin> reads more of the book *Periarchon* <note>Greek: *Peri Archon*, Latin: *De Principiis* ("On First Principles"), Origen's major theological work</note> will see him proceed in this order: that first he places those things which seemed to him expressly determined in the Scriptures, and in those he wanders not at all from the Church. Other things he says are doubtful to him and he wishes to inquire about them, asserting concerning all things that only that truth is to be received which in no way opposes apostolic and ecclesiastical dogmas.

For the third article, which is as it were a confirmation of the second, I state this proposition: that if there is someone <margin>Note this proposition.</margin> holding an erroneous opinion concerning matters of faith not yet determined by the Church, provided that in his will there is no stain, but a firm purpose to always believe those things consistent with Scripture and the Church, he neither sins mortally nor is he properly to be called a heretic. From which proposition it follows as a corollary that it is possible for the holding of a certain opinion at one time to be a mortal sin, which will not be so at another time. <margin>Corollary.</margin> and this is because one can believe something without obstinacy at one time which at another time he could not believe without obstinacy—for example, after a determination by the Church or a clarification of Holy Scripture. Concerning the opposite of what is believed, the opinion of all the Doctors bears witness, saying that it is not precisely an error of the intellect that makes a man a heretic, but there must be malice and perversity in the will. Therefore Augustine used to say: "I am able to err; I am not able to be a heretic." <margin>Augustine.</margin> This is confirmed by the determination of the universal Church, <margin>Confirmation.</margin> which has canonized many who nevertheless until death persisted in erroneous opinions...

->JOHN PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...who, asserting the opposite not dogmatically but as it seemed more probable to him, could be called a heretic; and this I evidently prove from a certain saying of Jerome himself cited above. For where Jerome says that even if in the works of Clement <note>Likely Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Church Father</note> (the disciple of the apostles) and others of such kind, some faulty things are found, he would not immediately judge them as heretics for that reason. He adds a fourfold cause. First, that the books could be corrupted. Second, that they wrote in another sense <note>meaning they intended a different interpretation</note>. Third, that they simply erred. Fourth, that they spoke less cautiously. 

In these words we must notice that, even if it is granted that Clement's book—in which he says the Son of God is a creature—is not corrupted, and granted that the author did not intend another sense, still Clement is not immediately to be judged a heretic, because he could have "simply erred." What then is "to have simply erred" <note>original: "simpliciter erravisse"</note> except to have erred from a defect of the intellect and an erroneous judgment of reason, and not from malice or perversity of the will? For if in that heresy—that the Son is a creature (which is the greatest of those charges leveled against Origen)—someone can simply err because there did not yet exist a determination of the Church about it, or a more certain verification through a greater clarification of the Scriptures (after which this would finally no longer be possible), and if at that time Clement was not bound under penalty of mortal sin to believe that with explicit faith, what can we say to show that Origen was obligated to believe explicitly in those matters where he is said to have erred? 

It must be noted, however, that because heresy can exist both in words spoken badly and out of order (as Augustine says) and in the underlying sense. <margin>Note</margin> <margin>Augustine</margin> <margin>Jerome</margin> Therefore Jerome, providing a way of excusing one who has erred in both together or separately solely from a defect of the intellect and not the will, says either that he "spoke less cautiously" (if heresy appears in the words) or "simply erred" (if the sense is heretical but produced by a simple and upright will though from a weak and erring intellect). And those words of Jerome are to be well noted and weighed, because in them a useful and sound doctrine <term>dogma: a settled opinion or principle</term> concerning heretical obstinacy is rightly founded.

<margin>Regarding the fourth article</margin> Regarding the fourth article, some who say Origen repented cite the *Lament of Origen*. <margin>Apocryphal book</margin> But that book is considered <term>apocryphal: of doubtful authenticity</term>, as is found in the Decretals, Distinction 15. <margin>Jerome</margin> But I cite the testimony of Jerome himself, who cannot be considered apocryphal, who expressly witnesses that Origen repented of his errors. 

I do not assert this because it is reasonably necessary for believing in Origen's salvation (as will be shown in the following article), but because these masters never cease shouting: "I show you that Origen erred; you show me that he repented! You will never show this; you will never find it written that Origen repented of what he wrote." 

Let the reverend fathers therefore hear Jerome himself—by whose authority they strike Origen with condemnation—in his *Apology to Pammachius and Oceanus*, in which he shows that he followed Origen's teaching, but not his dogma. After Jerome recounted Origen's errors, he added these words: "Origen himself, in the letter he writes to Fabian <margin>Pope Fabian</margin>, Bishop of the city of Rome, performs penance for why he wrote such things, and attributes the causes of his rashness to Ambrose <margin>Ambrose</margin>, who brought into public things that were issued in secret." 

These are Jerome's words, verbatim. What could be clearer? What more express? How now, or with what face, can they say it is nowhere found that Origen repented? 

I will also say what happened to me recently with two of those who were condemning this conclusion in a similar discussion. <margin>Note this witty remark</margin> For when I—in order to defend Origen against the charge of obstinacy—said to one who insisted much that the Church had determined Origen was damned in soul for obstinacy, that I held from Greek histories that Origen's dogmas were condemned many years after his death. I referred him (if he did not have the books at home) to the Bishop of Trau <margin>Bishop of Trau</margin> <note>Trogir, in modern Croatia</note>, a man no less outstanding in learning and character than in his dignity, at whose house I had seen a Greek book in which many things about the councils were collected. That good father said: "Why do you refer me to the Greeks, whom you know [to be...]?"

-># APOLOGIA<-

...to be utterly ignorant of those letters. "Let us seek," he said, "Latin ones. Do we not have the *Bundle of Times* <note>original: *fasciculus temporum*, a very popular world history book printed in the late 15th century</note> which treats these matters most elegantly?" "Let that *Bundle* be brought," I said, though I added: "If you prepare a fire for me as if I were a heretic by placing this 'bundle' <term>fasciculus: a Latin word meaning both a 'small book' and a 'bundle of sticks' used for fuel</term> beneath me, I will immediately drive both you and your bundle to the 'bad cross' <note>a Latin idiom equivalent to "go to the gallows" or "go to hell"</note>. For there is no faith to be placed in it." He became as inflamed as if I had blasphemed the Trinity. "Do not be so angry," I said. "Let the *Bundle* be brought. And do not think you can make me yield just because your 'bundles' are untied." It was brought, and in it we read these things concerning Origen:

*Origen was an outstanding teacher, incomparable in the holiness of his life, and most famous in the Church of God.*

And after a few words at the end, it says:

*A great labyrinth is woven by various men concerning Samson, Solomon, Trajan, and this Origen—namely, whether they were saved or not. Because these things can be left unknown without danger, and since the Church has not reached a certain judgment on them, they must be committed entirely to the Lord.*

This is your "good" bundle. When he had read this—hearing that the Church was not certain about the damnation of Origen—it was amazing how he turned pale. <margin>Note another point.</margin> Though the authority of the most proven experts could do nothing to move him, this little *Bundle* was so powerful that he changed his opinion on the spot. 

The following day, another man challenged me even more sharply, carrying a quite large book in his hand. "By what way," he said, "or by what path at all do you dare to defend Origen from the punishment of eternal fire? Look, I will show you testimony that you cannot contradict, which says Origen cannot be defended." "Produce it," I said, "venerable man, if you have your witnesses." Then he said: "This is a certain great witness," and he added the name. I, however, wish to keep the name quiet. "These are his sermons and preachings." Then I replied: "What 'sermons' are you bringing me? What trifles?" "Trifles!" he responded, now totally incensed. "Trifles," I said, "in which—if he has a sermon on this matter (for heaven forbid I should ever read such things)—unless some most manifest error is found, I am willing to have Origen’s head broken on Ixion's wheel <note>A reference to Greek mythology; Ixion was punished by being bound to a perpetually turning, fiery wheel</note> along with you." 

Impatient now and boiling with bile, he opened the book and began to read, raging in a very loud voice: *"Wednesday, Sermon 11: On the Origenists."* Then, in the pursuit of what was written, he shouted at every single word: "Is this not an error?" And look, while he was shouting with the envy of Stentor <note>A Greek herald in the Iliad known for having a voice as loud as fifty men</note>, he read these words written in the book: *Finally, Jerome confesses that he himself read six thousand books by Origen.* And immediately, as if playing a lyre, he shouted again: "Is this not an error?" "This," I said, "is indeed an error, and a great one! This is an open lie; here is a manifest falsehood!" 

To restrain the man immediately, I ordered the letters of Jerome to be brought. <margin>Pope Epiphanius <note>Pico notes the critic's error; Epiphanius was a Bishop, not a Pope</note></margin> And immediately running to the second book of his *Invective Against Rufinus*, I showed him Jerome saying to Rufinus that Bishop Epiphanius boasted of having read six thousand of Origen’s books. Jerome responded with these words: 

*Regarding the six thousand books which you falsely claim were read by him: who will believe either that you are telling the truth or that he could have lied? For if Origen had written six thousand books, it might be possible that a learned man, instructed in sacred letters from infancy, might have read the works of others out of curiosity and knowledge. But since Origen did not write that many, how could he have read them? Count the index of his books, which are contained in the third volume of Eusebius (in which he wrote the Life of Pamphilus), and you will not find six thousand, nor even a third part of that number.*

<margin>Epilogue</margin> These were Jerome’s words exactly. The man blushed, and my case was saved. 

But let us return now to the proposal. In conclusion: either we must concede with Rufinus and others (whom we cited above in the first article) that Origen never sinned; or, if we contend with Jerome that he did sin, we must also know that we must concede—along with Jerome—that Origen repented of his sin in a small book given to the Bishop of Rome. For my part, after I have diligently weighed and examined those things said about Origen by Eusebius, Rufinus, and Jerome, I conjecture that Origen, laboring for a long time in the deep scrutiny of the Scriptures, was hesitant regarding many arduous and principal questions of theology, since the truth was not yet certain and indubitable...

[Main Text]
...he himself might see whether he could assert anything regarding those matters from the testimony of the Scriptures. Because of this, regarding many mysteries of the faith, he perhaps said many things by way of inquiry and debate in the earlier years of his life which the Catholic faith does not accept. Therefore, Origen—who, as he himself says, was not ignorant of his own ignorance <note>This is a play on the Socratic idea of knowing what one does not know.</note> and clearly recognized that he had not yet attained the truth of those questions—never wanted what he preached in the churches to be recorded publicly by notaries before his sixtieth year, as Eusebius relates. Let us observe, therefore, what Eusebius writes in chapter twenty-six <margin>Eusebius</margin> of the sixth book of his *Church History*: that Origen, in the third year of the reign of Emperor Philip and under Pope Fabian, when he was already sixty years old, began to commit his sayings and letters to public record. And let us observe what he says above in chapter seventeen: that under Pope Urban, who was succeeded by Pontianus—already before the time of Fabian—Origen began the task of writing commentaries on the Holy Scriptures, with Ambrose <note>This refers to Ambrose of Alexandria, Origen's wealthy patron and friend, not the famous Saint Ambrose of Milan.</note> compelling him and forcing him by much pressure of prayers and entreaties. Eusebius says that Ambrose seemed most worthy of having this service bestowed upon him, and to whom whatever was secret and hidden, covered in the sacred letters, should be opened. From these two passages of Eusebius, in which an apparent contradiction appears, it is clearly gathered: that at the urging of Ambrose, he dictated certain things in his earlier years before he had yet discovered anything certain, which were nevertheless to be communicated to Ambrose privately and not published to the public. This was because he did not yet know them to be well-secured or in harmony with Apostolic truth. However, Ambrose brought those things, which had been produced in secret, into the public eye. 

Later, when the Catholic truth was discovered by Origen (now sixty years old), he began to write boldly and in a Catholic manner for the public. He was deeply grieved that those things he had written for Ambrose's private use had already been published by him. For his own justification <note>original: "purgatiōem," referring here to a formal legal or theological defense of one's reputation.</note> regarding this matter, as I gather from the words of Jerome and Eusebius, he wrote to Fabian, the Bishop of Rome, concerning the sequence of the whole affair, offering testimony of his Catholic faith. He explained that those things found written by him earlier were not written by him so that they would be published; he himself had been doubtful about whether they were Catholic or not. But Ambrose had published them. This is indeed what Jerome says: Origen himself, in the letter he writes to <margin>Jerome</margin> Fabian, the Bishop of Rome, expresses regret <note>original: "pniām agit," likely *poenitiam agit*, meaning he performs penance or expresses repentance.</note> for why he wrote such things, and he attributes the cause of the rashness to Ambrose, who brought into the public what had been produced in secret. 

Furthermore, Eusebius, recounting what he wrote after his sixtieth year—after he had counted his book *Against Celsus*, twenty-five books of *Commentaries on Matthew*, and twenty on the Prophets—adds: "He also wrote to Fabian, the Bishop of Rome, and to very many other leaders of the churches concerning his Catholic faith." Thus let it be true that before his sixtieth year, Origen was in doubt concerning many mysteries of the faith. And let it be true that he communicated many things in writing to Ambrose in secret, which he then held not by adhering to them firmly, but by inquiring tentatively, and which now ought not to be received by Catholics. And thus Jerome speaks the truth when he says that the things found in many of Origen’s books that are not Catholic belong to Origen, because they were truly dictated by him—though not as things believed, but as things sought after rather than found. Consequently, these things should not be blamefully attributed to Origen, who later discovered the Catholic truth. In these works, many things were also devised by heretics, according to Rufinus. We can also accept as true that Origen himself complained about this very thing while he was still alive. 

Let it be true then, according to Eusebius in the *Church History* (approved as true by Jerome), that Origen does not hold as his own works—that is, those in which he says something definitively and with adherence—except those which he wrote after his sixtieth year. And let it also be true, according to Jerome, that he repented of the things previously written and rashly published by Ambrose, and consequently died a Catholic. Thus, not only according to Rufinus, Pamphilus, and Eusebius, but even according to Jerome, it is more reasonable to believe that he <margin>Regarding the fifth article.</margin> is saved than to believe that he is damned. Regarding the fifth article, I say this proposition: <margin>First proposition</margin> however much anyone may sin gravely and mortally in this life, and it is certain that he [sinned] mortally...

# **APOLOGIA**

<margin>Correlative proposition</margin> ...unless his final impenitence <note>The theological state of refusing to repent for sins up until the very moment of death.</note> is certain, it is rash to truly assert that he is damned. The truth of this proposition is evident from the common opinion of all the doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church," authoritative theologians and teachers whose writings carry great weight.</note> who agree on this stated proposition. From this proposition, I infer two correlative propositions. The first is this: Not because someone has sinned mortally <note>A "mortal sin" is a grave offense that, in Catholic theology, results in the loss of divine grace and leads to hell if not repented.</note> during their life—and it is not certain to us that they did not repent—must we firmly judge that person to be in hell. This is clear because, while the mortal sin is present, the full condition for eternal damnation—final impenitence—is not yet established. One must go beyond the sin and be certain of their final refusal to repent. And I, who deny that we should firmly believe such a person is in hell, do not have to prove their repentance to you. But you, who assert that they are damned, must provide proof of their impenitence.

<margin>Henry of Hesse</margin> Much support for this is found in the saying of Henry of Hesse <note>A prominent German theologian and scientist (1325–1397).</note> who, in his exposition of the third chapter of the book of Genesis, says these formal words: "If the argument used by some were effective—by which they persuade themselves that someone is damned, as they do with Solomon <note>King Solomon’s salvation was a major debate in medieval theology because the Bible records his later idolatry but not his repentance.</note>, because Scripture commemorates his sin and makes no mention of his justice or repentance—then the first man [Adam] would be convicted as damned for his sin just as the first angel [Lucifer] was." Thus says Henry. For nowhere is mention made of Adam's repentance, but only of his sin. Similarly, in Judges chapter 8, we read of the sin of Gideon and not of his repentance; and yet the doctors rightly believe in his salvation. You can also see that by this same argument, some were so deceived that they erroneously said Moses was damned, because his sin at the 'waters of contradiction' <note>A biblical incident (Numbers 20) where Moses disobeyed God; he was barred from entering the Promised Land as a result.</note> was read, but nothing was expressly held regarding his repentance. And yet God said to Joshua: "Moses my servant is dead" <note>original: "Moyse servus meus mortuus est." The title "servant" implies he remained in God's favor.</note>.

<margin>Second correlative proposition</margin> The second correlative proposition is this: no one can be certain that someone is damned to hell unless they have this from a special revelation from God, or from those to whom it is believed God has revealed it. The truth of this is clear from the previous propositions, because no one can be certain of final repentance or impenitence except the one who knows the secrets of the heart and to whom He wished to reveal them. Since no one is as certain of anyone's state as they are of their own—for "no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him," as it says in the second letter to the Corinthians—and since a man cannot even be certain of himself, whether he is "worthy of hatred or love" as Ecclesiastes chapter 9 says, how much more will he be unable to be certain of another unless he has a special revelation?

From this main proposition and its correlatives, I infer the conclusion for my purpose: that even granted that Origen <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was a prolific early Christian theologian whose speculative ideas led to posthumous condemnations.</note> sinned mortally by erring in those matters, since we are uncertain of his final impenitence or repentance, to assert that he is damned is an entirely rash judgment and is to be rejected. Since we can be certain neither of his salvation nor of his damnation, it is nonetheless pious and highly reasonable to believe, as I have said, that God saved him—a man of such and so great knowledge.

<margin>The words of Jerome</margin> Regarding him, Jerome says in his preface to the Song of Songs: "While in other matters he surpassed all others, in this he surpassed himself." And of him, this is verified: "The king brought me into his chamber." And elsewhere, Jerome, wishing to imitate Origen in part, says: "Whom no one except the unskilled denies to be the master of the churches after the Apostles." And elsewhere:

<margin>Origen Adamantius</margin> "Origen sweated with such labor over the Scriptures that he justly received the name *Adamantius* <note>original: "Adamantius" (Greek for "man of steel" or "unbreakable"), a nickname referring to Origen's legendary endurance and tireless writing.</note>." And after certain remarks, he adds this: "Who could ever read as much as he wrote? And what reward did he receive for this sweat? He is condemned by Bishop Demetrius—except for the priests of Palestine, Arabia, Phoenicia, and Achaea, who did not join in his condemnation. The city of Rome itself consented to this and gathered a senate against him, not because of the novelty of his doctrines, nor because of heresy (as rabid dogs now falsely pretend against him), but because they could not bear the glory of his eloquence and knowledge." Why I have written this and dictated it by the small flame of a poor man's lamp with a quick but not cautious speech, you can understand if you consider the followers of Epicurus and Aristippus <note>Ancient philosophers often associated in the Renaissance with a lack of spiritual depth or hostility to wisdom.</note>. These are the words of Jerome, verbatim. Each of these words, I ask you, O ingenious reader...

<summary>This page argues that judging the eternal damnation of figures like Origen, Solomon, or Moses is rash and impossible without divine revelation, as only God knows the heart's final state. The author cites Henry of Hesse and Jerome to defend Origen’s reputation against those who condemn him out of jealousy rather than for heresy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s defense of the 3rd-century theologian Origen, arguing that Origen’s intense devotion and suffering for the faith outweigh any intellectual errors he may have committed.</meta>

GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...reader, pay diligent attention, and through these points understand for yourself the things I do not express explicitly. In the preface to his *Hebrew Questions* <note>original: "hebraicaꝝ quæstionū"</note>, Jerome says this of the same Origen: "I say this one thing: I would wish to have his knowledge of the Scriptures, even if it meant sharing the envy directed at his name." He regarded the "images and shadows of ghosts" as worthless—creatures whose nature is said to terrify little children and chatter in dark corners.

I pass over what the same Jerome proclaims about him: how he trampled upon greed; how he castrated himself out of zeal for God (though not according to knowledge <note>A reference to Romans 10:2; Origen was famously said to have taken Matthew 19:12 literally, a move later theologians criticized</note>); and how he toiled over the explanation of Scripture by day and by night. Those who clarify the Scriptures shall have eternal life, as the Wise Man says. And as Jerome writes to Vigilantius, Origen explained the obscure parts of the prophets and revealed the greatest sacred mysteries of both the New and the Old Testaments. I also pass over the fact that <margin>Note.</margin> he was not only the son of a martyr, but he himself came very close to the merit of martyrdom. 

For Eusebius says that even as a small boy, he burned with such a great passion for seizing martyrdom that he threw himself into dangers of his own accord. Later, in the time of the <margin>Decian</margin> Decian persecution, <margin>persecution</margin> he endured new crosses, new kinds of punishments, and torments unheard of in all ages. Eusebius says he was tormented by "a thousand deaths" so that the single death he longed for might not occur; the persecutor worked with the greatest effort to ensure that neither death was granted nor the pain ceased. See how little he lacked the praise of martyrdom, which so many of his disciples achieved under his leadership and encouragement. I say again, he lacked very little of the praise of martyrdom; indeed, he earned a merit that was essentially equal. 

For Augustine also says in his book *On the Good of Marriage*: <margin>Augustine</margin> "The merit of martyrdom is not unequal in John, who did not suffer [death], and in Peter, who did." Note these words of Augustine well. Just as John, although he did not pass by the sword, was nevertheless ready to undergo martyrdom when he was cast into the vat of boiling oil, so too was Origen. Although he did not undergo death by martyrdom, he was nonetheless ready—indeed, most eager—to undergo it. He suffered so many torments, as Eusebius says, that he underwent a thousand deaths for the sake of one. This is what Bernard says in <margin>Bernard.</margin> his sermon on the holy martyrs: <margin>Triple</margin> that there is a triple martyrdom—a martyrdom of <margin>martyrdom</margin> will only, a martyrdom of deed only, and a martyrdom of both deed and will. John the Evangelist suffered the martyrdom of will only, to whom it was said (as it was to his brother), "You shall drink my cup" <note>Matthew 20:23</note>. Hence, Cyprian <margin>Cyprian.</margin> says that among the servants of God, where martyrdom is contemplated and the mind is dedicated to the good, the person is crowned with God as judge. For it is one thing for martyrdom to be missing from the soul, and another for the soul to be missing from martyrdom.

If, therefore, Origen’s soul never failed the test of martyrdom and he underwent a thousand deaths for one, how can we not believe him to be crowned by God the judge, unless the martyr Cyprian is lying? And if he is damned, who, I ask, damned him to the death of hell? Was it Jesus Christ, for whom he himself wished to die so many times? Rather, just as Augustine says of the same Cyprian, <margin>Augustine.</margin> that the blood of martyrdom washed away every stain of heresy in him, so too let us piously believe regarding Origen: that the blood of martyrdom—poured out by him not so much outwardly upon the earth as inwardly upon his celestial soul, burning with zeal for God and charity—washed away every stain of heresy. 

Let us say with David <note>Referencing Psalm 1:1-2</note>: Blessed is Origen, who, even if he sometimes "walked in the counsel" of those who err, nevertheless did not "stand in the way" of sinners through impenitence, and never "sat in the seat" of pestilence through obstinacy; but "his will was in the law of the Lord, and he meditated on His law day and night." Blessed is Origen, whose "iniquities are forgiven" through baptism, whose "sins are covered" through penance, and to whom the "Lord did not impute sin" because of his martyrdom. Finally, concerning such a great man: even if he sometimes erred in the mysteries of faith due to a defect of intellect <term>ingenii defectu | a lack of mental capacity rather than a moral failing</term> and not from any malice of will, let us believe that he was not abandoned by the Lord in his final moments. Rather, by the visitation of His most clement mercy, he was illuminated regarding the secrets of faith (if he was erring in any points) and was called back from the erroneous path to the path of salvation. 

And this is what I meant in my brief response when I said elsewhere: since he was not found to be obstinate <note>In canon law, "obstinacy" or persistence in error after correction is required for a charge of heresy</note>, it is likely to believe that God saved him—that is, by visiting him with the "visitation" I have described...

<summary>Pico argues for the salvation of the controversial church father Origen, asserting that his extreme sufferings during the Decian persecution and his desire for martyrdom functioned as a "baptism of blood" that cleared him of any intellectual errors or heresies.</summary>

# APOLOGY

...placed him most mercifully in a state worthy of salvation; and by illuminating him regarding the secrets of the faith in which he had erred, God called him back to a saving repentance for those errors. Whether this actually occurred or not, no one can know with certainty unless it has been revealed to them from above. However, to one considering the acts and life of Origen, it seems more consistent and thus more reasonable to believe that it did happen rather than that it did not. For in doubtful matters, one should always reasonably adhere to the more favorable side. These things are said so that they may carry weight even if Origen's repentance were not certain—though we have already shown most fittingly in the preceding pages, through the testimony of the most blessed Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was a scholar who originally admired Origen but later became a harsh critic, though he preserved accounts of Origen's life.</note>, that his repentance is indeed established.

<margin>Regarding the sixth article.</margin> Regarding the sixth article, I say that it does not seem believable that the Church ever determined that Origen's soul was damned to hell. I prove the truth of this proposition by two reasons. The first

<margin>First reason.</margin> reason is this: concerning a matter where one side or the other cannot be determined with certainty except by rashness, it should not be believed that a determination was made by the Church. But regarding this question of whether Origen is saved or damned, neither side can be determined without being rash, at least without a special revelation from God. Therefore, since no such revelation is established, it should not be believed that a determination was made by the Church on this matter. The major premise is well-known: it would be harmful to the reputation of the Church to believe the opposite—namely, that anything could be judged by her without counsel and rashly.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin> The minor premise is clear from the articles mentioned above. It is confirmed because the Church could not be made certain of Origen's damnation except through a special revelation made concerning him; but there is no mention anywhere that such a revelation was made, therefore, etc. 

<margin>Second reason.</margin> The second reason is this: if there is anything that might persuade one that the Church has decided on Origen’s damnation, it consists of certain texts of the decrees <note>Referring to Canon Law / Decretals.</note> which seem to sound that way to those who interpret them in a crude manner. However, when these texts are correctly examined, they work against such people rather than for them. These are the texts they usually bring forward: First, from Distinction 15, the chapter "The Holy Roman Church," as written by Pope Gelasius <note>Pope Gelasius I (reigned 492–496 AD) issued a famous list of authorized and prohibited books.</note>. It says: "Likewise, we accept for reading certain small works of Origen which the blessed Jerome does not reject. But we say all his other works must be rejected along with their author." Also, in Case 24, Question 3, the chapter "Sane": "Likewise, if someone recurs to the times of Theophilus <note>Theophilus of Alexandria (died 412 AD), a fierce opponent of Origen.</note> of holy memory or earlier, they will find Origen was anathematized <note>formally cursed or excommunicated</note> after his death; which your Holiness also does, as does Julius, the most religious bishop of Rome." And the gloss there says: "Since he was damned, wouldn't his writings also be excluded?" and from the chapter "Fraternitis" regarding heretics. 

<margin>The Council of Ephesus.</margin> There it is written: "Since Celestine and Pelagius were damned in the Council of Ephesus, how can their chapters be received when their authors are damned?" From these authorities, some believe the damnation of Origen's soul to hell is proven. But I say that nothing more is held by these premises except that the Church condemns the opinions and dogmas attributed to Origen as heretical, and thus condemns and detests him as a teacher of dogma <note>original: "dogmatizante"</note>, intending nothing at all regarding the damnation or salvation of his soul. That this is true is clear for many

<margin>First.</margin> reasons. First, because it does not pertain to the Church to damn or save the souls of men; for that pertains only to Him who is the judge of the living and the dead <note>A reference to Christ as described in the Nicene Creed.</note>. Therefore, it is ridiculous if one reads in the decrees, "We damn Origen," to interpret it as "We damn his soul to the damnation of hell." 

<margin>Gelasius</margin> And it is also clearly evident from the manner of speaking used by Gelasius himself, who says the other works...

<summary>The author argues that while the Church condemns Origen's heretical writings, it has never officially pronounced his soul to be in hell, as judging the eternal fate of a soul belongs to God alone. He refutes common legal citations used to claim Origen's damnation, distinguishing between the condemnation of a teacher's errors and the condemnation of their eternal spirit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of Origen, specifically addressing the logical distinction between a person’s spiritual salvation and the official rejection of their academic or theological writings.</meta>

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

Secondly, I argue against those people using the very gloss <note>A "gloss" refers to the standard marginal commentaries used by medieval scholars to interpret law and scripture.</note> they cite, which asks: "If the man himself is damned, are not his writings also damned?" <margin>Secondly</margin> I ask these people whether this logic holds: "Origen himself is damned, therefore his writings are also damned." How is the term "damned" being used in that first statement? <margin>He argues against them.</margin> If it means his **doctrine** is not approved and he is not accepted as a **teacher**, then I have already proven my point. But if it means he is damned in his soul to hellish punishment, then the logic is completely invalid. It is entirely possible for many teachers whose writings are Catholic—and are read daily by Catholics—to be in hell. This is because a person may err in nothing regarding the faith and hold correct views on every article of belief, yet still fall into some other mortal sin and die in it. The damnation of a soul is entirely irrelevant to the damnation of a doctrine. The former is a matter of the malice of the **will**, while the latter is a matter of a defect in the **intellect**. Therefore, the reverse is also not true: "This man is in paradise, therefore his sayings are Catholic." For Papias is in paradise, as are Irenaeus, Victorinus, Cyprian, <margin>Papias</margin> <margin>Irenaeus</margin> and many others, yet many of their statements are rejected as heretical—statements which they are never recorded to have revoked. <margin>Victorinus</margin> <margin>Cyprian</margin> I confirm this from the very legal passage the gloss refers to regarding heretics (in the *Decretals*, the chapter *Fraternitatis*), <margin>Confirmation</margin> where it is asked: "If Celestinus and Pelagius <note>original: "Celestinus atque Pelagius." These were figures associated with the Pelagian heresy, which concerned human free will and divine grace.</note> were damned in the Synod of Ephesus, how could those chapters be accepted whose authors are damned?" It is certain, however, that in that synod Celestinus and Pelagius were not damned in themselves—that is, in their souls—but rather their **doctrine** was damned. This is partly because, as stated earlier, the Church is neither accustomed to nor able to damn men to hell, and partly because we must understand a judgment to be about the specific thing that was being questioned and debated. In that synod, as is clear from the records of the council, the question was not whether the souls of Celestinus and Pelagius were in paradise or in hell, but whether their sayings and teachings were Catholic or not. Therefore, we must understand the judgment to be about the truth of their teachings and whether they should be approved or rejected as authors of those specific doctrines.

Thirdly, it is foolish to say that the Church has officially determined that Origen’s soul is damned. <margin>Thirdly</margin> The Church does not have a custom of "damning" people—that is, issuing a formal sentence decreeing they are in hell—in the same way it has a custom of canonizing people. The reason it does one and not the other is that to decree someone is saved, we must be certain they died in a state of grace. We can find signs of this, though not absolute proof, from their life; however, life alone is not enough, because as long as a person is "on the way" <note>A common theological metaphor for being alive; a person in this life is a *viator* or traveler.</note> there is always room for merit or failure, and for changing from one intention to another. But we have signs after death, such as **miracles** or something similar. It is not easy to find such a sign that would prove someone's damnation after death; indeed, no sign can be had unless there is a specific revelation from God on the matter. If such a revelation were to happen, the Church—just as it testifies to miracles when it canonizes someone—would surely mention that a special revelation had been made so that it would not seem to have reached such a decree rashly or without counsel. Yet the Church tells no such story about Origen. We must therefore understand "damned Origen" in the way the Church's own records and testimonies suggest he was judged. Nothing is reported about him except that he erred regarding the mysteries of the faith. From such an error, it does not follow that Origen is absolutely damned in himself, but only in his writings and his doctrine, as is clear from what was said before. This is how we should judge him "damned" by the Church, and not otherwise. Furthermore, we know he was not "obstinate" <note>In canon law, heresy requires "pertinacity" or obstinacy—refusing to change one's mind after being corrected by the Church.</note> against the Church’s decisions, because the councils that condemned those opinions took place long after Origen’s death, as is clear from Greek and Latin histories. Whether he remained unrepentant of those views is something we can in no way know; in fact, we have already proven using Jerome’s testimony that either he did not write those things, or if he did, he repented of them.

<summary>Pico argues that the Church condemns doctrines (intellectual errors), not souls (willful malice), and notes that Origen could not have been a formal heretic because the councils that condemned his ideas happened long after his death.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's defense of his "theses," specifically addressing the psychological nature of faith and whether belief is a choice of the will. He cites medieval authorities and classical philosophy to argue that one cannot simply "will" oneself to believe something is true without evidence.</meta>

**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

[Main Text]

<margin>Henry of Oyta</margin>
<margin>Henry of Hesse</margin>
Henry of Oyta <note>A 14th-century German theologian and philosopher</note> and Henry of Hesse <note>Also known as Henry of Langenstein, a prominent theologian at the University of Paris and Vienna</note> hold this view. And when I was in Paris, almost the entire <margin>University of Paris</margin> University of Paris held it; indeed, many Catholic doctors <note>Teachers/scholars of the Church</note> consider it so true that they regard the opposite as impossible. In fact, I have not yet read a single doctor who contradicts this opinion. 

<margin>Clarification of the corollary proposition.</margin>
The corollary proposition <note>A secondary statement that follows naturally from an established one</note> is not to be understood or accepted in any way other than with the restriction or definition set down in the preceding statement: namely, that it is not within the free power of the will to believe an article of faith is true whenever it pleases, and to believe it is false whenever it pleases. This means that the intellect does not believe something precisely because the will desires it to believe; nor is such an interpretation of one proposition by another linked to it unusual. Indeed, in Holy Scripture, the meaning of the literal text is often taken from what precedes or follows it, which is exactly what must be done in our case regarding the statement "this is not in our power," etc. I do not propose this as a standalone statement or a separate conclusion, but as a corollary following from the previous one. 

If they do not wish to accept the meaning of the present corollary from its principal statement to which it is attached and linked, let them consider that there are <margin>Two ways something is said to be in the freedom or free power of the will.</margin> <margin>First.</margin> <margin>Second.</margin> two ways something is said to be "in the freedom" or "in the free power" of the will. In one way, once an apprehension is present in the intellect, no other act of the intellect is required, and it is within the commanding power of the will to perform that act. This is what is denied in this conclusion: that the act of believing is in the free power of a person. Nor is it necessary for every commanded, meritorious, or demeritorious act to be in a person's power in such a way. For to believe, the mere apprehension of terms is not enough. 

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
<margin>Argument first.</margin>
Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential early Christian theologian</note> affirms this in many places, as I have said, and also with the most effective reasons. And first, he argues thus: It is not in a person’s free power to have an <term>opinion</term> <note>A mental acceptance of something as likely, but with some doubt</note> that things are this way or that way just because they wish it. Therefore, it is not in a person's free power to <term>believe</term> <note>A firm mental acceptance of something as certain</note> things are this way or that way just because they wish it. 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
The logic of this follows clearly. Because if a power is not present where it would most likely be expected (in forming an opinion), then it is certainly not present elsewhere. It requires less effort to cling to something with a fear of the opposite (opinion) than without that fear (belief). Therefore, the premise is expressed by Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "ii. de anima"</note>, text of the commentary 153. This is also clear through experience. For anyone can experience in themselves that if a doubtful proposition is offered, if it is purely doubtful to them, they are not inclined to hold an opinion by <term>assent</term> <note>The mental act of agreeing to the truth of a statement</note> toward either side until some new "appearance" of truth comes upon them—either through a <term>syllogistic reason</term> <note>A formal logical argument or deduction</note>, or through intuitive knowledge, or through the testimony of many, or through the authority of the speaker, or something similar.

<margin>Second.</margin>
Second, it is argued thus: It is not in a person’s free power to make something appear true to their own intellect and to make it appear not true. Therefore, it is not in a person's power to believe in this or that way, that it is or is not true. The logic holds because it is a contradiction for someone to believe something and assent to it when it does not appear true to them. 

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
The premise is proven because for this or that to "appear" such and such to the intellect is for this or that to be represented to the intellect in a certain way. And this cannot depend on the command of the will, because this appearance precedes the act of the will. This is confirmed because something appearing a certain way to the intellect happens because the object being represented is such as it is, and the evidence (or whatever makes it credible or incredible) is such as it is, and the intellect itself is such as it is. But to make the object be a certain way, or the intellect be a certain way, is not within the choice of the will.

<summary>Pico argues that religious belief is not a simple choice of the will but a reaction of the intellect to evidence and "appearances" of truth. He supports this by citing Aristotle and Augustine, claiming that we cannot force ourselves to find something true if it does not seem true to us.</summary>

<keywords>free will, intellect, nature of belief, Aristotle, St. Augustine, University of Paris, Henry of Oyta, Henry of Hesse, epistemology, logic, assent</keywords>

<meta>This page continues a logical defense regarding the faculties of the soul, specifically focusing on why the human will cannot control what the intellect perceives as true.</meta>

->**APOLOGIA**<-
<note>original: "Apologia" — A formal defense or justification of a position, likely in a theological or philosophical context.</note>

...[neces]sity. Therefore, it is not within the power of the will for a thing to appear in one way or another to the intellect.

**Thirdly.** It is argued thirdly as follows: Whenever there is a certain power that is merely neutral and indifferent toward two opposing <term>secondary acts</term><note>In scholastic philosophy, a "secondary act" refers to the actual exercise of a capacity, such as the specific act of thinking about a tree.</note>, it cannot move into either of them unless it is first determined by something that is a <term>first act</term><note>A "first act" is the underlying state of readiness or the presence of a quality that allows a faculty to function.</note>, or something that stands in the place of a "first act" regarding one of those secondary acts. 

But it is the case that the intellect is a power that is merely neutral and indifferent toward the <term>specification</term><note>Specification refers to the mind focusing on a specific object or truth.</note> of any of its secondary acts. Therefore, it cannot be determined toward any such specification unless something else arrives that is either a "first act" or stands in the place of a "first act" regarding that determination. 

Then, following this reasoning, I propose this consequence: a mere act of the will cannot function as a "first act" regarding the specification of the acts of the intellect. Therefore, by the sole command of the will, the intellect cannot be determined toward such a specification. This consequence is well-known from the previously assumed reasoning, and the premise is evident from <note>original: "communi sententia"</note> common opinion.

<summary>This page argues that the intellect is a neutral faculty that requires external evidence or specific "first acts" to function; it cannot be forced to perceive a specific truth simply because the will commands it to do so.</summary>

<keywords>intellect, will, first act, secondary act, logic, scholasticism, cognitive faculty, Apologia</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his condemned propositions, specifically focusing on the nature of belief and whether the act of faith is a matter of free will or necessity, leading into a new question regarding the Eucharist.</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

For the defense of my conclusion, these points should suffice. However, I also wish to say this: there was a certain doctor—and I must confess that I have never read of his condemnation on this point—who simply held that the act of believing was not free. This was held assertively by Robert Holcot, <margin>Robert Holcot, a most subtle doctor.</margin> <note>Robert Holcot (c. 1290–1349) was an English Dominican theologian known for his "subtle" logic.</note> a most subtle doctor of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note> in his first book on the *Sentences*. <note>The "Sentences" of Peter Lombard was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages; scholars wrote "commentaries" on it to prove their expertise.</note> And when it is argued that it would follow that the act of believing or not believing would not be meritorious or demeritorious, he says this objection is null and frivolous. For an act is not meritorious because it is free, but because it conforms to some law promising a reward for that same act to the one performing it or to another. Consequently, he says the act of believing is not meritorious because it is free, but because it conforms to the divine law which promises such a reward—namely, eternal life—to anyone who believes. He argues that God could change this law and decree that whoever should happen to fall upon a cornerstone tomorrow by chance should be saved; in that case, that fall would be meritorious of eternal life. This is because our acts are not meritorious because they are free, but because they are accepted by God for eternal life. God can accept natural acts just as He accepts voluntary acts. Thus, He seems to have accepted the death of the Innocents <note>The "Holy Innocents," the infants killed by Herod in the Gospel of Matthew.</note> for eternal life, <margin>In the case of the innocents, there was no use of free will, according to Augustine.</margin> among whom there was no use of free will. Nor does God act irrationally in doing so, for His will is a sufficient reason for all things that He decrees or ordains. Therefore, Holcot concludes that if we take "to believe" to mean adhering with firm assent to those things whose truth is not evident to us except through the testimony of others—according to the way Augustine defines it in his homily on John, saying: "What is faith but to believe what you do not see?" <note>original: "quid est fides nisi credere quod non vides"</note>—then such an act of believing is not in the free power of man. But if "to believe" is taken to mean assenting to whatever has been revealed by God and testified to by miracles, <margin>To believe according to the terminology of Augustine.</margin> and being willing to live and work according to them, then—because this "believing" includes both an act of the intellect and the will—he concedes that it is free. According to this second definition, Augustine says in his homily on John that "to believe in God is to love by believing, to go to Him by believing, to adhere to Him by believing, and to be incorporated into His members." It is of this kind of belief it is said: "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." But of the first kind, it is said "the demons believe and tremble." The first <note>meaning the second type mentioned above: active, loving faith</note> is meritorious; the second <note>mere intellectual assent</note> is not meritorious. And when it is said that "faith exists only in those who are willing," Holcot says this must be understood as <margin>Holcot</margin> formed faith <term>Formed faith (fides formata): faith "formed" or completed by the presence of love/charity.</term> according to this second mode, which is "faith working through love," and not concerning faith taken in the first way. For he maintains that a believer can be necessitated to believe by the witnessing of miracles. I do not believe this opinion is true; however, after his inquiry, the same doctor, re-examining several of his own opinions, says that although the will might be necessitated to believe when evidence is present to the reason that something should be believed, nevertheless, because it was the cause of such necessity for itself, it is therefore imputed to it as a sin. He says the cause was that the person neglected to consider, diligently scrutinize, and discuss the things that created the false evidence for him; if he had done so, it would not have appeared so to the intellect, but otherwise. And therefore he concludes that when someone believes wrongly or disbelieves, his primary sin is negligence. This is the opinion of Robert Holcot on the freedom of belief, which never appeared good or probable to me. Let these fathers consider, however, whether they will also anathematize this doctor as a heretic along with Durandus, Henry, and others. <note>Pico is pointing out that if the Church censors him, they must also censor famous established theologians like Durandus of Saint-Pourçain and Henry of Ghent.</note>

In the miracle of the Eucharist, Catholic doctrine holds that these properties remain while the "substance" of bread turns into Christ. Pico is discussing the physics of how this happens.</note> could still hold the sacrament while also holding that the substance of bread does not remain. Indeed, these masters have not said that this conclusion is heretical or that it "savors of heresy," but only that it is "erroneous." If they had brought forward any reasons for this opinion of theirs, I would be able to either believe them or respond to them; but they, neither in the condemnation of this nor of other conclusions, offered any <margin>Note</margin>...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his "900 Conclusions." He is specifically addressing the nature of the Eucharist (Transubstantiation) and the linguistic function of the priest's words during the Mass. **GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...according to common opinion. However, the essence of bread agrees with the essence of the body of Christ in matter and in genus <note>original: "materia & genere"; Pico uses the Aristotelian categories of 'matter' (the stuff something is made of) and 'genus' (the general class of things it belongs to) to argue they are compatible for transformation.</note>. Whence one can be converted into the other even by nature, if the body were mortal; but the *being* <term>esse: the act of existing, as opposed to "essence," which is what a thing is</term> of bread does not share in matter nor in genus with the substantial *being* of the body of Christ, since that [Christ's being] is uncreated and divine, belonging to the divine person <note>original: "suppositi divini"</note>, since in Christ there is only one *being* of actual substantial existence. Therefore, [some argue] it is impossible for the *being* of bread to be converted, and it is necessary for it to remain. 

I am of the opinion that it is not necessary for it to remain: <margin>The author's opinion</margin> both because if it cannot be converted, it can nonetheless be annihilated, or it can be corrupted by yielding into the "potency of matter" <note>This refers to the idea of a thing breaking down into its most basic, unformed state—the raw potential to become something else.</note>. Just as humanity could be assumed [by Christ] without its own *being* being assumed, but rather remaining in the potency of matter, so too the essence can be converted without the *being* being converted, but rather reduced into the potency of the essence—though, to tell the truth, these "reductions" are easier to say than to understand. 

Likewise, although the *being* of bread cannot be converted into uncreated *being*, it can nonetheless be converted into a created essence, because things that share in matter are mutually transmutable—even granted that they do not share in "proximate" matter but only in "remote" matter, just as an element can be converted into a living thing and vice versa. However, the *being* of bread and the essence of the body of Christ agree in "prime matter," which is the remote potency of both, even if they do not agree in proximate matter. This is because matter is pure potency, whereas essence is potency joined with act. Indeed, if that previous argument were valid, it would conclude that of all the food Christ ate before his Passion, only the essence was converted into him and not the *being*; but it remained, or was corrupted in some way other than by conversion. For the substantial *being* of Christ was uncreated before the resurrection just as it was after. 

Likewise, some say that just as water—which by ordained power cannot be converted into the blood of Christ—is first converted into wine and afterwards the whole is converted into blood, so too, if *being* cannot by absolute power be converted into anything of Christ, it is first by nature converted into its own essence, passing into it like a "form" which yields into the potency of matter; and after that, the whole essence is converted into the [divine] essence, and thus it is not necessary for the *being* to remain. However, just as it seems erroneous to me to say that it is *necessary* for the *being* to remain, it is no less erroneous to say that it *cannot* remain.

**TENTH QUESTION: ON THE WORDS OF CONSECRATION.**

**T**hose words, "This is [my] body," which are spoken in the consecration, are held *materially* and not *significatively*. <note>In medieval logic, to use a word "materially" means you are quoting it or talking about the word itself; to use it "significatively" means you are using it to point to a real-world object or to perform an action yourself.</note>
These masters have said that this conclusion is scandalous and against the common opinion of the holy doctors, and that the opinion of the Glossator <note>A "glossator" refers to a standard commentator on Church law or scripture.</note> should not be held in this matter. 
I, however, say that *their* determination is scandalous and against the common opinion of many doctors, and that the Glossator's opinion is to be held in this matter rather than theirs. How this is so will be clearly evident once the meaning of the conclusion is understood. 

It must first be noted, therefore, <margin>Note</margin> that I do not intend for these words to have been taken "materially" when they were uttered by Christ, but only when they are uttered by the Gospel priest while consecrating. And therefore I said in the conclusion: "the words which are spoken *in the consecration*," that is, those which are now uttered by those who consecrate. 

For it is certain that the priest, in consecrating, recites the aforementioned words of Christ, so that the prayer uttered by such a priest stands for the prayer uttered by Christ when taken significatively. And such an opinion is not only not erroneous or scandalous, but rather the opinion opposed to the aforementioned sense seems to be contrary to the "form" of consecration, in which the priest speaks those words *recitatively*. For the consecrating priest *recites* that Christ said to the apostles: "Take and eat, etc." But the consecrating priest is neither speaking to the apostles, nor saying to them "Take, etc." except recitatively. For he alone receives the sacrament, nor does he say to those standing by, "Take and eat, etc." Similarly, when he says, "This is my body," that which is recited by the priest is that prayer, "This is my body," taken materially for a similar prayer...

->APOLOGY<-

...composition and from similar words, uttered significatively by Christ, which is evident through those words spoken before or after the consecration of the blood: "which will be shed for you and for many," etc. <note>original: "qui pro uobis & pro multis effundet"</note> For these words would be false if taken <term>significatively</term> <note>Meaning the words are intended to describe a literal, physical shedding of blood occurring at that exact moment.</note> because the blood of Christ will not be shed from now on; therefore, those words are taken only <term>recitatively</term>. <note>Meaning the priest is reciting or quoting Christ’s historical words rather than speaking them as a personal, present-tense declaration.</note> And what is recited but a voice uttered by another, for which the voice of the one reciting stands in place? And for that reason, this voice, as a recitation of another’s voice, is to be taken materially. Furthermore, even if these words were taken significatively rather than recitatively, they would denote that Christ’s blood is shed for others and not for the one consecrating, since it says "which will be shed for you and for many." It should rather be said "which for us," etc. I do not say these things because I believe the opposite opinion cannot be defended, but so that it may be clear that my conclusion is not only Catholic but more probable than its opposite. From this, it is clear that the present conclusion is not scandalous but probable, and the opinion of the <term>solemn glosser</term> <note>A reference to a standard legal commentator on Canon Law, specifically regarding Gratian's Decretum.</note> concerning the consecration <note>original: "di. ii. c. timore"</note> is not to be rejected in this matter but approved, just as it has never been rejected by the Church up to these times.

### ELEVENTH QUESTION ON THE MIRACLES OF CHRIST.

**M**iracles of Christ are the most certain argument of his divinity, not by reason of the thing done, but by reason of the manner of doing it.
In declaring this conclusion, I said that it is the firm knowledge of theologians that those miracles which Christ performed could be performed by a mere human through the power of God. For Christ says in John 14: "Truly I say to you, he who believes in me will do the works that I do, and will do greater things than these." Therefore, it is unanimously concluded by these same theologians that the thing from which we can conclude Christ was God is not the deed itself, but the *manner of doing* it; for he acted in the same way as those act who work by their own power and not by power received from elsewhere. This is the unique property of God: to act independently and not by another's power, a manner of acting that cannot be communicated to a creature. Because Christ performed many things in such a way—not by praying or asking, but by commanding and ordering as one having authority—it is clear that he operated as God himself, and not merely as a man existing in the power of God. 

Upon seeing this declaration of mine, they said my conclusion could be pulled toward an evil meaning because it includes things found among magicians, even granted that my declaration is true. I marvel at their judgment so much that I could not marvel more. First, let them tell me whether my conclusion could have any meaning other than the one I stated to anyone interpreting my words rightly and according to the correct and customary way of speaking. For what could be clearer than these words, what more expressive: "the miracles of Christ are the most certain argument of his divinity, not by reason of the thing done but by reason of the manner of doing"? 

Second, let them tell me if this is the sentence of a right judge: "This conclusion, although it is true and Catholic, must nevertheless be condemned because it can be pulled toward an evil meaning." If so, then that statement "Christ cast out demons" must be condemned because the Jews pulled it toward an evil meaning, saying that "he cast out those demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons." And "the Father is greater than I" <note>John 14:28</note> must be condemned because Arius <note>A 4th-century priest whose teachings led to the Arian heresy, which denied the full divinity of Christ.</note> used it to think of the inequality of the Son to the Father. And "he did not know her until she brought forth her firstborn son" <note>Matthew 1:25</note> must be condemned because Helvidius <note>A 4th-century writer who used this verse to argue that Mary did not remain a virgin after the birth of Jesus.</note> derived a heresy from it against the perpetual virginity of Mary. And "neither does the Son know that day" <note>Mark 13:32</note> must be condemned because from it some want to know more through the Father than the Son knows. Indeed, almost all Gospel propositions would have to be condemned because they could be pulled toward an evil meaning by heretics. When I have placed my proposition in the very same terms in which it is placed by many Catholic doctors, why should we condemn it even though it is true, simply because some can pull it toward an evil meaning? Surely, if any interpret it poorly, it is their meaning that is evil...

He critiques his opponents for wanting to condemn orthodox statements simply because they might be misinterpreted by others.</summary>

APOLOGIA

<margin>Augustine.</margin> I marvel at the teaching of those fathers and their extensive reading of sacred matters, who claim that it is never said of an angel—neither <term>properly</term> nor <term>improperly</term>—that he is "rational." <note>In medieval theology, "properly" means using a word in its strict, literal sense, while "improperly" refers to an analogical or metaphorical usage. Usually, humans are called "rational" because we reason step-by-step, while angels are called "intellectual" because they understand things instantly.</note> But let them read Augustine in his book *On Music*, in his book *On True Religion*, in the *Acts Against Fortunatus*, and in the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*. For in all these places, I remember that angels were called by the name of "souls" <note>original Latin: *animarum*</note> by Augustine. To be sure, I have not seen every text, nor am I able to remember every single location where I might have read in the works of the holy doctors that angels were called by this name. Indeed, it is a matter that, when read, is not even worthy of much attention.

However, when I said that it is more "improperly" said of God that He is "intellect," I intended nothing other than this: that angelic knowledge—which claims the name of "intellectual knowledge" for itself—is further distant from the infinite knowledge of God (who knows all things through His very essence) than it is distant from the reasoning knowledge of the rational soul...
