<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense (Apologia) of his nine hundred theses. He is addressing the controversy surrounding his proposed public debate in Rome, which was halted by Pope Innocent VIII.</meta>

-># GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

These words were dictated by me with a hurried pen, as things stand now; at another time, with more leisure and care, I shall perhaps write more and better things. This work itself, such as it is, was composed by working through the night over the span of twenty days. In publishing it, speed was more necessary to me than diligence. For it was necessary to provide my friends with something to throw to my barking enemies—as if throwing a morsel to Cerberus <note>In Greek mythology, Cerberus is the three-headed dog guarding the gates of the Underworld. Pico compares his critics to this beast.</note>—and thus to immediately confront the sickness of unjust infamy that was coming my way. 

Whatever I have written <margin>Note.</margin> and shall write in the future is always said with this preface: that I hold as valid and holy only that which the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> and all those whose judgment he approves shall decree to be valid and holy. And I wish that he had already decreed something regarding these opinions of ours which have been called into doubt, according to his own wisdom and authority. It was not my place to take up this work to defend what he might have condemned (which would be rash) or what he might have approved (which would be superfluous). 

Therefore, while we are not yet able to make use of the sentence of such a great judge, we have written these things so that there is no reason for my detractors to speak maliciously, or for the unrefined and simple to suspect something sinister regarding the questions I proposed for debate. For it can happen that when someone less educated encounters them, reading this proposition: *“Christ did not descend into hell truly and as far as real presence is concerned, in the way the common path posits,”* <note>Pico is debating the technical nature of Christ’s "Descent into Hell" between his death and resurrection.</note> they might be immediately offended by that phrase “not truly.” They might believe the meaning of the proposition is that the article of faith concerning the descent of Christ is not true. 

Likewise, when they read that *“infinite punishment is not owed to a mortal sin of finite duration,”* <note>Pico argued that a sin committed in a limited time shouldn't logically result in an eternal punishment, a view that bordered on heresy regarding the nature of Hell.</note> they might suspect me of supporting the heresy that the punishment of Gehenna <note>term: Gehenna. A biblical term for Hell or a place of fiery suffering.</note> is not eternal. And when they understand that I hold a good opinion regarding the salvation of Origen, <note>term: Origen. An early Christian scholar whose views on the eventual salvation of all souls were controversial and later condemned.</note> they might suspect that I love Origen's dogmas rather than his life, character, learning, and repentance. 

The same is true for many other propositions which might, at first glance, offend “holy simplicity”—that is, ears that are as pious as they are unlearned. For that reason, I have written these things, which ought to be read so that no one thinks ill of us or of the orthodox teachings of our holy religion. I would not want our people to read the propositions themselves while they are “raw,” so to speak, and unexplained, unless they have first encountered these explanations; for from those raw statements, many things could be conjectured that are as alien to the Catholic faith as they are to my own mind.

<meta>This page begins a list of formal theological "conclusions" or theses. Based on the content, the author is defending specific interpretations of Church doctrine—specifically the nature of Christ’s descent into hell and the mechanics of mortal sin—likely in response to accusations of heresy or for a formal academic disputation.</meta>

->THE CONCLUSIONS WHICH I DEFEND AS CATHOLIC IN THIS WORK ARE WRITTEN BELOW.<-

### First conclusion.
The soul of Christ descended to hell by a true and real descent. Thus, Christ was in hell during the three days <note>original: "triduo"; this refers to the three days between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection</note> according to the true and real presence of his soul.
**Corollary.** I do not approve of the opinion of Durandus <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334) was a philosopher-theologian known for independent views that often diverged from standard Church teachings.</note> regarding the descent of Christ to hell.

### Second conclusion.
Although this is so, the underlying reason for the true and real descent—and the true and real location of Christ's soul in hell—was not its essence or substance. This latter view is held by the "common path" <note>The "common path" refers to the mainstream academic consensus of the time.</note> of the **Scotists** <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus.</note> and the **nominalists** <note>A school of thought that argued universal concepts are just names, not real things.</note> which is commonly held at Paris, and which **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, the highly influential 13th-century theologian.</note> seems to adhere to in the third part of his *Summa*. Instead, it was only by effect or operation.

### Third conclusion.
The meaning explained through the conclusions written above is the meaning I intended through this proposition: Christ did not descend to hell truly and in terms of "real presence" as Thomas and the common path posit, but only in regards to the effect.

### Fourth conclusion.
The question of whether the aforementioned proposition—by the strictness of logic and the force of the words themselves—permits that meaning is not a question of faith <note>The author is arguing that even if his phrasing is technically debated by logicians, it does not constitute a religious error or heresy.</note>.

### Fifth conclusion.
One who believes that this proposition permits that meaning by the "virtue of the sermon" <note>original: "uirtute sermonis"; a technical term meaning the literal or customary sense of the words used.</note> does not err in faith.

### Sixth conclusion.
He who believes something is a matter of faith when it is not actually a matter of faith does not judge correctly regarding the faith.

### Seventh conclusion.
When one puts forward a proposition that has a double meaning, if he asserted it (and continues to assert it) in a Catholic sense, he is not bound to revoke the proposition, but only to clarify it.

### Eighth conclusion.
Given the aforementioned case and the multiplicity of possible meanings, we ought to judge a proposition according to the meaning intended by the person proposing it, rather than according to the meaning the words seem to suggest more strongly.

### Ninth conclusion.
**Mortal sin** is, by its demerit, worthy of eternal punishment.

### Tenth conclusion.
Anyone dying in mortal sin, even if they die with only one such sin, will be punished forever.

### Eleventh conclusion.
Unless the **guilt** <term>original: "reatus"; the legal or moral debt/obligation to undergo punishment for a sin</term> of mortal sin persevered eternally in the soul of the sinner, the punishment of the sinner would not persevere forever.

### Twelfth conclusion.
Just as this term "mortal sin" is sometimes taken to mean the act of sinning (whether by leaving something undone or by committing an act), it is also—and often and properly among Catholic doctors—taken to mean the **guilt**.

### xiii. conclusion.
When we say that a punishment or a reward is "owed" in some case, we can understand this in two ways: either that the person is demeritoriously or meritoriously worthy of such punishment or reward, or that such punishment or reward is actually being paid to them at that moment.

### xiiii. conclusion.

<meta>This page continues the list of 900 theses or "conclusions" proposed by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola in 1486 for public debate in Rome. The heresies attributed to Origen are impious and detestable, and have been justly condemned by the Church. 
<note>original: "Hærefes Origeni attributæ" — Origen (c. 185–253 AD) was a prolific early Christian theologian whose works became controversial centuries after his death due to his views on the pre-existence of souls and universal salvation.</note>
xxviii. conclusion.

Since it is the case that either Origen never believed those opinions but they were falsely attributed to him by heretics—as Rufinus, Pamphilus, Methodius, Didymus, and Haymo maintain—or if he did believe them at one time, he eventually repented of them—as Jerome maintains—it is reasonable to believe well concerning the salvation of his soul, and we are not bound by necessity of salvation to believe the opposite.
<note>Pico is arguing for a "charitable hope" regarding Origen's salvation, a controversial stance at the time since Origen had been formally condemned.</note>
xxviiii. conclusion.

The act of believing is a free act.
xxx. conclusion.

The act of believing is not so much in the power of a human being that, when a purely doubtful proposition is presented, the intellect can adhere to one side rather than the other by the mere and sole command of the will.
<note>Pico suggests that we cannot simply "force" ourselves to believe something is true if the evidence seems completely uncertain; the intellect requires some degree of conviction beyond just wishing it were true.</note>
xxxi. conclusion.

One who believes this proposition—that it is not in the free power of the will to believe an article of faith to be true when it pleases them, and to believe it to be false when it pleases them—provided they allow for the explicit meaning established in the preceding conclusion, does not err in faith.
xxxii. conclusion.

The accidents in the <term>Sacrament of the Altar</term> are in no subject.
<note>In medieval philosophy, "accidents" are qualities like color, taste, and smell. In the Eucharist (the Sacrament of the Altar), Catholic doctrine held that while the "substance" of bread changes into Christ, the "accidents" (the appearance of bread) remain without being "attached" to any physical substance.</note>
xxxiii. conclusion.

It is possible by the <term>absolute power of God</term> for the existence of the bread to remain without its essence, and for the accidents of the bread to be supported within that existence; this assumes a real distinction between essence and existence.
<note>Absolute power (potentia absoluta) refers to what God could theoretically do, even if He chose a different path in the actual world.</note>
xxxiiii. conclusion.

One who believes this proposition—namely, that whoever says an accident cannot exist unless it exists within the <term>Eucharist</term> could hold the sacrament while also holding that the substance of the bread cannot remain—can be verified by what was said in the preceding conclusion, and does not err in faith.
xxxv. conclusion.

The "bread-ness" does not remain in the sacrament of the Eucharist supported by Christ as God-man, but through conversion, it passes into the essence of the body of Christ.
<note>original: "Paneitas" — a technical term for the "nature of bread." Pico is defending the orthodox view of Transubstantiation against "Impanation" (the idea that bread and Christ exist together).</note>
xxxvi. conclusion.

If one holds the common view that God can support any nature, it is possible that Christ assumes "bread-ness" into the unity of the divine <term>suppositum</term>; and it is possible that through such support, Christ is present on the altar where the bread is, and thus, without the conversion or annihilation of the bread-ness, Christ is on the altar according to a possible truth of the sacrament of the Eucharist—not indeed the one instituted by Christ, but one that was possible to be instituted.
<note>Pico is exploring a hypothetical: God *could* have made the Eucharist work by having Christ "become" bread (like he became man), even though that isn't what actually happens in Catholic teaching.</note>
xxxvii. conclusion.

One who believes this proposition—namely: if the common view regarding the possibility of God supporting any creature is held, I say that without the conversion of the substance of bread into the body of Christ or the annihilation of the bread-ness, it could happen that the body of Christ is on the altar according to the truth of the sacrament (speaking of what is possible, not what is the case)—provided they allow for the explicit meaning in the preceding conclusion, does not err in faith.
xxxviii. conclusion.

These words, "This is my body," etc., when they were uttered by Christ, were held <term>significantly</term>, not materially.
<note>When Christ first said the words, he was performing the act of changing the bread (significantly/meaningfully).</note>
xxxix. conclusion.

These same words, when they are uttered by a gospel priest while consecrating, are held <term>materially</term>, that is, recitatively, not significantly.
<note>When a priest speaks, he is "reciting" or "quoting" Christ's original act rather than originating the command himself.</note>
xl. conclusion.

The miracles of Christ, as far as the actual deed performed is concerned, are an argument that they were performed by <term>divine power<note>original: "virtute diuina." In this context, 'virtus' refers to the inherent power or efficacy of a divine being.</note></term>.

<meta>This is the opening page of Pico della Mirandola's "De Ente et Uno" (1491). It establishes the scholarly friendship between Pico, Angelo Poliziano, and Lorenzo de' Medici, setting the stage for Pico’s famous project to harmonize the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle.</meta>

-> **ON BEING AND THE ONE** <-

-> GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON BEING AND THE ONE, TO ANGELO POLITIAN. PREFACE. <-

**N** <note>Decorative initial</note> You were telling me the other day, Angelo, about the conversation Lorenzo de' Medici had with you concerning "being" and "the one." He was disputing against Aristotle—whose *Ethics* you are publicly lecturing on this year—while leaning on the arguments of the Platonists. Lorenzo is a man of such effective and versatile genius that he seems naturally made for all things; what I admire most in him is that, although he is always deeply occupied with the affairs of the Republic, he is always either speaking or meditating on some literary matter. <margin>The harmony of Aristotle and Plato</margin> Because those who believe Aristotle disagrees with Plato also disagree with me—since I make the philosophy of both men concordant—you asked how Aristotle could be defended in this matter and how he might agree with his master, Plato. I told you then what came to mind, confirming the things you had replied to Lorenzo during the dispute rather than bringing forward anything new. But this was not enough for you. You demand that, even though I intend to write more extensively on these matters in the work I am currently laboring on—the *Concord of Plato and Aristotle*—I should nevertheless briefly outline for you in a short commentary the things I said to you in person about this question. <margin>Solution to the previous reasoning</margin> Since Domenico Benivieni happened to be present, a man very dear to both of us for his learning and integrity. Truly, what could I deny you, especially in a literary matter, being my almost inseparable companion? However, permit me, with your leave as a defender of refined language, to use certain words that have perhaps not yet been granted the "right of Latin citizenship" <note>original: "nondum fortasse Latii iure donatis"; Pico is apologizing for using technical Scholastic terms that would have sounded "un-Latin" to a humanist like Politian</note>. Yet the novelty of the subject matter and a certain necessity have forced these terms out. Do not look for the allure of an elegant style here; for as <margin>Manilius</margin> Manilius says: "The subject itself refuses to be adorned, content to be taught." These, then, if I remember correctly, were the points we were discussing.

### Chapter One, in which he recounts the arguments of the Platonists, by which they wish to prove that "the One" is superior to "Being."

**A** <note>Decorative initial</note> Aristotle says in many places that these terms correspond to each other and are of equal scope: namely, "the One" and "Being"; <margin>What Aristotle thinks</margin> likewise "the True" and "the Good," though we will speak of those later. <margin>What the Platonists think</margin> The Academy <note>Followers of Plato's school</note> resists this view, holding that the One is "prior" to Being. When they say "prior," they want it to be understood as both simpler and more universal. For this reason, they say that God (who is of supreme simplicity) is "the One," but is not "Being." Likewise, they claim that the first matter of all things—crude and formless—is included within the boundaries of the One, though it lies outside the limits of Being. Then they argue that the thing opposed to the One is not the same as the thing opposed to Being. For "nothingness" is opposed to Being, but "multiplicity" is opposed to the One. Therefore, by the same law by which opposites are judged, they believe these two—Being and the One—do not <term>convert: in logic, terms "convert" if they refer to the same set of things; Pico is discussing if everything that is "one" is also a "being"</term> nor correspond to each other.

### Chapter Two, in which he asks where Plato spoke about Being and the One, and shows that Plato’s words favor the opinion that the One and Being are equal, rather than those who want the One to be superior to Being.

**H** <note>Decorative initial</note> They rely on these arguments. Before we dissolve them, it would not be out of place to bring forward what I find expressed by Plato on this question. <margin>Names, reason, the good</margin> I find Plato disputing about Being and the One in two places: namely, in the *Parmenides* and the *Sophist*. The Academics contend that in both places, the One is placed above Being by Plato. <margin>What must be thought concerning Plato</margin> But I will first say this about the *Parmenides*: that in that whole dialogue, nothing is actually asserted as a definitive claim. Even if it were strongly asserted, nothing can be clearly found from which we could ascribe such a dogma to Plato. Certainly, the book is not to be counted among the dogmatic ones, since it is entirely nothing other than a kind of dialectical exercise. The words of the dialogue themselves are so far from contradicting our opinion that there are no interpretations more arbitrary and forced than those brought by those who [interpret it] in another sense...

O

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of the harmony between Plato and Aristotle, specifically addressing the metaphysical relationship between "Being" (ens) and "the One" (unum).</meta>

->OF MIRANDOLA<-

### Chapter three, in which he declares how "being" is understood by Aristotle when he makes it equal to "the one" and encompassing all things.

**T**his word "being" <note>original: "ens"</note>, about which there is a dispute as to whether it is equal to "the one," can be understood in two ways. <margin>Being can be understood in a twofold way</margin> The first is that when we say "being," we understand everything that is "outside of nothing." This is how Aristotle used the term when he made "being" equal to "the one." Nor did he use the word this way without reason: for as it is truly said, we should think like the few, but speak as we ought <note>meaning: speak like the majority so as to be understood</note>. We think and hold opinions for ourselves, but we speak to others—that is, to the multitude—and therefore we speak so that we may be understood. Now, the common people and anyone from the general public understand "being" in such a way that everything is called "being" which does not lack "existence" <note>original: "esse"</note>, and which cannot truly be called "nothing." But even those who are held to be the wisest among the very people who disagree with us <note>referring to the Neoplatonists</note> are found to have used this word in this way. For Parmenides the Pythagorean <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who argued that reality is a single, unchanging Being</note>, when he said that "the one is that which is," understood "God." This is true if we believe Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> and many others who wish to defend Parmenides against those who misrepresent him as if he had said that "all things are one." <margin>First testimony</margin> For they respond with one voice that Parmenides never believed there was no division, multitude, or plurality in things—which he himself openly confesses elsewhere in his poems—but when he said "the one is that which is," he judged that the name of "being" truly fits that which truly "is" <margin>and the second according to Simplicius</margin> as one thing only: and that "one" is God. Therefore, if we believe Parmenides and his defenders and the Platonists, "the one" cannot be above "being" unless it is also above God; and Parmenides is so far from denying that God is "being" that he grants the true name of "being" to God alone. And so, the solution to the first argument of the Platonists <margin>Solution to the first argument of the Platonists</margin> occurs to us in passing. But even Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian (Pseudo-Dionysius) highly respected in the Renaissance</note>, whom those who dispute against us claim as a supporter of their opinion, will not deny that it was truly said by God to Moses: *I am who I am* <note>original: "ego sum qui sum"</note>. In Greek, we read this as *I am the Being* <note>original: "εγω ειμι ο ωv" (egō eimi ho ōn)</note>. <margin>Dionysius</margin> Indeed, since they themselves say that "nothing" or "non-being" is opposed to "being" just as "multitude" is opposed to "the one," they must necessarily grant that that which is "not being" is "nothing" or "non-existence." Just as that which is "not one" is "many" or "a multitude." Therefore, if they observe the same law of speech, they must admit either that God is "nothing"—which the ears themselves dread to hear—or that He is "being." In this way, when "being" is accepted, we establish that first axiom and universal principle: of anything, it is necessary to say that it either "is" or "is not"; <margin>Fourth</margin> of nothing can both be said at once, or be thought possible. Since, therefore, there is nothing outside of everything except "nothing" itself, if "being" accepted in this way excludes only "nothing" from itself, it must undoubtedly encompass all things. Therefore, "the one" cannot encompass more things than "being" unless it encompasses "nothing"—which Plato denies in the *Sophist* <margin>Fifth</margin> when he says that "non-being" or "nothing" cannot be called "one." If, then, it does not encompass fewer things, as they wish, then "being" and "the one" are equal.

### Chapter four, in which he declares how something can be said to be higher than "being."

**W**e have explained one of these ways by which we said "being" can be understood, which people use; and just as they can use it correctly, they most truly affirm that nothing is more common than "being." <margin>Concrete and abstract names</margin> It remains for us to explain the other way, according to which it will be manifest that nonetheless it can be truly said that there is something placed above the eminence of "being." Of names, some are **concrete**, others are **abstract**. <margin>Difference</margin> Concrete names are *hot*, *shining*, *white*, *man*. Abstract names are *heat*, *light*, *whiteness*, *humanity*. Now, the force and difference between them is this: that what is called "abstract" denotes that which is such of itself, and not from another. The "concrete," on the other hand, signifies that which is such not of itself, but by the benefit of another. Thus, a *shining thing* shines by *light*. A *white thing* is white by *whiteness*. And a *man* is a man by *humanity*. Since, truly, nothing "participates" in itself, and the same condition cannot exist in the same thing both of itself and by the participation of another, it follows that what is called "abstract" cannot be named by the "concrete." Therefore, it is not fitting to say "whiteness is white" or "blackness is black." Indeed, anyone who uttered such things would be ridiculous—not because whiteness is black or heat is cold, but because the former is so far from blackness and the latter from coldness that...

O ii <note>Printer's signature mark</note>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s "On Being and the One" (De Ente et Uno), a treatise dedicated to Angelo Poliziano, where Pico attempts to reconcile the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle regarding the nature of existence.</meta>

->OF MIRANDOLA.<-

In many places, Aristotle’s philosophy was altered; from this arose those great intellectual battles fought with <term>Averroes</term><note>Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval university life.</note>. Yet, as far as this matter is concerned, there is little actual discord. For these thinkers divide what Plato understands under the "One" into "One" and "Something"—a distinction that is not foreign to Plato, who in the *Sophist* lists "Something" among the most common terms. Furthermore, what is contained under "Being," they partition into "Being" and "Thing." But more on these matters elsewhere. Let us follow what we have begun: these four <note>Being, One, True, and Good—often called the "Transcendentals" in philosophy.</note> exist one way in God and another way in those things that come after God. For God possesses these of Himself, while other things have them from Him.

Let us first see how they exist in created things. All things that exist after God have an efficient, an exemplary, and a final cause from Him. For "from Him, through Him, and unto Him" all things exist. Therefore, if we consider things as they are established by God as the efficient cause, they are called **Beings**, because they participate in existence through that efficient power. If we consider them in relation to their exemplar—which we call the **Idea**, according to which God established them—then they are called **True**. For an image of Hercules is called "true" when it actually conforms to the real Hercules. If we consider them as they tend toward Him as their ultimate end, they are called **Good**. But if each thing is taken absolutely according to itself, it is called **One**.

The order is as follows: first, each thing should be conceived under the <margin>Order in these four</margin> category of "Being," because an agent makes a thing exist before that thing can be "something" in itself; otherwise, its entire essence would not come from the agent. Thus, nothing exists after God that we do not understand as a "being from another"—a finite being, a participating being. **One** succeeds **Being**. The third is **Truth**, because after a thing exists in itself, <margin>Plato.</margin> it must be seen whether it is such as the exemplar to which it was formed. If it is found to be similar to that exemplar, it remains for the thing to turn itself toward it—as toward its kin and relative—through **Goodness**.

Who does not see that these four are equal in scope? Grant that something exists, and it is certainly **One**. For he who does not say "one" says "nothing," as Plato says in the *Sophist*. For whatever a thing is, it is undivided from itself and divided from other things which are not itself. When we say this, we understand "One"; or, to use Plato's words, it is "the same as itself and different from others," which he confirms in that same dialogue belongs to every single thing.

It is also necessarily **True**. <margin>Truth is convertible with Being.</margin> For if it is a man, it is certainly a "true man." It is the same as saying "this is not true gold" and "this is not gold." For when you say it is not "true gold," you mean it looks like gold and is something similar to gold, but it is *not* gold. <margin>Augustine.</margin> Therefore, Aurelius Augustine, defining truth in his *Soliloquies*, said: <note>original: "verum est id quod est"</note> "The true is that which is." This should not be taken to mean that "Being" and "True" are the exact same thing. Although they are the same in reality, they are different in their logic and definition; therefore, one should not be defined by the other. Rather, Augustine wanted to express that a thing is called "true" when it is what it is called and said to be—just as gold is "true" when it is gold and nothing other than gold. This, then, is what he meant by "the true is that which is," though some, failing to notice this, find fault with the definition.

Similarly, it is also **Good**, because whatever exists is good insofar as it exists. <margin>Goodness is convertible with Being.</margin> In my opinion, <term>Olympiodorus</term><note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> is greatly mistaken in believing he can prove that "Good" and "Being" are different. <margin>Dispute against Olympiodorus.</margin> He argues that we desire "Good" simply, but we do not desire "Being" simply, but rather "Well-being" <note>The Greek concept of *eudaimonia* or "living well" as opposed to merely existing.</note>; thus, it can happen that if we are in a bad state, we might desire not to exist. Setting aside whether those who are in a bad or miserable state can truly and naturally desire non-existence, he fails to notice that just as "Being" is manifold, so "Goodness" is manifold. First, there is the **natural being** of things—as for a man to be a man, a lion a lion, a stone a stone. An inseparable **natural goodness** follows this being. There are other types of being which can be called **accidental**, such as for a man to be wise, or beautiful, or healthy. Just as wisdom and beauty are different "beings" from humanity, so they are different "goods." For the goodness of humanity (by which a man is a man) is one thing, and the goodness of wisdom (by which he is not just a man, but becomes a wise man) is another; just as the latter is one type of being and the former another. Therefore, just as all things seek "Good," so all things seek "Being." And first, they seek that goodness which follows natural being, because this is the foundation...

<summary>Pico explains that Being, One, Truth, and Goodness (the Transcendentals) are distinct in definition but identical in reality, originating from God's role as efficient, exemplary, and final cause. He defends the idea that existence itself is a natural good, countering Olympiodorus's argument that suffering makes non-existence preferable.</summary>

**ON BEING AND THE ONE**

[The foundation] of subsequent goodnesses: which all come to it so that they cannot stand without it. For how will he be happy who does not exist at all? It is true that the goodness they acquire when they first exist is not sufficient for them; rather, they desire to attain the remaining goodnesses which might complete and adorn that first existence. Just as we truly say that other goodnesses are sought in addition to the first goodness, so we can truly say that other ways of being are desired beyond the first being: because it is one thing to be happy and another to be a man. And if someone grants that it is possible for someone not to wish to exist if they are not happy, it does not follow (as <note>Olympiodorus the Younger was a 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote commentaries on Plato and Aristotle.</note> Olympiodorus thinks) that the good is one thing and being is another. Rather, it means that being a human is one thing and happiness is another; likewise, the goodness of a human is one thing and the goodness of happiness is another. Therefore, a man does not want the one (the first) unless he also has the second. I pass over whether, by the same reasoning, something is called "simply good" and "simply being," or whether that which is called "being" is called "simply good" in such a way, and that which is "simply good" is called "such a being." This is not the place for all such disputes. Therefore, I was saying truly: each thing that exists is good to the extent that it is. For "God saw all the things he had made, and they were very good." <note>A reference to the Book of Genesis 1:31.</note> And why not? They are from a good craftsman, who impresses his likeness upon all things that come from him. In "being," therefore, we can admire the power of God the efficient cause; in "truth," we can venerate the wisdom of the artist; in "goodness," we can proclaim the liberality <note>Generosity or kindness.</note> of the lover; in "unity," we can receive the unique simplicity (so to speak) of the creator. This unity has joined each thing to itself and all things to each other, just as it calls everything to the love of itself, of others, and finally of God. Let us examine also whether their opposites are equally similar in scope: "falsehood" and "nothing" 

<margin>Evil and nothing are interchangeable. <note>In formal logic, "convertible" terms refer to the same set of things.</note> Against the error of the Manicheans. <note>The Manicheans were a religious group that believed in two equal powers: one good and one evil. Therefore, to "do evil" is "to do nothing"; and it is often said that evil has no "efficient cause" <note>A cause that brings something into being.</note> but rather a "deficient cause." It remains in "potentiality" as the parts which were previously in potentiality then begin to exist in actuality. For while they were in the whole, they did not have their own separate unity in actuality, which they only obtain when they subsist by themselves, separated from the whole.

However, if we assign these four names <note>original: "appellationes has quattuor." Pico refers to the four transcendentals: One, Good, True, and Being.</note> to God insofar as He is the cause of all things, the entire order is reversed. 

For first, He will be **One**, because He is understood in Himself before He is understood as a cause. Second, He will be **Good**. Third, **True**. Fourth, **Being**. 

This is because the cause which is called the **end** <term>Final Cause: The purpose or goal for which something is done (the "why").</term> is prior to that which is the **exemplary** cause, and the exemplary is prior to the **efficient** cause. 

For example:
1. First, we desire a goal—to be protected from the harshness of storms. 
2. Then, we conceive the **idea** <term>Exemplary Cause: The mental blueprint or model used by a creator.</term> of a house in our mind. 
3. Finally, we form that house in physical matter through the act of construction <term>Efficient Cause: The actual agent or force that brings something into existence.</term>. 

Therefore, if—as we defined in the previous chapter—the **Good** relates to the final cause, the **True** to the exemplary cause, and **Being** to the efficient cause, then God, as He is the Cause, will first possess the character of the **Good**, then the **True**, and finally of **Being**. 

We touch upon all these things briefly here, though they are otherwise a source <note>original: "sceta," likely a printer's error for "scatebra," meaning a bubbling spring or overflowing source.</note> of many great and significant questions.

<meta>This page contains the opening of a critique by Antonio of Faenza against Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's famous 1491 treatise "De Ente et Uno" (On Being and the One). Antonio challenges Pico’s attempt to reconcile the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle regarding the nature of God and existence.</meta>

-># ON BEING AND THE ONE<-
->## THE FIRST OBJECTIONS OF ANTONIO OF FAENZA AGAINST THE LITTLE BOOK ON THE ONE AND BEING.<-

<margin>First objection.</margin>
**S** If any little book deserves to be inscribed with the title *On Being and the One*, it is necessary that it explain the nature and properties of both Being and Unity. However, in this little work that recently came into my hands, and which is titled *On Being and the One*, several things are treated that are almost foreign to that title and inscription. Indeed, the author's primary purpose is to dispute whether, according to Plato, Being and the One follow one another mutually, or whether, as the Academics <note>The "Academics" here refers to the followers of Plato's Academy, specifically the Neoplatonists who believed the "One" was superior to "Being."</note> believe, the One is more universal than Being. But this is not to treat "Being and the One" in general, but rather the mutual conversion <note>In logic, "conversion" refers to the idea that two terms are interchangeable—for example, if everything that is "One" is also a "Being."</note> of Being and the One, and even then, only according to Plato. For if a philosopher were to debate only the question of whether the soul is immortal, he would not be disputing "On the Soul" in an absolute sense, but would only be treating the soul's immortality.

<margin>Second</margin>
Furthermore, the author of the work says that the Academics think that God, according to Plato, is not truly and properly "Being." This I greatly wonder at. For if he means all the Academics or Platonists—as his phrasing seems to suggest—he should not have made such an absolute pronouncement. 

<margin>Themistius</margin>
To claim that the Academics feel this way is perhaps not without falsehood. For Themistius <note>Themistius (c. 317–387 AD) was a philosopher and rhetorician who wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle.</note>, a far from ignoble author among the Platonists, testifies that according to Plato’s opinion, the Idea which is the principle of all things is truly and properly "Being" and "One." Indeed, all or most Platonists do not think the "Idea" is one thing and God, the craftsman of the world, is another.

<margin>Third.</margin>
Following this, he says: if it can be defended in any way according to Plato that the One is more universal than Being, it must be judged thus. He says that words which are called "concrete" in the Latin language—such as "white," "shining," or "being"—signify something "other" than the thing by which they particularly receive their name. For "whiteness" is one thing and "white" is another; "man" is one thing and "humanity" another. Therefore, something will be called "being" in which "existence" <term>esse: the act of existing</term> is one thing, and the "subject" <term>subsistit: that which stands under or carries the existence</term> is another. Therefore, God, who is existence itself, cannot be considered "Being," but rather "the One," because he contains and encloses all things. But does not this kind of defense lack internal consistency? For by whatever reason "white," "man," and "being" signify something "other," by that same reason "one," "blessed," "God," and many similar terms must also signify something "other." Therefore, God—who is unity, blessedness, and divinity all at once—could not be called "One," nor "Blessed," nor even "God." How then is he not "Being," but is "the One"?

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
Furthermore, "Being" <term>ens</term> is so called because it "is" <term>est</term>. Just as it is impossible that someone who sits is not a "sitter," it is impossible that he who truly and properly "is" should not be "Being." For He said: <note>original: "ego... deus sum qui sum"</note> "I am the God who is." <note>A reference to Exodus 3:14: "I am that I am."</note>

<margin>Fourth.</margin>
But it may seem more admirable that he not only tries to defend the idea that God is not "Being" according to Plato, but also tries to drag Aristotle himself into this same opinion. For he says that in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*, Being is divided into "being through itself" <term>ens per se</term> and "being by accident" <term>per accidens</term>. But "being through itself," he says, is divided into the ten categories. However, God cannot be placed in any category, as he thinks Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> has demonstrated. Therefore, if God is not "being through itself" nor "being by accident" (as is established according to Aristotle), he will not be "Being." Furthermore, "Being" is separated into "substance" and "accident" according to the most common division. But God is neither accident nor substance; for the author says God exceeds the limits of any category. Yet truly, I do not see by what reasoning the author of this work ascribes this Platonic opinion to our Aristotle (if indeed it is even the opinion of Plato). For the division of Being into "being through itself" and "being by accident" is a division of "complex being" <note>Referring to "being" as it exists in a mental proposition or statement, rather than just the essence of a thing.</note> as Blessed Thomas, 

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
to whom he grants much authority, subtly writes in that place. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
The same is manifest from examples. For "being by accident" according to Aristotle is threefold: either an accident is predicated of a subject, or a subject of an accident, or an accident of an accident. All of these pertain to a "complex" <term>complexionem: a mental combination or proposition</term>. In the same way, those things are called "beings through themselves" in which something is predicated that pertains either to the substance...

->**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**<-

...pertains either to quantity or another genus, provided that what is predicated of the subject fits it essentially <term>per se; a Latin term meaning 'in itself' or 'intrinsically'</term>, as "white" fits Socrates, but not necessarily "man" in general; or "animal" fits a horse. Moreover, the division of Being into substance and accident <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, a 'substance' is something that exists on its own (like a person), while an 'accident' is a quality that must exist in something else (like the color of that person's hair).</note> also encompasses God; for it is a division made through affirmation and negation. For a substance is that which rests upon nothing else but exists through itself, while an accident is that which exists in another, as if in a subject. Between these two, there is no middle ground, as Saint Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian.</note> believes; for indeed, no middle ground can be imagined between "having a subject" and "not having one." Therefore, substance, which is opposed to accident, will not be a genus if God is not contained within any genus. Furthermore, it is not an undisputed <margin>Confirmation</margin> opinion of Aristotle's that God is essentially contained in no genus; for there are some followers of Aristotle <margin>of the</margin> who think that God is essentially placed within a category. And I indeed think that the distinguished philosopher Boethius <margin>argument</margin> held this view; and I would show, if it were necessary, from the words of Boethius <margin>Boethius</margin> and also Augustine, that this can be aptly gathered. Again, he says that the negation of the "one" is distributive <note>original: "divisuam"</note>; <margin>Augustine.</margin> which he proves by the fact that a thing is destroyed when it is torn apart and divided. But how can "divided" and "united" be opposed as a negation? For between affirmation and negation, there is a contradiction; <margin>Fifth.</margin> however, a chimera <note>A mythical beast often used in logic puzzles to represent something that does not exist.</note> is neither one nor divided; nor is the fact that a diameter is commensurable <note>A reference to the mathematical proof that the diagonal of a square is incommensurable with its sides.</note> either one or divided. He also thinks that "falsehood" is the negation of "truth"; <margin>Sixth.</margin> which, although it might be defended in some way, is nevertheless a contrary rather than a negation, as Saint Thomas shows. For a chimera is not true <margin>Saint Thomas.</margin> or false, unless we utterly abuse the vocabulary; for that is "true" which is—that is, as he explains it, that which is what it seems and is said to be. Therefore, "false" will be that which is not what it seems and is said to be, like a counterfeit coin. Nothing, therefore, happens to be false except that which seems to be something else which it is not. But between that which seems to be what it is, and that which is not what it seems, no contradiction shines forth. Therefore, falsehood and truth are not opposed by any opposition of affirmation and negation. <margin>Seventh.</margin> He also thinks "evil" is the negation of "good." But Aristotle affirms that good and evil are <margin>Aristotle.</margin> genera of contraries in his *Categories*; and that which is a negation cannot be a genus. Furthermore, good is to be sought for the reason that it is good; but evil is to be fled. Seeking <margin>Confirmation</margin> and fleeing are contraries to each other, just as "gathering" and "separating" are. Therefore, good and evil will be contraries, which Boethius also asserts in his commentary on the *Categories*, whatever others may have said about it.

## **Response to the first objections.**
### **GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO ANTONIO OF FAENZA, GREETINGS.**

**Q**uestions of yours against that little book which I recently published *On Being and the One* I have read with as much pleasure as the love and freedom of spirit with which they were written by you. I owe you much in the name of this service; if we either bestowed this more freely upon our friends, or more willingly required it from them, we would certainly be far better and more learned than we are. But this deadly persuasion has seized the minds of men: that we think we do not please those whom our errors do not please; and we interpret the free judgment of friends as either hatred or moodiness, while we see flattery as love and natural goodness. So it happens that while we prefer to be praised even when undeserving rather than to be corrected even when deserving it, we are always mocked and never deserve praise. See how greatly we err! For almost all praise is always useless, and often harmful. For if it is true, what utility does it bring? If it is false, it surely makes us, who are praised, insane; and those who praise us, ridiculous. Reprehension is certainly always useful: if it is just, it leads to knowledge; if it is less than just, it excites us to the defense of the truth. Finally, what else is it to be corrected than to become better through another's labor? Or what else is it for a friend's book to shine under the file <note>The "file" (latin: *lima*) is a classic metaphor for the painstaking process of editing and refining a literary work.</note> than for you to profit from his sleepless nights while you sleep? I cannot, therefore, as I was saying, help but owe you very much, you who have freely signaled to me what you felt about those things in my book that pleased you less. I recognized in your writings, besides your benevolence, also that famous...

**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...declaring what it is and how it is that all things, in whatever way they exist, come from Him. For Dionysius <margin>Dionysius</margin> says that God is called "One" because He is all things uniquely; again, He is called "One" because He is the principle <note>original: "principium"; in this context, it means the foundational source or starting point</note> of all things that exist, just as unity is the principle of all numbers. These are my words there, verbatim. Therefore, if when we call God "One" we wish to declare *what* He is, I admit to you that He cannot be called "One" for the same reason that He cannot be called <term>Being</term> <note>original: "ens"; a central philosophical term for anything that exists</note>: because both are "concrete" names <note>A "concrete" name refers to a thing that has a quality (like "a white thing"), whereas an "abstract" name refers to the quality itself ("whiteness"). Pico argues God is the quality itself, not just a thing possessing it.</note>. Indeed, I was the first to openly assert this in that same book with these words: "these names—Being, True, One, Good—denote something concrete and, as it were, participated. For this reason, we say again that God is above Being, above Truth, above the One, and above the Good: because He is Existence itself, Truth itself, Unity itself, and Goodness itself." Those are the words from that passage.

It did not escape me, therefore, when I was writing, that both "Being" and "One" are equally concrete, and by reason of that concreteness, either neither or both should be removed from our description of God. But as I cautioned above: when we say God is "One" but not "Being," we are not signifying *what* God is, but *how* He is that which He is. We mean that He is all things in the most primary and simple way. This "manner" of existence can in no way be indicated or symbolized by the title of "Being," but it can be through the model and name of "Unity." For as Aristotle writes, existing things relate to each other just as numbers do; <margin>Aristotle</margin> and among numbers, unity is both the most primary and the most simple.

You add that you are surprised that I wish to defend the idea that "God is not Being" not only according to Plato, but even according to Aristotle. <margin>Solution to the fourth objection</margin> Truly, if you have run through the book more attentively, my primary aim in this whole work is to show that God both is and is properly called "Being"—not only according to the dogma of Aristotle but also following Plato—on the grounds that the "One" is not superior to "Being." <margin>Aristotle / Plato</margin> However, lest those who said God is "not Being but above Being" should seem entirely insane—among whom, if neither Plato nor Aristotle is included, certainly Dionysius <margin>Aristotle / Plato</margin> the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian and philosopher whose writings blended Neoplatonism with Christianity; Pico considers him "greater" than the Greek philosophers.</note> is, who is greater than both—I have attempted <margin>Dionysius</margin> to prove that there is a certain way of speaking which, if we follow it, makes it not absurd to say God is greater than the title of "Being." This way of speaking is even occasionally used by the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the "covered walkways" where they walked while discussing philosophy.</note>, even if you shrink from it. Yet you cannot deny it unless you deny their authority—to whom, even in your opinion, the first place in that school is owed.

For who does not know that the division of Being into "substance" and "accident" is frequent among the Aristotelians? When Being is divided in this way, it is the opinion of your own Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the most influential medieval theologian.</note> that God is not "Being" but "above Being." <margin>Thomas</margin> Concerning him, you used to say, "Take away Thomas, and Aristotle becomes mute." <note>original: "aufer Thomam; Mutus fiet Aristoteles." A famous proverb suggesting that Aquinas was the most perfect interpreter of Aristotle's difficult philosophy.</note> Thomas's words are roughly these: "God is neither an accident, nor can He properly be called a substance; both because a substance is so called because it 'stands under' <note>A play on the Latin "substantia," which literally means "standing under" attributes.</note> [attributes], and because substance indicates a 'quiddity' <note>The "what-ness" or essence of a thing.</note> which is different from its existence." Therefore, that division of Being into substance and accident is a division of *created* Being. These are his words. Furthermore, when Aristotle says that the "First Philosopher" deals with Being insofar as it is Being, and with the causes and principles of Being, there are many among the Peripatetics who would have it that God is not placed there by Aristotle among "Beings," but among the "causes of Being."

However, I have not only not denied, but have asserted and confirmed with many reasons in the third chapter of that same work, that by another way of speaking, God can properly be called Being. <margin>Solution to the confirmation</margin> I do not know why you, who are always an imitator of illustrious authors, now abandon those most famous Peripatetics. <margin>Boethius</margin> I have no doubt that Boethius <note>An early 6th-century philosopher who bridged the gap between Classical and Medieval thought.</note> would by no means wish to be numbered among those who place God under a "genus" <note>A general category or classification.</note>. <margin>Solution to the fourth objection</margin> Finally, you contend that neither is the division of the One a negation, nor is Falsehood a negation of Truth, nor Evil a negation of Good. You claim that a **chimera** <note>A mythical creature composed of parts from different animals; used in logic to represent an impossible object that can be thought of but cannot exist.</note> is neither "one" nor "divided." But I argue that the chimera we conceive in our minds does not exist precisely because the parts from which we understand it to be composed are, in the nature of things, divided rather than united. 

And just as a thing does not exist if the parts that would constitute it are divided; so too, a thing not only does not exist, but *cannot* exist, if its parts are neither united nor capable of being united by any force of nature. Therefore, the only reason we say a chimera does not exist—and the reason we believe it can never come into being—is that it is incredible that the beasts from which we imagine it could ever combine into a single living composition.

-># ON BEING AND THE ONE<-

...a question might arise concerning the speed of motions: whether it follows an arithmetic or a geometric proportion. Since at the beginning of the work the author promises to take many things from geometry, the book could be titled "On Geometry," as it deals so much with motion. But let us dismiss these matters as frivolous. In another small book, I have written my opinion on this matter. No one, I say, has said that the Platonists feel differently unless all or most of them feel that way. If, however, Themistius <note>Themistius (c. 317–388 AD) was a statesman and philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note>—who is not ignoble among the Platonists—affirms from Plato’s own opinion that the **Idea**, which is the principle of things, is truly and properly **Being**, then it should not have been declared absolutely that the Platonists, following Plato, do not think God is truly and properly Being. For the **Idea** is God.

But you respond that an "Idea" is one thing and God is another. Even if it were granted that the Idea is God, you argue it does not follow that God is properly and truly Being; for "God" and "Idea," though they are the same in reality, differ in our mental definition. However, I would not wish to dispute in this place whether the Platonists think God and the Idea are different, since that question is far removed from our current purpose. Nevertheless, many authors, both Greek and Latin alike, place the Ideas of Plato within God, imitating Plato himself. I believe I have done enough for my purpose by showing that a certain Platonist—and by no means an ignoble one—asserts that according to Plato, the **Idea**, and therefore God, is truly and properly **Being**.

The difference in definition to which you flee does nothing to change this. For "Idea" is a relative term <note>The term "Idea" implies a relationship to the things created in its image.</note>, while "God" is an absolute reality. If, therefore, God is truly and properly Being in that part where he relates to external things, how much more should He be considered **Being** by that reason through which He is God and exists in His own nature? Why, indeed, is the Idea—insofar as it is an Idea—truly and properly Being? No reason can be assigned, I say, unless it is said to be truly and properly Being because it truly and properly **is**. Therefore, God, by the very reason that He is God, will be even more truly and properly Being. He says: *I am who I am.* <note>original: "ego sum qui sum" — A reference to the Name of God revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14.</note>

Furthermore, the following objection was raised: if the Platonists can be rightly defended when they say God is not truly and properly "Being" but rather "The One" (because the name "Being" <term>ens: a "concrete" term in medieval logic that implies a subject possessing the act of being</term> is a concrete term that signifies something separate from what it is), then by the same logic it could be concluded that God is not "The One." For "The One" is also a concrete name. Indeed, He would be neither "Blessed" nor "God," for both words are concrete.

But you respond that God is not called "The One" as if the substance of God were shown by the name of one, but rather to explain how He is what He is. But I ask, what is the point of this? For the objection is not yet solved. You say God is not Being, but The One, because the name of "Being" is concrete. If, therefore, "The One" is also concrete, must it not be concluded by the same reasoning that God is not The One, nor even "God"—a name which pertains to His substance just as "Being" does? Furthermore, if He is "One" because He is uniquely that which He is, why should He not also be called "Being"? For in being One, He is all things that He is: namely, Wisdom, and Goodness, and Power. For He is not called "One" because He is a solitary "one." Therefore, by the same logic, He can be called "Being," even though He is not Being alone: for He is Being in the highest degree.

Furthermore, that argument has not yet been resolved which stated: God is truly and properly Being; for He says, *I am who I am.* Again, I wondered how you could defend the idea that even according to Aristotle, God is sometimes not considered by the name of "Being" because He is not "being through itself," nor "being by accident," nor "substance," nor "accident." For I have shown that God is neither being through itself nor by accident, and that nothing can be thought of as a middle ground between substance and accident. <note>In Aristotelian logic, everything that exists is either a "substance" (a thing itself) or an "accident" (a quality of a thing, like its color).</note>

You, however, answer nothing to the first objection. Against the second, you allege only one interpreter of Aristotle, namely **Blessed Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian.</note> <margin>Confirmation</margin>, who says that God is not properly a "substance" because He does not stand under any accidents, nor is the essence of God anything other than God Himself. But see, most excellent man, whether Thomas does not bear witness against you. For if the division of Being into substance and accident is, according to Blessed Thomas, a division of *created* being (as you yourself claim), how can it be ignored that there is such a thing as *uncreated* Being, which is God? By what reasoning, then, can you maintain—according to the interpretation of Blessed Thomas—that Aristotle thinks God is not properly and truly Being? For although Blessed Thomas seems in a certain place to deny that God is properly a substance...

## 10. FROM MIRANDOLA.

<margin>The Platonists</margin> Truly, I do not know why you so stubbornly contend to count Themistius <note>Themistius (c. 317–387 AD) was a statesman and philosopher who wrote "paraphrases" of Aristotle.</note> among their number. <margin>Themistius</margin> If you were to ask the ancients, they would all reply that Themistius is a Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: a follower of Aristotle's school of philosophy</term>, <margin>Not a Platonist</margin> not a Platonist. If you were to ask the man himself, I believe he would call himself a "paraphrast" and a follower of Aristotle, not of Plato. <margin>But rather a Peripatetic</margin> But perhaps (allow me to joke) you are dragging him into the Academy <note>The Academy refers to Plato's school/tradition.</note> against his will so that you do not appear entirely ignorant of Platonist and Greek thought—you who have at least read Themistius thanks to the efforts of <margin>Hermolaus</margin> our friend Hermolaus, <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493), a famous humanist who translated Themistius into Latin.</note> who made him available in Latin. But let us grant that Themistius is a Platonist. Let it also be entirely true—as we have declared abundantly enough both in this and the previous letter—that what he says in no way contradicts our opinion. This is because the Platonists will speak of God in one way as He is God, and in another way as He is an "Idea."

<margin>Solution to the other argument</margin> Let us come to this point: how "One" is said of God, even though "Being" is not. Recall what I wrote to you in my first letters. When the Platonists call God "One," they are not stating *what* He is, but *how* He is that which He is. But you do not yet sufficiently understand this. I shall speak more aptly. If you ask a man of the Academy <term>Academic: a Platonist philosopher</term> what God is, he will reply not only that he cannot answer you, but that you have no right to ask this—it is an unworthy question to ask of Him. For He who is above all essence <note>original: "essentia"</note> and above all that can be understood, can only be asserted by him to be most similar to "Unity." Just as unity is to numbers, so is He to all things that exist as their principle. Just as unity embraces all numbers, both even and odd, while being neither even nor odd itself in its individual simplicity, so He encloses and contains all things in His indivisible infinity. Do you see what was said? That through the name "One," we do not indicate *what* God is, but rather *how* He is that which He is. Finally, if we say "God is like Unity," we will certainly be truthful in what we wish to signify when we give Him the name of "the One." If we say to an audience "God is like Being," we will certainly make them laugh. But why should I use more words on you? For either these are enough, <margin>Why God is under no genus</margin> or I do not know what words could ever be enough.

He also concludes from this why God is under no "genus." <note>In logic, a "genus" is a category like "animal" or "substance."</note> For the genera of things belong to essence, <margin>How it happens</margin> but God is neither an essence nor does He "have" an essence. Therefore, since "Being" <note>original: "ens"</note> is sometimes understood by the Peripatetics to encompass only the ten categories, it is manifest that God is not contained under the name of "Being" as the followers of Aristotle sometimes use it. But you insist that Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> and others of that same family often use "substance" and "being" in such a way that God is called both a "substance" and "being." As if I were ignorant of this—which no one is—or as if it were not enough for me if they occasionally act otherwise. I did not say they *always* used the word that way, but only *sometimes*.

<margin>Solution to the other objection</margin> Move on to the things you object to regarding the opposition of "the One" and "the Divided." <margin>Namely, of the third principal point</margin> Truly, I think you are testing me with childish quibbles in jest. For if you say a "divided" thing is false, then surely "falsehood" is not false? For falsehood is not divided from itself. Furthermore, you say that the dead do not fight amongst themselves, for they are dead who are already dead. <note>Pico is likely responding to a joke or a semantic trap set by his correspondent.</note> Furthermore, Antonio, when I said that things which are false "fight with themselves," if this "fight" must happen with fists or even a weapon, then I confess the dead do not fight each other, nor are they "false." But just as a "simple" thing is false, so for "falsehood" to be false is not false, but true; therefore it is not divided, but one.

<margin>A clearer solution</margin> You add that it is falsely said by me that whatever is false "closes a contradiction" <note>i.e., contains an inherent logical impossibility.</note>. You say this because many things are false which, by the power of nature or man, could be true. But consider this: everything that is false, *as long as it is false*, contains a contradiction. But just as some things are false in a way that they *could* become true, <margin>Example</margin> others are false in a way that they can *never* be true. So there are some things so contradictory to themselves and fighting with themselves that they can never return to friendship and concord. Some things hate each other so much, yet can still return to favor. This will be manifest by an example: "A man is a lion" is always false, because it always contains a contradiction; and just as it can never be reduced to unity, so it can never be reduced to truth. But "that I am sitting" is neither [always] true nor false. If, however, you add that I am sitting *while I am standing*, immediately it becomes a falsehood. So...

...you even introduce a contradiction. For "me sitting while I stand" includes a contradiction: and as soon as it ceases to be false—as when I begin to sit—at that same moment it returns from division to unity. 

<margin>Solution to another point.</margin>
Furthermore, the objections you raise concerning the opposition of both types of falsehood were already resolved in my previous letter. For you say: "if it is true that what is seen, is; then it is false that what is seen, is not." Since there is no contradiction between "seeing what is" and "seeing what is not," then falsehood will not be the negation of truth. 

However, I do not accept the definition of falsehood in that way—that it consists of something "seeming to be" what it is not. Rather, I maintain that its definition lies in this: that it *is not* that which it is said to be. For example, false gold is false for this reason: because it is not gold; and as far as the definition of falsehood is concerned, it happens to either seem to be or actually be something other than gold. 

As for your claim that I have not resolved your argument by which you prove that 

<margin>Solution to another point.</margin>
good and evil are contraries, I will speak frankly. I did not think a solution was needed where 

<margin>Note.</margin>
there was no real knot to untie. Your argument is of this sort: "Good is to be sought; evil is to be avoided. Seeking and avoiding are contrary motions. Therefore, good and evil are contraries." To me, your reasoning seems so effective and of such great strength that it would prove not only that good and evil (about which someone might perhaps doubt) are contraries, but even that "being" and "non-being" (which everyone knows are contradictories) are contraries. For we would conclude thus: "Being is to be sought; non-being is to be avoided. Seeking and avoiding are contrary motions. Therefore, being and non-being are contraries." Either you must grant me that being and non-being are contraries, or I shall not grant you that good and evil are contraries. 

But you will say another reason must be unraveled. For "non-being" is not a genus <note>A 'genus' in logic is a general category under which specific things are classified.</note>. How then is it that "evil is nothing," when Aristotle says in the

Aristotle are full of solutions to this question, to whom I had referred you in my previous letter, so that I would not involve us both in unnecessary work. 

To set aside the fact that

I respond with what you could have also read in Simplicius: that good and evil are called "genera of contraries" because one side of a pair of contraries always has the quality of evil or deficiency; for instance, black when compared to white, or bitter when compared to sweet. In this way, all contraries are reduced to good and evil, insofar as every defect has the nature of evil. For this reason, in the first book of the *Lectures on Physics* <note>original: "physicæ auscultationis," referring to Aristotle's Physics.</note>, it is said that contraries are always compared to one another according to the logic of "better" and "worse."

For what else does he primarily do in that disputation but prove that "evil is nothing"? <note>In medieval philosophy, evil was often defined as a "privation" or lack of a due good, rather than a positive existing thing.</note> But if evil is nothing, it cannot be the "contrary" to good, since both parts of a pair of contraries must, by nature, be "something." And this is exactly what Thomas confirms there using the authority of Simplicius. See how far you wander—you who believe an opinion is confirmed by the testimony of Simplicius, when Thomas himself uses Simplicius’s testimony to weaken that very opinion! Perhaps you would not have fallen into this error if you had at some point read Simplicius's book itself, in which no mention is ever made of a "contrary opposition" between good and evil. 

If you object to me regarding eye disease and sickness—in which Thomas seems to acknowledge contrariety—I will bid you to look more closely at his words. For he does not say these are truly contraries, but that since they are privations <note>A lack of something that should naturally be present.</note>, they are nevertheless sometimes *called* contraries.

...is altogether ignorant. By what logic then do you claim that, according to Thomas's view, good is opposed to evil by some kind of contrary opposition? Surely you should have considered this: what is conceded regarding certain "imperfect" evils—due to the mixture of goodness they still retain—cannot be applied to the unmixed and absolute nature of evil itself.

->**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**<-

**Being** is said to be that which can answer the question "Does it exist?": whether it is a true and positive being or not. For this reason, he adds an example: "and thus evil is," just as "blindness is." This means that evil is a "being" in the same way that blindness is a "being." For in <term>Thomas Aquinas</term> <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theologian of the Middle Ages whose works Pico is reconciling with Plato.</note> there is no difference in words whether one says "it is" or "it is a being." 

However, when he adds that "to be something" does not only signify this, he does not mean to suggest that if someone asks "What is the moon?" or "What is thunder?" it is a reasonable answer to say "it is a being" or "it is something," as you seem to have thought. Such a solution is **ridiculous**. <margin>**Ridiculous:** Because you do not ask ridiculously, you do not solve it ridiculously; though many things are asked ridiculously which are then solved ridiculously when they are addressed, lest they appear unsolved because they cannot be solved. To one asking if the moon is a being, it will rightly be answered that it is a being. But to one asking further what kind of being it is, it is certainly ridiculous to answer that "it is a being."</margin> But this is what "to be something" signifies: especially according to the first mode, it signifies that which can be reasonably answered to the question "What is it?" For instance, it signifies that it is a substance, or an accident, or an animal, or a color, or something of this sort which can be rightly answered to a seeker of "What is it?" Blindness and evil, however, are none of these things. <margin>**To be something:** You say nothing. For who does not know that it is not "something" because it is neither a substance nor an accident?</margin>

That Blessed Thomas did not intend to interpret the first part of the division in that way, he himself explains in the *First Part, Question 48, Article 2*, where it is asked whether evil exists in things. <margin>**He says thus:** These same things follow for those in the prior question on evil, and they favor me, as do those others.</margin> For in responding to the second argument, he says: "As it is said in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, **Being** is used in two ways. In one way, it signifies the entity of a thing as it is divided into the ten <term>predicaments</term> <note>The ten categories of Aristotle (substance, quality, quantity, etc.) which define everything that exists in the physical world.</note>; and in this way, 'being' is interchangeable with 'thing,' and in this way, no <term>privation</term> <note>The absence of a quality that should be present, like blindness being the absence of sight.</note> is a being; thus, neither is evil. In the other way, 'being' is said of that which signifies the truth of a proposition which consists in composition, the sign of which is this word 'is'; and this is the 'being' that answers the question 'Does it exist?' And in this way, we say blindness is in the eye, or any other privation; and in this way also evil is called a being." These are the words of Thomas.

Do you not see, then, how he declares the first part of the division to be interchangeable with "thing"? Yet he does not deny that God is a "thing," nor whatever is good; for he confesses that every good is a thing, both in that argument and in the first question on evil. <margin>**A thing truly:** In that way, "thing" is both said of God and denied of Him, just as "being" is.</margin> If these things are true, the reasoning I used against the Platonists has not yet been refuted: **Being** is so called because it **is**, just as a "sitter" is so called because he "sits." <margin>**But if:** We have shown, however, that they are not true; therefore, the reasoning is refuted.</margin> Now, God not only "is," but he exists properly and truly; therefore, He is truly and properly **Being**. For you wished to solve the argument not from the Platonists, but from Thomas, ascribing things to Thomas which anyone who has read Thomas knows are entirely foreign to the man’s thought. <margin>**But from Thomas:** But you yourself, in explaining the words of Thomas above, fell into our opinion when you said God is called "being" insofar as it answers the question "Does it exist?", but not insofar as it signifies the essence of a thing.</margin>

Hence, that other reason I gave is not refuted: if God is "Being" in that respect where He is an "Idea," He is much more so in that respect where He is "God." For the latter is something absolute, while the former is relative. <margin>**To Thomas:** I do not ascribe false things to Thomas, for I do not imitate you, my fellow-father <note>original: "compater"</note>, who say that from Thomas's opinion good and evil are properly and truly contraries, and that this is even confirmed by the authority of Simplicius. When I showed that not a word of this exists in Simplicius, you responded that you had "gathered" that it was said by Simplicius. But the book is in our hands, fellow-father. Simplicius does not say it; therefore, you have gathered poorly.</margin> It is not true, as you just responded, that God is an essence in that respect where He is an Idea, but not in that respect where He is God; for it has already been shown that He is both Being and Essence. <margin>**Already shown:** It has also been demonstrated that you have not demonstrated well.</margin>

Furthermore, if God is Being and Essence in that respect where He is an Idea, it is necessary that there be **composition** in God, which is easily proved in this way: <margin>**Formerly:** For God and Idea are the same. Nor is the being of the Idea anything other than the being of God; but because the reasons are different, one thing is pronounced of God as He is God, and another as He is an Idea.</margin> for you previously said that according to the Platonists, God is not Being because God's existence is not different from God Himself. If, therefore, the Idea is "Being," it must be because the existence of the Idea is different from the Idea itself. But the existence of the Idea cannot be located or imagined outside of God, if God is the Idea (as has been granted); therefore, it is necessary that there be **composition** in God. <margin>**Composition:** This composition is according to reason (conceptual), not according to the thing (real).</margin>

You say, furthermore, that God is called "The One" by the Platonists because He is like unity; which, although it contains all numbers in its power (namely even and odd), is itself neither even nor odd. A **subtle** reason for naming, by Hercules! <margin>**Subtle:** So subtle that you still cannot understand it after it has been repeated a hundred times, as will soon be clear; from which you present us with a task.</margin> Aside from the fact that God cannot be "like" things—as Cicero and Thomas say—for the model of the world is not "like" the world, nor is a man "like" a painting; this reason cannot stand for any other cause.
