-># **OF BEING AND THE ONE**<-

<margin>It is not possible: One is not permitted to speak with you except within defined limits. <note>original: "Non põt: Non licet te cũ nisi p̃finito loq.ar"</note> Know that this kind of expression is often used by distinguished authors, even in the sacred texts, such as that passage concerning the "likeness of Melchizedek." <note>A reference to Hebrews 7:1-3, discussing Christ’s priesthood as being "after the likeness" of the biblical figure Melchizedek.</note></margin>

<margin>Furthermore: The "One" which the Platonists predicate of God is not a derivative description, but a substantive name. This is the case because you are entirely ignorant of Platonic thought and cannot understand the Greek language. See, therefore, how subtle this method of naming really is.</margin>

<margin>Furthermore: It is clear from this how "one" is said of matter in one way, and of God in another.
**Of the Platonists:** Why do you say I follow the reasoning of the Platonists rather than Dionysius <note>Likely Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian who blended Christian thought with Neoplatonism.</note>, when—as you boast with a loud voice—you have never read either the Platonists or Dionysius? You should know that among the Platonists, the model of God is "Unity," and according to Dionysius, God is uniquely "all things."</margin>

<margin>The root on which you rely: See how firm that "root" is, which you can neither conquer with any strength nor tear up with hard iron.
**I therefore:** All these points were satisfied in the previous letters.
**This is true:** You love gold too much, my fellow-godfather <note>term: <term>compater</term> (godfather/close friend). This suggests a personal, perhaps collegial, relationship between the debaters.</note>, that you attribute so much to it as to believe it could exist even if God did not.
**They think there are worlds:** Those who say these things—and say that gold exists—speak contradictions and are ignorant of their own words.
If God did not exist and gold existed: gold would be gold, and gold would not be gold; for the impossible gives birth to the impossible.</margin>

For that which borrows a name from another due to likeness or <term>analogy</term> <note>The philosophical method of naming God by comparing earthly things to divine perfections.</note> is usually called by the proper name of that thing. For instance, we call a statue that imitates a man a "man," not merely "human." Likewise, a "place" <note>term: <term>topos/locus</term>. In logic, a "place" is a source of an argument.</note> which is a distinction of propositions, or a "maximal proposition," is called a "place" by analogy to a natural physical place, and we do not call it "spatial." Therefore, if God received His name from "Unity" because of a likeness, He should not be called "One," but rather "Unity" itself. 

Furthermore, if every <term>concrete name</term> <note>A word that refers to a subject possessing a quality (e.g., "white" or "one") rather than the quality itself ("whiteness" or "unity").</note> signifies one thing and implies another, why do the Platonists call God "Likeness" rather than "Like"? Furthermore, if matter, according to the Platonists, is "one" as you write, and the unity of matter is not one thing and the matter itself another—which I do not think you would deny—by what reasoning can it be defended as "one"? For it is not similar to "Unity"; otherwise, it would also be similar to God. 

Furthermore, you previously said that God is "One" because He is uniquely all things; but now you seem to approve of the reasoning of the Platonists rather than that of Dionysius, perhaps having cast aside the former view. If you still hold it, it remains for you to answer the arguments that have been written down. For the "root" on which you rely to solve my objections is not true: namely, your claim that God is not "Being" nor "Essence," as I have already fully demonstrated.

But let us now come to the definition of "truth" set forth by you. You said in your earlier pamphlet that "truth" is defined by Augustine as: *Truth is that which is.* <note>original: "verum est quod est"</note> And so that the definition of "truth" and "being" should not seem to be the same, you say one must add: *Truth is that which is what it is said to be.* 

I, therefore, opposed your definition in this way: "to be what it is said to be" seems to signify nothing other than "to be what it is called." But for a thing to be called by this name or that is simply for it to *appear* as this or that. Therefore, it finally seemed to be concluded that "to be what it is said to be" is nothing other than "to be what it appears to be." Since there is no contradiction in appearing to be what is, and appearing to be what is not, I was proving that "falsehood" would not be the negation of "truth" if your definition held firm. 

Since you have now explained your definition more clearly, there is no lack of points which seem, to many, to further disprove your formal definition. For you say: "Truth is that which is said." That is, a thing is "true" because it is what it itself is. For example, "gold is true gold because it is gold." But against this is the fact that if God did not exist and gold did exist, gold would still be what it itself is, and it would be "true," yet it would not "be"—because it would not correspond to any divine <term>Idea</term> <note>The eternal patterns in the mind of God according to which all things are created.</note>. For you later say that true things are those that match and correspond to the Ideas. 

If the true definition of "man" is "rational animal," it is a contradiction to think that if God did not exist and man were a rational animal, man would not be man. Nor can one respond with what has been said elsewhere: namely, that it involves a contradiction for God not to exist and gold to exist. For there is no such contradiction, as theologians themselves and philosophers and logicians openly admit. For one can imagine that gold exists, but that God does not exist, nor a first cause, nor a first being. For those who think there are infinite worlds, or that the heavens are infinitely multiplied, or other similar things, do not therefore deny that the gold which is seen with the eyes and handled with the hands exists. Furthermore, whether there is a contradiction or not, the argument is not yet settled. For I say this: If God did not exist and gold existed, gold would be gold, but it would not be "true." Therefore—

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's critique of a contemporary's definition of "truth" and "being," likely addressed to Antonio Civran or a similar philosophical opponent. It follows a discussion on the transcendental properties of being.</meta>

->**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**<-

...the formal definition of the true is "to be that which it is itself." <note>Pico is critiquing a definition of truth that equates it simply with self-identity.</note> Just as it would not be a formal definition of man if I said: "If God did not exist and man were a rational animal, then man would not be man for that reason." For nothing can be deprived of its own definition, nor can a definition apply to anyone to whom the defined name cannot be fitted. Moreover, you cannot deny that gold is gold by nature before it corresponds to the idea of God; for the absolute is prior to the relative. <margin>The Absolute. For this is not an accidental relation distinct from the gold, but a substantial one; regarding this, see Henry of Ghent <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293) was a major scholastic theologian; Pico here cites him as an authority on substantial relations.</note>, unless you disdain him.</margin> Therefore, even if gold is gold, yet it cannot *be* unless some likeness arrives beyond the nature of gold, by which it corresponds to its archetype—whether the likeness is one thing and the gold another, or not, which is a separate question of its own.

Furthermore, you seem to posit the definition of being <term>being: translation of the Latin "ens," referring to anything that exists</term> in this way: "being is that which is." Otherwise, you would not say that Augustine's definition should be completed in this manner: "The true is that which it is itself," lest if we said only "that which is," the definition of the true and of being would seem the same. <margin>We said the same. Everything that is, is this: the very thing which it is. Wherefore every being is true, and every true thing is a being. But the underlying reason is different in each case.</margin> If, therefore, the definition of being is "that which is," by that logic: since being is "that which is," it is also itself and being. Therefore, by the same logic that something is a being, it must also be true; which is completely false.

Moreover, if the true is "that which it is itself," then blindness will be true, and death, and falsehood, and utterly non-being. For blindness is blindness, death is death, and falsehood is falsehood. Non-being is also non-being; any of these would be true without any intellect thinking about it at all. But if any of these is true, it must be "one." <note>In Scholastic philosophy, Being, Truth, and Unity were considered "transcendentals" that were interchangeable; Pico is arguing that if death is "true," it must also be "good" and "one," which leads to an absurdity.</note> But I know you will soon say: "Did I not concede that any of these is, and is therefore true, in those words I wrote to you: just as falsehood is falsehood, so that 'falsehood is falsehood' is not false, but true; and therefore not divided, but one?" <margin>Blindness however: It is one thing for blindness to be true; it is another for "blindness is blindness" to be true. Therefore, you labor in vain with many words to show that blindness is not true.</margin> 

But against this is the fact that every "one" is good, and in the same way true. Blindness, however, is not only evil, but according to what you write, it is entirely evil, and tastes of nothing good. Similarly with death; for you seem to call the nature of blindness and death the nature of absolute evil, unmixed with good. Therefore, none of these is true, nor "one," especially when the soul is not thinking. Furthermore, the true is that which corresponds to an idea; but blindness and death have no idea. <note>Following Plato and Augustine, Pico argues that "evil" and "lack" (privation) have no divine Idea or Form because they are absences of being, not things themselves.</note>

Moreover, if God did not exist, nor anything else capable of intelligence, nonetheless non-being would be non-being, and nothing would be nothing; for it is either something or nothing. Certainly not something, as is clear; therefore nothing and non-being. It would therefore be what it is now, and would be then. If, then, the true is that which is what it itself is, non-being and nothing would be true; which cannot happen, for it would correspond to no idea. Therefore, the formal definition of the true is not "to be that which it itself is."

Furthermore, you attempt to defend what you previously said: that any falsehood involves a contradiction. You say that every falsehood involves a contradiction as long as it is false. You also add these words: "But for me to sit is neither true nor false. If, however, you add that I am sitting while I am standing, immediately you bring in contradiction just as you do falsehood; for 'me sitting while I am standing' involves a contradiction, and as soon as it ceases to be false—as when I begin to sit—it returns from division to unity." But see, I ask you, if this agrees with you...

Q ii <note>Signature mark for a printer's quire.</note>

**ON BEING AND THE ONE, 10.**

<margin>Truly: for "that I am sitting" to be either true or false is always the case, because I am always either sitting or not sitting. And when it is said that "my sitting" is neither true nor false, it means that this proposition, by itself, determines neither truth nor falsehood—unlike necessary propositions <note>Necessary propositions are those that must be true by their nature, like "2+2=4," whereas "I am sitting" depends on physical circumstance.</note>. But since it can happen that it is true (namely, when I sit) and false (when I do not sit), the statement is indeterminate in itself toward either possibility. But undoubtedly, my dear friend <note>original: "compater" — a term for a close companion or "godfather" in a social/spiritual sense</note>, you must have an abundance of both paper and leisure time to stoop to these matters that are known even to schoolboys.</margin>

<margin>But it is true that Good and Evil are found in things, while Falsehood and Truth are found in the soul <note>The author is referencing the Aristotelian principle that "truth" is a property of how we think about things, not a physical property of the objects themselves.</note>. Therefore, a true proposition can signify an evil thing, because the proposition itself, insofar as it is true, is good; yet the thing itself, insofar as it is evil, may be considered "false" <note>In this context, "false" implies a lack of being or a deviation from the ideal state of that thing.</note>. It is one thing to say, "It is true that Judas sins," but another to say, "The sin of Judas is a truth."</margin>

<margin>Furthermore: every "falsehood" is divided, as we said in the previous booklet. But "not being false" is not equally false, which is why "not being false" is [not] equally divided, as we said in the letters to you. For those things which are necessarily false and always false are not false in the same way as those which are not necessarily false nor always false. Therefore, the former and the latter do not share the same logic of division. See if there is anything here that I should have feared to say, or that you might be able to refute.</margin>

[Main text]
...you might agree. For you think that Truth and Falsehood are opposed not as contraries, but as affirmation and negation. How then can a middle ground be found, unless there is a middle between affirmation and negation? <note>This refers to the "Law of the Excluded Middle," a pillar of logic stating that a statement is either true or its negation is true; there is no third option.</note> Moreover, every proposition is either true or false, unless you deny the first principle: which is that in any contradiction, one part is true and the other is false.

How, then, is "that you are sitting" neither true nor false? Indeed, I do not see by what reasoning you could maintain this, unless you do away with all philosophy and the entire concept of contraries. Furthermore, if every falsehood entails a contradiction, then as long as it is false that "God does not exist," that falsehood will entail a contradiction so long as God exists in the nature of things. 

If, therefore, God did not exist, it would neither be false that "God does not exist," nor would it be a contradiction. If, then, falsehood is the negation of truth, just as you posit, it would be true that "God does not exist" if God were not to exist. But every truth is a good, as you grant; therefore, if God did not exist, it would be a good thing for God not to exist—which seems absurd. For neither...
